unbloody.c: unbloody (un-blud’i), a. 1. Not stained with blood. This hath brought Sweet peace to sit in that bright state she ought, Unbloody, or untroubled. B. Jonson, King James’s Coronation Entertainment. 2. Not shedding blood; not eruel.—3. Not accompanied with bloodshed. Many battails, and some of those not wnbloodie. Milton, Hist. Eng., ii. Unbloody sacrifice, a sacrifice which does not involve the shedding of blood, such as the meat-offering (meat-offering) of the Old Testament; specifically, the eucharistic sacrifice.

unblotted.c: unblotted (un-blot’ed), a. Not blotted, or not blotted out; not deleted; not erased. Spenser... seems to have been satisfied with his first unblotted thoughts. J. D’Israeli, Amen. of Lit., II. 126. unblown! (un-blon’), a. [< wn-1+ blown.] 1. Not blown, inflated, or otherwise affected by the wind. A fire unblown (shall) devour his race. Sandys, Paraphrase of the Book of Job, p. 31. Leisure..). Might race with wnblown ample garments. S. Lanier, Sunrise on the Marshes. 2. Not caused to sound, as a wind-instrument. The lances unlifted, the trumpets unblown. Byron, Destruction of Sennacherib. unblown? (un-blon’), a. [< wn-l + blown?.] Not blown; not having the bud expanded; hence, not fully grown or developed. My tender babes! My unblown flowers! Shak., Rich. III., iv. 4. 10.

unblushing.c: unblushing (un-blush’ing), a. Not blushing; hence, destitute of or not exhibiting shame; impudent; shameless: as, an unblushing assertion. That bold, bad man,... pretending still, With hard unblushing front, the public good. T. Hdwards, Sonnets, xiv.

unblushingly.c: unblushingly (un-blush’ing-li), adv. Inanun- blushing or shameless manner. 4

unboastful.c: unboastful (un-bost’fil), a. Not boasting; unassuming; modest. Thomson, Summer.

unbodied.c: unbodied (un-bod’id), a. 1. Having no material body; incorporeal. He’s such an airy, thin, unbodied coward, That no revenge can catch him. Beau. and Fl., King and No King, v. 1. 2. Freed from the body; disembodied. Like an unbodied joy whose race is just begun. Shelley, To a Skylark, iii.

unboding.c: unboding (un-bo’ding), a. Not anticipating; not looking for. I grow in worth, and wit, and sense, Unboding critic-pen. Tennyson, Will Waterproof, vi.

unbodkined.c: unbodkined (un-bod’kind),a. Unfastened with a bodkin; freed from fastening by a bodkin. Mrs. Browning, Duchess May. [Rare.]

unbody.c: unbody (un-bod’i), v. 7. To be deprived of the body; become disembodied. The fate wolde his soule sholde unbody. Chaucer, Troilus, v. 1550.

unbolt.c: unbolt (un-bolt’), v. [< wn-2 + bolt1.] I. trans. To release or allow to be opened by withdrawing a bolt: as, to unbolt a door. He shall unbolt the gates. Shak., T. and C., iv. 2. 3. unbolt II, intrans. To withdraw a bolt and thus open that which it confined; hence (rarely), to open; unfold; explain. Pain. How shall I understand you? Poet. I will unbolt to you. Shak., T. of A., i. 1. 51. unbolted! (un-bdl’ted), a. [See bolt, v.] Not bolted; not fastened by bolts. unbolted? (un-bdl’ted), a. [See bolt?, v.] 1. Not bolted or sifted; not having the bran or coarse part separated by a bolter: as, unbolted meal. Hence—2}. Coarse; gross; not refined. I will tread this unbolted villain into mortar. Shak., Lear, ii. 2. 71.

unbone.c: unbone (un-b6n’),v. t [< un-2 + bone.] 1. To deprive of a bone or of bones. [Rare.]—2. To fling or twist about as if boneless. [Rare.] In the Colleges so many of the young Divines, and those in next aptitude to Divinity, have bin seene so oft upon the Stage writhing and unboning their Clergie limes to all the antick and dishonest gestures of Trinculo’s. Milton, Apology for Smectymnuus.

unbonnet.c: unbonnet (un-bon’et), v. I. intrans. To uncover the head by taking off the bonnet or, by extension, any head-dress. Scott, Li. of the Mie Vis Li. II. trans. To remove the bonnet or, by extension, any head-dress from, as the head, or the wearer of the head-dress.

unbonneted.c: unbonneted (un-bon’et-ed), a. 1. Having no bonnet on; by extension, without any head-dress; bareheaded. Unbonneted he runs. Shak., Lear, iii. 1. 14. 2. Without taking the bonnet or cap off; making no obeisance. I fetch my life and being From men of royal siege, and my demerits May speak unbonneted to as proud a fortune As this that I have reach’d. Shak., Othello, i. 2. 23.

unbooked.c: unbooked (un-bukt’), a. Unbookish. | [Rare.] With compass of diction unequalled by any other public performer of the time, ranging... from the unbooked freshness of the Scottish peasant to the most far-sought phrase of literary curiosity. Lowell, Study Windows, p. 139.

unbookish.c: unbookish (un-buk’ish), a. 1. Not addicted to books or reading. It is to be wondered how museless unbookish they were, minding nought but the feats of war. Milton, 2. Not cultivated by study; unlearned. His unbookish jealousy must construe Poor Cassio’s smiles, gestures, and light behaviour Quite in the wrong. Shak., Othello, iv. 1. 102.

unbooklearned.c: unbooklearned (un-buk’lér’ned), a. Illiterate. Rare.] Un-book-learn’d people have conn’d by heart many psalms of the old translation. Fuller, Ch. Hist., VII. i. 32. (Davies.)

unbored.c: unbored, a. A Middle English form of inborn. Gower, Conf. Amant., vi.

unborn.c: unborn (un-bérn’), a. [< ME. wnboren, unborn; < un-1 + born1.] Not born; not brought into life; not yet existing. The woe’s to come; the children yet unborn Shall feel this day as sharp to them as thorn. Shak., Rich. II., iv. 1. 322.

unbosom.c: unbosom (un-buz’um), v. [< wn-2 + bosom.] I. trans. To reveal in confidence; disclose, as one’s secret opinions or feelings: often used with a reflexive pronoun. Their several counsels they unbosom shall. Shak., L. L. L., v. 2. 141. The rest of this winter I spent in a lonesome, solitary life, having none to converse with, none to unbosom myself unto, none to ask counsel of, none to seek relief from, but the Lord alone, who yet was more than all. T. Ellwood, Life (ed. Howells), p. 227. II. intrans. To make a revelation in confidence; disclose one’s innermost feelings. + Princes usually treat such persons familiarly; and, quitting their throne like Luna, think they may with safety unbosom to them. Bacon, Political Fables, iv., Expl.

unbosomer.c: unbosomer (un-biz’um-ér), m. One who unbosoms, discloses, or reveals. An unbosomer of secrets.

unbottomed.c: unbottomed (un-bot’umd), a. bottom; bottomless. The dark, wnbottom’d, infinite abyss. Milton, P. L., ii. 405. 2+. Having no solid foundation; having no reliance. This is a special act of Christian hope, to be thus wnbot- tomed of ourselves, and fastened upon God. Hammond.

unbought.c: unbought (un-bat’), a. [< ME. wnbouht, un- bocht, unboht, < AS. unboht; as un-1 + bought?.] 1. Not bought: obtained without money or purchase. The unbought dainties of the poor. Dryden, Horace, Epod. 2. Thackeray. 1. Having no 6584 2. Unsold; without a purchaser: as, an unbought stock of books. The merchant will leave our native commodities unbought upon the hands of the farmer. Locke. 3. Not bought over; unbribed. Unbribed, unbought, our swords we draw. Scott, War Song of the Edinburgh Light Dragoons.

unbounded.c: unbounded (un-boun’ded), a. 1. Having no bound or limit; unlimited in extent; hence, immeasurably great: as, unbounded space; unbounded power. The wide, the unbounded prospect. Addison, Cato, vy. 1. 2. Having no check or control; unrestrained. He was a man Of an unbounded stomach, ever ranking Himself with princes. Shak., Hen. VIIL, iv. 2. 34, =Syn. 1, Boundless, illimitable.— 2, Uncontrolled.

unboundedly.c: unboundedly (un-boun’ded-li), adv. In an unpounded manner; without bounds or limits. Byron.

unboundedness.c: unboundedness (un-boun’ded-nes), ». The state or condition of being unbounded; freedom from bounds or limits; specifically, that character of a continuum by virtue of which, if any point be taken, and then any other indefinitely near the first, a third point may be found indefinitely near the first, and situated opposite to the second with reference to the first. In the extension of space-construction to the infinitely great we must distinguish between unboundedness and infinite extent; the former belonging to the extent relations, the latter to the measure relations. That space is an unbounded threefold manifoldness is an assumption which is developed by every conception of the outer world; according to which at every instant the region of real perception is completed and the possible positions of a sought object are constructed, and which by these applications is forever confirming itself. The wnbownded- ness of space possesses in this way a greater empirical certainty than any external experience. But its infinite extent by no means follows from this. Riemann, tr. by Clifford.

unboundent.c: unboundent (un-boun’den), a. [< ME. wnboun- den; pp. of unbind, v.] Set free; unwedded. Were I unbounded, also mote I thee, I wolde never eft comen in the snare. Chaucer, Prol. to Merchant’s Tale, 1. 14. unbow} (un-bou’), v. t [« wn-2 + bowl.] To unbend, Looking back would unbow his resolution. Fuller, Holy War, p. 118.

unbowable.c: unbowable (un-bou’a-bl), a. Incapable of being bent or inclined. Stubbes.

unbowed.c: unbowed (un-boud’), a [< ME. unbowed; < un-1 + bowed, pp. of bowl, v.] 1. Not bowed or arched; not bent. He... passeth by with stiff, unbowed knee. Shak., 2 Hen. VL., iii. 1. 16. Hence —2. Not subjugated; unsubdued; not put under the yoke. Shak., Tempest, i. 2. 115.

unbowel.c: unbowel (un-bou’el), v. t [< wn-2 + bowel.] To deprive of the entrails; eviscerate; disembowel. Dr. H. More.

unboy.c: unboy (un-boi’),v. t [< wn-2 + boy.] To free from boyish thoughts or habits; raise above boyhood. Clarendon. [Rare.]

unbrace.c: unbrace (un-bras’), v. [< wn-2 + brace.] I, trans. 1. Toremove the points or braces of; free from tension or constraint; loose; relax: as, to unbrace a drum; to unbrace the arms; to unbrace the nerves. His joyful friends unbrace his azure arms. Weis: Pope, Iliad, vii. 142. 2t. To carve; disjoint. Vnbrace that malade. Babees Book (E. E. T.8.), p. 265. II, intrans. To grow flaccid; relax; hang loose. Dryden.

unbraced.c: unbraced (un-brast’), a. Not braced, in any sense. With his doublet all unbraced. Shak., Hamlet, ii. 1.78.

unbraid.c: unbraid (un-brad’),v.t. [< wn-2 + braid.] To separate the strands of; unweave; unwreathe. aueiinell (un-brand’), a. Deprived of brains; not brained. Beau. and Fl. [Rare.]

unbranched.c: unbranched (un-brancht’), a. Not branched; not provided with branches.

unbreaking.c: unbreaking (up-bra’king), a. dissolving. An unbreaking and disparting storm. J. Wilson, Lights and Shadows of Scottish Life, p. 104.

unbreast.c: unbreast (un-brest’), v. t [« un-2 + breast.] To disclose or lay open; unbosom. Could’st thou unmask their pomp, unbreast their heart, How would’st thou laugh at this rich beggerie. P. Fletcher, Piscatory Eclogues, iv.

unbreathed.c: unbreathed (un-brérHd’), a. 1. Not breathed; not having passed through the lungs: as, air wn- breathed.— 2+. Not exercised; unexercised; unpractised. And now have toil’d their wnbreathed memories. Shak, M. N. D., v. 1. 74.

unbreathing.c: unbreathing (un-bré’rHing), a. Not breathing. Byron, Saul. ae unbuild

unbred.c: unbred (un-bred’), a. 1+. Unbegot; unborn. Hear this, thou age unbred: Ere you were born was beauty’s summer dead. Shak., Sonnets, civ. 2. Not well bred; destitute of breeding. My Nephew’s a little wnbred; you'll pardon him, Madam. Congreve, Way of the World, iii. 17. 3. Not taught or trained. Unbred to spinning. Dryden, Eneid, vii. 1095.

unbreech.c: unbreech (un-bréch’), v. t. [< un-2 + breech.] 1. To remove breeches from.—2. To free the breech of, as a cannon, from its fastenings or coverings. Let the worst come, I can unbreech a cannon, and without much help Turn her into the keel. Beau. and Fl., Double Marriage, ii. 1.

unbreeched.c: unbreeched (un-brécht’), a. Wearing no breeches; not yet of the age to wear breeches. Methoughts I did recoil Twenty-three years, and saw myself unbreech’d, In my green velvet coat, my dagger muzzled. Shak., W. T., i. 2. 155. unbrent}, a. A Middle English form of unburnt.

unbrewed.c: unbrewed (un-bréd’), a. Not brewed or mixed; pure or genuine. P They drink the stream Unbrew’d, and ever full. Young, Night Thoughts, vii.

unbribable.c: unbribable (un-bri’ba-bl), a. Ineapable of being bribed. Feltham.

unbridle.c: unbridle (un-bri’dl), v. ¢. To free from the bridle; let loose. Shak., Lear (Qq.), iii. 7. 86.

unbridled.c: unbridled (un-bri’dld), a. Not having a bridle on; hence, unrestrained; unruly; violent; licentious. This is not well, rash and unbridled boy, To fly the favours of so good a king. Shak., All’s Well, iii. 2. 80. He, mad with rage And with desires unbridled, fled, and vow’d That ring should me undo. Webster and Dekker, Northward Hoe, i. 3.

unbridledness.c: unbridledness (un-bri’dld-nes), n. The character or state of being unbridled; freedom from control or restraint; license; violence. The presumption and unbridledness of youth. Leighton, Com. on 1 Pet. v. unbroident, a. [< un-1 + broiden, braided: see ME. braid, broid.] Unbraided. Hire mighty tresses of hire sonnysshe heres, Unbroiden, hangen al aboute hire teres. Chaucer, Troilus, iv. 817.

unbroken.c: unbroken (un-brok’), a. Unbroken. God keep all vows unbroke that swear to thee! Shak., Rich. I1., iv. 1. 215. By age unbroke. Pope, Odyssey, viii. 147.

unbroken (un-bré’kn), a. 1. Not broken; whole; entire; hence, left in its integrity; not violated. The clergy met very punctually, and the patriarch’s letter was produced in the assembly, the seal examined, and declared to be the patriarch’s and unbroken. Bruce, Source of the Nile, IT. 460. 2. Not weakened; not crushed; not subdued: as, a mind unbroken by age.—3. Not tamed or rendered tractable; not taught; not accustomed to the saddle, harness, or yoke: as, an unbroken horse or ox.— 4, Not interrupted; undisturbed: as, unbroken slumbers; hence, regular. The allied army returned to Lambeque unpursued and in unbroken order. Macaulay, Hist. Eng., xix.

unbrokenness.c: unbrokenness (un-bro’kn-nes), n. The character or state of being unbroken.

unbrotherly.c: unbrotherly (un-brutH’ér-li), a. Not brotherly; not becoming or befitting a brother. Bacon.

unbrute.c: unbrute (un-brét’), v. t. [< wn-2 + brute.] To take away the character of a brute from. Penn, Liberty of Conscience, iv. [Rare.]

unbuckle.c: unbuckle (un-buk’l), v. t [< ME. wnbokelen, unboclen; < un-2 + buckle2.] To release from a fastening by buckles: as, to unbuckle a shoe.

unbuckramed.c: unbuckramed (un-buk’ramd), a. Not stiffened or lined with buckram; hence, not stiff; easy; natural; informal. Colman the Younger. [Rare.]

unbudded.c: unbudded (un-bud’ed), a. Not having put forth a bud; unblown. The hid scent in an unbudded rose. Keats, Lamia, ii.

unbuild.c: unbuild (un-bild’), v. t.; pret. and pp. unbuilt, unbuilded, ppr. unbuilding. [< un-2 + build, v.] To demolish, as that which is built; raze; destroy. [Rare.] To unbuild the city and to lay all flat. Shak., Cor., iii. 1. 198. unbuilt

unbuilt.c: unbuilt (un-bilt’), a. Not yet built; not erected; unconstructed. Unbuilt Babel. Drayton, Polyolbion, iv.

unbundle.c: unbundle (un-bun’dl),.v. t [< wn-2 + bundle.] To unpack; open; disclose; declare. [Rare.] Unbundle your griefs, madam, and let us into the particulars. Jarvis, Don Quixote, II, iii. 6. (Davies.)

unbuoyed.c: unbuoyed (un-boid’ or un-béid’),a. Not buoyed or borne up. Edinburgh Rev.

unburdened.c: unburdened (un-bér’dnd), a. Not burdened. Wholly unburdened with historical knowledge or with any experience of life. The Academy, Aug. 2, 1890, p. 96.

unburdenunburthen.c: unburden, unburthen (un-bér’dn, -run), v. ¢. [< wn-2 + burden, burthen.] 1. To rid of a load; free from a burden; ease. While we Unburthen'd crawl toward death. Shak., Lear, i. 1, 42. 2. To throw off as being a burden; discharge; hence, to disclose; reveal. To unburden all my plots and purposes. Shak., M. of V., i. 1. 138. 8. To relieve, as the mind or heart, by disclosing what lies heavy on it; also, reflexively, to relieve (one’s self) in this way: as, he wnbur- dened himself to his confessor. Well, now we are alone, there is a subject, my dear friend, on which I wish to unburthen my mind to you. Sheridan, School for Scandal, iv. 3. Georgina, when not unburdening her heart to me, spent most of her time in lying on the sofa, fretting about the dullness of the house. Charlotte Bronté, Jane Eyre, xxi.

unburiable.c: unburiable (un-ber’i-a-bl), a. Not capable of being buried; unfit to be buried. Tennyson, Gareth and Lynette.

unburied.c: unburied (un-ber’id), a. [< ME. unburied; < wn-1 + buried.] Not buried; not interred. The dead carcasses of unburied men. Shak., Cor., iii. 3, 122.

unburnedunburnt.c: unburned, unburnt (un-bérnd’, un-bérnt’), a. [<x ME. unbrent; <un-1 + burned, burnt.] 1. Not burned; not consumed or injured by fire. : He said ’twas folly, For one poor grain or two, to leave unburnt, And still to nose the offence. Shak., Cor., v. 1. 27. The source of the heat taken up by the vessel is nothing but unburnt gases. Seti. Amer. Supp., XXII. 8783. 2. Not baked, as brick. Ci (un-bér’ning), a. away by fire. [Rare.] The unburning fire called light. Sir K. Digby, Of Bodies, vii.

unburnt.c: unburnt (un-bérnt’), a. See unburned. O bush unbrent, brenning in Moyses syghte. Chaucer, Prioress’s Tale, 1. 16.

unburrow.c: unburrow (un-bur’6), v.t. [< wn-2 + burrow?.] To take from a burrow; unearth. [Rare.] He can bring down sparrows and unburrow rabbits. Dickens, Uncommercial Traveller, x. (Davies.) unburthen, v. t. See unburden.

unbury.c: unbury (un-ber’i), v. t.; pret. and pp. unburied, pr. unburying. [< un-2 + bury3.] 1. To ex- ume; disinter. [Rare.] The hours they are not at their beads, which are not a few, they employ in speaking ill of us, unburying our bones, and burying our reputations. Jarvis, Don Quixote, II. iii. 5. (Davies.) 2. Figuratively, to uncover; reveal; disclose. Since you have one secret, keep the other; Never unbury either. Lytton, Richelieu, i. 1.

unbutton.c: unbutton (un-but’n), v. t. [« un-2 + button.] To unfasten or open, as a garment, by separating the buttons and the buttonholes. What is the life of man! Is it not to shift from side to side, from sorrow to sorrow?—to button up one cause of vexation, and unbutton another? Sterne, Tristram Shandy, iy. 31.

unbuxom.c: unbuxom (un-buk’sum), a. [< ME. unbuxom, unbuxom, unboxum, unbuhsum; <un-1 + buxom.) Disobedient. Piers Plowman (C), iii. 87.

unbuxomly.c: unbuxomly (un-buk’sum-li), adv. In a disobedient manner. Gower, Conf. Amant., i.

unbuxomness.c: unbuxomness (un-buk’sum-nes),. [<¢ ME.*un- buxomness, unbuxsumnes; < unbuxom + -ness.} Disobedience. Sen Lucifer oure lear es lighted so lawe For hys vnbuxummnes in bale to be brente. York Plays, p. 6.

uncabled.c: uncabled (un-ka’bld), a. Not fastened or secured by a cable. Within it ships.. Not consuming . uncabled ride secure. Cowper, Odyssey, xiii. 117.

uncage.c: uncage (un-kaj’), v. t. Toset free from a cage or from confinement. The uncaged soul flew through the air. Fanshaw, Poems (ed. 1676), p. 299. 6585

uncalled.c: uncalled (un-kald’), a. [< ME. uncalled; < un-1 + called.) Not called; unsummoned; not invited; not demanded. Mild Lucina came uncalled. Dryden, tr. of Ovid’s Cinyras and Myrrha. Uncalled for, not required; not needed or demanded; improperly brought forward. In other people’s presence I was, as formerly, deferential and quiet; any other line of conduct being uncalled Sor. Charlotte Bronté, Jane Kyre, xxiv. Also written unealled-for, when used attributively: as, most uncalled-for remarks,

uncallow.c: uncallow (un-kal’6),. The name given in Norfolk, England, to the deposits of gravel resting on the chalk,

uncalm.c: uncalm (un-kim’), v. t. [¢ un-2 + calm.] To deprive of calm; disturb. [Rare.] What strange disquiet has uncalm’d your breast. Dryden.

uncamp.c: uncamp (un-kamp’), v.¢. [<wn-2+camp1.] To cause to decamp; dislodge; expel. [Rare.] If they could but now wncamp their enemies. Milton, Hist. Eng., ii.

uncandid.c: uncandid (un-kan’did), a. Not candid, frank, or true. The American, VIII. 232.

uncandor.c: uncandor (un-kan’dor), n. [Rare.] “Tt seems to me it was an utter failure,” suggested Annie. “Quite. But it was what I expected.” There appeared an uncandor in this which Annie could not let pass. Howells, Annie Kilburn, xxi.

uncanniness.c: uncanniness (un-kan’i-nes), ». The character of being uncanny. Your general uncanniness. George Eliot, Mill on the Floss, p. 277.

uncanny.c: uncanny (un-kan’i), a. [Se. and North. Eng. See canny.) 1. Not canny, in any sense.—2. Eery; weird; mysterious; apparently not of this world; hence, noting one supposed to possess preternatural powers. I wish she binna uncanny. Scott, Guy Mannering, iii. What does that inexplicable, that uncanny turn of countenance mean? Charlotte Bronté, Jane Eyre, xxiv. He... rather expected something uncanny to lay hold of him from behind. C. Kingsley, Alton Locke, xxi. 3. Severe, as a fall or blow. An uncanny coup I gat for my pains. Scott, Waverley, Ixvi. Same as wunca- In an uncan- Lack of candor.

uncanonic.c: uncanonic (un-ka-non’ik), a. conical. This act was uncanonic and a fault. Browning, Ring and Book, IT. 170.

uncanonical.c: uncanonical (un-ka-non’i-kal), a. 1. Not canonical; not agreeable to the canons. If ordinations were uncanonical. Jer. Taylor, Episcopacy Asserted, § 32. 2. Not conformed or conforming to rule; not determined by rule.—3. Not belonging to the paren (of Scripture).—Uncanonical hours. See OUr,

uncanonicalness.c: uncanonicalness (un-ka-non’i-kal-nes),n. The character of being uncanonical. Bp. Lloyd.

uncanonize.c: uncanonize (un-kan’on-iz), v. t. [<wn-2 + canonize.] 1. To deprive of canonical authority.—2. To reduce from the rank of a canonized saint.

uncanonized.c: uncanonized (un-kan’on-izd), a. Not canonized; not enrolled among the saints. The members of it [the Romish communion] boast very much of mighty signs and wonders wrought by some canonized and some uncanonized saints. Bp. Atterbury, Sermons, II. i.

uncap.c: uncap (un-kap’),v.; pret. and pp. uncapped, ppr. uncapping. [< un-2 + call.] I, trans. To remove a cap, as a percussion-cap, from, as a gun or a cartridge, or a protecting cap from, as a lens-tube. II. intrans. To remove the cap or hat.. I felt really like uncapping, with a kind of reverence. H. James, Jr., Trans. Sketches, p. 247.

uncapable.c: uncapable (un-ka’pa-bl), a. Incapable. An inhuman wretch, Uncapable of pity. Shak., M. of V., iv. 1. 5. He who came to take away the sins of the world was uncapable of pollution by sin. Bp. Hall, Contemplations, V. 176.

uncape.c: uncape (un-kap’),v. [< wn-2 + cape?.] In hawking, to prepare for flying at game by taking off the cape or hood. Various explanations are given to the word as used by Shakspere, “Merry Wives,” iii. 3. 176: “T warrant we'll unkennel the fox. Let me stop this way first. So now wneape.” According to Steevens, it means to turn the fox out of the bag; according to Warburton, to dig out the fox when earthed; according to Nares, to throw off the dogs or to begin the hunt; according to Schmidt, to uncouple hounds.;

uncaptious.c: uncaptious (un-kap’shus), a. Not captious; not ready to take objection or offense. unce Uncuptious and candid natures. Feltham, Resolves, ii. 43,

uncardinal.c: uncardinal (un-kar’di-nal), v. t. [< wn-2 + cardinal.] To divest of the cardinalate. [Rare.] Borgio... got a dispensation to uncardinal himself. Fuller.

uncareful.c: uncareful (un-kar’ful), a. 1. Having no care; free from care. This journey... has been one of the brightest and most uncareful interludes of my life. Hawthorne, French and Italian Note-Books, p. 272. 2. Taking no care; not watchful; incautious. —3t+. Producing no care. Uncareful treasure. [Rare in all senses.]

uncaria.c: Uncaria (ung-ka’ri-ii), n. [NL.(Schreber,1789), <L. uncus, a hook: see unce2, uncus.] A genus of gamopetalous plants, of the order Rubiaceze and tribe Naucleee. It is distinguished from the type-genus Nau- clear by its valvate corolla and _ septicidal capsule. There are about 82 species, mostly natives of India beyond the Ganges, with one in Africa and one in Guiana and Brazil. uncas.c: Uncas (ung'kas). Died about 1682. An Indian chief, a Pequot by birth. Cooper introduces a character TJncas in his “ Last of the Mohicans.”

uncate.c: uncate (ung’kat), a. [< LL. wncatus, hooked, curved, < L. incus, a hook: see unce2, uncus.] Same as wneinate. uncathedraled, uncathedraled (un-ka-thé’- drad), a. Destitute of cathedrals. ([Rare.] Tf he [Longfellow] had, like Whittier, grown old among the uncathedraled paganisms of American scenery and life, etc. Encyc. Brit., XIV. 862.

uncaused.c: uncaused (un-kizd’), a. Having no precedent cause; existing without an author; uncreated; self-existent. The idea of uncaused matter. Baxter, On the Soul, ii. 359.

unceremonious.c: unceremonious (un-ser-é-m0’ni-us), a. Not ceremonious; familiar; informal. No warning given! unceremonious fate! Young, Night Thoughts, iii.

unceremoniously.c: unceremoniously (un-ser-é-m6/ni-us-li), adv. In an unceremonious manner; without ceremony; informally.

uncertain.c: uncertain (un- ser'tan), a. Notecertain; doubtful. (a) Not known in regard to nature, quailed or general character. The things future, being also events very vneertaine, and such as can not possibly be knowne because they be not yet, can not be vsed for example nor for delight otherwise then by hope. Puttenham, Arte of Eng. Poesie, p:.82. For many days Has he been wandering in uncertain ways; Through wilderness, and woods of mossed oaks. Keats, Endymion, ii. (b) Not known as regards quantity or extent; indefinite; problematical: as, an uncertain number of independent voters; a person of uncertain age. She was not old, nor young, nor at the years Which certain people call a certain age, Which yet the most wneertain age appears, Because I never heard, nor could engage | A person yet by prayers, or bribes, or tears, To name, define by speech, or write on page The period meant precisely by that word. Byron, Beppo, st. 22. (c) Having doubts; without certain knowledge; not sure. Uncertain of the issue. Shak., 1 Hen. IV., i. 1. 61. Thir [the Saxons’] multitude wander’d yet uncertain of habitation. Milton, Hist. Eng., iii. (ad) Not sure as to aim or effect desired. Soon bent his bow, uncertain in his aim. Dryden, Aneid, vii. 691. Or whistling slings dismiss’d the uncertain stone. Gay. (e) Unreliable; insecure; not to be depended on. The uncertain glory of an ey day. Shak., T. G. of V., Gan I, then, Part with such constant pleasures to embrace Uncertain vanities? Fletcher and another, Elder Brother, i. 2. (f) Not firm or fixed; vague; indeterminate in nature; fluctuating. Unceasing. i. 3. 85. All around Are dim uncertain shapes that cheat the sight. Bryant, The Journey of Life. (g) Undecided; hesitating; not resolved. The uncertain sickly appetite to please. Shak., Sonnets, exlvii. (h) Not steady; fitful. Amid the strings his fingers strayed, And an uncertain warbling made. Scott, L. of L. M., Int. I could see by that uncertain glimmer how fair was all, but not how sad and old Howells, Venetian Life, xi. (i) Liable to change; fickle; inconstant; capricious; irresolute. Thou art constant; I an uncertain fool, a most blind fool. Be thou my guide. Beau. and Fl., Double Marriage, i. 1. Oh, woman! in our hours of ease Uncertain, coy, and hard to please. Scott, Marmion, vi. 30.
uncertain (un-sér’tan), v. & [< uncertain, a.] To make or cause to be uncertain. Raleigh.

uncessant.c: uncessant (un-ses’ant), a. Incessant. There is in this land also a mountains, which. continueth alwayes burning, by incessant belching out of flames. Hakluyt’s Voyages, I. 556.

uncessantly.c: uncessantly (un-ses’ant-li), adv. Incessantly. Whare-fore, what may do fail vn-to hym that couaytes vn-cessandly for to life the name of Ihesu? Hampole, Prose Treatises (EZ. E. T. 8.), p. 3.

unchain.c: unchain (un-chan’),v.¢. [< wn-2 + chain.] To free from chains, slavery, or restraint; let loose. Unchain your spirits now with spelling charms. Shak., 1 Hen. VI., v. 3. 31.

unchallengeable.c: unchallengeable (un-chal’en-ja-bl), a. Not to be challenged; secure. His title and his paternal fortune... might be rendered unchallengeable. Scott, St. Ronan’s Well, xxxiii. (Davies.)

unchallenged.c: unchallenged (un-chal’enjd), a. Not challenged; not objected to or cai to. account.

unchance.c: unchance (un’chans),”. [<un-1+ chance. Cf. wanchancy, mischance.| Mischance; calamity. [Seoteh.]

unchancy.c: unchancy (un-chan’si), a. [< unchance + -~y1. Cf. wanchancy.] 1. Unlucky; unfortunate; ill-fated; uncanny. I cannot but think that there is no safety in having such unchancy creatures (as angels, or ghosts, or fairies, or the like) about ane. Scott, Monastery. 2. Dangerous. Down the gate, in faith, they’re worse, Aw mair unchancy. Burns, Epistle to John Kennedy. I never tried him [a dragon-fly] with a hornet, they being unchancy insects to hold while one hand is otherwise engaged. J. G. Wood, Out of Doors, p. 95. 8. Inconvenient; unseasonable; unsuitable. Why had his Grace come at so unchancy a moment? Trollope. [Chiefly Scotch in all uses.]

unchangeability.c: unchangeability (un-chan-ja-bil/i-ti), n. The state or character of being unchangeable.

unchangeable.c: unchangeable (un-chan’ja-bl), a. Not capable of change; immutable; not subject to variation: as, God is an unchangeable being. Hooker, Eecles. Polity.

unchangeableness.c: unchangeableness (un-chan’ja-bl-nes),. The state or character of being unchangeable; immutability. Newton.

unchangeably.c: unchangeably (un-chan’ja-bli), adv. Soas not to suffer change; without changes immutably.

unchanged.c: unchanged (un- chanjd’), a. Not changed or altered; unvaried. Naught do I see unchanged remain. Scott, Marmion, iv. 24.

unchanging.c: unchanging (un-chan’jing),a. Not changing; suffering no alteration; always the same. Thy face is visard-like, unchanging. Shak., 3 Hen. VI., i. 4. 116,

To leave free of blame or accusation; acquit of blame; acquit. Even his mother shall wncharge the practice, And call it accident. Shak., Hamlet, iv. 7. 68.

uncharitable.c: uncharitable (un-char‘i-ta-bl), a. Not charitable; harsh; censorious; severe. Stone-hearted men, uncharitable, Passe careless by the poore. W. Browne, Britannia’s Pastorals, i. 4. How unequal, how uncharitable must it needs be, to impose that which his conscience cannot urge him to impose, upon him whose conscience forbids him to obey? Milton, True Religion. unchristen

uncharitableness.c: uncharitableness (un-char’i-ta-bl-nes),. The state or character of being uncharitable. Heaven and hell are the proper regions of mercy and uncharitableness. Bp. A ry.

uncharity.c: uncharity (un-char’i-ti), n. Want of charity; uncharitableness. Much uncharity in you. Webster. Fought with what seem’d my own wneharity. Tennyson, Sea Dreams.

uncharm.c: uncharm (un-chirm’), ». ¢ [< wn-2 + charm.] To release from some charm, fascination, or secret power. [Rare.]; Nor is there magic In the person of a king that plays the tyrant But a good sword can easily uncharm it. Shirley, Grateful Servant, iv. 2.

uncharming.c: uncharming (un-chir’ming), a. Not charming; no longer able to charm. [Rare.] Uncharming Catherine.: Dryden, Hind and Panther, iii. 209.

uncharnel.c: uncharnel (un-chir’nel), v. t [« wn-2 + charnel.) To remove from a tomb; disinter; exhume. [Rare.] Whom would’st thou uncharnel? Byron, Manfred, ii. 4.

unchartered.c: unchartered (un-chir’térd), a. Not chartered; hence, without restriction. Me this unchartered freedom tires. Wordsworth, Ode to Duty.

Lecky, European Morals, I. 116. unchet, ». A Middle English form of inch1.

(6) Not willing; grudging: as, uncheerful service. Niggardly in her grants, and uncheerful. Bp. Hall, Contemplations, i. 153.

To divest of the character of a child in relation to parents. [Rare in both uses.] They do justly unchild themselves that in main elections dispose of themselves without the consent of those which gave them being. Bp. Hail, Cont., Samson’s Marriage.

unchildish.c: unchildish (un-chil’dish), a. Not childish; not fit or proper for children. Webbe.

unchivalric.c: unchivalric (un-shiv’al-rik), a. Unchivalrous. I distrusted her, and such vague distrust seemed an wn- chivalric disloyalty. Winthrop, Cecil Dreeme, xviii.

unchristen.c: unchristen (un-kris’n),v. t. [¢€wn-2 + christen.] 1. To annul the baptism of; deprive of the rite In an unchaste unchristen or sacrament of baptism. Imp. Dict.—2. To render unchristian; deprive of sanctity. Hath, as it were, unhallowed and unchristened the very duty of prayer itself. Milton, Hikonoklastes, § 1. unchristian! (un-kris’tian), a. [< ME. un- cristen; <un-1 + Christian.) 1. Not Christian; opposed to Christianity or to its spirit; contrary to Christianity or a Christian character. Not in accordance with the civilization that Christianity insures; rude; cruel: often used colloquially to signify improper, unusual, and the like. My aunt has turn’d me out adoors; she has, At this unchristian hour. Fletcher and Shirley, Night-Walker, iii. 2. unchristian? (un-kris’tian), v. ¢ [< wn-2 + Christian.) “To deprive of the constituent qualities of Christianity; make unchristian. The papists, under the pretence of the church’s union, are the great dividers of the Christian world, unchurching the far greatest part of the church, and separating from all that be not subjects of the pope of Rome. Baxter, Self-Denial, xxxiii. unci, ». Plural of wneus.

A copper coin of the ancient Roman republic, the twelfth part of the as. See as4, 3.—8}+. A former name for the numerical coefficient of any term of the binomial theorem.

Pg. uncial, < ML. wncialis, of a twelfth part, of an ounce or an inch, an inch high, LL. litter uncials, lit. ‘inch letters,’ letters of considerable size; < L. wncia, a twelfth part, an ounce, an inch: see uncia, owncel, inch1.] I. a. 1}. Of or pertaining to an ounce. L. Phillips.— 2. In paleog., noting that variety of majuscule character, or writing, usually found in the earlier manuscripts, as opposed to the later minuscule, or cursive. Uncial characters are distinguished from capitals (that is, capital letters similar to the simplest form of those still in use) by relatively greater roundness, inclination, and inequality in height. unciatim.c: unciatim (un-si-a’tim), adv. [L., by twelfths, by ounces, ¢ wncia, a twelfth part, an ounce: see ounce.] Ounce by ounce. Imp. Dict.

unciferous.c: unciferous (un-sif’e-rus), a [< L. wneus, a hook, + ferre = E. bear.] In entom., bearing a curved process or hook: specifically applied to ovipositor with strongly curved tips, as those of certain grasshoppers.

unciform.c: unciform (un’si-form), a. and n. [< L. wneus, a hook, + forma, form.] I, a. Uneinate in form; hooked or crooked; hook-like: specifically applied in anatomy to certain hook-like processes of bone: as, the unciform process of the ethmoid; the unciform process of the wnci- form bone.—Unciform eminence of the brain, the calcar, or hippocampus minor. II.. In anat. and zool., one of the bones of the wrist, so called from its hook-like process; a carpal bone of the distal row, the innermost one on the ulnar or little-finger side, in special relation with the heads of the fourth and fifth metacarpals, supposed to represent carpalia IV and V of the typical carpus. See carpus, and cuts under Artiodactyla, Perissodactyla, hand, pisiform, and scapholunar.

uncinal.c: uncinal (un’si-nal), a. and n. [< LL. wneinus, a hook: see uncinus.] I, a. Same as wneinate; in conch., specifically noting one of the several lateral teeth of the radula. See admedian. II, ». An uncinal tooth of the radula; an uncinus.

uncinata.c: uncinata (un-si-na’tia), n.; pl. uncinate (-té). [NL., fem. sing. of L. wncinatus, hooked: see uncinate.] In sponges, a rod-like spicule bearing recurved hooks throughout its length. Uncinata2 (un-si-na’ti), m. pl. [NL., neut. pl. of L. uncinatum, hooked: see uncinate.] 1. A division of marine cheetopod worms, containing those whose tori are provided with minute chitinous hooks or uncini. The serpulas, sabellas, and other tubicolous worms belong to this section.— 2. [l.¢.] Plural of uncinatum.

uncinate.c: uncinate (un’si-nat),a@.andn. [< L. wncinatus, hooked, barbed, < LL. wneinus, a hook, barb: see uncinus.] I, a. Hooked or crooked; hooked at the end; forming a hook; unciform. Also uncate.—Uncinate abdomen, in entom., an abdomen in which the terminal segments are turned underneath the others, asin the males of certain Diptera.—Uncinate antenne, in entom., antenne in which the last joint is curved and pointed, bending back on the preceding one. —Uncinate convolution, gyrus, or lobe. (a) The hippocampal gyrus (which see, under gyrus). (6) The anterior extremity of the hippocampal gyrus. See cuts under cerebral, gyrus, and sulcus.—Uncinate process. See processus uncinatum, under processus.—Uncinate wing-nerv- ures, in entom., wing-nervures which run from the base toward the apex of the wing, but at the end are turned back in a hook-like form.; . n. An uncinate sponge-spicule.

uncinatum.c: uncinatum (un-si-na’tum), ”.; pl. uncinata (-t%). [NL., neut. of Li. wneinatus, hooked: see wnei- uncivility nate.| In anat., the unciform bone of the carpus: more fully called os uncinatum. uncini, ». Plural of wneinus.

uncinia.c: Uncinia (un-sin’i-i), n. [NL. (Persoon, 1807), < LL. uncinus, a hook: see uncinus.] A genus of sedges, distinguished from the related genus Carex by the hooked or barbed apex of the rachilla or spikelet-pedicel. There are about 25 species, mostly natives of the temperate and cold parts of the southern hemisphere, a few in the Hawaiian Islands, the West Indies, and the mountains of tropical America and Mexico. They are herbs with the habit of those species of Carex which have a simple androgynous continuous inflorescence. See hamulus, 1 (6).

uncinitaria.c: Uncinitaria (un-sin-i-ta’ri-i), n. pl. [NL.,<L. uncinatum, hooked: see wneinate.} In Sollas’s classification of sponges, a group, called a suborder, of dictyonine hexactinellidan Stlicispon- gin, characterized by the presence of uncinate spicules, and divided into two tribes, Clavularia and Scopularia, the former having one family, the latter five.

uncinitarian.c: uncinitarian (un-sin-i-ta’ri-an), a. [« Uncini- maria + -an.] Having uncinate spicules, as a sponge; of or pertaining to the Uncinitaria.

uncinula.c: Uncinula (un-sin’u-li), ». [NL. (Léveillé, 1851), < LL. uncinus, a hook: see uncinus.] A genus of parasitic (pyrenomycetous) fungi, of the family Lrysiphex, having the appendages free from the mycelium and recurved or coiled at the tip. Each perithecium contains several asci. U. ampelopsidin (U. spiralis) is the common or powdery grape-mildew, and is highly injurious to the grape. See grape-mildew, Erysiphee, Pyrenomycetes, and mildew.

uncinus.c: uncinus (un-si’/nus), 7.; pl. wneini (-ni). [< LL. uncinus, a hook, barb.] 1. A hook or hooklet; a hamulus; something small, hard, and crooked; specifically, in conch., one of the uncinal teeth of the radula. In the Heteropoda, it [the radula] is so far more highly developed that the outermost uncini of the transverse rows may not only be very long, but also be articulated in such a manner as to be movable. When, therefore, the radula is protruded, these teeth are erected, and when it is drawn back they come together like pincers. Gegenbaur, Comp. Anat. (trans.), p. 360. 2. One of the hooked cilia of infusorians.—3$. One of the numerous minute chitinous hooks of the tori of some annelids. See Uncinata.— 4, A weapon used in the eleventh century, resembling a martel-de-fer, but thought to have only one point or edge..

uncipher.c: uncipher (un-si’fér), v. t. To decipher. Which letter was intercepted by Captain Abbots, a Captain of Dragoons in the army, and is now enciphered. Rushworth Hist. Coll., Pt. IV. I. 491 (1647). (Davies.)

uncircumcision.c: uncircumcision (un-sér-kum-sizh’on),n. 1. Absence of circumcision; the condition of being uncireumeised. Rom, iy. 9,10.—2. Hence, people who are not circumcised; the Gentiles: often with the. If the uncircumcision keep the righteousness of the law, shall not his uncircumcision be counted for circumcision? Rom. ii. 26.

uncircumscript.c: uncircumscript (un-sér’kum-skript), a. [ME., <un-1 + cirewmscript.] Not circumscribed. Thou Oon and Two and Thre, eterne on lyve, That regest ay in Three and Two and Oon, Uncircumseript and al maist circumscrive. Chaucer, Troilus, v. 1879.

uncircumstantial.c: uncircumstantial (un-sér-kum-stan’shal), a. 1. Not circumstantial; not entering into minute particulars.— 2}. Not important. The like particulars, although they seem uncircumstantial, are oft set down in Holy Scripture. Sir T. Browne, Vulg. Err., vii. 1.

uncirostrate.c: uncirostrate (un-si-ros’trat), a. [< L. wneus, a hook, + rostratus, beaked: see rostrate.] In ornith., having a hooked beak; hamirostrate.

uncivil.c: uncivil (un-siv’il), a. Not civil. (a) Notpertain- ing to a settled government or settled state of society; not civilized; barbarous; savage; hence, not exhibiting refinement; unacquainted with the customs and manners of good society. The savage and vnetuill, who were before all science or ciuilitie, euen as the naked by prioritie of time is before the clothed. Puttenham, Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 7. The wneivil kerns of Ireland are in arms. Shak., 2 Hen. VI., iii. 1. 310. (6) Not courteous; ill-mannered; rude; coarse: as, an uncivil answer; an uncivil fellow. Let go that rude wneivil touch! Shak., T. G. of V., v. 4. 60. (c) Improper; unusual; not customary. With midnight matins, at wneivil hours. Dryden, Hind and Panther, iii. 1010.

uncivility.c: uncivility (un-si-vil’i-ti), ». Incivility. You were never the gentlemen offered any uncivility to me, which is strange, methinks, in one that comes from beyond seas, Webster and Dekker, Westward Ho, i. 2. uncivilized

uncivilized.c: uncivilized (un-siv’i-lizd),a. 1. Not civilized or reclaimed from savage life; rude; barbarous; savage: as, uncivilized hordes.— 2}. Coarse; indecent. The most uncivilized words in our language. Addison,

uncivilly.c: uncivilly (un-siv’i-li), adv. In an uncivil manner; not courteously; rudely.

unclad.c: unclad (un-klad’). Preterit and past participle of unclothe. Tennyson.

unclasp.c: unclasp (un-klasp’), v. t [« w-2+clasp.] 1. To loosen the clasp of, as a purse or a belt. Unclasps a huge tome in an antique guise, Primitive print and tongue half obsolete. Browning, Ring and Book, I. 45. 2t. To lay open; reveal; disclose. Gentle father, To you I have wnelasp’'d my burden’d soul. Ford, ’Tis Pity, i. 1.

unclassable.c: unclassable (un-klas’a-bl), a. Not capable of being classed or classified. Mind remains unclassable, and therefore unknowable. H. Spencer.

uncle.c: uncle (ung’kl), ». [Early mod. E. also uncle, ankle; < ME. uncle = G. Sw. Dan. onker, < OF. uncle, onely, FE. once = Pr. once, avoncle = It. avun- cul = Wallach. wnchiu, an uncle, a mother’s brother, <¢ L. avunculus,in inscriptions also avon- culus, avomeulus, avunculus, a mother’s brother (a father’s brother being patruus), lit. ‘little grandfather,’ dim. of avus, a grandfather. Cf. avuncular, atavism. See also nuncle.] 1. The brother of one’s father or mother; also, the husband of one’s aunt: correlative to aunt. Then pleas’d and parted; both go live apart; The Vnele kept the Mountain for his part. Sylvester, tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Vocation. 2. A familiar title of address to an old man: used especially in the southern United States as a kindly title for a worthy old negro: as, “Uncle Tom’s Cabin”: correlative to aunt or aunty in similar use. The bleating of goats was heard from the darkey settlement... as queer old aunties and aneles hobbled out to milk them. S. Bonner, Dialect Tales, p. 121. 38. A pawnbroker: so called in humorous allusion to the financial favors often expected and sometimes received from rich uncles. [Slang.] Fourscore pounds draws deep. Farewell, Doll. Come, sergeants, I’ll step to mine wele not far off, hereby in Pudding-lane, and he shall bail me. Webster and Dekker, Northward Ho, i. 2. Brothers, wardens of City Halls, And uneles, rich as three golden balls From taking pledges of nations. : Hood, Miss Kilmansegg. To talk like a Dutch uncle, See Dutch.—Uncle Sam, the government or the people of the United States: a jocular extension of the initials U. S. -uncle. [F. -uncle,< Li. -unculus, a dim. term. < -un-, -on-, part of the orig. noun, + -cu-lus, a double dim. suffix: see -cle, -cule, -culus.] <A termination of some diminutive words of Latin origin, as homuncle (also homuncule), ratiuncle, etc.

unclean.c: unclean (un-klén’), a. [< ME. wnclene, onclene, < AS. uncléne, unclean; as un-1 + clean.] 1. Not clean; foul; dirty; filthy. Thi lande wnelene alle dolven upper mot be, Of rootes, fern, and weed, to make it free. Palladius, Husbondrie (E. E. T. 8.), p. 46. 2. Ceremonially impure. (a) Not free from ceremonial defilement: said of persons. (0) Causing ceremonial defilement: said of animals or things, and specifically applied to animals forbidden by Jewish law to be used in sacrifice and for food. Lev. xi. 26, 8. Morally impure; foul with sin; wicked; evil; especially, lewd; unchaste. Als longe als thei ben of foule and of unclene Lyvynge (as thei ben now), wee have no drede of hem, in no kynde: for here God will not helen hem in no wise. Mandeville, Travels, p. 138. Where an wnelean mind carries virtuous qualities, there commendations go with pity. Shak., All’s Well, i. 1. 48. An unclean spirit, a wicked spirit; demon. Mark i. 27.

uncleanliness.c: uncleanliness (un-klen’li-nes), n. Want of cleanliness; filthiness; foulness.

uncleanly.c: uncleanly (un-klen’li), a. [< ME. wnclenlich, onclenlich; < wn-l + cleanly.) 1. Not cleanly; not clean; foul; filthy; dirty. The very uncleanly flux of a cat. Shak., As you Like it, iii. 2. 70. 2. Not chaste; unchaste; obscene. "Tis pity that these harmonious writers have indulged anything uncleanly or impure to defile their paper. Watts.

uncleanness.c: uncleanness (un-klén’nes), n. [< ME. unelen- nes, unclannes, onclennes, < AS. uncl&nnes, uncleanness; as unclean + -ness.] The state or character of being unclean. 6588

unclear.c: unclear (un-klér’), a. Not clear, in any sense of that word. Leighton, 1 Pet. iii.

uncleciate.c: uncle ciate (an-chek’a-bl),a. 1. Not capable of being checked or hindered; that may not be stopped suddenly or forcibly. J. Peacock, Sermon on Rom. il. 4.—2. Incapable of being checked or examined. His lordship used him in his most private and wncheck- able trusts. North, Life of Lord Guilford, ii. 285. (Davies.)

uncleesek.c: Uncle Esek (ung'kl e'zek). The pseudonym of Henry W. Shaw. Uncle Remus. See Remus, Uncle.

unclenchunclinch.c: unclench, unclinch (un-klench’, -klinch’), v. t. andi. [< ME.unclenchen; <un-2 + clench, clinch.] To open, or to force open, as the closed hand. The fist wnelenches, and the weapon falls. Garth, Dispensary, v.

unclesam.c: Uncle Sam (sam). The government of the people of the United States: a jocular extension of the initials U. S. Uncle Tom’s Cabin. A novel by Mrs. Harriet Beecher Stowe, published in book form in 1852. It was directed against negro slavery in the Southern States. The scene is laid chiefly in Kentucky and Louisiana. It has appeared in numerous editions and translations. It came out as a sort of feuilleton in the “National Era,” a Washington paper. The death of Uncle Tom was the first portion published, indeed the first that was written. It appeared in the summer of 1851, and excited so much attention that Mrs. Stowe added a beginning and middle to her end, by composing and printing from week to week the story as we now have it, until it was concluded in March, 1852. Before the end of 1852 it had been translated into Italian, Spanish, Danish, Swedish, Dutch, Flemish, German, Polish, and Magyar. There are two Dutch translations and twelve German ones; and the Italian translation enjoys the honour of the pope’s prohibition. It has been dramatised in twenty forms, and acted in every capital in Europe, and in the free States of America. Senior, Essays on Fiction, p. 397. Uncommercial Traveller, The. A volume of sketches by Dickens, first published serially in “All the Year Round” in 1860.

uncleship.c: uncleship (ung’kl-ship), ». [« wele + -ship.] The state of being an uncle; the relation of an uncle. Lamb, Essays of Elia, p. 388.

unclewt.c: unclewt (un-klé’), v. t [< wn-2 + clew.] To unwind; figuratively, to undo or ruin. If I should pay you for ’t as ’tis extoll’d, It would unclew me quite. Shak., T. of A., i. 1. 168.

uncling.c: uncling (un-kling’), vi. [< un-2 + cling.] To cease from clinging, adhering, entwining, embracing, or holding fast. Milton. [Rare.]

uncloak.c: uncloak (un-kl6k’), v. [< wn-2 + cloak.] I. trans. To deprive of the cloak; remove the cloak from; hence, to reveal; bring to light. II. intrans. To take off the cloak, or the outer garments generally.

unclog.c: unclog (un-klog’), v. t.; pret. and pp. unclogged, ppr. unclogging. [< un-2 + clog.) To disencumber of what clogs; relieve of difficulties or obstructions; free from encumbrances. It would unclog my heart Of what lies heavy to ’t. Shak., Cor., iv. 2. 47.

uncloister.c: uncloister (un-klois’tér), v. t [< wn-2 + cloister.] To release from a cloister or from confinement; set at liberty. Norris.

unclosed.c: unclosed (un-klozd’), pa. [< ME. wnelosed; < un-1 + closed.] 1. Not separated by inclosure; open; uninclosed. I have to longe in this manere Left hem unclosed wilfully. Rom. of the Rose, 1. 3921. The king’s army would, through those unclosed parts, have done them little harm. Clarendon, Great Rebellion. 2. Not finished; not brought to a close; of accounts, not balanced; not settled. I don’t love to leave any Part of the Account unclos’d. Steele, Conscious Lovers, iv. 1. 3. Not closed. His unclosed eye yet lowering on his enemy. Byron, Giaour.

unclosel.c: unclosel (un-kl6z’),v. [<¢ ME. wnelosen; < un-2 + close.] I, trans. 1. To open. Whenne Somer cometh, unclose hem, thai beth sure. Palladius, Husbondrie (E. E. T. §.), p. 120. Thy letters trembling I wnelose. Pope, Eloisa to Abelard. 2+. To uncover; take off the covers from.—3. To disclose; lay open. Than thei loked a-boute and be-helde toward the see where thei saugh the cristin a litill vn-closed. Merlin (E. E. T. 8.), iii. 597. II. intrans. To open; be laid open. This flour, when that it shulde unclose Agayn the sonne. Chaucer, Good Women, 1. 111. The goddess spoke; the rolling waves wneclose. Pope, Iliad, i. 562. unclose? (un-kl6s’), a. [< wn-1 + close2.] Not close; unreserved; babbling. [Rare.] Knowen designs are dangerous to act, And th’ vnelose chief did never noble fact. Sylvester, The Captaines, 1. 1075. (Davies.)

unclothe.c: unclothe (un-klorH’), v. t.; pret. and pp. wn- clothed or unclad, ppr. unclothing. [Formerly also unloath, uncloth; < ME. unclothen, un- lethen; < un-2 + clothe.| 1. To strip of clothes; make naked; divest of covering. The ceremonies, dances, and sacrifices ended, they went to vneloth themselues. Purchas, Pilgrimage, p. 808. 2. Figuratively, to divest; free; strip. The fame of Pyrocles and Musidorus greatly drew him to a compassionate conceit, and had already unclothed his face of all show of malice. Sir P. Sidney, Arcadia, v.

unclothed.c: unclothed (un-klérHd’), a. Not clothed; being without clothes.

uncloud.c: uncloud (un-kloud’),v.¢. [< wn-2+ cloud1.] To free from clouds; unveil; clear from obscurity, gloom, sadness, dullness, or the like. Beau. and Fi., Philaster, iv. 2.

unclouded.c: unclouded (un-klou’ded), p. a. Not cloudy; free from clouds; not darkened or obscured; free from gloom; clear: as, an wnclouded sky; an unclouded intellect.

uncloudedness.c: uncloudedness (un-klou’ded-nes), x. The state of being unclouded. Boyle.

uncloudy.c: uncloudy (un-klou’di), a. Not cloudy; free from clouds. Gay.

unclubable.c: unclubable (un-klub’a-bl), a. Not clubable; unsocial. uncombine “Sir John was a most unclubable man!” How delighted was I to hear this master of languages [Dr. Johnson] so unaffectedly and socially and good-naturedly make words, for the promotion of sport and good humour! Mme. D’ Arblay, Diary, i. 41. unclue}t, v. t. Same as unclew.

unclutch.c: unclutch (un-kluch’), v. t. [< wn-2 + clutch.] To open, as something clutched, clenched, or closely shut. Dr. H. More.

unco.c: unco (ung’k6), a. and. [A dial. reduction of uncouth.] I, a. Unknown; strange; unusual. Leesome Brand (Child’s Ballads, Il. 342). [Scoteh.] II.. 1. Anything strange or prodigious. Galt.—2. A strange person; a stranger. Galt.

unco (ung’k6), adv. [< unco, a.] Wonderfully; remarkably; very: as, unco glad; unco guid. [Seotech.] In this prison there grew a tree, And it was unco stout and strang. Lord Beichan and Susie Pye (Child’s Ballads, IV. 254), uncock! (un-kok’), v. t. [< wn-2 + cock.] 1.

uncoffined.c: uncoffined (un-kof’ind), a. Not furnished with a coffin; not put into a coffin. Unknelled, uncofined, and unknown. Byron, Childe Harold, iv.

uncogitable.c: uncogitable (un-koj’i-ta-bl), a. Not capable of being cogitated or thought. Sir T. More.

uncoif.c: uncoif (un-koif’),v.t. [< wn-2 + coif.] To pull off the cap or head-dress of. [Rare.] Two apple-woman scolding and just ready to uncoif one another. Martinus Seriblerus.

uncoifed.c: uncoifed (un-koift’), a. Without a coif; not wearing a coif. Her majesty’s renown’d though wncoif’d counsel. Young, Night Thoughts, viii.

uncoin.c: uncoin (un-koin’), v. ¢ To deprive (money) of its character as coin. [Rare.] These are the people who frequently wncotn money, either by melting it or by exporting it to countries where it is sooner or later melted. Jevons, Money and Mech. of Exchange, p. 81.

uncoined.c: uncoined (un-koind’), a. 1. Not coined: as, uncoined silver. Locke.—2. Not minted; lacking the stamp of conventionality; hence, natural, unfeigned. A fellow of plain and uncoined constancy. hak., Hen. V., v. 2. 161.

uncollected.c: uncollected (un-ko-lek’ted), a. 1. Not collected; not brought to one place; not received: as, uncollected taxes; debts wncollected.—2. Not having one’s thoughts collected; not having control of one’s mental faculties; not recovered from confusion, distraction, or wandering. What a wild beast is uncollected man! Beau. and Fl., Maid’s Tragedy, iv. 2.

uncoloreduncoloured.c: uncolored, uncoloured (un-kul’ord), pa. 1. Not colored; not stained or dyed; hence, unclouded; clear; specifically, white. Things uncoloured and transparent. To deck with clouds the uncolour’d sky, Or wet the thirsty earth with falling showers. Milton, P. L., v. 189. 2. Not heightened in description; truthful; unbiased: as, an uncolored statement.—3, Unadorned; plain; chaste. The contrast was remarkable between the uncolored style of his [John Foster’s] general diction, and the brilliant felicity of occasional images embroidered upon the sober ground of his text. De Quincey, Biog. and Hist. Essays, p. 350.

uncolt.c: uncolt (un-k6lt’), v. t. [< un-2 + colt.] To unhorse; deprive of a colt or horse. [Rare.] Thou liest; thou art not coated, thou art wneolted. Shak,, 1 Hen. IV., ii, 2042.

uncombine.c: uncombine (un-kom-bin’), v. [< wn-2 + combine.] I, trans. To sever or destroy the combination, union, or junction of; separate; disconnect. Outbreaking vengeance uncombines the ill-joined plots. Daniel, Civil Wars, iii. II. intrans. To become separated or disconnected. [Rare in both uses.] = Bacon. uncombine The rude conjuncture of wncombining cable in the violence of a northern tempest. Jer. Taylor, Sermons, II. ii.

uncomeatable.c: uncomeatable (un-kum-at’a-bl), a. [< un-1 + come-at-able.| Not accessible; not attainable; beyond reach or comprehension. [Colloq.] He has a perfect art in being unintelligible in discourse, and uncomeatable in business. Steele, Tatler, No. 12.

uncomeliness.c: uncomeliness (un-kum’‘li-nes),». 1. Want of comeliness; want of beauty or grace: as, wn- comeliness of person, of dress, or behavior.— 2. Unbecomingness; unseemliness; indecency. He... gave such orderly and well-behaved reproof to all uncomeliness that I would have sworn his disposition would have gone to the truth of his words. Shak., M. W. of W., ii. 1. 60.

uncomely.c: uncomely (un-kum‘li), a. [< ME. uncomely, on- comely, uncumelich; < un-1 + comely.) 1. Not comely; wanting grace: as, an uncomely person; uncomely dress.— 2. Unseemly; unbecoming; unsuitable; indecent. Thinke nothing uncomly which is honest, for nothing is comely that is not honest. Booke of Precedence (KE. E. T. S., extra ser.), i. 71. Besides (to say truth) nakedness is uncomely, as well in mind as in body. Bacon.
uncomely (un-kum‘li), adv. In an uncomely or unbecoming manner; indecently. 1Cor. vii. 36. Tis most uncomely spoken. Fletcher (and Massinger?), False One, iii. 1.

uncomfortable.c: uncomfortable (un-kum’fér-ta-bl), a. 1. Not comfortable; affording no comfort; causing bodily or mental discomfort; giving uneasiness; disquieting: as, an uncomfortable seat or condition. Christmas is in the most dead and the most uncomfortable time of the year. Addison. How uncomfortable will the remembrance be of all your excesses, oaths, injustice and profaneness, when death approaches, and judgment follows it? Stillingfleet, Sermons, I. v. 2. Disagreeably situated; uneasy; ill at ease: as, to feel uncomfortable. How surely dost thou malice these extremes, Uncomfortable man. Ford, Lady’s Trial, iii. 3.

uncomfortableness.c: uncomfortableness (un-kum’feér-ta-bl-nes), n. The state of being uncomfortable, uneasy, or miserable. Jer. Taylor.

uncomfortably.c: uncomfortably (un-kum’fér-ta-bli), adv. In an uncomfortable manner; with discomfort or uneasiness; in an uneasy state.

uncommendable.c: uncommendable (un-ko-men’da-bl), a. Not commendable; not worthy of commendation; illaudable. [Rare.] The uncommendable licentiousness of his poetry. Feltham, On Eccles. ii. 11.

uncommerciable.c: uncommerciable (un-ko-mér’shia-bl), a. [< un-1 + *commerciable, equiv. to commerceable. | Not capable of being made an article of commerce. [Rare.] By prohibiting all his Majesty’s subjects from dealing in tobacco, one third of the exports of the United States are rendered uncommerciable here. Thos. Jefferson, To Count De Montmorin (Works, II. 188).

uncommercial.c: uncommercial (un-ko-mér’shal), a. 1. Not commercial; not carrying on or familiar with or devoted to commerce. The Uncommercial Traveller. Dickens, The wisdom of taking measures to keep the river in good condition is made plain to even the uncommercial mind. S. L. Clemens, Life on the Mississippi, p. 310. 2. Not in accordance with the principles of commerce. You did not think it uncommercial to tax the whole mass of your manufactures, and, let me add, your agriculture too. Burke, American Taxation. (EHncyc. Dict.)

uncommitted.c: uncommitted (un-ko-mit’ed), a. [< ME. uncommitted; < un-1 + committed.) 1. Not committed or done. Offys uncommitted ofte anoyeth. Chaucer, Parliament of Fowls, 1. 518. The uncommitted sin. Hammond. 2. Not committed or intrusted.—3. Not referred to a committee.—4. Not pledged by anything said or done: as, uncommitted by rash promises or statements; an uncommitted delegation to a convention.

uncommon.c: uncommon (un-kom’on), a. Not common; not usual; infrequent; rare; hence, remarkable; extraordinary; strange. Steele, Englishman, No. 26. The spiritual is ever foreign to the material, the wn- common to the common.. Sharp, D. G. Rossetti, iii. =Syn. Scarce, unusual, unwonted, unique, singular, queer. uncommon (un-kom’on), adv. [< uncommon, a.) Exceedingly; very: as, uncommon cheap. (Vulgar.]

uncommonly.c: uncommonly (un-kom’on-li), adv. 1. In an uncommon manner; rarely; not usually. We are not uncommonly told that Henry VII. had not in his own person the shadow of hereditary right. uncommonness.c: uncommonness (un-kom’on-nes),. The state or character of being uncommon; rareness of occurrence; infrequency.

uncommunicable.c: uncommunicable (un-ko-mii/ni-ka-bl), a. 1. Incommunieable. Burke.—2. Not communicative; reserved; taciturn. Imp. Dict. [Rare.]

uncommunicative.c: uncommunicative (un-ko-mi’ni-ka-tiv), a. 1+. Not communicative or disposed to impart one’s wealth; not liberal; parsimonious. A little too uncommunicative for their great circumstances. Richardson, Clarissa Harlowe, ii. 90. 2. Not communicative; not disposed to impart one’s thoughts; not free to communicate to others; reserved; taciturn. A churlish and uncommunicative disposition. Chesteryield. uncommunicativeness (un-ko-mw’ni-ka-tiy- nes), ”. The state or character of being uncommunicative, reserved, or taciturn; reserve. Richardson.

uncompacted.c: uncompacted (un-kom-pak’ted), a. Not compact; not firm or settled. Feltham.

uncompanied.c: uncompanied (un-kum’pa-nid), a. Having no companion; unaccompanied. Fairfax.

uncompanionable.c: uncompanionable (un-kom-pan’yon-a-bl), a. Not companionable or sociable. Miss Burney.

uncompanioned.c: uncompanioned (un-kom-pan’yond), a. Unaccompanied; without a companion; alone; - solitary; having no equal. In his hours of uncompanioned darkness. J. Wilson, Lights and Shadows of Scottish Life.

uncomplainingly.c: uncomplainingly (un-kom-pla’ning-li), adv. In an uncomplaining manner; without murmuring or complaint.

uncomplaisant.c: uncomplaisant (un-kom’pla-zant), a. Not complaisant; not civil; not courteous. Locke.

uncompliable.c: uncompliable (un-kom-pli’a-bl), a. Unready or unwilling to yield or comply. Cudworth, Morality, 1V. v. § 3.

uncomposable.c: uncomposable (un-kom-p0’za-bl), a. Incapable of being composed; not to be reconciled or arranged. Roger North, Examen, p. 63.

Milton, P. L., i. 425. 2. Not intricate or complicated. That uncompounded style. Hammond, On Fundamentals. uncomprehensible} (un-kom-pré-hen’si-bl), a. Incomprehensible. Bp. Jewell.

unconceiledt.c: unconceiledt, a. An obsolete variant of wn- counseled. unconceivable+ (un-kon-sé’va-bl), a. ceivable. Locke.

unconceivableness.c: unconceivableness (un-kon-sé’va-bl-nes), n. Inconeeivableness. Dr. H. More, Immortal. of Soul, i. 4. unconceivably} (un-kon-sé’va-bli), adv. Inconceivably. Locke.

unconcern.c: unconcern (un-kon-sérn’), n. Want of concern; absence of anxiety; freedom from solicitude; indifferentism; indifference; apathy. I can’t bear to hear her spoken of with Levity or Unconcern. Steele, Conscious Lovers, ii. 1. =Syn. Indifference, Insensibility, etc. See apathy.

unconcerned.c: unconcerned (un-kon-sérnd’), a. Not concerned; not anxious; feeling no concern or solicitude; easy in mind; not interested; not affected. Incon- The morn, All unconcern’d with our unrest. Milton, P, L., xi. 174. Calm Villain! how unconcern’d he stands, confessing Treachery and Ingratitude! Congreve, Double-Dealer, i. 6. =Syn. Unconcerned at, for, about. With at, unconcerned means not anxious in view of something that is or happens; with for it means not anxious for the safety or success of some object of interest or desire: unconcerned at the successes of a rival; unconcerned for one’s own safety. With about it generally means the same as with Jor, but sometimes the same as with at.

unconcernedly.c: unconcernedly (un-kon-sér’ned-li), adv. Inan unconcerned manner; without concern or anxiety.

unconcernedness.c: unconcernedness (un-kon-sér’ned-nes), n. Freedom from concern or anxiety. South. unconcerning+ (un-kon-sér’ning), a. Not interesting; not affecting; not belonging to one. Dy. H. More.

unconcernment.c: unconcernment (un-kon-sérn’ment), ». The state of having no interest or concern. South. unconcludent+ (un-kon-klé’dent), a. Not decisive; inconclusive. Sir M. Hale. unconcludible+ (un-kon-klé’di-bl), a. be concluded or determined. That which is unconcludible... tothe understanding. Dr. H. More, Philos. Poems, notes.

unconcluding.c: unconcluding (un-kon-kl6’ding), a. Inconclusive. False and unconcluding reasonings. Locke.

unconcludingness.c: unconcludingness (un-kon-klé’ding-nes), n. The character of being inconclusive. The uncertainty of the truth,... by reason of the unconcludingness of the arguments brought to attest it. Jer. Taylor, Works (ed. 1835), IT. 344. Not to

unconcocted.c: unconcocted (un-kon-kok’ted), a." 1. Not concocted; not digested. Sir T. Browne.—2. Figuratively, rude; indigested.

unconcurrent.c: unconcurrent (un-kon-kur’ent), a. Not concurring or agreeing. Daniel.

uncondemned.c: uncondemned (un-kon-demd’), a. Not condemned; not judged guilty; not disapproved; not pronounced criminal. They have beaten us openly uncondemned. Acts xvi. 37. A familiar and uncondemned practice. Locke. uncondited+ (un-kon-di’ted), a [< wn-l+ L. conditus, pp. of condite, season, spice, flavor.] Unseasoned. [Rare.] While he estimates the secrets of religion by such measures, they must needs seem as insipid as cork, or the wn- condited mushroom. Jer. Taylor, Works (ed. 1835), IT. 60.

unconditional.c: unconditional (un-kon-dish’on-al), a. Not conditional; absolute; unreserved; not limited by any conditions: as, an unconditional surrender. O pass not, Lord, an absolute decree, Or bind thy sentence unconditional, Dryden, Annus Mirabilis.

unconditionality.c: unconditionality (un-kon-dish-on-al’i-ti), n. The character or state of being unconditional. J. Ward, Encye. Brit., XX. 82.

unconditionally.c: unconditionally (un-kon-dish’on-al-i), adv. In an unconditional manner; without conditions: as, to surrender unconditionally.

unconditionalness.c: unconditionalness (un-kon-dish’on-al-nes), n. The character of being unconditional. J. Fiske, Cosmic Philos., I. 151.

unconditioned.c: unconditioned (un-kon-dish’ond), a. Not subject to conditions; not an effect, accident, or result of circumstances. vi are =e unconditioned This step from conditioned to unconditioned [existence] implies a pure a priori synthesis. E.
