undigestible.c: undigestible (un-di-jes’ti-bl), a. Indigestible. undight} (un-dit’), v. t [< wn-2 + dight.) To put off, as ornaments or apparel. From her fayre head her fillet she undight. Spenser, F. Q., I. iii. 4. undigne, a. [ME., < wn-1 + digne.] Unworthy. Undigne and unworthy Am I to thilke honour that ye me bede. Chaucer, Clerk’s Tale, 1. 303.

undignified.c: undignified (un-dig’ni-fid), a. Not dignified. (a) Not honored; not rendered dignified. (6) Not consistent with dignity; exhibiting an absence of dignity. The attempts of Henry III. to influence the chapters were undignified and unsuccessful; his candidates were seldom chosen. Stubbs, Const. Hist., § 705.

undignify.c: undignify (un-dig’ni-fi), v. t To render undignified; deprive of dignity; debase. [Rare.] Rowells, Venetian Life, xii.

undilution.c: undilution (un-di-la’shon), ». The character or state of being undiluted. [Rare.] The three primary colours assumed in the... figure (of the prismatic spectrum) are red, green, and blue, each in its highest degree of purity and undilution. Herschel, Popular Lectures on Scientific Subjects, p. 258.

undinal.c: undinal (un-dé’nal), a. [< wndine + -al.] Of or pertaining to an undine, or the belief in such creatures.

undine.c: undine (un-dén’), n. [= F.ondine, f. (odin, m.), = G. undine, < NL. *undine, a water-spirit, ¢ L. unda, wave, water: see undulate, found.] A wa- ter-spirit of the female sex, resembling in character the sylphs or spirits of the air, and corresponding in some measure to the naiads of classical mythology. According to Paracelsus, when an undine married a mortal and bore a child she received a soul.

undinted.c: undinted (un-din’ted), a. Not impressed by blows; unbattered. Shak., A. and C., ii. 6. 39.

undiocesed.c: undiocesed (un-di’d-sést), a. Not possessed of or preferred to a diocese. Milton, Reformation in Eng., i. undirect+ (un-di-rekt’), v. t [« wn-2 + direct.] To misdirect; mislead. Fuller.

undirectly.c: undirectly (un-di-rekt’li), adv. [Rare.] Directly or undirectly, secretly or openly. Strype, Eccles. Mem., Henry VIII. No. 64.

undiscernable.c: undiscernable (un-di-zér’na-bl), a. Same as undiscernible. Indirectly. undiscernedly

undiscernedly.c: undiscernedly (un-di-zér’ned-li), adv. In such a manner as not to be discerned or discovered or seen. Boyle, Works, II. 447.

undiscernible.c: undiscernible (un-di-zér’ni-bl), a. Indiscernible. Shak., M. for M., v. 1.373. Also wndiscern- able.

undiscernibly.c: undiscernibly (un-di-zér’ni-bli), adv. Indis- eernibly. Jer. Taylor, Repentance, v. § 5.

undiscerning.c: undiscerning (un-di-zér’ning), a. Not discerning; not making just distinctions; lacking judgment or the power of discrimination. Donne.

undischarged.c: undischarged (un-dis-chirjd’), a. Not dises (a) Not dismissed; not freed from obliga- Ion. Hold still in readiness and undischarged. B. Jonson, Sejanus, v. 3. (b) Not fulfilled; not carried out; unexecuted: as, an undischarged duty.

undisciplinable.c: undisciplinable (un-dis’i-plin-a-bl), a. Incapable of being disciplined. Sir M. Hale, Of Self-Denial.

undisciplined.c: undisciplined (un-dis’i-plind), a. Not disciplined; not duly exercised and taught; not properly trained or brought to regularity and order; raw: as, undisciplined troops; undisciplined valor; undisciplined minds. An armed disciplined body is, in its essence, dangerous to liberty; undisciplined, it is ruinous to society. Burke, Speech on Army Estimates, 1790.

undiscloset.c: undiscloset (un-dis-kl6z’), v. t. To refrain from disclosing; keep close or secret. Daniel.

undiscomfited.c: undiscomfited (un-dis-kum’fi-ted), a. Not discomfited. He may his cheese holde undescounfited. Chaucer, Boéthius, i. meter 4.

undiscording.c: undiscording (un-dis-kér’ding), a. Not discording; not disagreeing; not discordant in sound; harmonious. [Rare.] With undiscording voice. Milton, Solemn Music, 1. 17.

undiscoursed.c: undiscoursed (un-dis-kdérst’), a. Not discoursed about; not made the subject of talk or discussion; silent. [Rare.] We would submit to all with indefinite and wndis- coursed obedience. Bp. Hacket, Abp. Williams, i. 130. (Davies.)

undiscoverable.c: undiscoverable (un-dis-kuy’ér-a-bl), a. That cannot be discovered or found out: as, undiscoverable principles.

undiscoverably.c: undiscoverably (un-dis-kuy’ér-a-bli), adv. In a manner not to be discovered. Milton, Tetrachordon.

undiscovered.c: undiscovered (un-dis-kuv’érd), a. Not discovered; not seen; not descried; not laid open to view; lying hid. The undiscover'd country, from whose bourn No traveller returns. Shak., Hamlet, iii. 1. 79.

undiscreet.c: undiscreet (un-dis-krét’), a. [Harly mod. E. also wndiserete; < ME. undiscreet; < un-1 + discreet.| Indiscreet. So undiscreet of governance. Chaucer, Nun’s Priest’s Tale, 1. 614. The wndiserete hastiness of the emperour Claudius caused hym to be noted for foolisshe. Sir T, Elyot, The Governour, ii. 6.

undiscreetly.c: undiscreetly (un-dis-krét’li), adv. Indiscreetly. Tyndale, Ans. to Sir T. More, ete. (Parker Soe., 1850), p. 95.

undiscreetness.c: undiscreetness (un-dis-krét’nes), ». Indiscretion; imprudence. Udall, tr. of Apophthegms of Erasmus, p. 328.

undiscretion.c: undiscretion (un-dis-kresh’on), ». [< ME. wn- discretion; < un-1 + discretion.] Indiseretion. Lydgate, Story of Thebes, iii.

undiscriminating.c: undiscriminating (un-dis-krim‘i-na-ting), a. Not discriminating; not distinguishing or making a difference. Cowper, Odyssey, xxii.

undiscussed.c: undiscussed (un-dis-kust’), a. Not discussed; not argued or debated. Bp. Hall, Christ Transfigured, ii.

undisguisable.c: undisguisable (un-dis-gi’za-bl), a. of being disguised. Quarterly Rev.

undisguised.c: undisguised (un-dis-gizd’), a. Not disguised; not covered with a mask or with a false appearance; hence, open; frank; candid; plain; artless: as, undisguised anxiety. Plaine English wndisgwised. The Isle of Ladies, 1. 1450. Himself he view’d with undisguised respect. Crabbe, Tales, Works, IV. 129.

undisguisedly.c: undisguisedly (un-dis-gi’zed-li), adv. In an undisguised manner; openly; frankly.

undishonored.c: undishonored (un-dis-on’ord), a. Not dishonored; not disgraced. Shak.,C. of E., ii. 2. 148,

undisjoined.c: undisjoined (un-dis-joind’), a. Not disjoined; not separated or parted. Cowper. Incapable 6602

undismayed.c: undismayed (un-dis-mad’), a. Not dismayed; not disheartened by fear; not discouraged. The exhortation to be confident and undismayed. J. A, Alexander, Com. on Mark xiii. 11.

undispensable.c: undispensable (un-dis-pen’sa-bl), a. 1. Indispensable. Milton.—2. Unavoidable. A necessary and indispensable famine in a camp. ‘uller. 3. Excluded from dispensation. Lord Herbert.

undispensed.c: undispensed (un-dis-penst’), a. 1. Not dispensed.— 2. Not freed from obligation. Canon Tooker.

undispensing.c: undispensing (un-dis-pen’sing), a. That cannot be dispensed with. Milton, Divorce, ii. 5.

undispersed.c: undispersed (un-dis-pérst’), a. Not dispersed; not scattered. Boyle. undispleased+ (un-dis-plézd’), a. displeasure; not resentful. He would forgive all old respace, And undispleased be of time past. The Isle of Ladies, 1. 925.

undispose.c: undispose (un-dis-p6z’), v. t [< un-2 + dispose.| Toindispose. Jmp. Dict. [Rare.]

undisposed.c: undisposed (un-dis-p6zd’), pa. 1. Indisposed as regards the health. Jmp. Dict. [Rare.]— 2+. Not disposed; not inclined. Careless and undisposed to joyne with them. Hooker. 8. Not sold, settled, decided, allocated, or arranged: with of: as, goods remaining wndis- posed of. undisposedness} (un-dis-pd’zed-nes), ». Indisposition.

undisprivacied.c: undisprivacied (un-dis-pri’va-sid), a. Not disprivacied; not deprived of privacy. Lowell, Cathedral. [Rare.]

undisputable.c: undisputable (un-dis-pi’- or un-dis’pi-ta-bl), a. Indisputable. Spectator. [Rare.] A wealth of indisputable evidence is at hand. Stedman, New Princeton Rey., Sept., 1886, p. 156. undisputableness (un-dis-pu’- or un-dis’pi-ta- bl-nes),”. The quality or state of being undisputable.

undisputably.c: undisputably (un-dis-pi’- or un-dis’pu-ta-bli), adv. Indisputably. The Engineer, LXX. 31. [Rare.]

undisputed.c: undisputed (un-dis-pa’ted), a. Not disputed; not contested; not called in question: as, an undisputed title; undisputed truth. Congreve, Hymn to Harmony.

undissembled.c: undissembled (un-di-sem’bld), a. Not dissembled; open; undisguised; unfeigned. Undissembled and unlimited veneration for the Holy Scriptures. Bp. Atterbury, Sermons, I. xviii. The anguish in his inmost soul, and the undissembled expression of it in his aspect. - Hawthorne, Scarlet Letter (1875), p. 169.

undissipated.c: undissipated (un-dis’i-pa-ted), a. Not dissipated; not scattered. Boyle.

undissolvable.c: undissolvable (un-di-zol’ va-bl), a. 1. Incapable of being dissolved or melted.—2. Incapable of being loosened or broken: as, the undissolvable ties of friendship. Rowe, Tamer- lane, iii.

undissolved.c: undissolved (un-di-zolvd’), a. Not dissolved; not melted; not loosened, dispelled, broken, etc. Tennyson, Day-Dream.

undissolving.c: undissolving (un-di-zol’ving), a. ing; not melting; not loosening. To link soft hearts in undissolving bands. Beaumont, Masque of Inner-Temple.

undistempered.c: undistempered (un-dis-tem’pérd), a. Free from distemper, disease, or perturbation; free from any disordering influence. Any unprejudiced and undistempered mind. Barrow, IIT. 36.

undistinctive.c: undistinctive (un-dis-tingk’ iv), a. Undiserim- inating; making no distinctions; impartial. Undistinetive Death. Dickens. undistinctly+ (un-dis-tingkt’li), adv. Indis- tinety. Hooker, Eccles. Polity, v. § 68.

undistinguishable.c: undistinguishable (un-dis-ting’wish-a-bl), a. Not distinguishable; indistinguishable. The quaint mazes in the wanton green For lack of tread are undistinguishable. Shak., M. N. D., ii. 1. 100. undistinguishableness (un-dis-ting’gwish-a- bl-nes),”. The state or character of being undistinguishable. Natwre, XLIII. 159.

undistinguished.c: undistinguished (un-dis-ting’gwisht), a. 1. Not distinguished; not so marked as to be dis- tinety known from another; not discerned or discriminated. Lacking in Not dissolv- undividual Often shrieking undistinguish'd woe, In clamours of all size, both high and low. Shak., Lover’s Complaint, 1. 20. Beauty, strength, and youth, with old age, weakness, and deformity, lay undistinguished in the same promiscuous heap of matter. Addison, Thoughts in Westminster Abbey. His ashes undistinguished lie. Scott, L. of L. M., v. 2. The slopes and rills in undistinguished gray Melt away. Browning, Love Among the Ruins. 2. Not treated with distinction or marked respect. Pope.—8. Not separated from others by extraordinary qualities; not famous; not distinguished by particular eminence: as, wn- distinguished people.—4. Not having an air of distinction: as, an undistinguished appearance or mien.

undistinguishing.c: undistinguishing (un-dis-ting’gwish-ing), a. Making no difference; not discriminating: as, undistinguishing favor. A general undistinguishing suspicion is altogether as apt to mislead a man as a too easy and unwary credulity. Bp. Atterbury, Sermons, I. v.

undistracted.c: undistracted (un-dis-trak’ted), a. Not distracted; not perplexed by contrariety or variety of thoughts, desires, or concerns. Boyle, Works, I. 276.

undistractedly.c: undistractedly (un-dis-trak’ted-li), adv. With-out distraction. Boyle, Works, I. 254.

undistractedness.c: undistractedness (un-dis-trak’ted-nes), n. The state of being undistracted. Boyle, Works, I. 3.

undistracting.c: undistracting (un-dis-trak’ting), a. Not distracting; not confusing the mind by drawing it toward a variety of objects. Leighton, Expos. on Psalm xix.

undisturbed.c: undisturbed (un-dis-térbd’), a 1. Free from disturbance or interruption; not molested or hindered: as, undisturbed with company or noise; undisturbed friendly relations.— 2. Not agitated; hence, free from perturbation of mind; calm; tranquil; placid; serene; composed: as, undisturbed by danger. The undisturbed and silent waters. Dryden. =Syn. Quiet, peaceful, unmoved, unruffled.

undisturbedly.c: undisturbedly (un-dis-tér’bed-li), adv. In an undisturbed or tranquil manner; calmly; peacefully. Locke.

undisturbedness.c: undisturbedness (un-dis-tér’bed-nes), n. The state of being undisturbed; calmness; peacefulness.

undiversified.c: undiversified (un-di-vér’si-fid), a. Not diversified; not varied; uniform. A particle of mere undiversified matter. Dr. T. Cogan, On the Passions, note R.

undiverted.c: undiverted (un-di-vér’ted), a. 1. Not diverted; not turned aside. These grounds have not any patent passages,... and 0 therefore must suffer the greatest part of it (the river) run by them undiverted. Boyle, Works, II. 408. Her young friend, apparently, was an interesting study; she wished to pursue it undiverted, H. James, Jr., Pass. Pilgrim, p. 221. 2. Not amused; not entertained or pleased. The reader, however, may not be undiverted with its unaffected simplicity and pathos. Wakejield, Memoirs, p. 8.

undivestedly.c: undivestedly (un-di-ves’ted-li), adv. With the absence (of); free. [Erroneous.] You will (as undivestedly as possible of favour or resentment) tell me what you would have me do. Richardson, Clarissa Harlowe, ii. 64. (Davies.)

undividable.c: undividable (un-di-vi’da-bl), a. and ». I, a. Incapable of being divided or separated; indivisible. Shak., C. of E., ii. 2. 124, II, ». Something which cannot be divided. Reducing the undivideables into money. Jarvis, tr. of Don Quixote, IT. y. 9.

undivided.c: undivided (un-di-vi’ded), a. 1. Not divided; not separated or disunited; unbroken; whole: as, undivided attention. God should be the object of our undivided respect. J, Edwards, Works, IV. 177. 2. Not made separate and limited to a particular sum: as, to own an undivided share of a business.—38. In bot., not lobed, cleft, or branched.—4. In entom., composed of a single piece: as, an undivided pygidium.

undividedly.c: undividedly (un-di-vi’ded-li), adv. Without division or separation; unbrokenly. Creation, nature, religion, law, and policy make them {man and wife) undividedly one. Feltham, On St. Luke xiv. 20.

undividedness.c: undividedness (un-di-vi‘ded-nes),. The quality or state of being undivided; wholeness.

undividual.c: undividual (un-di-vid’a-al), a. [< wl + dividual. Cf. individual.) Not capable of being 4 divided; indivisible. as undividual True courage and courtesy are individual companions, Fuller, Worthies, Worcestershire,

undivined.c: undivined (un-di-vin’), a. Not divine; opposed to what is divine or elevated. Ruskin.

undivorced.c: undivorced (un-di-vorst’), a Not divorced; not separated. These died together. Happy in ruin, undivorced by death, Young, Night Thoughts, v,

undivulged.c: undivulged (un-di-vuljd’), a. Not divulged; not revealed or disclosed; secret. Shak., Lear, iii. 2. 52. undo! (un-dé’), v. t.; pret. undid, pp. undone, ppr. undoing. [<un-1+dol.] To leave unperformed or unexecuted: usually in opposition with do. [Rare.] What to your wisdom seemeth best, Do or undo, as if ourself were here. Shak., 2 Hen. V1, iii. 1. 196. undo? (un-dé’), v. t.; pret. undid, pp. undone, ppr. undoing. [< ME. undon, london (pret. undye, undee, pp. undon, london), < AS. undon (= OFries. india), put back, open, undo, < w-, back, + don, put, do: see wn-2 and dol.] 1. To put back into a former condition; reverse, as something which has been done; annul; bring to nought. Oute of the place swithe thei gode And the tube thei vndede; No thing ther Inne thei ne founde, But a manere floure at the grounde. King Horn (E. E. T. 8.), p. 98. Let her not still undo, with peevish Haste, All that her Woman does. Congreve, tr. of Ovid’s Art of Love. 2. To untie or unfasten; unloose; unfix; open. Undo this button. Shak., Lear, v. 3. 309. A knife, a knife, I say!— O, Master Allum, if you love a woman, draw out your knife, and undo me (cut her stay lace], undo me! Webster and Dekker, Northward Ho, ii. 1. But, at the Prioress’ command, A monk undid the silken band That tied her tresses fair. Scott, Marmion, ii. 20. 3. To find the answer or explanation of; solve. [Rare.] Pray you, undo this riddle, And tell me how I have vex’d you? Fletcher (and another), False One, iv. 2. 4. To bring ruin or distress upon; ruin the morals, character, reputation, or prospects of; destroy; annihilate; spoil; ruin. This love will undo sall. Shak., T. and C., iii. 1. 120. Fool that Iam! I have undone myself, And with my own hand turn’d my fortune round, That was a fair one. Beau. and Fl., King and No King, iv. 2. "Twas I betray’d your sister, I undid her. Fletcher, Loyal Subject, v. 2. The Wretch by Fortune or by Love undone! Congreve, To Sleep. 5+. To reveal; disclose; unfold; explain. Melakketh bothe English and wit For to undo hit at the fulle. Chaucer, Death of Blanche, 1. 899, 6+. To be too much for the power of; baffle. Which lames report to follow it and undoes description to do it. Shak., W. T., v. 2. 63.

undock.c: undock (un-dok’), v. ¢ [< un-2 + dock3.] To ee out of dock: as, to dock and wndock a ship.

undoer.c: undoer (un-d6’ér), m. [< wndo2 + -erl.] One who undoes, in any sense; one who reverses what has been done; one who ruins. Sandys,

undoing.c: undoing (un-dé’ing), n. [Verbal n. of wndo2, v.| 1. The reversal of what has been done: as, there is no undoing of the past.— 2. Ruin; destruction. The ytter vndoyng of some honest families. Babees Book (E. EB. T. 8.), p. 242. Of havoc tired and rash undoing, Man left this Structure to become Time’s prey. Wordsworth, Sonnets, iii. 47.

undomesticate.c: undomesticate (un-d6-mes’ti-kat), v. t. 1. To estrange from home life or duties. Richardson, Grandison, ii. 11.—2. To make wild or roving; untame: as,to undomesticate an animal. [Rare. }

undomesticated.c: undomesticated (un-d6-mes’ti-ka-ted), p. a. 1. Not domesticated; not accustomed to a family life.—2. Not tamed, as an animal. -undomestication (un-do-mes-ti-ka’shon), 7. The act or process of making wild, as an animal, 6603 or the state of being undomesticated. Millican, Evolution of Morbid Germs, iv. 60. [Rare.] undone! (un-dun’), a. [< wn-1 + done.] Not done. These ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone, Luke xi. 42. undone? (un-dun’). Past participle of undo, undo2,

undose.c: undose (un’dos), a. [< L. wundosus, wavy, < unda, a wave: see found, undulate.] In entom., wavy; undate; undulated; having undulating parallel lines.

undoubtable.c: undoubtable (un-dou’ta-bl), a. Not to be doubted; indubitable. Bp. Hall, Specialties.

undoubtably.c: undoubtably (un-dou’ta-bli), adv. Without doubt; undoubtedly. The Lngineer, LX VI. 266.

undoubted.c: undoubted (un-dou’ted), a. [< ME. wndouted; <un-1 + doubted.] 1. Not doubted; not called in question; indubitable; indisputable. The undoubted splendour of the line of Hastings needs no illustration from fable. Macaulay, Warren Hastings. 2. Not filled with doubt, apprehension, fear, or the like; hence, confident; bold; fearless; redoubted. Hardy and undoubted champions. Shak., 3 Hen. VI., v. 7. 6. 38. Not being an object of doubt or suspicion; unsuspected. More should I question thee, and more I must, Though more to know could not be more to trust, From whence thou camest, how tended on; but rest Unquestion’d welcome, and undoubted blest. Shak., All’s Well, ii. 1. 211.

undoubted (un-dou’ted), adv. [< ME. undoubted, undowted; < undoubted, a.) Undoubtedly. And wndowted this lytell Chapell of the byrthe of our Lorde is the most glorious and deuoute place that euer I come in. Sir R. Guylforde, Pylgrymage, p. 37. Undoubted it were moche better to be occupied in honest recreation than to do nothing. Str T. Elyot, The Governour, i. 26.

undoubtedly.c: undoubtedly (un-dou’ted-li), adv. [Early mod. E. undowghtedly; < undoubted + -ly2.] With-out doubt; without question; indubitably. Undowghtedly in a prince... may be nothing more excellent... than to aduaunce men after the estimation of their goodness. Sir T. Elyot, The Governour, iii. 13.

undoubtful.c: undoubtful (un-dout’fil), a. 1. Not doubtful; not ambiguous; plain; evident. His fact... came not to an undoubtful proof. Shak., M. for M., iv. 2. 142. 2. Harboring no doubt or suspicion; unsuspicious. Our husbands might have looked into our thoughts And made themselves undoubtful. Beau. and Fl., Honest Man’s Fortune.

undoubting.c: undoubting (un-dou’ting), a. Not doubting; not hesitating respecting facts; not fluctuating in uncertainty: as, an undoubting believer; an undoubting faith. They are captivated into a confident and undoubting persuasion that they are savingly wrought upon. J. Hdwards, Works, III. 27.

undoubtingly.c: undoubtingly (un-dou’ ting-li), adv. In an undoubting manner; without doubting; certainly. We know undoubtingly what good is, and what evil is. H. S. Holland, Logic and Life, p. 62. undoubtoust, @. [ME. wndoutous, wndowtous; <un-l + doubtous.] Undoubting; certain. Undowtous ferth. Chaucer, Boéthius, v. prose 1.

undrainable.c: undrainable (un-dra’na-bl), a. Not capable of being drained or exhausted; inexhaustible. Mine undrainable of ore. Tennyson, none.

undrape.c: undrape (un-drap’), v.¢. [< wn-2 + drape.] To strip of drapery; uncover.

undraped.c: undraped (un-drapt’), a. Not draped; not arranged in folds pleasing to the eye, or so as to hang artistically; also, not covered with drapery; not clothed; nude: as, an undraped statue.

undraw.c: undraw (un-dra’), v. t.; pret. andrew, pp. undrawn, ppr. undrawing. [< un-2 + draw.] To draw aside or open. Angels undrew the curtains of the throne.

undrawn.c: undrawn (un-drin’), a. Not drawn. pulled, dragged, or hauled. Forth rushed with whirlwind sound The chariot of paternal Deity, Flashing thick flames, wheel within wheel, undrawn, Itself instinct with spirit. Milton, P. L., vi. 751. (b) Not portrayed or delineated, The deathbed of the just is yet undrawn By mortal hand. Young, Night Thoughts, ii. (c) Not drawn, as from a cask. [< wn-2 + double.] Young. (a) Not undulary And beer wndrawn, and beards unmown, display Your holy reverence for the Sabbath-day. Byron, English Bards and Scotch Reviewers,

undreaded.c: undreaded (un-dred’ed), a. Not dreaded; not feared. Unnamed, undreaded, and thyself half-starved. Milton, P. L., x. 595. undreamed, undreamt (un-drémd’, un- dremt’), a. Not dreamed; not thought of; not imagined: often followed by of. Many things fall out by the design of the general motor, and undreamt of contrivance of nature. Sir T. Browne, Vulg. Err., iii. 10. Unpath’d waters, wndream’d shores. Shak., W. T., iv. 4. 578.

undreaming.c: undreaming (un-dré’ming), a. Not dreaming; unmindful: with of. The days when, undreaming of Theatres and Managerships, thou wert a scholar, and an early ripe one, under the roofs builded by the munificent and pious Colet. Lamb, Elia (1877), p. 295. undress! (un-dres’ orun‘dres), nanda. [< un-1 + dress, n.] I, ». Ordinary dress, as opposed to full dress or uniform, regarded as ‘‘dress” in a special sense; a loose negligent dress. The Queen came to Lady Bathurst’s to see the review, and held a sort of drawing-room;.. everybody was in undress except the officers. Greville, Memoirs, July 20, 1830. Iam woman of quality... for all I am in an undress this morning. Vanbrugh, Provoked Wife, iv. 3. II, a. Pertaining to ordinary attire; hence, informal; unostentatious; simple: as, an wn- dress uniform. His undress life (if we may use the phrase). Swift. Undress guard-mounting. See parade guard-mount- ing, under parade.— Undress parade. See parade. undress? (un-dres’), v. [< wn-2 + dress, v.] I. trans. 1. To take off the clothes of; strip: as, to undress a child. Madam, undress you and come now to bed. Shak., T. of the S., Ind., 1. 119. 2. To divest of ornaments or elegant attire; disrobe. Pope.—8. To take the dressing, bandages, or covering from, as a wound. I. intrans. To take off one’s dress or clothes. To make me dress and undress. Fletcher (and another), Noble Gentleman, ii.

undressed.c: undressed (un-drest’), p. a. Not dressed, in any sense.

undrossy.c: undrossy (un-dros’i), a. Not drossy; free from dross or other impurities. Pope.

undry.c: undry (un-dri’), v. 7. [<« ME. undrien; < un-2 + dry.) To become moist. There is warm and drie, Ablaqueate hem that thai may undrie. Paliadius, Husbondrie (E. E. T. 8.), p. 189.

undue.c: undue (un-dti’), a. 1. Not due; not yet demandable by right; not yet owing: as, a debt, note, or bond undue.— 2. Not right; not lawful; improper; unworthy: as, an undue proceeding. Having first try’d in vaine all undue ways to procure Mony,... upon meer extremities he summoned this last Parlament. Milton, Hikonoklastes, i. 8. Erring by excess; excessive; inordinate; misproportioned: as, an undue regard to the externals of religion; an undue attachment to forms; an undue rigor in the execution of law. Pleasure admitted in undue degree Enslaves the will, nor leaves the judgment free. Cowper, Progress of Error, 1. 269. Undue influence, that control which one obtains over another whereby the latter is made to do in important affairs what of his free will he would not do. It differs wholly from persuasion, in which falsehood does not mingle, for that merely leads the will, while undue influence coerces it. (Cooley.) The undue influence which renders void a will procured by it is such as imposes a restraint on the will of the testator, so that the act represents not his will, but the will of another.

undueness.c: undueness (un-du’nes), x. The state or quality of being undue. Roget. [Rare.]

unduke.c: unduke (un-dik’), v. # [< wn-2 + duke.] To deprive of the rank of duke. He hath letters from France that the King hath unduked twelve Dukes. Pepys, Diary, Dec. 12, 1663.

undulant.c: undulant (un’di-lant), a. [= F. undulant = Sp. ondulante, < NL. *undulan(t-)s, ppr. of *undu- lare, undulate: see undulate.] Undulating; undulatory. And on her deck sea-spirits I descried Gliding and lapsing in an undulant dance. Taylor, St. Clement’s Eve, ii. 2. (Davies.) Naked arms More white and undulant than necks of swans. Lowell, Parting of the Ways.

undulary.c: undulary (un’dia-la-ri), a. [< L.*wndula, dim. of unda, wave (see undulate), + -ary.] Undulating. undulary The blasts and undulary breaths thereof maintain no certainty in their course. Sir T. Browne, Vulg. Err., vii. 17.

undulate.c: undulate (un’du-lat),a. [< L. undulatus, waved, wavy, diversified as with waves, waved, < *wn- dull, a wave, dim. of unda, a wave: see found, and ef. undine, undulous, etc.] Wavy; having a waved surface. (a) In bot., wavy; repand; bending, or having a margin which bends, slightly inward and outward: as, an undulate leaf; undulate strike. Also undate, undulated. Compare sinuate (b). (b) In zoidl., marked with wavy lines. Specifically, in entom.: (1) Wavy; forming a series of gentle curves which meet in reversed curves: as, an undulate line or margin. (2) Rising and falling in gentle curves: said of surfaces and also of margins. (8) Marked with parallel wavy lines.

undulate (un’du-lat), v.; pret. and pp. wndu- lated, ppr. undulating. [< undulate, a.; ef. F. ondule = Sp. undular, nodular = It. ondulare, wave, have a waving motion, ¢ NL. as if *wn- tulare, rise and fall in waves, wave; ef. L. undulatus, waved, wavy, diversified as with waves, < *unduly, dim. of unda, wave: see undulate, a.] I. intrans. To have a wavy motion; rise and fall in waves; move in waves. The dread ocean undulating wide. Thomson, Summer, 1. 982. Tall spire from which the sound of cheerful bells Just undulates upon the list’ning ear. Cowper, Task, i. 175. “we Waver, etc. See fluctuate.; I, trans. To cause to wave, or move in waves; cause to vibrate. Breath vocalized, that is, vibrated and undulated. Holder.

undulately.c: undulately (un’da-lat-li), adv. In an undulate manner or form. Sinuately or undulately cut at the apex. H. C. Wood, Fresh-Water Algee, p. 144.

undulating.c: undulating (un’di-la-ting), pa. 1. Waving; vibrating; moving in waves. All the winds wandering along the shore Undulate with the undulating tide. Shelley, Epipsychidion. 2. Having a form or outline resembling that of a series of waves; wavy. Astretch of country is said to be undulating when it presents a succession of elevations and depressions, resembling the waves of the sea. The Christ is a better character, has more beauty and grace than is usual with Rubens; the outline remarkably undulating, smooth, and flowing. Sir J. Reynolds. 38. In zool., undulate.

undulatingly.c: undulatingly (un’du-la-ting-li), adv. In an undulating manner; in waves.

undulation.c: undulation (un-di-la’shon), ». [= F. ondula- tion = Sp. undulation = Pg. undulagdo = It. on- colazione, < NL. *undulation-), < *undulate, an- dilate: see undulate.] 1. The act of undulating; a waving motion; fluctuation; in physics, wave-motion: as, the undulations of water or air or the ether. Undulations are said to be progressive when they successively traverse the different parts of a body, as the waves of the sea; and they are said to be stationary when all the particles of a body begin their vibrations simultaneously and end them at the same instant. See wave and wave-motion. Worms and leeches move by undulation. Sir T. Browne, Vulg. Err. Wide dash’d the Waves in undulation vast. Thomson, Spring, 1. 314. 2. A wavy form; a form resembling that of a wave or waves; waviness. The root of the wilder sort [is] incomparable for its crisped undulations. Evelyn, Sylva, ii. 4. This Wideness had been excusable, if your Lines had been straight, but they were full of odd kind of Undulations and Windings. If you can write no otherwise, one may read your Thoughts as soon as your Characters. Howell, Letters, I. v. 28. 3. In pathol., a particular uneasy sensation of unundulatory motion in the heart.— 4. Inswrg., a certain motion of the matter of an abscess when pressed, which indicates its fitness for opening.— 5. A set of waved lines; a surface so marked, or such an appearance; vermiculation; waviness.—6, In geom., the coming of a plane curve into a higher contact than usual with its tangent without contrary flexure.

undulationist.c: undulationist (un-di-la’shon-ist), n. [« wndu- lation + -ist.] One who advocates some undulatory theory, especially (and originally) the undulatory theory of light. Whewell.

undulatory.c: undulatory (un’du-la-to-ri), a. [= F. ondula- tire = Sp. Pg. wndulatorio = It. ondulatorio; as undulate + -ory.) 1. Having the character of an undulation; moving in or marked by undulations; undulating: as, an undulatory current of electricity; the undulatory motion of water, of air, or other fluid.i— 2. Having the form or appearance of a series of waves. 6604 Between their [mountains’] summits and inland plain, on which the celebrated deposit of nitrate of soda lies, there is a high undulatory district. Darwin, Geol. Observations, II. x. 302. 3. Of or pertaining to undulation; assuming undulating movements of some medium as the physical explanation of some class or group of phenomena: as, the undulatory theory of light. —Undulatory current. See electric current, under current.— Undulatory theory of light. See light1. undull!} (un-dul’), a. [< ME. undull; < un-1 + dull.] Not dull; sharp. With a dart undull that the duke bare. Destruction of Troy (E. E. T. 8.), 1. 13908. undull?t (un-dul’),v.t. [<wn-2 + dull.] To remove dullness from. Undulling their grossness. Whitlock, Manners of Eng. People, p. 477. Mrs. Tulliver,... after running her head against the same resisting medium for thirteen years, would go at it again to-day with undulled alacrity. George Eliot, Mill on the Floss, I. viii.

undulose.c: undulose (un’di-lés), a [< NL. *uwndulosus, wavy: see undulous.] Undulous. Quart. Jour. Geol. Soc., XLY. 343. [Rare.]

undulous.c: undulous (un’di-lus), a. [< NL. *wndulosus, wavy,< L.*undula, a wave: see undulate.] Undulating; rising and falling in waves or like waves. He felt the undulous readiness of her volatile paces under him. R. D, Blackmore, Lorna Doone, Ixy.

unduly.c: unduly (un-di’li), adv. In an undue manner or degree; wrongly; improperly; excessively; inordinately.

undurably.c: undurably (un-di’ra-bli), adv. ble manner; not lastingly. undust} (un-dust’), v. t [« un-2 + dust.] To free from dust. W. Montague, Devoute Essays, dis;

undutiful.c: undutiful (un-du’ti-fal), a. 1. Not dutiful. I know my duty; you are all undutiful. Shak., 3 Hen. VL, v. 5. 33. 2. Not characterized by a sense of duty or obedience; rebellious; irreverent. Undutiful proceedings and rebellions against the supreme natural power. Jer. Taylor, Rule of Conscience, iii. 5.

undutifully.c: undutifully (un-dv’ti-ful-i), adv. Inan undutiful manner; not according to duty; in a disobedient manner. Dryden, tr. of Juvenal’s Satires, iy.

undutifulness.c: undutifulness (un-du’ti-fil-nes), n. or character of being undutiful.

undying.c: undying (un-di’ing), a. Not dying; not subject to death; immortal; hence, unceasing; imperishable. Chains of darkness, and the undying worm. Milton, P. L., vi. 739. The undying barytone of the sea. Lowell, Among my Books, 2d ser., p. 240.

undyingly.c: undyingly (un-di’ing-li), adv. Immortally; imperishably; unceasingly. Scribner’s Mag., IV. 102.

undyingness.c: undyingness (un-di’/ing-nes), n. The character or state of being undying; immortal. &., Broughton, Cometh Up as a Flower, xii.

uneared.c: uneared (un-érd’), a. Not eared or plowed; untilled. Shak., Sonnets, iii.

unearned.c: unearned (un-érnd’), a. [< ME. wnerned; < un-1 + earned.| Not earned; not merited by labor or services; not won: as, an unearned salary; unearned dividends.—Unearned increment, the increase of value of land resulting from general causes, such as the growth of population and consequent demand, as distinguished from increase due to the labor or improvements put upon the land by its individual owner. According to the views of some economists, the unearned increment rightfully belongs to the community whose growth is one of the causes or conditions of it, and should be taken from the owner by taxation in some form. According to the views of others, the individual enjoyment of it is an essential condition of securing general cooperation in the promotion of public and local improvements, and public spirit and enterprise.

unearth.c: unearth (un-érth’), v.t. [« w-2+ earth.) 1. To drive or bring forth from an earth or burrow; drive from any underground hole or burrow; draw from the earth. A rough terrier of the hills; By birth and call of nature preordained To hunt the badger and unearth the fox. Wordsworth, Prelude, iv. 2. To uncover from the earth; dig out of the ground; exhume, as fossils; exfodiate. To unearth the root of an old tree. Wordsworth, Simon Lee. Not durable; not In an undura- Dry- The state uneaths 38. To bring to light; discover; find out; disclose. It was the labours of Dr. Pertz and his agents that unearthed the Historia Pontificalis of John of Salisbury among the MSS. of the Bern Library. Stubbs, Medieval and Modern Hist., p. 68.

unearthliness.c: unearthliness (un-érth’li-nes), ». The character or state of being unearthly. W. Black, A Daughter of Heth, iii.

unearthly.c: unearthly (un-érth’li), a. Not earthly; not terrestrial; supernatural; not like, or as if not proceeding from, anything belonging to the earth; unworldly; hence, weird; appalling: as, an unearthly ery or sight. The night of our arrival was one of those unearthly moonlight nights which belong to Italy. Aldrich, Ponkapog to Pesth, p. 31.

unease.c: unease (un-éz’), 7. [< ME. nese; < un-1 + ease, n.] Trouble; misery; uncomfortable state or condition. [Obsolete or archaic.] My gret unease fulle ofte I meene [moan]. Rom. of the Rose, 1. 2596. It was not any palace corridor: There where we were, but dungeon natural, With floor uneven and unease of light. Longfellow, tr. of Dante’s Inferno, xxxiv. 99.

uneased.c: uneased (un-ézd’), a. Not eased or made easier. We leave their sorrows in many degrees unrelieved and uneased. Jer. Taylor, Holy Dying, i. 4.

uneaset.c: uneaset (un-éz’), v. t. [ME. wnesen; < un-1 + ease, v.}] To make uneasy. Cannetes olde eke tyme is nowe to wede, And of to kytte it that thaire roote wneseth. Paliadius, Husbondrie (E. E. T. 8.), p. 81.

uneasily.c: uneasily (un-6’zi-li), adv. 1. In an uneasy manner; with uneasiness or pain.—2. With difficulty; not readily. Milton, Hist. Eng., v.

uneasiness.c: uneasiness (un-6’zi-nes), n. The state of being uneasy; want of ease or comfort, physical or mental. Shak., Hen. V., ii. 2. 27.

uneasy.c: uneasy (un-é’zi),a. 1. Not easy either in body or in mind; feeling some lack of ease, either mental or physical; disturbed; unquiet. Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown. Shak., 2 Hen. IV., iii. 1. 31. 2. Not easy or elegant in manner or style; not graceful; constrained; stiff; awkward. Shall I live at Home a stiff melancholy poor Man of Quality, grow uneasy to my Acquaintance as well as myself, by fancying I’m slighted where I am not? Steele, Grief A-la-Mode, ii. 1. 3. Causing pain, trouble, constraint, discomfort, or want of ease; cramping; constraining; irksome; disagreeable. The wales were exceeding uneasie. For they were wonderful hard. Coryat, Crudities, I. 92. He puts a force and constraint upon himself which is uneasie to any man, and he lets the vizard fall off sometimes when it is more observed than he thinks. Stillingfleet, Sermons, II. v. This account was very uneasy to me. T. Ellwood, Life (ed. Howells), p. 220. Walpole had, it is plain, an greasy consciousness of the frivolity of his favourite pursuits. Macaulay, Horace Walpole. 4. Not easy to be done or accomplished; difficult. But this swift business I must uneasy make, lest too light winning Make the prize light. Shak., Tempest, i. 2. 451.

uneatable.c: uneatable (un-é’ta-bl), a. Not eatable; not fit to be eaten: as, uneatable fruit. Big scarlet hips—which are uneatable by us. Grant Allen, Colin Clout’s Calendar, p. 119.

uneatableness.c: uneatableness (un-é’ta-bl-nes),. The quality or state of being uneatable. Wallace, Natural Selection, iii. 120.

uneaten.c: uneaten (un-é’tn), a. Not eaten; not devoured; hence, not destroyed. Therefore I will outswear him and all his followers, that this is all that’s left wheaten of my sword. F Beau. and Fl., King and No King, iii. uneath (un-éPH’), a [< ME. onethe, onethe, < AS. unedthe, difficult, < wn-, not, + ethe, easy: see un-l and eath,a.] Not easy; difficult. [Obsolete or archaic.] Uneath it were to tell. Southey. uneath} (un-éfH’), adv. [< ME. onethe, neth, unnethe, unneth, onethe, onnethe, etc., < AS. un- ethe, not easily, < wn-, not, + ethe, easily: see eath, adv. scarcely. Atte last a forster came riding; And, wete ye wele, so sorrowful he was That he onnethe myght speke to the kyng. Generydes (EB. E. T. 8.), 1. 977. Uneath may she endure the rs fee Shak., 2 Hen, VI, ii. 4. 8.

uneaths.c: uneaths (un-éPHz’), adv. [< ME. unethes, unnethes; < uneath, adv., + adv, gen. -es.] Same as uneath. Cf. uneaths.] Not easily; hardly; aT ad a uneaths We are so now ordered and so straitly watched, that unnedths our servants dare do anything for us. Bp. Ridley, ia Bradford’s Letters (Parker Soc., 1853), II. 174.

unebriate.c: unebriate (un-6é’bri-at), a. Unintoxicating; also, unintoxicated. [Rare.] There were... wnebriate liquors, pressed from cooling fruits. Bulwer, My Novel, IV. xvii. (Davies.)

unecared.c: unecared (un-kard’), a. Not regarded; not heeded; not attended: with for. Their own... ghostly condition uncared for. Hooker, Eccles. Polity, v. § 1,

unedge.c: unedge (un-ej’), v. t. [< wn-2 + edge.] To deprive of the edge; blunt. Here our weapons, And bodies that were made for shining brass, Are both unedg’d. Fletcher, Valentinian, i. 3.

unedifying.c: unedifying (un-ed’i-fi-ing), a. Not edifying; not improving to the mind. Boyle. uneducatel} (un-ed’a-kat), a. [«< wn-1 + educate, a.) Not educated. Solyman and Perseda. uneducate? (un-ed’t-kat), vt = [« wn-2 + educate, v.| To deprive of education; reverse or annul what has been done by way of educating or training. H. Spencer, Social Statics, p. 388.

uneffectual.c: uneffectual (un-e-fek’ti-al), a. [Rare.] The glow-worm shows the matin to be near, And ’gins to pale his ineffectual fire. Shak., Hamlet, i. 5. 90.

unelected.c: unelected (un-é-lek’ted), a. Not elected; not chosen; not preferred. Shak., Cor., ii. 3. 207.

unelegantly.c: unelegantly (un-el’é-gant-li), adv. Inelegantly. Holland, tr. of Plutarch, p. 425. [Rare.]

unembarrassed.c: unembarrassed (un-em-bar’ast), a Not embarrassed, in any sense.

unembodied.c: unembodied (un-em-bod’id), a. 1. Disembodied. Byron, When Coldness Wraps. [Rare.] —2. Not embodied; not collected into a body: as, unembodied militia. Imp. Dict. [Rare.]

unemotional.c: unemotional (un-é-m0’shon-al), a. Not emotional; free from or unaccompanied by an exhibition of emotion or feeling; impassive; not inducing emotion: as, an wremotional person; an unemotional book. This little book [‘‘ Nature”] met with a very unemotional reception. 0. W. Holmes, Emerson (Amer. Men of Letters, p. 91).

unemotionally.c: unemotionally (un-é-m6’shon-al-i), adv. In an unemotional manner; impassively.

unemotioned.c: unemotioned (un-é6-m06’shond), a. Free from emotion; impassive. Godwin, Mandeville, iii. 98. [Rare.] ert (un-em-ploid’), a 1. Not employed; having no work or employment. Men sour with poverty and unemployed. Addison. The fact is, Africa is a nation of the unemployed. The Speaker, May 31, 1890. 2. Notin use: as, unemployed capital or money. An overflow of unemployed energy and vivacity. M. C. Tyler, Life of Patrick Henry, p. 16. 8. Not accompanied with work or employment. To maintain able-bodied men in unemployed imprisonment. Froude, Hist. Eng., xvi.

unemployment.c: unemployment (un-em-ploi’ment),”. The condition of being unemployed; the state of being unused. Science, XI. 192. [Rare.]

unemptiable.c: unemptiable (un-emp’ti-a-bl),a. Not capable of being emptied; inexhaustible. Hooker, Ec- eyes. Polity, ii. 1.

unencapsuled.c: unencapsuled (un-en-kap’suld), a. Not capsulated. Hncyc. Brit., XVI. 653. [Rare.]

unenchanted.c: unenchanted (un-en-chan’ted), a. Not enchanted; that cannot be enchanted. Milton, Comus, 1. 395.

unenclosed.c: unenclosed, a. See uninclosed. unencumber, unencumber (un-en-, un-in- kum’bér), v. t. [< wn-2 + encumber.] To free from encumbrance; disencumber.

unencumberedness.c: unencumberedness (un-en-kum’bérd-nes), n. The quality or state of being unencumbered. The Atlantic, LX VII. 182. [Rare.].

unendeared.c: unendeared (un-en-dérd’), a. Not attended with endearment. Milton, P. L., iv. 766.

unended.c: unended (un-en’ded), a [< ME. unended, < AS. wngeended; as un-1 + ended.] Endless; infinite.

unending.c: unending (un-en’ding), a. [« ME. *unending, unendande; < un-l + ending.) Not ending; having no end. My body in boys ay abydande Vne[n|jdande withouten any ending. York Plays, p. 1. The unending circles of laborious science. Feltham, On Eccles. ii. 11, Ineffectual. 6605

unendingness.c: unendingness (un-en’ding-nes), n. acter of being unending. unendly+ (un-end‘li), a. [< ME. *unendly (= G. unendlich); < un-1 + hendly, a.) Having no end; endless. Sir P. Sidney, Areadia, p. 224.

unendurable.c: unendurable (un-en-dir’a-bl), a. Not to be endured; intolerable. Without some touch of it [idealizing] life would be wa- endurable prose. Lowell, Among my Books, 2d ser., p. 189.

unengaged.c: unengaged (un-en-gajd’), a. Not engaged, in any sense.

unenglish.c: un-English (un-ing’glish),a@. Not English. (@) Not characteristic of Englishmen; opposed in character, feeling, etc., to what is English. (0) Not properly belong- ane ty. oF not in accord with the usages of, the English

unenglished.c: unenglished (un-ing’glisht), a. Not translated or rendered into English. Bp. Hall, Honour of the Married Clergy.

unenlightened.c: unenlightened (un-en-li’tnd), a. Not enlightened; not mentally or morally illuminated; also, not proceeding from or marked by mental a moral enlightenment: as, unenlightened zeal. Natural reason, unenlightened by revelation. Bp. Atterbury, Sermons, II., Pref.

unentangle.c: unentangle (un-en-tang’gl), v.t. [< wn-2 + entangle.| To disentangle. Donne, Devotions, p. 129. [Rare.]

unentangled.c: unentangled (un-en-tang’gld), a. Not entangled; not complicated; not perplexed. Unentangled through the snares of life. Johnson, Lives of the Poets, Collins.

unentering.c: unentering (un-en’tér-ing), a. Not entering; making no impression. Southey, Thalaba, ix.

unenterprising.c: unenterprising (un-en’tér-pri-zing), a. Not enterprising; not adventurous. Burke, Thoughts on French Affairs (1791).

unentertaining.c: unentertaining (un-en-tér-ta’ning), a. Not entertaining or amusing; giving no delight. Gray, To West, Letter xxv. (1740).

unentertainingness.c: unentertainingness (un-en-tér-ta’ning-nes), 7. The quality of being unentertaining or dull. Gray, To West, Letter xxvii. (1740).

unenthralled.c: unenthralled (un-en-thrald’), a. Not enslaved; not reducedtothraldom. Milton, Hikonoklastes.

unentombed.c: unentombed (un-en-témd’), a. Not buried; not interred. Dryden, Aineid, vi.

unentranced.c: unentranced (un-en-transt’), a. Not entranced; not under the influence of a charm or spell; disentranced. His heart was wholly unentranced. Taylor, Ph. van Art. (The Lay of Elena). (Davies.)

unenviable.c: unenviable (un-en’vi-a-bl), a. Not enviable. Milton, Animadversions, Pref.

unenvied.c: unenvied (un-en’vid), a. Not envied; exempt from the envy of others. Milton, P. L., ii. 23.

unenvious.c: unenvious (un-en’vi-us), a. Not envious; free from envy. Cowley, Pindarie Odes, xxi.

unequable.c: unequable (un-é’kwa-bl), a. Inequable. March and September,. the two most unsettled and wnequable of seasons. Bentley.

unequal.c: unequal (un-é’kwal), a. and nm. I, a. 1. Not equal; not of the same size, length, breadth, quantity, quality, strength, talents, age, station, etc. To shape my legs of an unequal size. Shak., 3 Hen. VI., iii. 2. 159. 2. Inadequate; insufficient; inferior: as, his strength was unequal to the task. Atlas becomes unequal to his freight, And almost faints beneath the glowing weight. Addison, tr. of Ovid’s Metamorph., ii. The Day Unequal to the Godhead’s Attributes Various, and Matter copious of your Songs. Prior, Second Hymn of Callimachus. 8. Not balanced or matched; misproportioned; one-sided; hence, inequitable; unfair; unjust; partial. To punish me for what you make me do Seems much unequal. Shak., A. and C., ii. 5. 101. We play unequal game, Whene’er we shoot by Fancy’s aim! Scott, Rokeby, i. 31. 4. Not equable; not uniform; irregular: as, unequal pulsations. I have called him the most original and the most unequal of living poets. Stedman, Vict. Poets, p. 338. 5. Not having the two sides or the parts symmetrical: thus, an unequal leaf is one in which the parenchyma is not developed symmetri- The char- So as not to oe unestablish cally on each side of the midrib or stalk. Also called oblique.—6. In entom., composed of parts or joints of different forms: as, unequal palpi or antenna.— Unequal surface, in entom., a surface having very slight and indeterminate elevations and depressions.— Unequal temperament. See temperament. —Unequal voices, in music, properly, voices of different quality or compass; but the term is often used in the sense of mixed voices.— Unequal wings, in entom., wings of which the anterior pair are longer or shorter than the posterior, generally the former. II, x. One not equal to another in station, power, ability, age, or the like. Milton, P. L., vi. 453. [Rare.]

unequalable.c: unequalable (un-é’kwal-a-bl), a. [« wn-l + equal + -able.| Not capable of being equaled; not capable of being matched or paralleled; matchless; peerless. Boyle, Works, I. 282.

unequaledunequalled.c: unequaled, unequalled (un-6’kwald),a. Not to be equaled; unparalleled; unrivaled. Milton, P. L., ix. 983.=Syn. Unmatched, matchless, unexampled, peerless.

unequally.c: unequally (un-6’kwal-i), adv. Unequally yoked together. Unequally pinnate leaf. See pinnate.

unequalness.c: unequalness (un-é’kwal-nes), ». The state of being unequal; inequality. Sir W. Temple, Essay on Poetry.

unequitably.c: unequitably (un-ek’wi-ta-bli), adv. Inequitably. Secker, Charge to Clergy of Oxford (1750).

unequity.c: unequity (un-ek’wi-ti), n. [< ME. wnequitie; < un-l + equity. Cf. miquity.] Want of equity; inequity; iniquity. Wyclif, Rom. iii. 5.

unequivocal.c: unequivocal (un-é-kwiv’6-kal), a. Not equivocal, in any sense.=Syn. Plain, unambiguous, unmistakable. See obscure.

unerrable.c: unerrable (un-ér’a-bl), a. Incapable of erring; infallible. Sheldon, Mirror of Antichrist (1616), p. 142.

unerrableness.c: unerrableness (un-ér’a-bl-nes), n. Incapacity of error. Decay of Christian Piety.

unerring.c: unerring (un-ér’ing), a. 1. Not missing the mark; certain: as, an unerring aim. Diana taught him all her silvan arts, To bend the bow, and aim unerring darts. Pope, Wiad, v. 68. 2. Committing no mistake; incapable of error; infallible: as, the unerring wisdom of God. Jer. Taylor, Dissuasive from Popery.

unerringly.c: unerringly (un-ér’ing-li), adv. In an unerring manner; without error, mistake, or failure; infallibly. Locke, Human Understanding, ii. 9.

unescapable.c: unescapable (un-es-ka’pa-bl), a. That cannot be escaped. Ruskin.

uneschewable.c: uneschewable (un-es-ch6’a-bl), a. [<¢ ME. wn- eschuable; < un-1 + eschew + -able.] Unavoidable. An uneschuable byndynge togydere. Chaucer, Boéthius, v. prose 1.

uneschewably.c: uneschewably (un-es-ch6’a-bli), adv. [< ME. uneschuably; < uneschewable + -ly2.] Unavoidably. They ben to comyn uneschewably. Chaucer, Boéthius, v. prose 3.

unespied.c: unespied (un-es-pid’), a. Not espied; not discovered; not seen. Spenser, Present State of Treland.

unessayed.c: unessayed (un-e-sad’), a. Not essayed; unattempted. Milton, Eikonoklastes.

unessence.c: unessence (un-es’ens), v. & [« wn-2 + essence.] To deprive of essence or distinctive characteristics. [Rare.] Not only does truth, in... long intervals, unessence herself, but (what is harder) one cannot venture a crude fiction, for the fear that it may ripen into a truth upon the voyage. Lamb, Essays of Elia, p. 178.

unessential.c: unessential (un-e-sen’shal), a.andn. I,a.1. Not essential; not constituting the essence or essential part; inessential; not of prime importance. The unessential parts of Christianity. Addison, Freeholder, Sundry wnessential points of church order. H. B. Smith, Christian Theology, p. 593. 2. Void of real being. The void profound Of wnessential night. Milton, P. L., ii. 488. II, ». Something not constituting essence, or not of absolute necessity: as, forms are among the wnessentials of religion.

unestablish.c: unestablish (un-es-tab’lish), v.t. [< un-2 + establish.] To deprive of establishment; disestablish. Milton, Hikonoklastes, xxvii. [Rare.] Not equally. 2 Cor. vi. 14. Inequitable. unethes unethes, adv.: See wreaths.

unevangelical.c: unevangelical (un-é-van-jel’i-kal), a. Not evangelical. Milton, Answer to Eikon Basilike, § 12,

uneven.c: uneven (un-é’vyn),a. [< ME. uneven, < AS. un- efen,< un-, not, + even, even: see wn-l and event.] 1. Not even. (a) Not level, smooth, or plain; rough; rugged. Shak., M. N. D., iii. 2.417. (b) Not straight or direct; crooked. Shak., R. and J.,iv.1.5. (c) Not uniform, equable, regular, or continuous; changeable; jerky. Light quirks of music, broken and uneven. Pope, To the Earl of Burlington, Ep. 4. (d) Not perfectly horizontal or level, as the beam of a scale; not at the same height or on the same plane; hence, not fair, just, or true. Belial, in much uneven scale thou weigh’st All others by thyself. Milton, P. R., ii. 173. (e) In arith., odd; not divisible by 2 without a remainder: as, 3, 5, 7, etc., are uneven numbers. 2t. Ill-matched; unsuitable; ill-assorted. Spen- ser, F. Q., VI. v. 9.—8}. Difficult; perplexing; embarrassing. Shak., 1 Hen. IV., i. 1. 50.— Uneven pages, pages with odd numbers, like 1, 3, 5, 7, etc.

unevenly.c: unevenly (un-é’yn-li), adv. [< ME. unevenly; < uneven + -ly2.) In an uneven manner; not smoothly or regularly._Unevenly even. Seeevenl.

unevenness.c: unevenness (un-é’yn-nes), x. The state or character of being uneven. (a) Inequality of surface: as, the unevenness of ground or of roads. (6) Irregularity; want of uniformity. (c) Want of equableness; unsteadiness; variableness. Unevenness of temper. Addison, Spectator. Her abruptness and unevenness of manner were plainly the result of her secluded and lowly circumstances. George Eliot, Mill on the Floss, vi. 6. (d@) Want of smoothness in regard to style or composition. Boyle, Works, II. 251.

uneventful.c: uneventful (un-é-vent’ful), a Not eventful: as, an uneventful reign or life. Southey.

uneventfully.c: uneventfully (un-6-vent’ful-i), adv. In an uneventful manner; so as to be without, striking occurrences.

unevident.c: unevident (un-ev’i-dent),a. Not evident, clear, obvious, or manifest; obscure. Bp. Hacket, Abp. Williams, i.197. (Davies.)

unexaminable.c: unexaminable (un-eg-zam’i-na-bl), a. Not capable of being or proper to be examined. The lowly, alwise, and unexaminable intention of Christ in what he went with resolution to doe. Milton, Reformation in Eng., i.

unexampled.c: unexampled (un-eg-zam’pld), a. Having no example or similar case; having no precedent or rival; unprecedented; unparalleled. Milton, P.L., iii. 410. . Her modest mien And carriage, marked by unexampled grace. Wordsworth, Prelude, vii.

unexceptionable.c: unexceptionable (un-ek-sep’shon-a-bl), a. Not liable to any exception or objection; unobjectionable; faultless; hence, excellent; admirable. Men of clear and unexceptionable characters. Waterland, Works, V. 296. unexceptionableness (un-ek-sep’shon-a-bl- nes), x. The state or character of being unexceptionable. Dr. H. More, Seven Churches, Pref.

unexceptionably.c: unexceptionably (un-ek-sep’shon-a-bli), adv. In an unexceptionable manner. South, Sermons, V. iv.

unexceptional.c: unexceptional (un-ek-sep’shon-al), a. Not forming an exception; in the regular course; usual.

unexceptionally.c: unexceptionally (un-ek-sep’shon-al-i), adv. Without exception; in a manner excluding nothing; entirely.

unexceptive.c: unexceptive (un-ek-sep’tiv), a. Not exceptive; admitting no exception. J. H. Sterling, Text-book to Kant, p. 11.

unexcised.c: unexcised (un-ek-sizd’), a. Not charged with the duty of excise; not subject to the payment of excise.

unexclusive.c: unexclusive (un-eks-kl6’siv),a. Not exclusive; general; comprehensive. His erudition was as wnexclusive as profound. Sir W. Hamilton.

unexclusively.c: unexclusively (un-eks-kl6’siv-li), adv. With-out exclusion of anything; so as not to exclude. Sir W. Hamilton, Reid’s Works, Supp. Diss., Note D, § 2.

unexcogitable.c: unexcogitable (un-eks-koj’i-ta-bl), a. Not excogitable; inconceivable. Sir W. Raleigh, Hist. World, I. 2.

unexcusableness.c: unexcusableness (un-eks-kii’za-bl-nes), n. Inexcusableness. Hammond, Works, IV. 642. Tnexcusa- 6606

unexecuted.c: unexecuted (un-ek’sé-ki-ted), a. 1. Not executed, in any sense. Burke, Letter to a Noble Lord.— 2+, Unemployed; not brought into use; inactive. You therein ... leave unexecuted your own renowned knowledge. Shak., A. and C., iii. 7. 45.

unexempt.c: unexempt (un-eg-zemt’), a 1. Not exempt; not free by privilege.—2+. Not exempting from or depriving of some privilege or the like. Milton, Comus, 1. 685.;

unexpectant.c: unexpectant (un-eks-pek’tant), a. Not expectant; not expecting, looking for, or eagerly waiting for something. With bent wneapectant faces. George Eliot, Romola, lv.

unexpectation.c: unexpectation (un-eks-pek-ta’shon), n. Want of previous consideration; want of foresight. Bp. Hall, Balm of Gilead, § 1.

unexpected.c: unexpected (un-eks-pek’ted), a. Not expected; not looked for; unforeseen; sudden: often used substantively with the definite article: as, it is the unexpected that happens. Thy speech doth please me; for it ever sounds As thou brought’st joyful, unexpected news. Beau. and Fl., King and No King, iv. 4.

unexpectedly.c: unexpectedly (un-eks-pek’ted-li), adv. In an unexpected manner; at a time or in a manner not expected or looked for; suddenly. Milton, S. A., 1. 1750.

unexpectedness.c: unexpectedness (un-eks-pek’ted-nes), n. The character of being unexpected. Sterne, Tristram Shandy, iv. 29.

unexpensive.c: unexpensive (un-eks-pen’siv), a Inexpensive. Milton, Apology for Smectymnuus. unexperience} (un-eks-pé’ri-ens), ». Inexperience. B. Jonson, Magnetick Lady, iii. 4.

unexperienced.c: unexperienced (un-eks-pé’ri-enst), a. 1. Inexperienced. Thou return unexperienced to thy grave. Shak., T. of the S., iv. 1. 86. Young at his first entrance, and wnexperienc’d, he {Ethelbert] was the first raiser of civill War among the Saxons. Milton, Hist. Eng., iii. 2. Untried; not yet known from experience; also, exhibiting inexperience: applied to things. Unexperienced art. G. Harvey, Four Letters.

unexpert.c: unexpert (un-eks-pért’), a. 1. Inexpert. Sir T. More, Utopia (tr. by Robinson), ii. 1. My sentence is for open war; of wiles More unexpert I boast not; them let those Contrive who need, or when they need. Milton, P. L., ii. 52. 2. Without knowledge; unacquainted; ignorant. Him you will find in letters and in laws Not wnexpert. Prior, Imit. of Horace, i. 9.

unexplored.c: unexplored (un-eks-plord’), a. Not explored, in any sense.

unexpressibly.c: unexpressibly (un-eks-pres’i-bli), adv. Inexpressibly. Bp. Hall, Character of Man.

unexpressive.c: unexpressive (un-eks-pres’iv), a. 1. Not expressive; deficient in expression.—2}. Not to be expressed; inexpressible; unutterable; ineffable. Shak., As you Like it, iii. 2. 10.

unextended.c: unextended (un-eks-ten’ded), a 1. Not extended or stretched out. Uneatended arms. Congreve, Mourning Bride, iii. 2. Not having extension; occupying no assignable space. A spiritual, that is, an wneatended substance. Loeke, Human Understanding, iv. 10.

unextinguishable.c: unextinguishable (un-eks-ting’gwish-a-bl), a. Inextinguishable. Uneatinguishable fire. Milton, P. L., ii. 88.

unextricable.c: unextricable (un-eks’tri-ka-bl), a. ble. Barrow, Sermons, II]. xxxvi. uneyed} (un-id’), a. Unobserved; unnoticed; unseen; unperceived. Beau. and Fi., Wit at Several Weapons, ii.

unfabled.c: unfabled (un-fa’bld), a. Not fabled or imaginary; not mentioned in fable; unconnected or unmixed with fable; real. They are more amusing than plain unfabled precept. Sydney Smith, Works, I. 176. (Davies.)

unface.c: unface (un-fas’), v. To remove the face or cover from; expose. Not exposed, in Inextrica- eS | ae unfaithful Unface these, and they will prove as bad cards as any in the pack. Rushworth, Hist. Collections, IL. ii. 917.

unfadable.c: unfadable (un-fa’da-bl), a. Incapable of fading, perishing, or withering. A crown incorruptible, unfadable. Bp. Halil, Contemplations, Ahasuerus Feasting.

unfadgingt.c: unfadgingt (un-faj’ing), a. Not suiting; of unsuitable shape, quality, or the like. The potter may err in framing his vessel, and so in anger dash the pile = dared clay against the walls, Rev. T. Adams, Sermons, III. 122. (Davies.)

unfading.c: unfading (un-fa’ding), a. 1. Not liable to lose strength or freshness of coloring.—2, Not la- ble to wither or decay. The unfading rose of Eden. Pope, Eloisa to Abelard.

unfadingly.c: unfadingly (un-fa’ding-li), adv. In an unfading manner; so as not tofade; imperishably.

unfadingness.c: unfadingness (un-fa’ding-nes), ». The character or state of being unfading. Polwhele, Hist. Devonshire.;

unfailable.c: unfailable (un-fa’la-bl), a. Not capable of failing; infallible.: This unfailable word of truth. Bp. Hall, Sermon on 2 Pet. i. 10.

unfailableness.c: unfailableness (un-fa’la-bl-nes),. The character or state of being unfailable; infallibility.

unfailing.c: unfailing (un-fa’ling), a. 1. Not liable to fail; incapable of being exhausted: as, an unfailing spring; unfailing sources of supply.—2. Not missing; always fulfilling a hope, promise, or want; not coming short; sure; certain. Thou, secure of my unfailing word, Dryden, Wiad, i. 322. Some god, propitious to the Trojan foe, * Has from my arm unfailing struck the bow. Pope, Iliad, xv. 551.

unfailingly.c: unfailingly (un-fa’ling-li), adv. In an unfailing manner; surely. 3

unfailingness.c: unfailingness (un-fa’ling-nes), n. The character of being unfailing. Bp. Hall, Sermon on 2 Pet. i. 10.

unfaint.c: unfaint (un-fan’), a. [< ME. unfain, unfein, un- Sawe, < AS. unfegen, < un-, not, + fegen, glad: see fail.] Not fain; sorry. All the folke were vnfayn, & of fyn will To haue reft hir the ryke, for ruth that thai had. Destruction of Troy (E. E. T, §.), 1. 12108. ‘‘A-las,” sche sayd, ‘‘I am vn-fayn To se my sone in this disseise.”” Political Poems, etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 210. unfainlyt+, adv. [< unfain + -ly2.] Sorrowfully. Halliwell.

unfainting.c: unfainting (un-fan’ ting), a. Not fainting; not sinking or succumbing or giving way. Thorow which [labyrinth it is] impossible to passe without the conduct of wisdom and exercise of unfainting fortitude. Sandys, Travailes, p. 88.

unfair.c: unfair (un-far’),a. [« ME. unfair, < AS. unfe- ger (= Goth. wnfagrs), < un-, not, + fever, beautiful: see fair1.] Not fair. (a) Not beautiful; not comely. (bt) Not glad; sad; sorrowful. Noght sesyng of sorrow, & sobbing vnfaire On dayes to Endure, with drooping on nights. Destruction of Troy (E. E. T. 8.), 1. 3290. (ct) Unseemly; disgraceful. He wag cursed for his vnclannes, & cached ther-inne, Done doun of his dyngneté for dede wnfayre. Alliterative Poems (ed. Morris), ii. 1801. (d) Not honest; notimpartial; disingenuous; using trick or artifice. You come, like an unfair merchant, to charge me with being in your debt. Swift. (e) Not based on honesty, justice, or fairness; inequitable: as, unfair advantages; unfair practices. =Syn, (d) (e) Unjust, inequitable, partial, one-sided, dishonest, dishonorable. See candid. ‘ ¥
unfair (un-far’), v.t. To deprive of fairness or beauty. Shak., Sonnets, v. [Rare.]

unfairly.c: unfairly (un-far’li), adv. In an unfair or unjust manner. Secker, Sermons, IV. xiii.

unfairness.c: unfairness (un-far’nes), x. The state or character of being unfair, in any sense. Bentley, Phileleutherus Lipsiensis.

unfaith.c: unfaith (un-fath’), x. Want or absence of faith; distrust. Unfaith in aught is want of faith in all. ‘ Tennyson, Merlin and Vivien (song).

unfaithful.c: unfaithful (un-fath’ful),a. [< ME. unfaythfull; < un-l + faithful.] 1. Not faithful; not observant of promises, vows, allegiance, or duty. Fro all fandyng vnfaythfull thou fende ys, Here in this worlde of life while we laste. York Plays, p. 241. His honor rooted in dishonor stood, And faith unfaithful kept him falsely true. Tennyson, Lancelot and Elaine. 2. Not performing the proper duty or function. My feet through wine unfaithful to their b eacna ope. unfaithful 8. Not possessing faith; unbelieving; impious; infidel. Milton, P. L., xii. 461.—4. Not trustworthy; inexact; not conforming to the letter and spirit: as, an unfaithful account; an unfaithful translation. He was a learned man, of immense reading, but is much blamed for his unfaithful quotations. Aubrey, Lives (William Prinne). =Syu. 1. Faithless, etc. (see perfidious); derelict.

unfaithfully.c: unfaithfully (un-fath’ful-i), adv. In an unfaithful manner; without faithfulness; perfidiously; negligently: as, work unfaithfully done.

unfaithfulness.c: unfaithfulness (un-fath’ful-nes), ». The character of being unfaithful. A pretext for unfaithfulness or negligence. J. A, Alexander, Sermons, II. 75.

unfalcated.c: unfalcated (un-fal’ka-ted), a. 1. Not faleated; not hooked; not bent. like a sickle.—2}. Not curtailed; having no deductions. I am of opinion that a real unfalcated income of six hundred pounds a year is a sufficient income for a country dean in this kingdom. Swift, On Bill for Clerical Residences.

unfallible.c: unfallible (un-fal’i-bl), a. Infallible. Shak., 1 Hen. VI., i. 2.59.

unfallowed.c: unfallowed (un-fal’6d), a. Not fallowed. Th’ unfallowed glebe. J. Philips, Cider, i.

unfaltering.c: unfaltering (un-f4l’tér-ing), a. Not faltering; not failing; not hesitating. Sustained and soothed By an unfaltering trust, approach thy grave. Bryant, Thanatopsis.

unfalteringly.c: unfalteringly (un-fal’tér-ing-li), adv. In an unfaltering manner; without faltering. He inspired all, so that “all felt ready to follow him unfalteringly into any... post of danger.” Amer. Antiquarian, IX. 112.

unfamed.c: unfamed (un-famd’), a. Not renowned; inglorious. [Rare.] Death unfamed. Shak., T. and C., ii. 2. 159.

unfamiliar.c: unfamiliar (un-fa-mil’yar), a. Not familiar; not well known or acquainted; not wonted by frequent use. Byron, Lara, i. The unfamiliar handwriting. W. D. Howells, Indian Summer, p. 192.

unfamiliarity.c: unfamiliarity (un-fa-mil-i-ar’i-ti),n. The state of being unfamiliar; want of familiarity. Johnson, Pref. to Dict.

unfamiliarly.c: unfamiliarly (un-fa-mil’ yar-li), adv. In an unfamiliar manner.

unfamous.c: unfamous (un-fa’mus), a [< ME. unfamous; <un-l + famous.| Not famous; lost to fame; forgotten. Chaucer, House of Fame, 1. 1146.

unfardle.c: unfardle (un-fir’dl), v. t. To unloose and open, as a pack (fardel); unpack. Nashe, Lenten Stuffe (Harl. Mise., VI. 171). (Davies.)

unfarrowed.c: unfarrowed (un-far’6d),@. Deprived of a farrow or litter. Tennyson, Walking to the Mail. [Rare.];

unfashionable.c: unfashionable (un-fash’on-a-bl), a. 1+. Incapable of being fashioned or shaped.—2. Not fashionable, in any sense. For there is no Charm in Words as to matters of Breeding, An unfashionable Name won’t make a Man a Clown. Jeremy Collier, Short View (ed. 1698), p. 221. 3+. Shapeless; deformed. Shak., Rich. III., Tlera2s

unfashionableness.c: unfashionableness (un-fash’on-a-bl-nes), 1. The character of being unfashionable; deviation from or opposition to the fashion.

unfashionably.c: unfashionably (un-fash’on-a-bli), adv. In an unfashionable manner; not in accordance with fashion.

unfashioned.c: unfashioned (un-fash’ond),a. Not modified by art; not molded; amorphous; shapeless; not haying a regular form. B. Jonson, Poetaster, ial

unfast.c: unfast (un-fast’), a. Not fast or safe; not secure. Johnson. unfast} (un-fast’), v.¢ [<¢ ME. unfasten, unves- ten, onfesten; < un-2 + fast1.] To loose.

unfasten.c: unfasten (un-fa’sn), v. [< ME. wnfastnen; < un-2 + fasten.) I. trans. To loose; unfix; unbind; untie; figuratively, to detach from any connecting link or agency; disconnect. : He doth unfasten so and shake a friend. Shak., 2 Hen. IV., iv. 1. 209. II. intrans. To come untied or unloosed.

unfastener.c: unfastener (un-fas’nér), ». One who or that which unfastens.

unfastnesst.c: unfastnesst (un-fast’nes), ». Lack of closeness, as of fiber; porousness. [Rare.] The insolidity and wnfastness of the tree. Rev. T. Adams, Works, II. 478.

unfathered.c: unfathered (un-fii’rHérd), a. 1. Having no father; fatherless; hence, produced contrary to the course of nature. Shak., 2 Hen. IV., iv. 6607 4, 122.—2. Not acknowledged by its father; having no acknowledged father, as an illegitimate child: used figuratively: as, an unfathered proposition.

unfatherly.c: unfatherly (un-fi’FHér-li), a. Not befitting a father. Cowper, Tirocinium, 1. 866.

unfathomable.c: unfathomable (un-fatH’um-a-bl), a. Incapable of being fathomed or sounded; too deep to be measured; hence, not capable of being sounded by thought or comprehended.

unfathomableness.c: unfathomableness (un-fafH’um-a-bl-nes), n. The state of being unfathomable. Norris, On the Beatitudes, p. 133.

unfathomably.c: unfathomably (un-fatH’um-a-bli), adv. So as not to be fathomed or sounded. Thomson, Winter.

unfathomed.c: unfathomed (un-fatH’umd), a. Not fathomed or sounded; not to be sounded. Gray, Hlegy.

unfatigueable.c: unfatigueable (un-fa-té’ga-bl), a. Incapable of being fatigued; unwearlable; indefatigable. Nashe, Pierce Penilesse, p. 58.

unfaulty.c: unfaulty (un-fal’ti), a. Free from fault, defect, or deficiency. Spenser, Heavenly Love, 1. 233.

unfavorableunfavourable.c: unfavorable, unfavourable (un-fa’vor-a-bl), a. 1. Not favorable; not propitious; discouraging; adverse. Macaulay, Mill on Government.—2. Not adapted to promote some specified object; somewhat prejudicial: as, weather unfavorable for harvest; unfavorable conditions.— 3}. Ill-favored; ugly; unattractive ; repulsive. unfavorableness, unfavourableness (un-fa’- vor-a-bl-nes), ». The character of being unfavorable. Adam Smith.

unfavorablyunfavourably.c: unfavorably, unfavourably (un-fa’vor-a-bli), adv. Inanunfavorable manner; so as not to countenance or promote; in a manner to discourage. Secker, Sermons, III. xy.

unfeared.c: unfeared (un-férd’), a. 1}. Not affrighted; not afraid; not daunted; intrepid. B. Jonson, Catiline, iv. 1.—2. Not feared; not dreaded.

unfearful.c: unfearful (un-fér’ful), a. Not fearful; not influenced by fear; courageous. Unfearefull preachers of my name. Udall.

unfearfully.c: unfearfully (un-fér’ful-i), adv. In anunfearful manner; bravely. Sandys, Travailes, p. 270.

unfeasible.c: unfeasible (un-f6’zi-bl), a. Not feasible; impracticable; infeasible. South, Sermons, III. ii. unfeastly, a. [ME. unfestlich; < un-1 + feastly.] Not festive; not cheerful. Hir liste nat appalled for to be, Nor on the morwe unfestlich for to se. Chaucer, Squire’s Tale, 1, 358.

unfeather.c: unfeather (un-ferH’ér), v. ¢. To strip or denude of feathers. Colman, The Oxonian in Town, i.

unfeathered.c: unfeathered (un-ferH’érd), a. Not provided with feathers; featherless. Dryden. unfeatly+ (un-fét’li), adv. Unadroitly; without skill; not dexterously. Udall, Luke, Pref.

unfeatured.c: unfeatured (un-fe’tird), a. Wanting regular features; deformed. Dryden, tr. of Juvenal’s Satires, x. [Rare.] unfeaty}+ (un-fé’ti), a. [<un-1+ feat, a.,+ -y1.] Not feat; unskilful; clumsy. They might talk of book-learning what they would, but, for his part, he never saw more unfeaty fellows than great clerks were. Sir P. Sidney, Arcadia, ii,

unfed.c: unfed (un-fed’), a. Notfed; not supplied with food; not nourished or sustained. Shak., Lear, iii. 4. 30.

unfeed.c: unfeed (un-féd’), a. Not feed; not retained by fee; unpaid. Shak., Lear, i. 4. 142.

unfeeling.c: unfeeling (un-fé/ling), a. 1. Devoid of feeling; insensible; void of sensibility. Shak., 2 Hen. VI., iii. 2. 145.— 2. Devoid of sympathy with others; hard-hearted; unsympathetic; cruel. Gray, Distant Prospect of Eton College.

unfeelingly.c: unfeelingly (un-fé’ling-li), adv. 1. In an unfeeling or cruel manner.— 2+. Without perception or comprehension. Chaucer, Troilus, ii. 19.

unfeelingness.c: unfeelingness (un-fé’ling-nes), n. The state or character of being unfeeling; insensibility; hardness; cruelty.

unfeigned.c: unfeigned (un-fand’), a. Not feigned; not counterfeit; not hypocritical; real; sincere: as, unfeigned piety; unfeigned thanks. Shak., T. of the S., iv. 2. 32.

unfeignedly.c: unfeignedly (un-fa’ned-li), adv. In an unfeigned manner; without hypocrisy; really; sincerely. Because it smells, vnfegneitlie, To verray percialytie. Lauder, Dewtie of Kyngis (E. E, T. 8.), 1. 481. He pardoneth and absolveth all them that truly repent and unfeignedly believe his holy gospel. Book of Common Prayer, Absolution. unfinishing

unfeignedness.c: unfeignedness (un-fa’ned-nes), n. The state of being unfeigned; truth; sincerity. Leighton, Com. on 1 Pet. ii. 24.

unfeigning.c: unfeigning (un-fa’ning), a. Not feigning; true. Cowper, Odyssey, Xxi.

unfellow.c: unfellow (un-fel’o), v.¢ To separate from being fellows or from one’s fellows; sunder; dissociate. Mrs. Browning. [Rare.]

unfellowed.c: unfellowed (un-fel’6d), a. Not matched; having no equal. Shak., Hamlet, v. 2. 150.

unfelt.c: unfelt (un-felt’), a. Not felt; not making its presence or action known; not perceived. An unfelt sorrow. Shak., Macbeth, ii. 3, 142.

unfeltlyt.c: unfeltlyt, adv. Imperceptibly. Into his [Pharaoh’s] brest she [Envy] blows A baneful ayr, whose strength wnfeltly flowers Through all his veins. Sylvester, tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Lawe.

unfence.c: unfence (un-fens’), v. t. 1. To strip of fence or guard. South, Sermons, IV. iv.—2. To remove a fence or wall from.

unfenced.c: unfenced (un-fenst’), a. Having no fence; not fenced in; also, without protection, guard, or security; defenseless. A town... unwalled and unfenced. Holinshed, Hist. Scotland, an. 1572. Spreading afar and unfenced o’er the plain. Longfellow, Evangeline, i. 1.

unfermented.c: unfermented (un-fér-men’ted), a. 1. Not haying undergone fermentation.—2. Not leayven- ed; not made with yeast, as bread.

unfertility.c: unfertility (un-fér-til’i-ti), n. Infertility. Nineteenth Century, XXIV. 834. unfestlich, a See unfeastly.

unfetter.c: unfetter (un-fet’ér), v. t. [< ME. unfeteren; < un-2 + fetter.] 1. To loose from fetters; unchain; unshackle; remove the fetters from. She went alone and gan her herte unfetter Out of desdaynous prison but a lite. Chaucer, Troilus, ii. 1216. 2. To free from restraint; set at liberty: as, to unfetter the mind.

unfettered.c: unfettered (un-fet’érd), pa@. Unchained; unshackled; free from restraint; unrestrained. Unfetter’d by the sense of crime. Tennyson, In Memoriam, xxvii.

unfeudalize.c: unfeudalize (un-fu’dal-iz), ».% To free from feudalism; divest of feudal rights or character. Also spelled unfeudalise. Carlyle, French Rev., Il. v.5. (Davies.)

unfigured.c: unfigured (un-fig’ard), a. 1. Not figured. specifically —(a) Representing no animal or vegetable figures or forms. (b) Devoid of figures of any kind; not spotted or dotted: as, an unfigured muslin; an unfigured vase. 2. Literal; devoid of figures of speech. Blair. —8s. In logic, not determined in reference to figure.

unfile.c: unfile (un-fil’), v. ¢ [< wn-2 + fill.] To remove from a file or record. Ford. unfiled! (un-fild’), a. [< wn-1 + filed, pp. of jill, v.] Not rubbed or polished with a file; not burnished. He was all army in rugged steele un/filde, As in the smoky forge it was compiled. Spenser, F. Q., III. vii. 30. unfiled?+ (un-fild’), a. [< ME. wnfyled; <un-1 + filed, pp. of file?, v.] Not soiled, polluted, corrupted, or contaminated; undefiled. Surrey, Adneid, ii.

unfilial.c: unfilial (un-fil’yal), a. Not filial. Shak., W.T., iv. 4. 417.

unfilleted.c: unfilleted (un-fil’et-ed), a. Not bound up with or as with a fillet. Coleridge, The Picture.

unfine.c: unfine (un-fin’), a. Not fine; shabby. [Rare.] The birthday was far from being such a show; empty and unjine as possible.

unfinish.c: unfinish (un-fin’ish),. Lack of finish; incompleteness. [Rare.] It is such a comfort to a tired American — tired of our fret and hurry and unfinish — to see something done and completed and polished. S. Bowles, in Merriam, I. 366.

unfinishable.c: unfinishable (un-fin’ish-a-bl), a. Incapable of being finished, concluded, or completed. Jarvis, tr. of Don Quixote, I. i. 1.

unfinished.c: unfinished (un-fin’isht), a. Not finished; not complete; not brought to an end; imperfect. A garment shapeless and unfinished. Shak., Venus and Adonis, 1. 415,

unfinishing.c: unfinishing (un-fin’ish-ing), ». The act of leaving unfinished, or not bringing to an end; the state of remaining unfinished. [Rare.] Noble deeds, the wnjinishing whereof already surpasses what others before them have left enacted. Milton, Apology for Smectymnuus, § & unfirm

unfirm.c: unfirm (un-férm’), a. Not firm; not strong or stable; feeble; infirm. The sway of earth Shakes like a thing wnjirm. Shak., J. C., i. 3. 4. So is the unfirm king In three divided. Shak., 2 Hen. IV., i. 3. 73.

unfirmamented.c: unfirmamented (un-fér’ma-men-ted), a. Not having a firmament; unbounded; boundless. Carlyle. (Rare.]

unfirmness.c: unfirmness (un-férm’nes), n. The state of being unfirm; want of firmness; instability. Imp. Dict.

unfit.c: unfit (un-fist’),v.t [< wn-1 + fist.] To unhand; release. [Rare.] You goodman Brandy face, wnjist her, How durst you keep my wife? Cotton, Scarronides, p. 85. (Davies.)

unfit (un-fit’), a. Not fit. (@ Improper; unsuitable; unbecoming; inappropriate: said of things. A most unit time. Shak., Hen. VIIL., ii. 2. 61. (b) Not suited or adapted; not fitted. It cannot be too carefully remembered that air containing so much carbonic acid gas that a candle will not burn therein is writ also to support human life. W. L. Carpenter, Energy in Nature (1st ed.), p. 73. (c) Wanting suitable qualifications, physical or moral; not competent; unable: said of persons. Unjit to live or die. Shak., M. for M., iv. 3. 68. =Syn. (a) Inapt. See apt. (ce) Unqualified, unmeet, unworthy, incompetent, insufficient.

unfit (un-fit’), v. t To make unsuitable; deprive of the proper or necessary qualifications for some act, activity, use, or purpose.. Age and blindness had unjitted Lord North for the duties of a public prosecutor. Macaulay, Warren Hastings.

unfitly.c: unfitly (un-fit’li), adv. In an unfit manner; not properly; unsuitably; inappropriately. B. Jonson, Alchemist, To the Reader.

unfitness.c: unfitness (un-fit’nes), n. The character of being unfit, in any sense. Shak., Lear, i. 4. 356.

unfitting.c: unfitting (un-fit’ing), a. [< ME. wnfittyng; < un-l + fitting.| Not fitting; unsuitable; unbecoming. To assail such a hideous creature Off so wonderful unjittyng stature. Rom. of Partenay (E. E. T. 8.), 1. 4758,

unfittingly.c: unfittingly (un-fit’ing-li), adv. In an unfitting manner; improperly. The Atlantic, LXV. 585.

unfix.c: unfix (un-fiks’), v. t 1. To make no longer fixed or firm; loosen from any fastening; detach; unsettle: as, to unfix the mind or affections; to unfix bayonets. /nix his earthbound root. Shak., Macbeth, iv. 1. 96. 2. To melt; dissolve. [Rare.] Nor can the rising sun Unjix their frosts. Dryden.

unfixed.c: unfixed (un-fikst’), a. Not fixed, in any sense.

unfixedness.c: unfixedness (un-fik’sed-nes), n. The state of being unfixed or unsettled. Barrow, Sermons, II. vi.

unfixity.c: unfixity (un-fik’si-ti),n. The state of being unfixed; fluctuation; variableness. [Rare.] The unjizity of the inflection of jutovs is shown by the existence of the variant juncos in Phocian inscriptions. Classical Rev., III. 35.

unflagging.c: unflagging (un-fiag’ing), a. Not flagging; not drooping; maintaining strength or spirit; sustained: as, unflagging zeal. South, Sermons, ay,

unflame.c: unflame (un-flim’), v. ¢ To unkindle; cool. [Rare.] Fear Unjlames your courage in pursuit. Quarles, Emblems, iii., Int.

unflated.c: unflated (un-fla’ted), a [< wn-1 + L. flatus, pp. of flare, blow (see flatus), + -ed2.] Not blown. The “jerk” or unflated aspirate. Encyc. Brit., XXII. 386,

unflattering.c: unflattering (un-flat’ér-ing), a. Not flattering, in any sense. Sir P. Sidney, Astrophel and Stella, xxvii.

unfledged.c: unfledged (un-flejd’), a. 1. Not yet fledged or furnished with feathers. Her unjledg’d brood, Cowper, Tliad, ix. 2. Not having attained to full growth or experience; not fully developed; immature. Unjledged actors. Dryden, Love Triumphant, i. 1.

unflesh.c: unflesh (un-flesh’),v.¢. [< wn-2 + flesh.] To deprive of flesh; reduce to a skeleton. [Rare.]

unfleshed.c: unfleshed (un-flesht’), a. Not fleshed; not seasoned to blood; untried: as, an unfleshed hound; unfleshed valor. In an 6608 Whene’er I go to the field, Heaven keep me from The meeting of an wrflesh’d youth or coward!: Beau, and Fi., Little French Lawyer, i. 2.

unfleshly.c: unfleshly (un-flesh’li), a. Not fleshly; not human; incorporeal; spiritual. Those unfleshly eyes with which they say the very air is thronged. C. Reade, Cloister and Hearth, 1. or (un-fiesh’i), a. Bare of flesh; fleshess. Gastly Death’s unfleshy feet. Sir J. Davies.
