unflinching.c: unflinching (un-flin’ching), a. Not flinching; not shrinking: as, unflinching bravery.

unflower.c: unflower (un-flou’ér), v. t. [« un-2 + flower.] To strip of flowers. G. Fletcher, Christ’s Victory and Triumph. [Rare.]

unfluent.c: unfluent (un-fl6’ent), a. Not fluent; unready in speech. Sylvester, tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, DOs

unflush.c: unflush (un-flush’), v.7. [< wn-2 + flush1.] To lose a flush of color. The west unflushed, the high stars grow bright. M. Arnold, Thyrsis.

unfoiled.c: unfoiled (un-foild’), a. Not vanquished; not defeated; not baffled. Milton, Hist. Eng., iii. unfold! (un-fold’), v. [< ME. unfolden, unfalden, unvolden, < AS. unfealdan, unfold, < un-, back, + fealdan, fold: see un-2 and fold, v.] I, trans. 1. To open the folds of; expand; spread out; change from a folded condition, in any sense of the word fold. Chaucer, Troilus, i. 1702; Pope, Iliad, ii. 978.—2. To lay open to view or contemplation; make known in all the details; develop; disclose; reveal: as, to wn- fold one’s designs; to unfold the principles of a science. The Holy Fader wondered on that he told, Off tho merueles that ther gan unfold. Rom. of Partenay (E. E. VT. §.), 1. 5124. Time shall unfold what plaited cunning hides. Shak., Lear, i. 1. 283. 3. To show, or let be seen; display. {Lightning] that in a spleen wnfolds both heaven and earth. Shak., M. N. D., i. 1. 146. II. intrans. To become opened out; be spread apart; become disclosed or developed; develop itself. I see thy beauty gradually unfold. Tennyson, Eleanore. unfold? (un-fold’), v. t. [< un-2 + fold?.] To release from a fold or pen. She [the milkmaid] dares go alone and unfold sheep in the night, and fears no manner of ill. Quoted in Walton’s Complete Angler, p. 82.

unfolder.c: unfolder (un-f6l’dér), n. One who or that which unfolds.

unfolding.c: unfolding (un-f0l’ding), ». [Verbal n. of wn- fold!, v.} The act of spreading out; disclosure; revelation; development. To my unfolding lend your prosperous ear. Shak., Othello, i. 3. 245.

unfoldment.c: unfoldment (un-f6ld’ment), ». [< wnfold1 + -ment.] Unfolding; development. [Rare.] The unfoldment of the power of voluntary motion. Pop. Sci. Mo., XX XIII. 4. unfoldress} (un-f6l’dres), n. [< unfold + -erl + -ess.] A female who unfolds or discloses. The unfoldresse of treacheries. Holinshed, Descrip. of Ireland.

unfoliated.c: unfoliated (un-f6’li-a-ted), a. Not having a foliated structure; not foliated. See foliation, 6.

unfool.c: unfool (un-f6l’), v. t [< wn-2 + fool.] To restore from folly; make satisfaction to (one) for calling one a fool; take away the reproach of folly from. [Rare.] Have you any way, then, to unfool me again? Shak., M. W. of W., iv. 2. 120.

unfooted.c: unfooted (un-fut’ed), a. Not trodden by the foot of man; unvisited. [Rare.] Until it came to some unfooted plains Where fed the herds of Pan. Keats, Endymion. unforbidden, unforbid (un-fér-bid’n, un-fér- bid’), a. Not forbidden; not prohibited: applied to persons; allowed; permitted; legal: applied to things.

unforbiddenness.c: unforbiddenness (un-fér-bid’n-nes), n. The state of being unforbidden. Boyle. unforced |(un-forst’), a. Not forced, in any sense of that word. This gentle and unforced accord. Shak., Hamlet, i. 2. 123.

unforcedly.c: unforcedly (un-f6r’sed-li), adv. Inan unforced manner. Sandys, tr. of Ovid’s Metamorph., xiii., note. ‘_ > ee ' Byers unfortunate

unforcible.c: unforcible (un-for’si-bl), a. Wanting force or strength: as, an wnforcible expression. Hooker, Eecles. Polity, v. § 65. [Rare.]

unforeboding.c: unforeboding (un-for-b6’ding),a. Not foretelling; not telling the future; giving no omens. Pope, Odyssey, ii.

unforeknowable.c: unforeknowable (un-for-n0’a-bl), a. ble of being foreknown. Cudworth.

unforeknown.c: unforeknown (un-for-nén’), a. Not previously known or foreseen. [Rare.] Which had no less proved certain, unforeknown. Milton, P. L., iii. 19.

unforesee.c: unforesee (un-for-sé’), v. t.; pret. unforesaw, pp. unforeseen, ppr. unforeseeing. [< un-1 + JSoresee.| Not to foresee or anticipate; have no previous view or impression of. Bp. Hacket, Abp. Williams, i. 171. (Davies.)

unforeseeable.c: unforeseeable (un-for-sé’a-bl), a. Incapable of being foreseen. South, Sermons, V. vi.

unforeseeing.c: unforeseeing (un-for-sé’ing), a. Not foreseeing; not provident. Daniel, Civil Wars, vi.

unforeseen.c: unforeseen (un-for-sén’), a. Not foreseen; not foreknown.: The sudden and unforeseen changes of things. Bacon, Political Fables, v., Expl. The unforeseen, that which is not foreseen or expected. Incapa- Nothing is certain but the unforeseen. Froude.

unforeskinned.c: unforeskinned (un-for’skind), a. [< un- + foreskin + -ed2.) Circumcised. Milton, 8. A., 1. 1100. [Rare.]

unforewarned.c: unforewarned (un-for-wirnd’), a. Not forewarned; not previously warned or admonished. Milton, P. L., v. 246.

unforfeited.c: unforfeited (un-fér’fit-ed), a. Not forfeited; maintained; not lost. Shak., M. of V., ii. 6.7.

unforged.c: unforged (un-forjd’), a. [< ME. unforged; < un-1 + forged.] Not forged; not made. Unforged was the hauberke and the plate. Chaucer, Former Age, 1. 49.

unforgetable.c: unforgetable (un-fér-get’a-bl), a. That cannot be forgotten. Also spelled unforgettable.

unforgivable.c: unforgivable (un-fér-giv’a-bl), a. Incapable of being forgiven; unpardonable. Carlyle, Life of Sterling, vii. Also spelled unforgiveable.

unforgiven.c: unforgiven (un-fér-giv’n), a. Not forgiven; not pardoned. Bp. Jewell, A Replie to M. Hardinge, p. 546.

unforgiver.c: unforgiver (un-fér-giv’ér), m. One who does not pardon or forgive; an implacable person. Richardson, Clarissa Harlowe, VII. 26. [Rare.]

unforgiving.c: unforgiving (un-fér-giv’ing), a. Not forgiving; not disposed to overlook or pardon offenses; implacable. Byron, Fare Thee Well.

unforgivingness.c: unforgivingness (un-fér-giv’ing-nes), n. The quality of being unforgiving; implacability. Richardson, Clarissa Harlowe, VII. 287. unforgotten, unforgot (un-fdr-got’n, un-fér- got’), a. Not forgotten; not lost to memory; not overlooked or neglected. Clime of the unforgotten brave, Byron, The Giaour.

unform.c: unform (un-férm’), v.t. [< w-2 + form.] To destroy; unmake; decompose, or resolve into parts. pan te (un-fé6r’mal), a. Not formal; informal.

unformalized.c: unformalized (un-fér’mal-izd), a. Not made formal; unreduced to forms. Charlotte Bronté, Villette, xix.

unformed.c: unformed (un-férmd’), a. Not having been formed; not fashioned; not molded into regular shape. Matter unform’d and void. Milton, P. L., vii. 233. Unformed stars, in anc. astron., stars not included in any constellation-figure, but considered as belonging to one of the constellations: generally used with reference to Ptolemy’s catalogue, as the shapes of the constellation- figures are not so determinate as to distinguish whether stars not given by Ptolemy are in all cases within or without the figure.:

unfortified.c: unfortified (un-fér’ti-fid), a. Not fortified, in any sense. A heart unfortified, a mind impatient. Shak,, Hamlet, i. 2. 96.

unfortify.c: unfortify (un-for’ti-fi), v. t [<un-2 + fortify.] To strip of fortifications; dismantle. [Rare.] On the kings name I command you to leaue your armour, to discamp your camp, and to bok Tordi- silas. Guevara, Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 272.

unfortunacyt.c: unfortunacyt (un-for’ta-na-si), n. [< wnfortu- nate) + -cy.] Misfortune. The king he tacitly upbraids with the wnfortunacies of his reign by deaths and plagues. Heylin, Life of Laud, p. 831. (Davies)

unfortunate.c: unfortunate (un-for’tu-nat), a and n. I. a. Not fortunate; not prosperous; unlucky; un- Not predicted or lt we, Ei, unfortunate happy: as, an unfortunate adventure; an unfortunate man. Men ever were most blessed, till cross fate Brought love and women forth, unfortunate To all that ever tasted of their smiles. Fletcher, Faithful Shepherdess, iv. 4. =Syn. Unsuccessful, ill-fated, ill-starred, disastrous, calamitous. See fortunate. II. x. One who or that which is unfortunate; one who has fallen into misfortune or misery. One more unfortunate, Weary of breath. Hood, Bridge of Sighs.

unfortunately.c: unfortunately (un-fér’tu-nat-li), adv. In an unfortunate manner; by ill fortune; unhappily. Shak., Venus and Adonis, 1. 1029.

unfortunateness.c: unfortunateness (un-fér’ti-nat-nes), n. The condition or state of being unfortunate; ill luck; ill fortune. His greatest Unfortunateness was in his greatest Blessing. Baker, Chronicles, p. 102.

unfossiliferous.c: unfossiliferous (un-fos-i-lif’e-rus), a. Destitute of fossils. Hneyc. Brit., XVIII. 622.

unfostered.c: unfostered (un-fos’térd), a. 1. Not fostered; not nourished.— 2. Not countenanced or favored; not patronized: as, a scheme unfostered.

unfought.c: unfought (un-fat’), a. Not fought. If they march along _ Unfought withal. ~ Shak., Hen. V., iii. 5. 12.

unfounded.c: unfounded (un-foun’ded), a. 1. Not founded; not built or established. Milton, P. L., ii. 829. —2. Having no foundation; vain; idle; baseless: as, unfounded expectations. Paley, Natural Theology. iatoundedy (un-foun’ded-li), adv. Ina baseless or unfounded manner.

unframable.c: unframable (un-fra’ma-bl), a. Not capable of being framed or molded. Hooker, Hecles. Polity, i. § 16.

unframableness.c: unframableness (un-fra’ma-bl-nes), n. The character of being unframable. Bp. Sanderson.

unframed.c: unframed (un-framd’), a. 1. Not formed; not constructed; not fashioned. Dryden.— 2. Not provided with a frame; not put into a frame: as, an unframed picture.

unframet.c: unframet (un-fram’), v. t. [< wn-2 + frame.] To destroy the frame of; take apart; hence, to make useless; destroy. You write unto me that you are much offended by many slanderers that deprave your doings and unframe your attempts. Guevara, Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 109.

unfrangible.c: unfrangible (un-fran’ji-bl), a. incapable of being broken; infrangible. Taylor.

unfrankable.c: unfrankable (un-frang’ka-bl), a. Incapable of being franked or sent by a public conveyance free of expense. Southey, Letters (1819), iii. 106. (Davies.)

unfraught.c: unfraught (un-frat’), a. Not fraught; not filled with a load or burden; unloaded. But would God that without lenger delayed These galees were unfraught in fortie dayes. Hakluyt’s Voyages, I. 195.

unfree.c: unfree (un-fré’), a. [< ME. unfre; < un-1 + free.) Not free, in any sense of the word Sree. Below the freeman there were unfree men, serfs bound to the soil and slaves, the conquered foes of past generations and the captives of his own. F. Pollock, Land Laws, i. 16. In no previous arrangement between Christian states had the rule ‘‘free ships, free goods” been separated from the opposite, ‘‘wnfree or hostile ships, hostile goods.” Woolsey, Introd. to Inter. Law, § 174. agen al (un-fréz’),v.t [<un-2+ freeze.] To thaw. Unfreeze the frost of her chaste heart. T. Hudson, Judith, iv. 196. (Davies.)

unfrequency.c: unfrequency (un-fré’kwen-si), n. The state of being unfrequent; infrequency. The unfrequency of apparitions. Glanville, Essays, vi.

unfrequent.c: unfrequent (un-fré’kwent), a. Not frequent; not common; not happening often; infrequent. Spectator, No. 472. In the German universities feuds were not infrequent. Encye. Brit., XXIII. 848.
unfrequent (un-fré-kwent’), v. # [« wn-2 + Srequent.| To cease to frequent. J Philips, Cider, i. [Rare.]

unfrequented.c: unfrequented (un-fré-kwen’ted), a. Not frequented; seldom resorted to by human beings; solitary: as, an unfrequented place or forest. Shak., T. G. of V., v. 4. 2

unfrequently.c: unfrequently (un-fré’kwent-li), adv. Infre- sei y. Cogan, On the Passions, i.2. [Rare.] 15 Not fran- Not frangible; Jer. 6609

unfrett.c: unfrett (un-fret’), v. t [< wn-2 + fret.] To smooth out; relax. Until the Lord unfret his angry brows. Greene and Lodge, Looking Glass for Lond. and Eng.

unfretted.c: unfretted (un-fret’ed), a. Not fretted; not worn orrubbed. Holinshed, Chronicles of Ireland, an. 1532.

unfriend.c: unfriend (un-frend’),». [< ME. wnfreond, on- Sreond (= MHG. wnvriunt), hostile person; <una friend.) One nota friend; an enemy. Car- yle.

unfriended.c: unfriended (un-fren’ded), a. Lacking friends; not countenanced or supported. Shak., T.N., i.3>) 10; He was unfriended and unknown. Ticknor, Hist. Span. Literature, II. 97.

unfriendedness.c: unfriendedness (un-fren’ded-nes), ». The quality or state of being unfriended. Atheneum, No. 3148, p. 236.

unfriendliness.c: unfriendliness (un-frend’li-nes), n. The quality of being unfriendly; want of kindness; disfavor. Leighton, Com. on 1 Pet. ii. 11.

unfriendly.c: unfriendly (un-frend’li), a. 1. Not friendly; not kind or benevolent; inimical: as, an wn- Sriendly neighbor. I would not breed dissention; Tis an unfriendly office. Beau. and Fl., Knight of Malta, ii. 3. They left their bones beneath unfriendly skies. Cowper, Expostulation, 1. 524. 2. Not favorable; not adapted to promote or support any object. The unfriendly elements. =Syn. Hostile, inimical, antagonistic. See amicable.
unfriendly (un-frend‘li), adv. In an unkind manner; notasafriend. Wollaston, Religion of Nature, vi.

unfrighted.c: unfrighted (un-fri’ted), a. Not frighted; not seared or terrified. B. Jonson, Epigrams, iv.

unfrightful.c: unfrightful (un-frit’fal), a. Not frightful; not or ne or repulsive. Carlyle, French Rev., . vii. 4.

unfrock.c: unfrock (un-frok’), v.t. [<un-2 + frock.] To deprive of a frock; divest of a frock; hence, referring to a monk’s frock, to deprive of ecclesiastical rank or authority. “Proud prelate,” she [Elizabeth] wrote,... “If you do not immediately comply with my request,... I will unfrock you!” J. R. Green, Short Hist. of Eng. People, vii. 3.

unfructed.c: unfructed (un-fruk’ted), a. In her., having no fruit: said of a branch or sprig of some plant which is usually represented fructed. More leaves or sprigs are usually shown as forming part of the branch than when there is fruit. unfructuous, a. [< wn-1 + fructuous.] Unfruitful. Wyclif.

unfruitful.c: unfruitful (un-frét’fal), a. Not fruitful, in any sense. Shak., Pericles, iii. 1. 58. In the midst of his unfruitful prayer. Shak., Lucrece, 1. 344.

unfruitfully.c: unfruitfully (un-frét’fil-i), adv. In an unfruitful manner; fruitlessly. B. Jonson, The Silent Woman, v. l.

unfruitfulness.c: unfruitfulness (un-frét’fil-nes), ». The state or character of being unfruitful; barrenness; infecundity; unproductiveness: applied to persons or things. unfruitoust, a. [ME., also unfruytous; < un-1 + fruitous, fruitful: see fructuous.| Unfruitful. Wyclif.

unfueledunfuelled.c: unfueled, unfuelled (un-fi’eld), a. plied with fuel; not fed with fuel. Thalaba, ii. (Davies.) [Rare.]

unfulfilled.c: unfulfilled (un-ful-fild’), a. Not fulfilled; not accomplished: as, a prophecy or prediction wn- fulfilled. Milton, P. L., iv. 511.

unfullt.c: unfullt (un-ful’), a. Not full or complete; imperfect. Sylvester.

unfumed.c: unfumed (un-fimd’), a 1. Not fumigated.— 2+. Not extracted or drawn forth by fumigation; undistilled: noting odor or scent. She... strows the ground With rose and odours from the shrub unfumed. Milton, P.L., v. 349.

unfunded.c: unfunded (un-fun’ded), a. Not funded; floating: as, an unfunded debt. See fund, v. t., and Junded. The unfunded debt of the United Kingdom exists in the form of exchequer bills and bonds, treasury bills, etc., issued by the government when it desires to raise money for temporary purposes, all bearing interest at fixed rates, and due at specified times; while the funded debt of that country is properly no debt at all, the government being under no obligation to repay the principal sum represented by the stock, but only to pay the interest Not sup- Southey, ungartered thereon, for the due performance of which a fund consisting of the product of certain taxes or sources of revenue is set aside.

unfurl.c: unfurl (un-férl’),v. [< wn-2 + furl.] I. trans. 1. To spread or shake out from a furled state, as a sail or a flag. Gallia’s proud standards, to Bavaria’s joined, Unfurl their gilded lilies in the wind. Addison, The Campaign. 2. Figuratively, to disclose; display. I am resolved to display my unfurled soule in your very face. NV. Ward, Simple Cobler, p. 56. The red right arm of Jove, With all his terrors there unfurl'd. Byron, tr. of Horace, II, intrans. To be spread out or expanded; open to the wind. As marks his eye the seaboy on the mast, The anchors rise, the sails unfurling fast. Byron, Corsair, i. 16,

unfurnish.c: unfurnish (un-fér’nish), v.¢. [<¢ wn-2 + furnish.] To deprive of furnishing, furniture, or necessaries of any kind. Puttenham, Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 170.

unfurnished.c: unfurnished (un-fér’nisht), a. Not furnished; not supplied with furnishings or furniture of any kind; unsupplied; unequipped: as, an wn- furnished house. We shall be much unfurnish’d for this time. Shak., R. and J., iv. 2. 10.

unfurrowed.c: unfurrowed (un-fur’od), a. Not furrowed; not formed into drills or ridges; hence, smooth: as, an unfurrowed field; the unfurrowed sea. The unseeded and unfurrowed soil. Cowper, Odyssey, ix. unfused! (un-ftizd’), a. Not fused; not melted. unfused?2 (un-fizd’), a. Not provided or fitted with fuse, asamineorabomb. Science, V.74.

ungained.c: ungained (un-gand’), a. Not yet gained; unpossessed. Shak., T. and C.,i. 1. 315.

ungainful.c: ungainful (un-gan’ful), a. Unprofitable; not producing gain. Daniel, Musophilus.

ungainliness.c: ungainliness (un-gan‘li-nes), ». The state or character of being ungainly; ungainly appearance ; clumsiness; awkwardness.

ungainly.c: ungainly (un-gan’li), a. [< ME. *ungainly (cf. ungainly, adv.); <un-1 + gainly, a.) 1+. Unfit; vain. Misusing their knowledge to ungainly ends, as either ambition, superstition, or for satisfying their curiosity. Hammond, Sermons, IV. 13. 2. Awkward; clumsy; uncouth: as, an wngain- ly carriage. LHverett, Orations, I. 213.=gsyn. 2. Uncouth, Bungling, etc. See awkward and clumsy.
ungainly (un-gan‘li), adv. [< ME. *wngaynly, ungeinliche; < un-1 + gainly, adv.) In an awkward manner; clumsily; uncouthly. Why dost thou stare and look so ungainly? Vanbrugh, Confederacy, i. 2.

ungaint.c: ungaint (un-gan’), a. [< ME. ungain, ungain; <un-1+ gain, a.) 1. Perilous; dreadful. [He] gird comes vnto grounde with vngayn strokes. Destruction of Troy (ER. E. ‘I. 8.), 1. 1832. 2. Ungainly; awkward; clumsy. A brown boy with a thin face, a huge nose, and as ungain as possible. Gray, Letters, I. 86.

ungallant.c: ungallant (un-gal’ant, -ga-lant’), a. Not gallant; uncourtly toadies. Gay, Letter to Swift, April 27, 1731.

ungalled.c: ungalled (un-gald’), a. uninjured. Why, let the stricken deer go weep, The hart ungalled play. Shak., Hamlet, iii. 2. 283,

ungarment.c: ungarment (un-giir’ment), v. t [< wn-2 + garment.| To unclothe; strip.

ungarmented.c: ungarmented (un-giir’men-ted), a. Not having garments; not covered with garments; unclothed. And round her limbs ungarmented the fire Curl’d its fierce flakes. Southey, Joan of Arc, iv. (Davies.)

ungarnished.c: ungarnished (un-giir’nisht), a. [<« ME. wgar- nest; < un-1 + garnished.] Not garnished or furnished; unadorned; not properly provided or equipped. The gome watz vngarnyst with god men to dele. Alliterative Poems (ed. Morris), ii. 187. A plain ungarnish'd present as a thanke-offering to thee, Milton, Animadversions.

ungartered.c: ungartered (un-giir’térd), a. Not held by garters, as the hose or stockings; not having or wearing garters. You chid at Sir Proteus for going ungartered. Shak., T. G. of V., ii. 1. 79. Unhurt; not galled; ungathered

ungathered.c: ungathered (un-garnH’érd), a. Not gathered together; not culled; not picked; not collected; specifically, noting printed sheets that have been folded, but not gathered in regular order for binding. Those persons whose souls are dispersed and ungathered by reason of a wanton humour to intemperate jesting are apt to be trifling in their religion. Jer. Taylor, Works (ed, 1835), I. 741.

ungavabay.c: Ungava Bay (ung-ga'va ba). An arm of Hudson Strait, projecting into Labrador.

ungear.c: ungear (un-gér’), v. t. [< un-2 + gear.] To strip of gear; also, to throw out of gear.

ungeneraledungeneraled.c: ungeneraled, ungeneraled (un-jen’e-rald), a. Made not general; local; particular. fuller. [Rare.]

ungenerated.c: ungenerated (un-jen’e-ra-ted), a. Not generated; not brought into being. Raleigh.

ungenerous.c: ungenerous (un-jen’e-rus), a. Not generous; not showing liberality or nobility of mind or sentiments; illiberal; ignoble; dishonorable. The victor never will impose on Cato Ungen’rous terms. Addison, Cato.

ungenerously.c: ungenerously (un-jen’e-rus-li), adv. In an ungenerous manner; illiberally; ignobly.

ungenial.c: ungenial (un-jé’nial), a. Not genial. (a) Not favorable to natural growth: as, ungenial air; ungenial soils. (b) Not kindly; unpleasant; disagreeable; harsh; unsympathetic: as, an ungenial disposition. (c) Not congenial; not suited or adapted. [Rare.] Critical explanations of difficult passages of Scripture . do well for publication, but are ungenial to the habits and taste of a general audience. Sydney Smith, in Lady Holland, iii.

ungenitured.c: ungenitured (un-jen’i-tird), a. Wanting genitals; wanting the power of propagation; impotent. Shak., M. for M., iii. 2. 184.

ungenteel.c: ungenteel (un-jen-tél’), a. Not genteel; impolite; rude: of persons or manners.

ungenteelly.c: ungenteelly (un-jen-tél’li), adv. In an ungenteel manner; impolitely; uncivilly. Hdinburgh Rev.

ungentle.c: ungentle (un-jen’tl), a. [< ME. wngentel; < un-1 + gentle.] 1. Not gentle; harsh; rough; rude; ill-bred; impolite, When nature biddeth thee to be good and gentle to other, she commandeth thee not to be cruel and ungentle to thyself. Sir 7. More, Utopia (tr. by Robinson), ii. 7. Cesar cannot live To be ungentle. Shak., A. and ©., v. 1. 60. 2. Not noble; plebeian. Sum man hath grete rychesses, but he is ashamed of his ungentel linage. Chaucer, Boéthius, ii, prose 4.

ungentleman.c: ungentleman (un-jen’tl-man), v.% Same as ungentlemanize. Some tell me home-breeding will ungentleman him. Gentleman Instructed, p. 545. (Davies.)

ungentlemanize.c: ungentlemanize (un-jen’tl-man-iz), v. t. [< wn-1 + gentleman + -ize.] To deprive of the character of a gentleman; make boorish. [Rare.] Unmanning and un-gentlemanizing themselves to any extent. C. A. Bristed, English University, p. 416.

ungentlemanlike.c: ungentlemanlike (un-jen’tl-man-lik), a. Not like a gentleman; not becoming a gentleman; ungentlemanly. Sydney Smith, To John Allen.

ungentlemanliness.c: ungentlemanliness (un-jen’tl-man-li-nes), n. The character of being ungentlemanly. Quarterly Rev.

ungentlemanly.c: ungentlemanly (un-jen’tl-man-li), a. Not befitting a gentleman; rude; uncivil; ill-bred. Swearing in the Playhouse is an ungentlemanly as well as an unchristian Practice. Jeremy Collier, Short View, p. 59. =Syn. See wneivil.

ungentlemanly (un-jen’tl-man-li), adv. In an ungentlemanly manner; not as a gentleman. To defraud and cousin them ungentlemanly of their parents love, which is the greatest and fairest portion of their inheritance. Holland, tr. of Plutarch, p. 148.

ungentleness.c: ungentleness (un-jen’tl-nes),. 1. Want of gentleness; harshness; severity; rudeness.— 2. Want of politeness; incivility. Shak., As you Like it, v. 2. 83.

ungently.c: ungently (un-jent’li), adv. Inan ungentle manner; harshly; with severity; rudely. Shak., Tempest, i. 2. 444.

ungenuine.c: ungenuine (un-jen’a-in), a Not genuine. His best Plays are almost always Modest and clean Complexion’d. His Amphitrio, excepting the wngenwine Addition, is such. Jeremy Collier, Short View, p. 18.

ungenuineness.c: ungenuineness (un-jen’i-in-nes), n. The character of being ungenuine; spuriousness.

unger.c: Unger (ong'er), Franz. Born in Styria, 1800; died at Gratz, Feb. 13, 1870. A distinguished Austrian botanist and paleontologist, professor of botany at Vienna from 1850. He was particularly noted* for his researches in the anatomy and physiology of plants and in fossil botany. Ungern-Sternberg (ong'ern-stern'berG), Baron Alexander von. Born near Reval, Esthonia, 1806: died at Dannenwalde, Mecklenburg-Stre- litz, Aug. 24, 1868. A German novelist. Among his best-known novels are “Der Missionar,” “ Diane,” and “Die Royalisten.” Unicorn, The. See Monoceros.

unget.c: unget (un-get’), 7. = [< wn-2 + get. Cf. wn- beget.| To treat as if unbegotten. [Rare.] T'll disown you; I'll disinherit you; I'll wnget you. Sheridan, The Rivals.

ungiculus.c: ungiculus (ung-gwik’a-lus), ”.; pl. unguicule (-h). ([NL., < L. wnguiculus, dim. of unguis, nail, claw: see wnguis.] In entom., an unguis; a small claw or hook-like appendage. Sometimes used to distinguish either tarsal claw, when both claws and the last tarsal joint are collectively called unguis. See unguis, 4.

ungifted.c: ungifted (un-gif’ted), a. Not gifted. @) Not endowed with peculiar faculties.: A hot-headed, ungifted, unedifying preacher. Arbuthnot, Hist. of John Bull, xxiii. (>) Not having received a gift; without a present. 6610 Lest thou depart the coast ungifted. Cowper, Odyssey, xv.

ungild.c: ungild (un-gild’), v. t. [< wn-2 + gilds.] To deprive of gilding. It will wngild one face of the object while the other face becomes gilt. Workshop Receipts, 1st ser., p. 196.

ungildedungilt.c: ungilded, ungilt (un-gil’ded, un-gilt’), a. Not gilt; not overlaid with gilding. Our mean ungilded stage. Dryden.

ungilding.c: ungilding (un-gil’ding), n. The act or process of depriving of gilding; hence, figuratively, a stripping off of decorations. By all this wee may conjecture how little wee need feare that the unbuilding of our Prelates will prove the woodening of our Priests. Milton, Animadversions. Articles of iron, steel, and silver, which cannot be submitted to the wngilding-bath. Workshop Receipts, 1st ser., p. 205.

ungill.c: ungill (un-gil’), v. t. [< wn-2+ gills.] To release the gills of (a fish) from the net; take or remove from a gill-net, as fish.

ungilt.c: ungilt (un-gilt’), v. 4 An obsolete variant of ungild. Bycause that there was none all that did vngilte it. Golden Boke, Prol. ungiltif},a. [ME.: see wnguwilty.] Without guilt; innocent. Is this an honour unto thy deye, That folk wngiltif suffren here injure? Chaucer, Troilus, iii. 1018.

ungird.c: ungird (un-gérd’), v. t= [< un-2 + gird.] To loosen by taking off the girdle, as arobe; also, to take the girdle or belt from. The sportive exercises for the which the genius of Milton ungirds itself. Macaulay.

ungivet.c: ungivet (un-giv’),v. [< wn-2 + give.] To give way; relax; slacken. That religion which is rather suddenly parched up than seasonably ripened doth commonly ungive afterwards. Fuller, Ch. Hist., II. ii. 40. (Davies.)

ungkaputi.c: ungkaputi (ung’kii-put-i), n. [Native name.] The active gibbon of Sumatra, Hylobates agilis. Also called wngha, ungka-pati, ungka-etam.

unglad.c: unglad (un-glad’), a. [ME. unglad,< AS. un- gled (=Ieel. ugladhr), not glad; as wn-1 + glad.] nen; sad. Alliterative Poems (ed. Morris), iii. 63.

ungladden.c: ungladden (un-glad’n), v.¢. [< wn-2 + gladden.] To deprive of gladness; leave uncheered; make sad. ([Rare.] It wears, to my eye, a stern and sombre aspect, too much ungladdened by genial sunshine. Hawthorne, Scarlet Letter, p. 49.

unglaze.c: unglaze (un-glaz’),v.t. [< wn-2 + glaze.] To ys the glass from, as a window or window-sash.

unglazed.c: unglazed (un-glazd’), a. 1. Unprovided with glass, or with glass windows.—2. Not coated or covered with vitreous matter: as, unglazed earthenware. See unglazed pottery, under pottery.

ungloomed.c: ungloomed (un-glémd’), a. Not darkened, overshadowed, or overclouded. [Rare.] With look ungloomed by guile. M. Green, The Spleen.

unglorified.c: unglorified (un-glo’ri-fid), a. Not glorified; not honored with praise or adoration. Dryden.

unglorify.c: unglorify (un-gl0’ri-fi), v. t._[< un-2 + glorify.) To deprive of glory. Watis, Remnants of Time, § 31. [Rare.]

unglorious.c: unglorious (un-gl0’ri-us), a. Not glorious; bringing no glory or honor; inglorious. Wyclif, Job xii. 19.

unglove.c: unglove (un-gluv’), v. ¢. [< un-2 + glove.] To take off the glove or gloves from. Unglove your hand. Fletcher (and Massinger?), Lovers’ Progress, ii. 1.

unglozed.c: unglozed (un-glozd’), a. [< ME. unglosed; < un-1 + glozed.| Not glozed or glossed. Late gore confessoure, sire kynge, construe this unglosed. Piers Plowman (B), iv. 145.

unglue.c: unglue (un-gli’), v. t. [< un-2+ glue.] To separate, as that which is glued or cemented; hence, figuratively, to free from any strong attachment. Unglue thyself from the world and the vanities of it. Bp. Hall, Christ Mystical, § 24.

unglutted.c: unglutted (un-glut’ed), a. Not glutted; not satiated or saturated; not cloyed. Seyd’s unglutted eye. Byron, Corsair, ii. 8.

ungnadia.c: Ungnadia (un-gnad’i-ii), ». [NL. (Endlicher, 1833), named for Ungnad, who wrote (1757) on = rs, ungovernably Persian fruits.] A genus of plants, of the order Sapindacez and tribe Sapindez. It is distinguished from the related genus d/sculus, the horse-chestnut, by its alternate pinnate leaves, and by its flowers with a tongue-shaped disk. The only species, U. speciosa, the Spanish buckeye, is a native of Texas and Mexico, having a soft satiny reddish wood. It is a small tree, or sometimes a low shrub, with leaves of from 3 to 7 serrate leaflets, the terminal leaflet being long-stalked. The rose-colored flowers are aggregated in lateral clusters or corymbs, followed by a coriaceous three-lobed capsule containing three globose seeds resembling those of the horse-chestnut, but with emetic properties, and reputed poisonous, ungoard}, a. See ungored. ungod! (un-god’), v. ¢.; pret. and pp. wngodded, ppr. unnodding. [< un-2 + god1.] 1. To divest of the divine attributes or qualities, real or supposed; divest of divinity; undeify. Dr. J. Scott. [Rare.]—2. To deprive of a god, or cause to recognize no god; make atheistical or godless. [Rare.] Thus men wngodded may to places rise, And sects may be preferred without disguise. Dryden, Hind and Panther, iii. 742. ungod?t, a. A Middle English form of ungood.

ungodlily.c: ungodlily (un-god’li-li), adv. In an ungodly manner; impiously; wickedly.

ungodliness.c: ungodliness (un-god’li-nes),. The quality of being ungodly; impiety; wickedness. The wrath of God is revealed from heaven ag: ungodliness. Rom. i. 18.

ungodly.c: ungodly (un-god’li), a. 1. Not godly; careless of God; godless; wicked; impious; sinful: as, ungodly men or ungodly deeds. 1 Pet. iv. 18. Glory to him whose just avenging ire Had driven out the ungodly from his sight. ‘Milton, P. L., vii. 185. 2. Polluted by wickedness. The hours of this ungodly day. Shak., K. John, iii. 1. 109. Such an ungodly sickness I have got That he that undertakes my cure must first O’erthrow divinity, all moral laws. Beau. and Fl., King and No King, iii. 1. 3. Outrageous; extremely annoying. [Slang.] The poisonous nature of the wind, and its ungodly and unintermittent uproar, would not suffer me to sleep. R. L. Stevenson, Olalla. 4. Squeamish; nice. Halliwell. [Prov. Eng.] =Syn. 1. Godless, Unrighteous, etc. See irreligious. ee (un-gtd’), a. [< ME. ungood, ungod, < AS. ungod (= OHG. MHG. ungot, G. uncut = Icel. agodhr), not good; as wn-1 + good.) Not good; bad.

ungoodly.c: ungoodly (un-gid‘li), a. [< ME. ungoodly; < un-1 + goodly, a.) Not goodly; not good; bad. I nolde holde hir ungoodly. Rom. of the Rose, 1, 3741.

ungoodly (un-gid/li), adv. [< ME. ungoodly, ungoodly; < un-1 + goodly, adv.] Not well; ill. He was ungoodly served ther in. Paston Letters, III. 125, ungored! (un-gérd’), a. [<un-1+ gore] + -ed?.] Not stained or marked with gore; unbloodied. [Rare.] ainst all Helms of gold Vngoard with bloud, Sylvester, The Vacation, p. 288. (Davies.) ungored2 (un-gérd’),a. [< wn-1 + gore2 + -ed?.] Not gored; not wounded as with a horn or spear. I have a voice and precedent of peace, To keep my name ungored. Shak., Hamlet, v. 2. 261.

ungorged.c: ungorged (un-gérjd’), a. Not gorged; not filled; not sated. Ungorged with flesh and blood. Dryden, Theodore and Honoria.

ungorgeous.c: ungorgeous (un-gér’jus), a. Not gorgeous; not showy or splendid. Carlyle, French Rey., IL. iv. 8. (Davies.) [Rare.]

ungottenungot.c: ungotten, ungot (un-got’n, -got’), a. 1. Not gained. Daniel, Civil Wars, vii.— 2+. Not begotten. Ungotten and unborn. Shak., Hen. V., i. 2. 287.

ungovernable.c: ungovernable (un-guv’ér-na-bl), a 1. Inea- pable of being governed, ruled, or restrained; not to be regulated by laws or rules; refractory; unruly.; So ungovernable a poet cannot be translated literally. Dryden. I trust... that our enemies, who predict that the indulgence will make us more insolent and ungovernable, may find themselves false prophets. Franklin, Autobiography, p. 380. 2. Licentious; wild; unbridled: as, wngovern- able passions.=Syn, Unmanageable, intractable, uncontrollable. See govern.

ungovernably.c: ungovernably (un-guv’ér-na-bli), adv. In an ungovernable manner; so as not to be governed - or restrained. Goldsmith. a Cr ungoverned

ungoverned.c: ungoverned (un-guv’érnd), a. 1. Not governed; having no government; anarchical. The estate is green and yet wngovern’d. Shak., Rich, TIL, ii. 2. 127. 2. Not controlled; not subjected to government or law; not restrained or regulated; unmanaged; unbridled; licentious: as, ungoverned passions. To serve ungoverned appetite. Milton, P. L., xi. 517.

ungown.c: ungown (un-goun’), vt [<wn-2+ gown.] To remove from the clerical function; degrade from the position of priest or clergyman. Compare uncowl, unfrock.

ungraced.c: ungraced (un-grast’), a. vored; not honored. Ungraced, without authority or mark. B. Jonson, Catiline, i. 1.

ungraceful.c: ungraceful (un-gras’ful), a. Not graceful; lacking grace or elegance; inelegant; clumsy: as, ungraceful manners. Nor are thy lips ungraceful. Milton, P. L., viii. 218. The other oak remaining a blackened and ungraceful Not graced; not fa- trunk, Scott.

ungracefully.c: ungracefully (un-gras’ful-i), adv. In an ungraceful manner; awkwardly; inelegantly. Spectator.

ungracefulness.c: ungracefulness (un-gras’fil-nes),n. The quality of being ungraceful; want of gracefulness; awkwardness: as, ungracefulness of manners. Locke.

ungracious.c: ungracious (un-gra’shus), a. 1. Rude; unmannerly; odious; hateful; brutal. How ungracious a thing this ambition is. Latimer, Mise. Sel. Ungracious wretch! Fit for the mountains and the barbarous caves, Where manners ne’er were preached. Shak., T. N., iv. 1. 51. 2. Offensive; disagreeable; unpleasing; unacceptable. Parts which are ungracious to the sight. Dryden, ty. of Juvenal, x. 543. Anything of grace toward the Irish rebels was as wn- gracious at Oxford as at London. Clarendon, Great Rebellion. 3. Showing no grace; impious; wicked. Swearest thou, ungracious boy? Shak., 1 Hen. IV., ii. 4. 490.

ungraciously.c: ungraciously (un-gra’shus-li), adv. In an ungracious manner; with disfavor: as, the proposal was received ungraciously. This that with gyle was geten wngraciouslich is pended. Piers Plowman (B), xv. 129.

ungraciousness.c: ungraciousness (un-gra’shus-nes), ». The character of being ungracious. Jer. Taylor.

ungraining.c: ungraining (un-gra’ning), ». The act or process of removing the grain of something. Gild- er’s Manual, p. 23.

ungrammatical.c: ungrammatical (un-gra-mat’i-kal), a. Not according to the established rules of grammar.

ungrammatically.c: ungrammatically (un-gra-mat’i-kal-i), adv. In a manner contrary to the rules of grammar.

ungrateful.c: ungrateful (un-grat’fil), a. 1. Not grateful; not feeling thankful or showing gratitude for favors; not making returns, or making ill returns, for kindness. I cared not to oblige an ungrateful age; and perhaps the world is delivered by it from a fardle of impertinences. Evelyn, To Samuel Pepys, Esq. 2. Exhibiting ingratitude; characterized by ingratitude: as, ungrateful conduct; ungrateful words.— 8. Giving no return or recompense; offering no inducement: as, ‘‘th’ ungrateful plain,” Dryden. To abate his zeal For his ungrateful cause. Wordsworth, Excursion, vi. 4, Unpleasing; unacceptable; disagreeable. It will not be altogether an ungrateful study. B. Jonson, Cynthia's Revels, ii. 1. =Syn. 1. See grateful.

ungratefully.c: ungratefully (un-grat’fil-i), adv. In an ungrateful manner. Fletcher, Humorous Lieutenant, iii. 7.

ungratefulness.c: ungratefulness (un-grat’fil-nes),n. The state or character of being ungrateful, in any sense.

ungratet.c: ungratet (un-grat’),a.andn. [< un-1 + grate3. Cf. ingrate and ungrateful.| I, a. 1. Not agreeable.— 2. Ungrateful. But, Carthage, fie! It cannot be wngrate, faithless through feare. Marston, Sophonisha, ii. 2. 5 me m. An ungrateful person; an ingrate. wife.

ungratified.c: ungratified (un-grat’i-fid), a. Not gratified; not satisfied; not indulged. 6611 Should turn thee away ungratified. Beau. and Fil., Honest Man’s Fortune, i.

ungrave.c: ungrave (un-grav’), a. [< un-1+ grave3.] Not grave or serious. Davies. ungraved! (un-gravd’),a. [< wn-l + gravel + -ed2.] Not engraved; not carved. ungraved? (un-gravd’), a. [< wn-2 + grave? + -ed2.] Unburied; not placed in a grave; not interred. Surrey, Aineid, iv.

ungravely.c: ungravely (un-grav’li), adv. Without gravity or seriousness; without dignity; indecently. Shak., Cor., ii. 3. 233, [Rare.]

ungravet.c: ungravet (un-grav’), v.t [« un-2 + grave2.] To take out of the grave; disinter. Fuller, Ch. Hist., IV. ii. 53. (Davies.)

ungreablet.c: ungreablet, a. An erroneous form of Middle English unagreeable, occurring in the sixteenth- century editions of Chaucer.

ungreediness.c: ungreediness (un-gré’di-nes), n. The character of being not greedy, in any sense. Hncyc. Brit., XX. 610.

ungreen.c: ungreen (un-grén’),a. [< ME. wngrene, < AS. wngréne; asun-1 + green.| Not green; decay- With seer branches, blossoms ungreen. Rom. of the Rose, 1. 4749.

ungrounded.c: ungrounded (un-groun’ded), a Having no foundation or support; not grounded; unfounded: as, ungrounded hopes or confidence. (She] confessed that what she had spoken against the magistrates at the court (by way of revelation) was rash and ungrounded. Winthrop, Hist. New England, I. 310.

ungroundedly.c: ungroundedly (un-groun’ded-li), adv. In an ungrounded manner; without ground or support; without reason. Bale.

ungroundedness.c: ungroundedness (un-groun’ded-nes), ». The state or quality of being ungrounded; want of foundation or support. Steele.

ungrown.c: ungrown (un-grdn’), a. Not grown; immature. My ungrown muse. P. Fletcher, Purple Island, vi.

ungrubbed.c: ungrubbed (un-grubd’), a. [< ME. wngrobbed; < un-2 + grubbed, pp. of grub.] Not dug about. Unkorven and ungrobbed lay the vine. Chaucer, Former Age, 1. 14.

ungrudging.c: ungrudging (un-gruj’/ing), a. Not grudging; freely giving; liberal; hearty. No ungrudging hand. Lamb.

ungrudgingly.c: ungrudgingly (un-gruj’ing-li), adv. In an ungrudging manner; without grudge; heartily; cheerfully: as, to bestow charity ungrudgingly. Receive from him the doom ungrudgingly. Donne.

ungual.c: ungual (ung’gwal), a. [Sometimes ungueal; < L. unguis, nail, claw (see unguis), + -al.] Of, pertaining to, shaped like, or bearing a nail, claw, or hoof; unguicular; ungular.—Ungual matrix, the root of the nail.—Ungual phalanx. See phalanx.

unguarded.c: unguarded (un-giir’ded), a. 1. Not guarded; not watched; not defended; having no guard. Her unguarded nest. Shak., Hen. V., i. 2. 170. Took a fatal advantage of some unguarded hour. Macaulay, Hist. Eng., xv. 2. Careless; negligent; not cautious; not done or spoken with caution: as, an unguarded expression or action; to be unguarded in conversation. Every unguarded word uttered by him was noted down. Macaulay, Hist. Eng., vi. I feel that I have betrayed myself perpetually;— so unguarded in speaking of my partiality for the church! Jane Austen, Northanger Abbey, p. 94.

unguardedly.c: unguardedly (un-giir’ded-li), adv. In an unguarded manner; without watchful attention to danger; without caution; carelessly: as, to speak or promise unguardedly.

unguardedness.c: unguardedness (un-giir’ded-nes), n. The state of being unguarded. Quarterly Rev.

unguardt.c: unguardt (un-gird’), v. t [< wn-2 + guard.] To deprive of a guard; render defenseless. Some wellchosen presents from the philosopher so softened and unguarded the girl’s heart that a favorable opportunity became irresistible. Fielding, Tom Jones, v. 5.

ungueal.c: ungueal (ung’gwé-al), a Same as ungual. Imp. Dict. (Rare.]

unguent.c: unguent (ung’gwent),”. [< ME. unguent = F. onguent = Pr. onguen, inguen, unguent = Sp. Pg. It. unguento, < L. unguentum, ointment, < unsere, unguere, smear, anoint, = Skt. air, smear, anoint. From the L. verb are also ult. E. unction, unctuous, oint, anoint, ointment, inunction, etc.] Any soft composition used as an ointment or for lubrication. Have odour like her unguent. Palladius, Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 109, And tho’ your Unguents bear th’ Athenian Name, The Wooll’s unsav’ry Scent is still the same. Congreve, tr. of Ovid’s Art of Love, unguiferous

unguentary.c: unguentary (ung’gwen-ta-ri), a. [=Sp. Pg. It. unguentaria, < L. unguentarium, of or pertaining to ointment, < unguentum, ointment: see wn- guest.) Of or pertaining to unguents.—Un- guentary vase, a small vase for unguents.

unguento.c: unguento (ung-gwen’to), n. [It. unguento: see unguent.] An unguent. ’Tis this blessed unguento, this rare extraction, that hath only power to disperse all malignant humours. B. Jonson, Volpone, ii. L

unguentous.c: unguentous (ung-gwen’tus), a [< waguent + -ous.] Like an unguent, or partaking of its qualities. Wright. [Rare.] ungues, ”. Plural of unguis.

unguessed.c: unguessed (un-gest’), a. Not arrived at or attained by guess or conjecture; unsuspected. Spenser. And there by night and there by day The worm unguent and breeding lay. Bulwer, tr. of Schiller’s Fight with the Dragon, p. 73.

unguical.c: unguical (ung’gwi-kal), a. [< L. unguis, nail, claw, + -ic-al.] Like a nail or claw; ungual; unguicular. [Rare.]

unguicorn.c: unguicorn (ung’gwi-kérn), ». [< L. unguis, nail, claw, hook, + cornu, horn.] In ornith., the horny sheath of the tip of the upper mandible, when distinct from the rest of the pieces composing the sheath of the bill, as it is in ducks, geese, petrels, ete.; the dertrotheca. The inferior unguicorn is the corresponding sheath of the tip of the under mandible. Also called myxotheca. The unguicorn or dertrotheca is large and strong [in the albatross]. Coues, Proc. Phila. Acad., 1866, p. 276.

unguicular.c: unguicular (ung-gwik’i-lir), a. [< L. wngui- culus, dim. of unguis, nail, claw, + -ar3.] 1. Of or pertaining to a nail or claw; bearing claws; ungual.—2. Of the length of an unguis or human finger-nail; about half an inch long.—Unguicular joint of the tarsus, in entom., the last tarsal joint, to which the ungues are attached.

unguiculata.c: Unguiculata (ung-gwik-a-la’ta), n. pl. [NL., neut. pl. of unguiculatus: see unguiculate.| In the Linnean classification, one of the primary divisions, a subclass or superorder, of the Mammalia, including the four orders Bruta, Glires, Fere, and Primates, or the edentates, rodents, carnivores, and quadrumane (including man): correlated with Ungulata, or hoofed quadrupeds, and the cetaceans. [Not now used in any exact classificatory sense, though available as a designation. |

unguiculate.c: unguiculate (ung-ewik’i-lat),a.andn. [=F. unguicule = Sp. unguiculado, < NL. unguiculatus, < L. ungiculus, nail, claw: see ungiculus.] I. a. 1. Having nails or claws, as distinguished from hoofs; not ungulate nor muticous, as a mammal; belonging to the Unguiculata.— 2, In bot., furnished with a claw or claw-like base; clawed: said of petals; also, ending in a point like a claw.—38. In entom., hooked, as if clawed.—Unguiculate antenne or palpi, antenne or palpi in which the last joint is slender and curved, resembling a claw.—Unguiculate maxilla, subchelate maxillae, whose lacinia or external lobe has at its apex a slender tooth which can be folded down on the lobe itself, as in the Cicindelide.—Unguiculate tibia, in entom., a tibia which has the external apical angle prolonged in a more or less incurved and pointed process: distinguished from the mucronate tibia, in which there is a similar prolongation on the inner side. I. n. A member of the Unguiculata.

unguidably.c: unguidably (un-gi‘da-bli), adv. In an unguidable manner. Carlyle.

unguided.c: unguided (un-gi’ded), a. led or conducted. [{< wn- Incapable of be- 1. Not guided; not A stranger Unguided and unfriended. Shak., T. N., iii. 3. 10. 2. Not regulated; ungoverned. The accidental, unguided motions of blind matter. Locke,

unguiferous.c: unguiferous (ung-gwif’e-rus), a. [< L. unguis, nail, claw, + ferre = E. bear.] 1. Bearing an unguis of any kind: as, the terminal or wn- guiferous phalanx of a digit.—2. Having unguiferous phalanges or digits; unguiculate or ungulate, as a quadruped.— Unguiferous prolegs, in entom., those false or deciduous legs of a caterpillar which are armed beneath with many minute hooks, unguiform

unguiform.c: unguiform (ung’gwi-férm), a. [= F. ongui- forme; < Li. unguis, nail, claw, + forma, form.] Shaped like a claw; hooked; unciform.—Un- uniform mandibles, in entom., mandibles which are on, parallel-sided, and curved downward, as in the lar- vee of many Diptera.

unguiltiness.c: unguiltiness (un-gil’ti-nes), ». The character or state of being unguilty or innocent; innocence. Your conscience knows my heart’s unguiltiness. Chapman, Alphonsus, Emperor of Germany, v. 2.

unguilty.c: unguilty (un-gil’ti), a [<¢ ME. wngylty, on- gulty (also, with F. term., wngiltif), < AS. ungyl- tig, not guilty; as wn-1 + guilty.) Not guilty; innocent. Wyelif.

unguinal.c: unguinal (ung’gwi-nal), a. [= Sp. inguinal, < L. wnguis, nail, claw: see unguis.} Of or pertaining to the unguis, or human nail. [Rare.] Dr. reports a case of reproduction of the entire unguinal phalanx of the thumb by a single bone-graft (Pacific Med. Jour.). Pop. Sci. News, XXIII. 143.

unguinous.c: unguinous (ung’gwi-nus), a. [< L. wnguinosus, full of fat or oil, < wngere, unguere, smear, anoint: see unguent.] Oily; unctuous; consisting of fat or oil, or resembling it.

unguirostral.c: unguirostral (ung-gwi-ros’tral), a. [« L. wn- guis, nail, claw, + rostrum, beak.] Having a nail at the end of the bill, as a duck or goose.

unguirostres.c: Unguirostres (ung-gwi-ros’tréz), n. pl. [NL.: see unguirostral.| In ornith., in Nitzsch’s classification, the duck family: so called from the nail at the end of the bill: equivalent to the Lamellirostres or Anseres of authors, exclusive of the flamingos.

unguis.c: unguis (ung’gwis),.; pl. wngues(-gwéz). [NL., < L. unguis, nail, claw, talon, hoof, = Gr. dove, nail, claw: see nail andonyx.] 1. Anail, claw, or hoof of any animal.— 2+. A measure of length, about half an inch.—3. In anat.: (a) The human lacrymal bone: so ealled because it resembles the human finger-nail: more fully called os unguis. (b) The hippocampus minor, or clear, of the brain. Also wnguis avis, unguis Halleri.—4. In entom., one of the curved claws at the extremity of an insect’s tarsus. Generally there are two of these on each tarsus, but they may be united; sometimes there is a projection or claw-like organ, the onychium or empodium, between the true claws. The ungues are attached to a very small piece, which, according to Huxley, is a true joint, though the preceding joint is generally called the last of the tarsus: this piece may be expanded beneath into a cushion-like organ, the pulvillus. Some entomologists apply the term unguis to the last tarsal joint, including the two claws, which are then distinguished as unguicule, The ungues assume various forms, which are of great importance in classification. The two claws may be more or less united or connate, even nearly to the tips. When forming only a slight angle with each other they are said to be divergent, and when spreading widely they are divaricate. They are cleft when each claw is split from the tip so that there is an upper and a lower division; unequally cleft when these divisions are of unequal size; cleft with movable parts when the divisions are movable on each other; bifid when the divisions are side by side instead of one over the other. According to the processes on the lower or concave surface, ungues are toothed when each has one pointed process; serrate when there are several small pointed teeth; serrulate when these processes are fine and bristle-like; pectinate when they are long, slender, and numerous; appendiculate when each claw has a membranous appendicle beneath. The claws may be unequal in size; and when they can be turned back on the last tarsal joint they are said to be subchelate. 5. In bot., the claw or lower contracted part of some petals, by which they are attached to the receptacle, as in the pink, the mustard, Cleome, etc. It is analogous to the petiole of a leaf. Also ungula. See cut under claw.

ungula.c: ungula (ung’gi-lii), ».; pl. angule (-1é). [NL., < L. ungula, claw, talon, hoof, dim. of wnguwis, nail, claw, talon, hoof: see wnguis.}] 1. A slightly hooked or blunt nail—that is, a hoof, as of the horse, ox, etc.; also, a claw or nail of any kind; a talon.— 2. In geom., a part cut off from a cylinder, cone, etc., by a plane passing obliquely through the base and part of the curved surface: so named from its resemblance to the hoof of a horse.—3. In surg., an instrument for extracting a dead fetus from the womb.—4, In bot., same as wnguis, 5.— 5. [ap.] [NL. (Pander, 1830).] A genus of brachiopods: same as Obolus, 3, and Ungulites.

ungular.c: ungular (ung’gi-lir), a. [< ungula + -ar3.] Of the character of an ungula; ungual.

ungulata.c: Ungulata (ung-gi-la’tii), n. pl. [NL., neut. pl. of LL. ungulates, having claws or hoofs: see ungulate.| In the Linnean classification, one of the primary divisions, a subclass or superorder, of Mammalia, including all the hoofed 5 te eds, the two Linnean orders Pecora and elle (except the elephant and walrus, which Not guiltily; in, 6612 Linneeus placed in Bruta, an order of his Unguiculata). The Ungulata were thus nearly equivalent to the orders Pachydermata, Solidungula, and Ruminantia, and correspond to the modern orders Artiodactyla (the ruminants, pigs, and hippopotamuses) and Perissodactyla (horses, tapirs, and rhinoceroses), together with the Proboscidea and Hyracoidea, and certain fossil groups, as the Ainblypoda. The term, like the correlated Unguwicu- lata, has lapsed from a strict classificatory sense, but is still used as a convenient designation of hoofed quadrupeds collectively or indiscriminately.

ungulate.c: ungulate (ung’ gi-lat), a. and». [< LL. w- gulatus, having claws or hoofs, ¢ L. wngula, claw, talon, hoof: see wngula, unguis.] I, a. 1. Shaped or formed into a hoof; hoof-like; ungulous.—2. Hoofed, as a quadruped, like the horse, ox, etc.; belonging to the Ungulata. See ee multungulate, solidungulate, subungu- ate. ITI, n. An ungulate or hoofed quadruped.

unguled.c: unguled (ung’guld), a. In her., having hoofs: noting ruminant animals. The epithet is used only when the hoofs are of a different tincture from the rest of the bearing.

unguligrada.c: Unguligrada (ung-gi-lig’ra-dii), v. pl. [NL., neut. pl. of wnguligradus: see unguligrade.| A division of ruminant ungulates; the ruminants proper, exclusive of the Camelidz; the Pecora unguligrade, contrasted as a series with the Pecora tylopoda or Phalangigrada, the latter including only the camel family. Also Ungu- lograda.

unguligrade.c: unguligrade (ung’gi-li-grad), a. and n. [< NL. unguligradus, ¢ L. ungula, hoof, + gradi, walk.] I, a. Walking upon hoofs; having true hoofs; cloven-footed, as a ruminant, or solidungulate, as the horse; belonging to the Ungu- ligrada; not phalangigrade or tylopod. II, ». An unguligrade quadruped.

ungulina.c: Ungulina (ung-gi-li’‘ni), m. [NL. (Bosco, or Oken, 1815), dim. of L. wngula, claw, hoof: see ungula.) A genus of bivalves, typical of the family Ungulinidz, whose few species are African, and live on coral.

ungulite.c: ungulite (ung’gi-lit), n. A brachiopod of the genus Ungulites (or Obolus).

ungulitegrit.c: ungulite-grit (ung’gi-lit-grit), m. A division of the Lower Silurian, extending from near Lake Ladoga to beyond Reval on the Gulf of Finland, and characterized by the presence of so-called ungulites (Obolus apollinis), one of the characteristic brachiopods of the primordial fauna. So named by Pander.

ungulites.c: Ungulites (ung-gu-li’téz), ». [NL. (Bronn, 1848), < L. ungula, a hoof.] A genus of brach- isopods: same as Obolus, 3. Also Ungula.

ungulous.c: ungulous (ung’gu-lus), a. [< L. wngula, hoof, + -ous.] Pertaining to or resembling a hoof; ungulate.

ungum.c: ungum (un-gum’), v. t [< wn-2 + gum2.] To remove gum from; free from gum or a gummy substance, or from stickiness; degum. When ungummed, bleached, and combed, it [ramie] forms the strong brilliant staple now used in the manufacture of Japanese silks. Bramwell, Wool-Carding, p. 67.

ungyve.c: ungyve (un-jiv’),v. t. [<un-2 + gyve.] To free from fetters or handcuffs. [Rare.] Commanded hym to be vngyued and set at libertie. Sir 7. Elyot, The Governour, ii. 6. unhabile} (un-hab’il), a. [< wn-1 + habile. Cf. unable.] Unfit; unsuitable. Puttynge out of their citie their women and all that were of yeres unhabile for the warres,... they [the Petilians] obstinately defended their walles. Sir T. Elyot, The Governour, iii. 6.

unhabitable.c: unhabitable (un-hab’i-ta-bl), a. Uninhabitable. [Obsolete or rare.] We offer vnto yowe the Equinoctiall line hitherto vn- knowen and burnt by the furious heat of the soonee, and wnhabitable after the opinion of the wolde writers, a fewe excepted. Peter Martyr (tr. in Eden’s First Books on America, [ed. Arber, p. 64). Hitherto they had all the like opinion, that vnder the line Equinoctiall for much heat the land was vnhabitable. Hakluyt’s Voyages, I. 219.

unhacked.c: unhacked (un-hakt’), a. Not hacked; not cut or mangled; not notched. With unhack’d swords and helmets all unbruised, We will bear home that lusty blood again. Shak., K. John, ii. 1. 254.

unhackneyed.c: unhackneyed (un-hak’nid), a. Not hackneyed; not worn out or rendered stale, flat, or common-place by frequent use-or repetition.

unhair.c: unhair (un-har’), v. [<« ME. wnheeren; < un-2 + hair.] I. trans. To deprive of hair; remove the hair from; depilate: as, to unhair skins or hides. Wyclif, Ezek. xxix. 18. I'll unhair thy head. Shak., A. and C., ii. 5. 64. unhandy Screens of willow matting or unhaired skins. Morgan, Contrib, to American Ethnology, p. 127 II. intrans. To become free from hair. The hide is said to unhair in 24 hours, Workshop Receipts, 2d ser., p. 370.

unhairingbeam.c: unhairing-beam (un-har’ing-bém), n. In lea- ther-manuf., a semicylindrical beam resting on a support at one end and on the floor at the other, so that it has an inclined position: used to support the hides as they come from the lime-pits, and to hold them for treatment with the unhairing-knife.

unhairingknife.c: unhairing-knife (un-har’ing-nif), n. In leather-manuf., a two-handled iron scraper used to scrape the hair from hides after they are taken from the lime-pits. Compare wnhairing-beam.

unhairingmachine.c: unhairing-machine (un-har’ing-ma-shén’), ». A machine for removing the hair from hides. It consists of two cylinders between which the hides are passed, one cylinder carrying spiral scrapers, and the other below it caused, by suitable gearing, to revolve at a less speed.

unhale.c: unhale (un-hal’),a. [< wn-1 + hale?. Cf. unwhole.] Unsound; not healthy. Waterhouse, Apology for Learning.

unhallow.c: unhallow (un-hal’6), v. ¢ To profane; dese- erate. Acvorth chyrche vnhalwed was, theruor hym was wo. Robert of Gloucester, p. 349, ThisKing hath as it were unhallowed and unchristened the very duty of prayer itself. Milton, Hikonoklastes, § 1.

unhallowed.c: unhallowed (un-hal’6d), a. 1. Not hallowed, consecrated, or dedicated to sacred purposes. Let never day nor night unhallow’d pass. . Shak., 2 Hen. VIL, ii. 1. 85. 2. Unholy; profane; impious. Unhallow’d hand I dare not bring so near yon sacred place. Fletcher, Faithful Shepherdess, v. 5.

unhallowing.c: unhallowing (un-hal’6-ing), n. The act or process of profaning or desecrating; profanation. Who cannot but see the mass, which maketh to the profanation and unhallowing both of body and soul, to be forbidden. J. Bradford, Works (Parker Soc., 1853), IT. 323.

unhampered.c: unhampered (un-ham’pérd), a. Not hampered, hindered, or restricted. Let soar The soul unhampered by a featherweight. Browning, Ring and Book, I. 116.

unhand.c: unhand (un-hand’),v.¢. [< un-2 + hand.] To take the hand or hands from; release from a grasp; let go. Unhand me, gentlemen. By Heaven, I'll make a ghost of him that lets me! Shak., Hamlet, i. 4, 84. What do you mean? Unhand me; or, by Heaven, I shall be very angry! this is rudeness. Beau. and Fl., Captain, i. 3.

unhandily.c: unhandily (un-han’di-li), adv. In an unhandy manner; awkwardly; clumsily.

unhandiness.c: unhandiness (un-han‘di-nes), ». The state or character of being unhandy; want of dexterity; clumsiness.

unhandled.c: unhandled (un-han’dld), a. 1. Not handled; not touched; not treated or managed. Left the cause o’ the king unhandled. Shak., Hen. VIII., iii. 2. 58. 2. Not accustomed to being used; not trained or broken in. [Rare.] Youthful and unhandled colts. hak., M. of V., v. 1. 72.

unhandsome.c: unhandsome (un-han’sum), a. 1+. Not well adapted for being handled or used; inconvenient; awkward; untoward; unmanageable; unhandy. Then the intermedial evil to a wise and religious person is like unhandsome and ill-tasted physick. Jer. Taylor, Rule of Conscience, i. 5. 2. Not handsome; not good-looking; not well-formed; not beautiful. Were she other than she is, she were unhandsome. Shak., Much Ado, i. 1. 177. 38. Not generous or decorous; not liberal; unfair; disingenuous; mean; unbecoming. Being taken before the Governor, he demanded my passe, to which he set his hand, and asked 2 rix-dollars for a fee, ch methought appeared very unhandsome in a Soldier of his quality. Evelyn, Diary, Oct. 2, 1641.

unhandsomely.c: unhandsomely (un-han’sum-li), adv. In an unhandsome manner, in any sense. A good thing done unhandsomely turns ill. Browning Ring and Book, IT. 88.

unhandsomeness.c: unhandsomeness (un-han’sum-nes), ». The state or character of being unhandsome, in any sense. Sir P. Sidney.

unhandy.c: unhandy (un-han’di), a. Not handy, in any sense; awkward; inconvenient. unhang

unhang.c: unhang (un-hang’), v. t.; pret. and pp. unhung _ or unhanged, ppr. unhanging. [< un-2 + hang.] 1. To take or remove from a hanging position, as a picture or a bell, or a rapier from its hangers; also, to remove from its hinges or similar supports, as a door, a gate, or a shutter. Lend me thy boy to unhang my rapier. B. Jonson, Case is Altered, v. 2. 2. To deprive of hangings, as a room. Sed, (an-hangd’), a. [< ME. unhanged, onhanged; < un-1 + hanged.) Not hanged; not punished by hanging. Also unhung. Thou on-hanged harlot, hark what I same. York Plays, p. 313. There live not three good men unhanged in England. Shak., 1 Hen. IV., ii. 4. 144.

unhappily.c: unhappily (un-hap’i-li), adv. 1. Inan unhappy manner; unfortunately; miserably; evilly: as, to live unhappily. LIucrece the chaste. Haply that name of ‘‘ chaste” unhappily set This bateless edge on his keen appetite. Shak., Lucrece, 1. 8. Unhappily deceived. Milton. 2. By ill fortune; as ill luck would have it; to some one’s misfortune: as, unhappily I missed seeing him. The commonplace is unhappily within reach of us all. Lowell, New Princeton Rev., I. 177. 8. Not suitably or appropriately; not aptly.— 4+. Trickishly; mischievously. ares.

unhappiness.c: unhappiness (un-hap’i-nes), n. 1. The state or character of being unhappy, in any sense.— 2. Misfortune; ill luck. It is our great unhappiness, when any calamities fall upon us, that we are uneasy and dissatisfied. Abp. Wake. 38+. A mischievous prank; wildness. _Iam Don Sanchio’s steward’s son, a wild boy, That for the fruits of his unhappiness Is fain to seek the wars. Fletcher and another, Love’s Pilgrimage, ii. 2.

unhappy.c: unhappy (un-hap’i), a. [< ME. unhappy, unhappi, unhappy; <un-1 + happy.) 1. Not happy. (a) Not cheerful or gay; in some degree miserable or wretched; cast down; sad. Ay me, unhappy! Tobeaqueen! Shak., 2 Hen. VL, iii. 2. 70. Unhappy consort of a king distrest! Partake the troubles of thy husband’s breast. Pope, Iliad, xxiv. 234. (0) Marked by or associated with ill fortune, infelicity, or mishap; inauspicious; ill-omened; calamitous; evil; lamentable. “T must,” quod he, “telle yow myn avise and extent; The quene is cause of this unhappy case.” Generydes (B. E. T. S.), 1. 982. Unhappy was the clock That struck the hour. Shak., Cymbeline, v. 5. 153. My dreams are like my thoughts, honest and innocent; Yours are unhappy. Fletcher and Rowley, Maid in the Mill, i. 1. Nothing indeed can be more unhappy than the condition of bankruptcy. Steele, Spectator, No. 456. (c) Not felicitous; not well suited or appropriate; not apt. 2. Not having good hap, fortune, or luck; unfortunate; unlucky. Tam little unhappy in the mould of my face, which is not quite so long as it is broad. Steele, Spectator, No. 17. 8+. Full of tricks; mischievous; tricksy. Laf. A shrewd knave, and an unhappy. Count. So he is. My lord that’s gone made himself much sport out of him. Shak., All’s Well, iv. 5. 66. Ay, and beat him well; he’s an unhappy boy. Beau. and I’l., Knight of Burning Pestle, ii. 4. =Syn. 1. Downcast, cheerless. unhappy} (un-hap’i), v. ¢. Shak., Rich. I1., iii. 1. 10.

unhapt.c: unhapt (un-hap’), ». [< ME. wnhappe, unhap, onhap, unhep (= Ieel. ihapp); < un-1 + hap!.) Tl luck; misfortune. Sadly the segge hym in his sadel sette, As non wnhap had hym ailed. Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight (E. E. T. 8.), 1. 438. Now certes, friend, I drede of thyn unhappy. Chaucer, Envoy to Scogan, 1. 29.

unharboredunharboured.c: unharbored, unharboured (un-hir’bord), a. Not sheltered; affording no shelter. [Rare.] Trace huge forests and unharbour’d heaths. Milton, Comus, 1. 423.

unharborunharbour.c: unharbor, unharbour (un-hir’bor),v.t. [<wn-2 + harbor.) To drive from harbor or shelter; dislodge: a hunters’ word. note, Devil upon Two Sticks, i.

unhardened.c: unhardened (un-hir’dnd), a. Not hardened; not indurated: literally or figuratively. Messengers Of strong prevailment in wnharden’d youth. Shak., M. N. D., i. 1. 35.

unhardy.c: unhardy (un-hir’di), a [<« ME. wnhardy, unhard; <un-1 + hardy.) 1. Not hardy; not able To make unhappy. Tae «(| f 6613 to endure fatigue or adverse conditions; tender.— 2. Not having fortitude; not bold; timorous. Irresolute, unhardy, unadventurous. Milton, P. R., iii. 243.

unharmed.c: unharmed (un-hirmd’), a. Not harmed or injured. Shak., R. and J., i. 1. 217.

unharmful.c: unharmful (un-hirm’fil), a. Not harmful or doing harm; harmless; innoxious. Themselves unharmful, let them live unharmed. Dryden, Hind and Panther.

unharmfully.c: unharmfully (un-hirm’ful-i), adv. Harmlessly; innoxiously. Contemporary Rev., LIV. 676.

unharmonious.c: unharmonious (un-hiir-m0’ni-us), a. Inharmonious. Those pure immortal elements that know No gross, no unharmonious mixture. Milton, P. L., xi. 51.

unharness.c: unharness (un-hir’nes), v. t. [< wn-2 + harness.) 1. To strip of harness; loose from har- poe or gear; hence, to set free from work; re- ease. An unmerciful day’s work of sorrow till death unhar- | ness them. Milton, Divorce, ii. 21. The sweating steers unharnessed from the yoke. Dryden, tr. of Virgil’s Eclogues, ii. 96. 2. To remove armor or military dress from.

unhasp.c: unhasp (un-hasp’), v. t [« ME. unhaspen; < un-2 + hasp.] To loose from a hasp; let go. While bolt and chain he backward roll’d, And made the bar unhasp its hold. Scott, L. of the L., vi. 12.

unhasty.c: unhasty (un-has’ti), a. Not hasty; not precipitate; not rash; deliberate; slow. From her unhaste beast she did alight. Spenser, ¥. Q., I. iii. 4. He isaperfect man... whohath... so unhastyand wary a spirit as that he decrees upon no act before he hath considered maturely. Jer. Taylor, Works (ed. 1835), I. 843.

unhat.c: unhat (un-hat’),v.; pret. and pp. unhatted, ppr. unhatting. [< un-2 + hat.] I. trans. To remove the hat from. II, intrans. To take off the hat; uncover the head, as from politeness, or in worship. Unhatting on the knees when the host is carried by. H. Spencer. unhatched! (un-hacht’), a. [< wn-1 + hatch? + -ed2.]_ 1. Not hatched; not having left the age.— 2. Not matured and brought to light; not disclosed. Some unhatched practice. Shak., Othello, iii. 4. 141. unhatched?t (un-hacht’), a. [< un-1 + hatch + -ed2; or perhaps for wnhacked, not hacked.] Not hatched or marked with cuts or lines; not scratched or injured: applied in the quotations to a rapier not yet used in fight, both literally and figuratively. He is knight, dubb’d with unhatched rapier and on carpet consideration. Shak., T. N., iii. 4. 257. Tender and full of fears our blushing sex is, Unharden’d with relentless thoughts, wnhatch'd With blood and bloody practice. Beau. and Fi., Knight of Malta, ii. 5.

unhatting.c: unhatting (un-hat’ing), n. A taking off of the hat, especially as an act of politeness, as in making a bow. [Rare.] Bows, and curtseys, and unhatting. A. Spencer.

unhaunted.c: unhaunted (un-hiin’ted), a. Not haunted; not frequented; not resorted to; unvisited. A lone unhaunted place. Donne, Prog. of the Soul, i.

unhazarded.c: unhazarded (un-haz’iir-ded), a. Not exposed or submitted to hazard, chance, or danger; not ventured. Milton, S. A., 1. 809.

unhazardous.c: unhazardous (un-haz’ir-dus), a. Not hazardous; not full of risk or danger; free from risk or danger. Dryden, Duke of Guise, Epis.

unhead.c: unhead (un-hed’), v. t. [< wn-2 + head.] To take the head from; remove the head of; deprive of the head or of a head. You... did not only dare to uncrown, but to unhead a monarch, T. Brown, Works, ii. 216. (Davies.) unheal}} (un-hél’),. [< ME. wnheele, unhele, < AS. unh#lu, infirmity; as un-l + hall, n.] Miserable condition; misfortune; wretchedness. Envy alone That sory is of other mennes wele, And glad is of his sorwe and his unheele. Chaucer, Physician’s Tale, 1. 115. unheal2+ (un-hél’), v. ¢. [Early mod. E. unhele, unheel; < ME. wnheelen, wnhelen, < AS. unhelan, uncover; as wn-2 + heal2.] To uncover. Yit wol this werk the roote, as sum men telle, Unhele, or kirve, and colde it after quell. Palladius, Husbondrie (E. E. T. 8.), p. 46. Then suddenly both would themselves unhele, And th’ amorous sweet spoils to greedy eyes revels. Spenser, F. Q., II. xii. 64. unheeding

unhealable.c: unhealable (un-hé’la-bl), a. being healed; incurable. An unhealable sprain. Fuller.

unhealth.c: unhealth (un-helth’),». [< ME. wnhelthe; < un-2 + health.) Want of health; unhealthiness. Tens of thousands... lead sedentary and unwholesome lives... in dwellings, workshops, what not?— the influences, the very atmosphere of which tend not to health, but to unhealth, and to drunkenness as a solace under the feeling of unhealth and depression. Kingsley, Health and Education, p. 6.

unhealthful.c: unhealthful (un-helth’ful), a. Not healthful; injurious to health; insalubrious; unwholesome ; noxious, physically or morally: as, an unhealthful climate or air. Dryden, tr. of Juve- nal’s Satires, iv.

unhealthfully.c: unhealthfully (un-helth’ful-i), adv. In an unhealthful manner; unhealthily.

unhealthfulness.c: unhealthfulness (un-helth’fil-nes), ». The state of being unhealthful; unwholesomeness; insalubriousness. Bacon.

unhealthily.c: unhealthily (un-hel’thi-li), adv. wholesome or unsound manner. voree, Pref.

unhealthiness.c: unhealthiness (un-hel’thi-nes),. The state or character of being unhealthy, in any sense.

unhealthy.c: unhealthy (un-hel’thi), a. 1. Not healthy; lacking health; without vigor of growth; unsound: as, an unhealthy child; an unhealthy plant.—2. Not promoting health; unhealthful; unwholesome: as, unhealthy habits or food.— 3. Not indicating health; resulting from bad health; morbid: as, an unhealthy sign or eray- ing; an unhealthy appearance.—4. Morally unhealthful: as, unhealthy literature.

unheard.c: unheard (un-hérd’), a. 1. Not heard; not perceived by the ear. Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard Are sweeter. Keats, Ode on a Grecian Urn, 2. Not admitted to audience or given a hearing; not permitted to speak for one’s self. What pangs I feel unpitied and unheard. Dryden. Yet it was thought unjust to condemn him [Russell] wn- heard. Macaulay, Hist. Eng., xix. 3. Not known to fame; not celebrated. Nor was his name unheard. Milton, P. L., i. 788. Unheard-of, unprecedented; such as was never known or heard of before. We deeming it proper to apply some speedy Remedy to so enormous and unheard-of piece of Villany. Milton, Letters of State, March 28, 1650.

unhearset.c: unhearset (un-hérs’), v. t [Early mod. E. wn- hearse; < un-l + hearse1.] To remove from a hearse or monument. And himselfe baffuld, and his armes wnherst. Spenser, F. Q., V. iii. 37.

unheartt.c: unheartt (un-hirt’),v. t. [< un-2 + heart.] To discourage; depress; dishearten. Yet, to bite his lip And hum at good Cominius much wnhearts me. Shak., Cor., v. 1. 49. [< un-2 + heaven.] [Rare.] Not capable of In an un- Milton, Di-

unheaven.c: unheaven (un-hev’n), v. ¢. To remove from or deprive of heaven. Unheav'n yourselves, ye holy Cherubins. Davies, Holy Roode, p. 28.

unheavenly.c: unheavenly (un-hev’n-li), a. Not heavenly; not pertaining to, characteristic of, or suitable for heaven. Byron, Manfred, iii. 1. [Rare.]

unhedged.c: unhedged (un-hejd’), a. Not hedged. Our needful knowledge, like our needful food, Unhedged, lies open in life’s common field. Young, Night Thoughts, v.

unheeded.c: unheeded (un-hé’ded), a. Not heeded; disregarded; neglected; unnoticed. The world’s great victor passed unheeded by. Pope.

unheededly.c: unheededly (un-hé’ded-li), adv. Without being noticed. [Rare.] Beneath the fray An earthquake reeled unheededly away. Byron, Childe Harold, iv.

unheedful.c: unheedful (un-héd’fil), a 1. Not heedful; heedless; not cautious; inattentive; careless. Tennyson, The Gardener’s Daughter.—2. Not marked by caution or consideration; rash; inconsiderate. Unheedful vows may heedfully be broken. Shak., T. G. of V., ii. 6. 11.

unheedfully.c: unheedfully (un-héd’ful-i), adv. Carelessly; incautiously. Shak., T.G. of V., i. 2. 3.

unheedilyt.c: unheedilyt (un-hé’di-li), adv. In an unheeding manner; carelessly; unheedingly. Spenser, 1D, Os UVee-em BF

unheeding.c: unheeding (un-hé’ding), a. Not heeding; careless; negligent; heedless. He passed unmark’d by my unheeding eyes. Dryden. unheedingly

unheedy.c: unheedy (un-hé’di),a. 1. Unheeding; careless. So have I seen some tender slip... Pluck’d up by some unheedy swain. Milton, Epitaph on Marchioness of Winchester, 1. 38. 2. Precipitate; sudden. Wings and no eyes figure unheedy haste. Shak., M. N. D., i. 1. 237. unheel}t, v. t. See wnheal2.

unheired.c: unheired (un-ird’), a. Without an heir. To leave him utterly unheired. Chapman. unhelet, ». See unheal.

unhelm.c: unhelm (un-helm’), v.¢ [« un-2 + helm2.] To deprive of helm or helmet. Scott, Ivanhoe.

unhelpful.c: unhelpful (un-help’fil), a 1. Affording no aid. Shak.,2 Hen. VI., iii. 1. 218.—2. Unable to help one’s self; helpless. Ruskin.

unhelpfully.c: unhelpfully (un-help’ful-i), adv. In an unhelpful manner; without giving aid. unhende} (un-hend’), a. [< ME. unhende, on- hende; <un-1 + hend?.] Ungracious; discourteous; ungentle; hard. Then Am I thyne Enemye moste unhende. Political Poems, etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 190. ‘unheppen (un-hep’en), a. [< wn-1 + heppen, for *helen, holpen, pp. of help: see help.] _Misshapen; ill-formed; clumsy; awkward. Tennyson, The Village Wife. [Prov. Eng.] unheritable} (un-her’i-ta-bl), a. Barred from inheritance; disqualified as an heir. Thereby you [are] justly made illegitimate and wnher- table to the crown imperial of this realm. Heylin, Reformation, ii. 207. (Davies.)

unheroism.c: unheroism (un-her’6-izm), n. That which is not heroic; unheroic character or action; cowardice. ([Rare.] Their greedy quackeries and wnheroisms. Carlyle, Cromwell, i. 65.

unhesitating.c: unhesitating (un-hes’i-ta-ting), a. Not hesitating; without misgiving or doubt; prompt; ready.

unhidden.c: unhidden (un-hid’n), a. Not hidden or concealed; open; manifest. Shak., Hen. V.,i.1. 86. unhide} (un-hid’), v. ¢. [< ME. wnhiden; < wn-1 + hide1.] To reveal the nature of; disclose. Tyl I this romance may unhide. Rom. of the Rose, 1, 2168. unhilly, v. ¢t [ME. wnhillen, unhilen; < un-2 + hill2. Cf. unheal2.]- To uncover; unroof. And if his hous be whiled and reyne on his bedde, He seeth and seeth til he slepe dry. Piers Plowman (B), xvii. 319.

unhinge.c: unhinge (un-hinj’), v. t. 1. To take from the hinges: as, to unhinge a door. Paul’s midnight voice prevail’d, his music’s thunder Unhing’d the prison-doors, split bolts in sunder. Quarles, Emblems, v., Epig. 10. 2. To displace; unfix by violence. Rather than not accomplish my revenge, Just or unjust, I would the world wnhinge. Waller. 8. To unsettle; loosen; render unstable or wavering; discompose; disorder: as, to whinge the mind; to whinge opinions. Wingy mysteries in divinity, and airy subtleties in religion, which have unhinged the brains of better heads. Sir T. Browne, Religio Medici, i. 9,

unhingement.c: unhingement (un-hinj’ment), ». The act of unhinging, or the state of being unhinged. Imp. Dict. (Rare.]

unhistoric.c: unhistoric (un-his-tor’ik), a. 1. Not historic; not containing or conveying history; not being a part of recorded history; not noticed in history; unrecorded. Through how many ages this unhistoric night of European man may have preceded the dawn of civilisation it is at present vain to speculate. Encye. Brit., 11. 342. 2. Contrary to history. [Rare.] Under the influence of crude and wnhistoriec discussion of the subject... this conception of the American state has passed from the minds of large bodies of our people. e Bibliotheca Sacra, XLVI. 545. Of Disraeli, in 1874, there is an equally speculative and unhistoric judgment. The Academy, Dec. 27, 1890, p. 606.

unhitch.c: unhitch (un-hich’), v. t. To disengage from a hitch or fastening; set free; unfasten: as, to unhitch a horse.

unhive.c: unhive (un-hiv’),v.¢. 1. To drive from a hive. —2. To deprive of habitation or shelter. In an un- Not hired. Milton, 6614

unhoard.c: unhoard (un-hérd’), v.¢, To dissipate; scatter. Milton, P. L., iv. 188. [Rare.] unhold!+ (un-hold’), v. t [< un-1+ hold1.] To cease to hold; let go the hold of. Otway. unhold?}, a. [< ME. wnhold, < AS. unhold (= OS. OHG. unhold), < un-, not, + hold, faithful: see hold2.] Unfavorable; hostile.

unholet.c: unholet, a. A Middle English form of unwhole.

unholily.c: unholily (un-h6’li-li), adv. In an unholy manner. Je. Taylor, Rule of Conscience, ii. 3.

unholiness.c: unholiness (un-ho’li-nes),. The character or state of being unholy; want of holiness. The unholiness of obtruding upon men remission of sins for money. Raleigh.

unholsomt.c: unholsomt, a. A Middle English form of wn- wholesome.

unholy.c: unholy (un-hd’li), a. and n. I, a. Not holy. (a) Not sacred; not hallowed or consecrated. Doth it follow that all things now in the church are unholy which the Lord himself hath not precisely instituted? Hooker, Eccles. Polity. (b) Impious; wicked. Blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, wn- holy. 2 Tim. iii. 2. sh Lae (a) Unhallowed, unsanctified. (%) Profane, ungodly. II. n.; pl. wnholies (-liz). That which is [unrare.] How many other Unholies has your covering Art made holy, besides this Arabian Whinstone. Carlyle, Sartor Resartus.

unhomogeneousness.c: unhomogeneousness (un-h6-m6-jé’né-us-nes), n. The character or state of being unhomogeneous; heterogeneousness.

unhonestly.c: unhonestly (un-on’est-li), adv. [< ME. wn- honestly; < unhonest + -ly2.] Dishonestly; improperly ; unchastely. Speke neuer unhonestly of woman kynde. Babees Book (&. BE. T. 8.), p. 306. unhonesty}+ (un-on’es-ti), m. Dishonesty; impropriety; improper conduct. Unhonesty hath ever present pleasure in it, having neither good pretence going before, nor yet any profit following after. Ascham, Toxophilus (ed. 1864), p. 39.

unhonestt.c: unhonestt (un-on’est), a [< ME. wnhonest; < un-1 + honest.| Dishonest; dishonorable; not virtuous; unchaste. Whenne yee er sette, take none wnhoneste tale. Babecs Book (KE. E. T. 8.), p. 4. Then, lady, you must know, you are held wnhonest; The Duke, your brother, and your friends in court, .With too much grief condemn you. Beau. and Fl., Woman-Hater, v. 5.

unhonoredunhonoured.c: unhonored, unhonoured (un-on’ord), a. Not honored; not regarded with honor or veneration. Unwept, unhonour’d, and unsung. Scott, L. of L. M., vi. 1.

unhonortunhonourt.c: unhonort, unhonourt (un-on’or),v.t. [< ME. unhonoured; < un-2 + honor.] To dishonor. IT honour my Fadir, and ye han wnhonourid me. Wyclif, John viii.

unhooded.c: unhooded (un-hud’ed), a. Not having or not covered with a hood. Up soars one falcon unhooded, while the other is drawn from its uncertain perch on the head of the Arab to join the others. Harper’s Mag., LXXVII. 82.

unhook.c: unhook (un-huk’), v. ¢ To loose from a hook; open or undo by detaching the hook or hooks of.

unhoop.c: unhoop (un-hép’), v. t. 1. To remove the hoops of, as a barrel or cask.— 2. To remove the stiff petticoats or hoop-skirts of, as a woman: probably jocose, and with allusion to def. 1. Unhoop the fair sex, and cure this fashionable tympany got among them. addison.

unhoped.c: unhoped (un-hdpt’), a. Not hoped or looked for; unexpected; not so probable as to excite hope. Whatsoevere thou mayst sen that is don in this world unhoped or unwenyd. Chaucer, Boéthius, iv. prose 6. With unhop’d success. Dryden, Aneid, vii. 400. Unhoped-for, unhoped; not hoped for.

unhopeful.c: unhopeful (un-hop’ful), a. Not hopeful; leay- ing no room for hope; hopeless. Shak., Much Ado, ii. 1. 392.

unhopefully.c: unhopefully (un-hop’fil-i), adv. In an unhopeful manner; without hope; hopelessly. Fortnightly Rev., N. S., XLI. 833.

unhorse.c: unhorse (un-hérs’), v.t. [< ME. wnhorsen, on- horse; < un-2 + horse.) 1. To throw or strike down from a horse; cause to dismount or fall from the saddle. But thei were clene onhorsid in the feld. Generydes (E. E. T. 8.), 1. 2464. He would unhorse the lustiest challenger. Shak., Rich, IL, v. 3. 19. Uniat 2. To deprive of a horse or horses; remove the horse or horsesfrom. [Rare.] Maidens wave Their kerchiefs, and old women weep for joy; While others, not so satisfied, unhorse The gilded equipage, and, turning loose His steeds, usurp a place they well deserve. Cowper, Task, vi. 701.

unhostile.c: unhostile (un-hos’til), a 1. Not hostile; friendly.—2. Not pertaining to or caused by anenemy. [Rare.] By unhostile wounds destroy’d. J. Philips, Blenheim.

unhouse.c: unhouse (un-houz’), v. t 1. To drive from the house or habitation; dislodge. Milton, On the Death of a Fair Infant, 1. 21.—2. To deprive of shelter. Imp. Dict.

unhoused.c: unhoused (un-houzd’), a. 1. Not housed or sheltered as by a house; having no house or home. Whittier, Tent on the Beach.—2. Deprived of or driven from a house, home, roof, or shelter. Shak., T. of A., iv. 3. 229. unhouseled, unhouseled+ (un-hou’zeld), a. Not having received the sacrament. Cut off even in the blossom of my sin, Unhousel’d, disappointed, unaneled,. Shak., Hamlet, i. 5. 77. 1. Not human; R. L. Stevenson, [Rare.]
