unkempt.c: unkempt (un-kemt’), a. [A later form of unkembed, also unkemmed; < ME. unkempt; < wn-+ + kembed, kempt, pp. of kemb.] 1. Uncombed; disheveled: as, unkempt hair; hence, disorderly, —2. Figuratively, rough; unpolished. But ah! too well I wote my humble vaine, And howe my rimes bene rugged and unkempt. Spenser, Shep. Cal., November, The aspect of some lawless, unkempt genius. C. Tyler, Life of Patrick Henry, p. 16.

unkenned.c: unkenned (un-kend’), a. [Also unkend, unkent; <un-l + kenned, pp. of ken1.] Unknown. [Obsolete or dialectal.] To travel through unkenned lands. Greene, Alphonsus, iv.

unkennel.c: unkennel (un-ken’el), v. #.; pret. and pp. wn- kenneled, unkennelled, ppr. unkenneling, unkennelling. [< un-2 + kennell.] 1. To drive or force from a kennel; take out of a kennel. Shak., M. W. of W., iii. 3. 174.—2. To rouse from secrecy or retreat. Observe mine uncle, if his occulted guilt Do not itself wnkennel in one speech. Shak., Hamlet, iii. 2. 86.

unkensome.c: unkensome (un-ken’sum), a. [< wn-l + kent + -some.] Not recognizable. It’s unkensome we wad be. Archie of Ca’field (Child’s Ballads, VI. 90).

unkept.c: unkept (un-kept’), a. 1. Not kept; not retained; not preserved.—2. Not sustained, maintained, or tended. He... stays me here at home unkept. Shak., As you Like it, i. 1. 9. 3. Not observed; not obeyed, as a command. Hooker, Eecles. Polity, iv. § 14.

unkiarskelessi.c: Unkiar-Skelessi (on'ke-ar-ska-les'se), or Hun- kiar-Skelessi. A small place in Asia Minor, near Constantinople, where, in 1833, Russia and Turkey concluded a treaty favorable to the former. Unlearned Parliament, The. See Parliament of Dunces. Unnatural Combat, The. A play by Philip Massinger, acted about 1619, printed in 1639. Unready, The. An epithet of the Anglo-Saxon king JEthelred. See JEthelred,

unkind.c: unkind (un-kind’), a. [< ME. wnkinde, unkynde, uncunde, unkuynde, onkynde, onkende, < AS. un- hynde, ungecynde, not natural, < wn-, not, + ge- hynde, natural, kind: see kind1.] 1+. Not natural; unnatural. Therfor he, of ful avisement, Nolde never wrote in none of his sermons Of swiche unkynde abhominaciouns. Chaucer, Prol. to Man of Law’s Tale, 1. 88. 2. Not sympathetic; lacking in or not springing from or exhibiting kindness, benevolence, or affection; not kind; harsh; cruel. Rich gifts wax poor when givers prove unkind. Shak., Hamlet, iii. 1. 101,

unkindliness.c: unkindliness (un-kind’li-nes), ». The character of being unkindly; unkindness; unfavorableness. Tennyson, Merlin and Vivien.

unkindly.c: unkindly (un-kind’li), a. [< ME. unkindly, un- kyndely, unkundeliche, < AS. ungecyndelic, unge- cyndlic, unnatural, < wn-, not, + gecyndelic, natural, kindly: see kindly, a.] 1+. Unnatural; contrary to nature. And gan abhor her brood’s unkindly crime. Spenser, F. Q., II. x. 9. 2. Unfavorable; malignant. Forbidding every bleak unkindly fog. Milton, Comus, 1. 269. 3. Not kindly; unkind; ungracious: as, an wn- kindly manner.

unkindly (un-kind’li), adv. [< ME. unkindly, unkyndely, unkuyndeliche, unkyndelike,< AS. *un- gecyndelice, unnaturally, ¢ wn-, not, + gecynde- lice, naturally: see kindly, adv.) 1+. In a manner contrary to nature; unnaturally. Dronken Loth unkyndely Lay by his doughtren two unwityngly. Chaucer, Pardoner’s Tale, 1. 23. 2. In an unkind manner; without kindness or affection; ungraciously. Something unkindly she does take it, sir, To have her husband chosen to her hands, Beau. and Fl., King and No King, iii. 1.

unkindness.c: unkindness (un-kind’nes), ». [< ME. wnkynd- nes; < unkind + -ness.) 1. The state or character of being unkind; want of kindness; want of natural affection; want of good will; ill will. Take hede, I praise thee, that our loue be not inuenimed with unkyndnes. Golden Book, ix. Ingratitude, commonly called w inesse. Sir T. Elyot, The Governour, ii. 13. 2. An unkind act; harsh treatment; an ill turn. In all those unkindnesses, rudenesses, &c., whereof you accuse yourself, I am enforced to acknowledge myself most justly condemned. J. Bradford, Letters (Parker Soc., 1853), IT. 4. unkindred}t (un-kin’dred), a. Not of the same kindred, blood, race, or kind; not related. One... of blood unkindred to your royal house. . Rowe, Lady Jane Grey, iii. unkindredly+ (un-kin’dred-li), a. Unlike kindred. [Rare.] Her unkindredly kin. 4 <i Richardson, Clarissa Harlowe, VI. 391. (Davies.) Southern. Not kingly; unbe- unkingship unkingship} (un-kind’ship), n. [ME. wnkynd- ship; < unkind + -ship.) An unnatural act. The childe his owne father slough; That was unkyndship enough. Gower, Conf. Amant., vi.

unking.c: unking (un-king’), v. t. [< wn-2 + king1.] To deprive of royalty. They would unking my father now To make you way.

unkingly.c: unkingly (un-king’li), a. coming a king; not noble. What shameful words (unkingly as thou art) Fall from that trembling tongue and tim’rous heart? Pope, Mliad, xiv. 90. nabtneehinl (un-king’ship), ». [< wn-1 + kingship.) The state or condition of being unkinged. Un-kingship was proclaim’d, and his Majesty’s statues thrown down at St. Paul’s Portico and the Exchange. Evelyn, Diary, May 30, 1649.

unkiss.c: unkiss (un-kis’), v. ¢ To retract or annul by kissing again, as an oath taken by kissing the book. Shak., Rich. IL, v. 1. 74.— [Rare.] unketh, a Same as waked.

unknelled.c: unknelled (un-neld’), a. Untolled; not having the bell tolled for one at death or funeral. Byron, Childe Harold, iv.

unknightly.c: unknightly (un-nit’li), a Contrary to the rules of chivalry; unworthy of a knight. Scott, The Talisman.

unknit.c: unknit (un-nit’), v. t.; pret. and pp. unknitted or unknit, ppr. unknitting. [< ME. unknytten; < un-2 + knit.] I. trans. To untie, as a knot; _unwrinkle or smooth out; undo, as knitted work. ‘The whiche wnknytteth alle care and comsyng is of reste. Piers Plowman (C), xxi. 225. Unknit that threatening, unkind brow. Shak., T. of the 8., v. 2. 186. Where they trick her [the Bride] in her richest ornaments, tying on her silken buskins with knots not easily unknit. Sandys, Travailes, p. 52. II. intrans. To become separated; relax. [Rare.] Loue is so natural to man or woman, and the desire to be beloved, that where loue amongst them doeth once cleave itis... bone that neuer unknitteth. Guevara, Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 187.

unknot.c: unknot (un-not’), v. ¢.; pret. and pp. unknotted, ppr. unknotting. [< un-2 + knot.] To free from knots; untie.

unknotty.c: unknotty (un-not’i),a. Not knotty; having no knots. Sandys, tr. of Ovid’s Metamorph., x. [Rare.]

unknow.c: unknow (un-n6’), v. t.; pret. unknew, pp. unknown, ppr. unknowing. [< ME. unknowen; < un-2 + know1.] 1. To become ignorant of, or unacquainted with, as something already known; lose the knowledge of. Can I unknow it?— No, but keep it secret. Dryden, Duke of Guise, v. 1. 2. Not to know; to have no knowledge of or acquaintance with. Wyclif, Rom.i.13. [Rare in both uses.]

unknowability.c: unknowability (un-n6-a-bil’i-ti), n. [< wnknow- able + -ity (see -bility).| The state or character of being unknowable. J. S. Mill.

unknowable.c: unknowable (un-n0’a-bl), a. [< ME. wnknow- able; < un-l + knowable.} 1. Incapable of being known; not capable of being ascertained or discovered; above or beyond knowledge. Their objects, transcending the sphere of all experience actual or possible, consequently do not fall under the categories, in other words are positively unknowable. Sir W. Hamilton. By continually seeking to know, and being continually thrown back with a deepened conviction of the impossibility of knowing, we may keep alive the consciousness that it is alike our highest wisdom and our highest duty to regard that through which all things exist as The Unknowable. H. Spencer, First Principles, § 31. 2+. Unknown. Liggeth thanne stille al owtrely unknowable. Chaucer, Boéthius, ii. meter 7.

unknowableness.c: unknowableness (un-n6’a-bl-nes), ». The character or state of being unknowable. Herbert Spencer insists on the certainty of the existence of things in themselves, but also on their absolute and eternal unknowableness. J. F. Clarke, Orthodoxy, p. 25.

unknowably.c: unknowably (un-n0’a-bli), adv. Not so as to be known.

unknowen.c: unknowen, a. A Middle English form of unknown. ‘

unknowing.c: unknowing (un-nd’ing), pa. [< ME. unknow- ends unknawynge; < un-l + knowing.) Not owing; ignorant: with of before an object. Gh aia vet 6625 Butte appe they rose, to say yow furthermore, And chaungyd horses onto them bothe vnknowyng. Generydes (E. BE. T. 8.), 1. 3396. The second victor claims a mare unbroke, Big with a mule, unknowing of the yoke. Pope, Iliad, xxiii. 334.

unknowingly.c: unknowingly (un-n0’ing-li), adv. Ignorantly; without knowledge or design. Unknowingly she strikes, and kills by chance. Dryden, Pal. and Arc., 1. 277.

unknowingness.c: unknowingness (un-n6’ing-nes), x. The state of being unknowing; ignorance. [Rare.] A confession of simple unknowingness. The American, VIII. 379.

unknowledged.c: unknowledged (un-nol’ejd), a. Not acknowledged or recognized. B. Jonson, The Satyr.

unknown.c: unknown (un-non’), @.and. [Karly mod. E. also unknowen; < ME. unknowen, unknown, wi- knawel; <un-1 + known.] I, a. 1. Not known; not become an object of knowledge; not recognized, discovered, or found out. Then shall come a knyght vn-knowen that longe hath be lost, and helpe this kynge, that the prince may not hym chace oute of the felde ne discounfite. Merlin (E. E. T. S.), iii. 417. For Frensh of Paris was to hire unknown. Chaucer, Gen. Prol. to C. T., 1. 126. Get thee into some unknown part of the world, That I may never see thee. Webster, Duchess of Malfi, iv. 2. Unknown in this sense is often used in the predicate, followed by to: asia man unknown to fame; a fact unknown to the public. In this use it is also often used absolutely: as, unknown to me (elliptically for it being unknown to me), he made a new contract. That he, unknown to me, should be in debt. Shak., C. of E., iv. 2. 48, 2. Not ascertained, with relation to extent, degree, quantity, or the like; hence, inealeula- ble; inexpressible; immense. The planting of hemp and flax would be an unknown advantage to the kingdom. Bacon. 3+. Not to be made known, expressed, or communicated. For divers unknown reasons, I beseech you, Grant me this boon, Shak., Rich. IIL, i. 2. 218. 4+. Not having had sexual commerce. I am yet unknown to woman. Shak., Macheth, iv. 3. 126. II, x. One who or that which is unknown. (a) An obscure individual; one without prestige. (0) In math., an unknown quantity.

unknownness.c: unknownness (un-ndn’nes), ». The state or condition of being unknown. Camden.

unlaboredunlaboured.c: unlabored, unlaboured (un-la’bord), a. 1. Not produced by labor or toil. Unlaboured harvests shall the fields adorn. 2. Not cultivated by labor; not tilled. Let thy ground not lie unlaboured. J. Philips, Cider, i. 3. Spontaneous; voluntary; natural; hence, easy; free; not cramped or stiff: as, an wn- labored style. And from the theme unlabour'd beauties rise. Tickell,

unlaboringunlabouring.c: unlaboring, unlabouring (un-la’bor-ing), a. Not laboring or moving with marked exertion. A mead of mildest charm delays the unlabouring feet. Coleridge, To Cottle.

unlaborious.c: unlaborious (un-la-bd’ri-us), a. Not laborious; not toilsome; not difficult; easy. Milton, Areopagitica.

unlace.c: unlace (un-las’), v. t [< ME. unlacen, unladen; < un-2 + lace.] 1. To loose from lacing or fastening by a cord, string, band, or the like passed through loops, holes, etc.; open or unfasten by undoing or untying the lace of: as, to unlace a garment or a helmet. However, I am not sure if they do not sometimes unlace that part of the sail from the yard. Cook, Second Voyage, ITI. ii. 2. To loosen or ease the dress or armor of. My lorde, vn-lase you to lye, Here schall none come for to cry. York Plays, p. 293. 3. To divest of due covering; expose to injury or damage. [Rare.] What’s the matter, That you wnlace your reputation thus? Shak., Othello, ii. 3. 194, Dryden. In an 4. To disentangle. So entrelaced that it is unable to be wnlaced. Chaucer, Boéthius, iii. prose 12. 5t. To carve. Vnlace that cony. Babees Book (E. E. T. 8.), p. 265.

unlade.c: unlade (un-lad’), v. t. [< un-2 + laden.] 1. To unload; take out the cargo of. unlawful St. Oge’s —that venerable town with the red fluted roofs and the broad warehouse gables, where the black ships unlade themselves of their burdens from the far north. George Eliot, Mill on the Floss, i. 12. Lading and unlading the tall barks. Tennyson, Enoch Arden, 2. To unburden; remove, as a load or burden; discharge. There the ship was to unlade her burden. Acts xxi. 3. Forth and unlade the poison of thy tongue. Chapman, Humorous Day’s Mirth. As much as filled three cars, Unladed now. B, Jonson, Alchemist, iii, 2.

unlaid.c: unlaid (un-lad’), a 1. Not laid or placed; not fixed. The first foundations of the world being yet inlaid. Hooker, Eccles. Polity. 2. Not allayed; not pacified; not exorcised; not suppressed. Blue meagre hag or stubborn unlaid ghost That breaks his magic chains at curfew time. Milton, Comus, 1. 484, 3. Not laid out, as a corpse. B. Jonson, Underwoods.—4. Naut., untwisted, as the strands of a rope.

unlamented.c: unlamented (un-lai-men’ted), a. Not lamented; whose loss is not deplored; not mounted; unwept. Thus unlamented pass the proud away. Pope, Unfortunate Lady, 1. 43.

unland.c: unland (un-land’), v. t. [< wn-2 + land1.] To deprive of lands. Fuller, Worthies, Monmouth, li. 117. (Davies.)

unlap.c: unlap (un-lap’), v. t.; pret. and pp. wilapped, ppr. unlapping. [< un-2 + lap3.] To unfold. Tapestry... unlapt and laid open. Hooker,

unlarded.c: unlarded (un-lir’ded), a. Not larded; not dressed with lard; hence, not mixed with something by way of improvement; not intermixed or adulterated. Speak the language of the company you are in; speak it purely and unlarded with any other. Chesterfield, Letter to his Son.

unlash.c: unlash (un-lash’), v. t. [< wn-2 + lash.] Naut., to loose, unfasten, or separate, as something lashed or tied down.

unlatch.c: unlatch (un-lach’), v. [< un-2 + latch.] I. trans. To open or loose, as a door, by lifting the latch; also, to loose the latchet of: as, to unlatch a shoe. Another unlatched Ben-Hur’s Roman shoes. L, Wallace, Ben-Hur, p. 253. II. intrans. To become open or loose through the lifting of a latch.

unlaw.c: unlaw (un-la’), ». [< ME. wnlawe, unlage, < AS. unlage, wilage, violation of law, < un-, not, + lagu, law: see wn-land law.) 1}. Violation of law or justice; lawlessness; anarchy; injustice. Cayphas herde that ilke sawe, He spake to Jhesu with wn-lawe, MS. Cantab. Ff. v. 48, f. 18. (Halliweill.) This state of things was what our fathers called unlaw, a state of things where law was in the mouths of men in power, but where law itself became the instrument of wrong. E. A. Freeman, Norman Conquest, IV. 421. 2. In Scots law: (a) Any transgression of the law; an injury, or act of injustice. (b) A fine or amercement legally fixed and exacted from one who has transgressed the law.

unlaw (un-la’), v. t [< ME. slawen; < un-2 + law.] 1}. To outlaw. Nyf me dude him wnlawe. Robert of Gloucester, p. 473. 2. To deprive of the authority or character of law. [Rare.] That also which is impious or evil absolutely, either against faith or manners, no law can possibly permit that intends not to unlaw it self. Milton, Areopagitica, p. 54. 8. In Scots law, to fine.

unlawed.c: unlawed (un-lid’), a. [< wn-1 + lawed, pp. of law1, v., 4.] See the quotation. The disabling dogs, which might be necessary for keeping flocks and herds, from running at the deer, was called lawing, and was in general use. The Charter of the Forest, designed to lessen these evils, declares that inquisition or view for lawing dogs shall be made every third year, and shall be then done by the view and testimony of lawful men, not otherwise; and they whose dogs shall be then found unlawed shall give three shillings for mercy; and for the future no man’s ox shall be taken for lawing. Such lawing also shall be done by the assize commonly used, and which is, that three claws shall be cut off without the ball of the right foot. Scott, Ivanhoe, note toi. (Davies.)

unlawful.c: unlawful (un-la’fil), a. [<« ME. *wnlaweful, un- lageful; < un-1 + lawful.) 1. Not lawful; contrary to law; illegal; not permitted by law, human or divine; not legalized: as, an wnlaw- Sul act; an unlawful oath; an unlawful society. unlawful Those that think it is unlawful business I am about, let them depart. Shak., W. T., v. 3. 96. 2. Begotten out of wedlock; illegitimate. Shak., A. and C., iii. 6. 7.—Unlawful assembly, in law, the meeting of three or more persons to commit an unlawful act. Mostauthorities restrict this phrase to a meeting contemplating riotous acts and in such manner alto give firm and courageous persons in the neighborhood of such assembly reasonable grounds to apprehend a breach of the peace in consequence of it. Technically it ceases to be termed an unlawful assembly when the unlawful act is executed, the offense then being riot, or when some steps are taken toward the execution of it, the offense then being deemed a rout. = Syn. Illegal, Lili- cit, etc. See lawful.

unlawfully.c: unlawfully (un-la’ful-i), adv. 1. In an unlawful manner; in violation of law or right; illegally.—2. Ilegitimately; not in wedlock. Shak., M. for M., iii. 1. 196.

unlawfulness.c: unlawfulness (un-l4’ful-nes), ». 1. The character or state of being unlawful; illegality; contrariety to law. The unlawfulness of lying. 2. legitimacy.

unlay.c: unlay (un-la’), v. t.; pret. and pp. inlaid, ppr. unlaying. [< un-2 + lay1.] Naut., to untwist, as the strands of a rope.

unlead.c: unlead (un-led’), v. t [«< wn-2 + lead?.] In printing, to remove the leads from (composed types).

unleal.c: unleal (un-lél’), a. [Early mod. E. (Se.) also unleill; < ME. unlele, hounlele; < un-1 + leal.] Not leal; disloyal. Halliwell (under hounlele).

unlearn.c: unlearn (un-lérn’), v. [< wn-2 + learn] I, trans. 1. To discard, put away, or get rid of (what one has learned); forget the knowledge of. When first began to learn to push, this last winter, my master had a great deal of work upon his hands to make me unlearn the postures and motions which I had got, by having in my younger years practised back-sword, with a little eye to the single falchion. Steele, Tatler, No. 173. 2+. To failto learn; nottolearn. Dr. H. More. II. intrans. To put away acquired knowledge; become ignorant. For only by unlearning Wisdom comes, And climbing backward to diviner Youth. Lowell, Parting of the Ways.

unlearnability.c: unlearnability (un-lér-na-bil’i-ti), m. [« wn-1 + learn + -ability.) Inability tolearn. [Rare.] You will learn how to conduct it [the camera], with the pleasure of correcting my awkwardness and unlearnability. Walpole, Letters (1777), iv. 85.

unlearned.c: unlearned (un-lér’ned), a. [< ME. wnlerned; < un-1 + learned.) 1. Not learned; ignorant; illiterate; not instructed; inexperienced. But how it semethe to symple men unlearned that men ne mowe not go under the Erthe, and also that men scholde falle toward the Hevene, from under! Mandeville, Travels, p. 184. 2. Not suitable to a learned man; not becoming a scholar. I will prove those verses to be very unlearned, neither savouring of poetry, wit, nor invention. Shak., L. L. L., iv. 2. 165. 3 (un-lérnd’). Not gained by study; not known; not acquired by investigation. They learned mere words, or such things chiefly as were better unlearned. Milton, Education. Unlearned Parliament. Sameas Parliament of Dunces (which see, under parliament).=Syn. 1. Illiterate, Uniet- tered, etc. See ignorant.

unlearnedly.c: unlearnedly (un-lér’ned-li), adv. In an unlearned manner; so as to exhibit ignorance; ignorantly. Sir T. More, Works, p. 1037.

unlearnedness.c: unlearnedness (un-lér’ned-nes), ». Want of learning; illiterateness. Sylvester, tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., Eden.

unleash.c: unleash (un-lésh’),v. ¢. [< wn-2 + leash.] To free from a leash, or as from a leash; let go. In chase of imagery unleashed and coursing, Stedman, Poets of America, p. 301. unleavet,v. [< wn-2 + leaf], leave3.] I, trans. To strip of leaves. Puttenham, Arte of Eng. Poesie, iii. 25. (Davies.) II, intrans. To lose leaves, as a tree; become bare. [Rare.] Of amorous Myrtles, and immortal Bays Never vn-leav'd. Sylvester, tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., Eden.

unleavened.c: unleavened (un-lev’nd), a. Not leavened: as, unleavened bread; hence, not affected as if by leaven.

unlectured.c: unlectured (un-lek’turd),a. 1. Not addressed in, or as if in, a lecture or lectures.—2. Not taught or inculeated by lecture. [Rare.] A science yet unlectured in our schools. Young, Night Thoughts, v. 518.

unled.c: unled (un-led’),a. Notled; without guidance; hence, in command of one’s faculties. South, Sermons, 6626 They will quaffe freely when they come to the house of a Christian; insomuch as I have seen but few goe away unled from the embassadours table. Sandys, Travailes, p. 51.

unlefult.c: unlefult, a. See wnleveful. unleisured} (un-lé’zhurd), a. Not having leisure; occupied. Sir P. Sidney. The hasty view of an wnleasw’d licencer. Milton, Areopagitica, p. 81.

unleisuredness.c: unleisuredness (un-lé’zhurd-nes), n. Want of leisure; the state of being occupied. Boyle, Works, I. 251.

unless.c: unless (un-les’), conj. [Harly mod. E. also wn- lesse, onless, onless, ones, earlier onless that, on lesse that (that being ultimately dropped, as with for, conj., lest, etc.), a phrase analogous to at least, at most, ete.: see on and less. Cf. lest.] 1. If it be not that; if it be not the ease that; were it not the fact that; if... not; supposing that... not. It is not possible for all things to be well, winless all men were good: which I think will not be yet these good many years. Sir T. More, Utopia (tr. by Robinson), i. Unless thou tell’st me where thou had’st this ring, Thou diet within this hour. Shak., All’s Well, v. 3. 284. You should not ask, less you knew how to give. Beau. and Fi., Laws of Candy, ii. 1. 2+. For fear that; in case; lest. Beware you do not once the same gainsay, Unless with death he do your rashness pay. Greene, Alphonsus, v. {By omission of a verb, implied in the context, unless may have the force of ‘except,’ ‘but for’: as, Here nothing breeds Unless the nightly owl. Shak., Tit. And., ii. 3. 97. Let not wine, Unless in sacrifice or rites divine, Be ever known of shepherds. Fletcher, Faithful Shepherdess, v. 5.] =Syn. ELacept, Unless. Except could once be used as a synonym for unless, but the words have now drawn entirely apart. Unless is only a conjunction; except is only a preposition. Hacept introduces an exception to a statement which is otherwise general: it may be followed by a clause when connection is made by a particle, as when, that, as, while, or especially another preposition: the omission of such connective makes the structure archaic. Unless introduces a clause, or the abbreviation of a clause, indicating a limitation or condition.

unlessoned.c: unlessoned (un-les’nd), a. Not taught; not instructed. Shak., M. of V., iii. 2.161. [Rare.] unletted, a. [< un-1 + letted, pp. of let2.] Not prevented; unhindered. Uniletted of every wight. The Isle of Ladies, 1. 1881.

unlettered.c: unlettered (un-let’érd), a. Unlearned; untaught; ignorant; illiterate. Milton, Comus, 1. 174.=Syn. Illiterate, Unlearned, etc. See ignorant.

unletteredness.c: unletteredness (un-let’érd-nes), n. The state of being unlettered. unleveful}, a. [ME., also unleful, unlefful; < un-l + leveful.| Unlawful. I deme it felony and unleveful. Chaucer, Boéthius, v. prose 3. A longing vnleffull light in his hert Gert hym hast in a hete, harmyt hym after. Destruction of Troy (B. E. T. §.), 1. 13686.

unlevel.c: unlevel (un-lev’1),v. ¢t. To make not level or uneven. [Rare.] It was so plain as there was scarcely any bush or hillock either to unlevel or shadow it. Sir P. Sidney, Arcadia, iii.

unlicensed.c: unlicensed (un-li’senst), a. 1. Not licensed; not having a license: as, an unlicensed innkeeper. —2. Done or undertaken without, or in defiance of, due license or permission: as, an wi- licensed traffic.

unlicked.c: unlicked (un-likt’), a. Not licked; not brought to proper shape by licking: from the old popular notion that the she-bear licked her cubs into shape; hence, ungainly; raw; unmannerly; uncultivated. A country squire, with the equipage of a wife and two daughters,... oh gad! two such unlicked cubs! Congreve, Old Bachelor, iv. 8. unlightsome}t (un-lit’sum), a. Dark; gloomy; wanting light. First the sun, A mighty sphere, he framed, unlightsome first. Milton, P. L., vii. 354,

unlike.c: unlike (un-lik’),a. [« ME. wnlic, unrich, unilich, < AS. angelic (= OF ries. unlike = G. ungleich = Teel. alike = Sw. olio = Dan. lig), ¢ un-, not, + gelic, like: see like?.] 1. Not like; dissimilar; diverse; having no resemblance. What occasion of import Hath all so long detain’d you from your wife, And sent you hither so unlike yourself? Shak., T. of the §., iii, 2. 106. unlimited Being unlike in troth of Religion, they must needs be vn- like in honesties of living. Ascham, The Scholemaster, p. 84. 2+. Not likely; improbable; unlikely. It ne is nat an unlyk miracle to hem that ne knowen it nat. Chaucer, Boéthius, iv. prose 6. It is not unlike that the Britons accompanied the Cimbrians and Gaules in those expeditions. Hakluyt’s Voyages, Il. 1. Unlike quantities, in math., quantities expressed by different letters or combinations of letters, or by the same letters with different exponents. Unlike signs, the signs plus (+) and minus (—). é ‘

unlike (un-lik’), adv. Not in a like or similar manner; not like or as. Oft have I seen the haughty cardinal... Swear like a ruffian and demean himself Unitke the ruler of a commonweal. Shak., 2 Hen. VI., i. 1. 189,

unlikelihood.c: unlikelihood (un-lik’li-hid), ». The state of being unlikely or improbable; improbability. Thus much may suffice to shew the unlikelihood or rather impossibilities of the supposed coming of our Saxon ancestors from elsewhere into Germanie. Verstegan, Rest. of Decayed Intelligence (ed. 1628), p. 39. The extreme unlikelihood that such men should engage in such a measure. Paley, Evidences, iii. 8.

unlikeliness.c: unlikeliness (un-lik’li-nes),”. [« ME. unlykly- nesse; < unlikely + -ness.] 1. The state of being unlikely; improbability. There are degrees herein, from the very neighbourhood of demonstration quite down to iraprobability and unlikeliness. Locke. 2. The state of being unlike; dissimilarity. Bp. Hall, Contemplations, Christ’s Baptism. Strange in its utter unlikeliness to any teaching, Platonist or Hebrew. Kingsley, Hypatia, xxi. 3+. Unattractiveness; the incapacity to excite liking or love. I that God of Loves servants serve, Ne dar to love for myn unliklynesse. Chaucer, Troilus, i. 16.

unlikely.c: unlikely (un-lik’li), a. [< ME. unlikely, un- likly; < un-1 + likely.]_ 1. Such as cannot be reasonably expected; improbable: as, an wn- likely event. That it wrung his conscience to condemn the Earle of high Treason is not unlikely. Milton, Rikonoklastes, ii. 2. Not holding out a prospect of success or of a desired result; likely to fail; unpromising. A very unlikely envy she hath stumbled upon against the princess’s unspeakable beauty. Str P. Sidney, Arcadia, ii. A strange unlikely errand, sure, is thine. M. Arnold, Balder Dead, I. 83. 3+. Not calculated to inspire liking or affection; not likable or lovable. Whan I considered youre beatee, And therewithal the wnlikly elde of me. Chaucer, Merchant's Tale, 1. 936.

unlikely (un-lik’li), adv. In an unlikely manner; with no or little likelihood; improbably. The pleasures... not unlikely may proceed from the discoveries each shall communicate to another. Pope. unliken} (un-li’kn), v. To make unlike; feign; pretend. Wyclif.

unlikeness.c: unlikeness (un-lik’nes), n. blance; dissimilarity. And he supplied my want the more As his unlikeness fitted mine. Tennyson, In Memoriam, 1xxix. unlimber! (un-lim’bér), a. [< wn-1 + limber1.] Not limber; not flexible; not yielding. Sir H. Wotton. unlimber? (un-lim’bér), v. —_ [< wn-2 + limber2.] I. trans. To detach the limbers from; take off the limbers of: as, to unlimber S. II. intrans. To detach the limbers from the guns. The battery unlimbers and whirls its black-muzzled guns to the front. Harper's Mag., LXXVI. 788.

unlime.c: unlime (un-lim’),v.t. [< wn-2 + lime.] To remove the lime from, as from hides sufficiently treated with it. Pop. Sci. Mo., XXXIV. 287. unlimitable+ (un-lim’i-ta-bl), a. Tlimitable. Milton, Eikonoklastes, xxviii. 1. Not limited; Want of resem-

unlimited.c: unlimited (un-lim’i-ted), a. having no bounds; boundless. So unlimited is our impotence... that it fetters our very wishes. le. The wnlinvited, though perhaps not indefinite, modifiability of matter. Hualey, Anat. Invert., p. 41. 2. Undefined; indefinite; proper exceptions. With gross and popular capacities, nothing doth more prevail than unlimited generalities, because of their plainness at the first sight. Hooker, Eccles. Polity. 3. Unconfined; not restrained; not restricted. An unguarded, unlimited will. = Jer. Taylor. ‘ not bounded by , unlimited Unlimited function. See function.— Unlimited problem, in math., a problem which may have an infinite ad of solutions.— Unlimited quantity. See quan-

unlimitedness.c: unlimitedness (un-lim’i-ted-nes),. The state of being unlimited or boundless, or of being undefined,

unline.c: unline (un-lin’), v. t. [< un-2 + line3.] To take the lining out of; hence, to empty. [Rare.] It wnlines their purses. Davies, Bienvenu, p. 6. (Davies.)

unlineal.c: unlineal (un-lin’é-al), a. Not lineal; not coming in the order of succession. Shak., Macbeth, iii. 1. 63.

unlining.c: unlining (un-li‘ning), ». [Verbal n. of unline, v.| In bot., Lindley’s name for the process of chorization or chorisis, the redoublement (deduplication) of Dunal. See chorisis.

unlink.c: unlink (un-lingk’), v. t. [< wn-2 + link.] To separate the links of; loose, as something fastened by a link; unfasten; untwist; uncoil. Seeing Orlando, it [a snake] unlinked itself. Shak., As you Like it, iv. 3. 112. I cannot mount till thou wnlink my chains; I cannot come till thou release my bands. Quarles, Emblems, v. 9.

unlinked.c: unlinked (un-lingkt’), a. Not connected by or as by links. J. Martineau, Materialism, p. 127.

unliquefied.c: unliquefied (un-lik’ wé-fid), a. Unmelted; not dissolved. Addison, Travels in Italy.

unliquidated.c: unliquidated (un-lik’ wi-da-ted), a. Not liquidated; not settled; unadjusted: as, an wnliqui- dated debt; unliquidated accounts. See liqui- date.—Unliquidated damages. See damage.

unliquored.c: unliquored (un-lik’ord), a 1. Not moistened or smeared with liquor; not lubricated; dry. [Rare.] Churches and states, like an unliquored coach,... on fire with their own motion. Bp. Hail, Sermons. 2. Not filled with liquor; not in liquor; not intoxicated; sober. [Rare.] I doubt me whether the very soberness of such a one, like an unlicour’d Silenus, were not stark drunk. Milton, Apology for Smectymnuus.

unlistening.c: unlistening (un-lis’ning), a. Not listening; not hearing; not regarding or heeding. Thomson, Liberty.

unliturgize.c: unliturgize (un-lit’ér-jiz), v. & [X wn-2 + liturgy + -ize.| To deprive of a liturgy. Bp. Gauden, Tears of the Church, p. 609. (Davies.) [Rare.] unlive! (un-liv’), v. t [< wn-2 + live.] To live in a manner contrary to; annul or undo by living. We must uniive our former lives. Glanville, Vanity of Dogmatizing, viii. unlive?t (un-liv’), v.t. [«< wn-2 + life (ef. alive, liwe2).] To bereave or deprive of life. If in the child the father’s image lies, Where shall I live now Lucrece is unlived? Shak., Lucrece, 1. 1754.

unliveliness.c: unliveliness (un-liv’li-nes), ». Want of liveliness; dullness; heaviness. Milton, Divoree,i.3.

unload.c: unload (un-lod’), v. [< wn-2 + load?.] I, trans. 1. To take the load from; discharge of a load or cargo; disburden: as, to unload a ship; to unload a cart.—2. To remove, as a cargo or burden, from a vessel, vehicle, or the like; discharge: as, to unload freight.— 3. Figuratively, to relieve from anything onerous or troublesome; remove and cause to cease to be burdensome. Nor can my tongue unload my heart’s great burthen. Shak., 3 Hen. VI, ii. 1. 81. From this high theme how can I part, Ere half unloaded is my heart! Scott, Marmion, Int, to i. 4. To withdraw the charge, as of powder and shot or ball, from: as, to unload a gun.—5. To sell in large quantities, as stock; get rid of: as, to wnload shares of the A and B railway. [Colloq.]| i. intrans. To go through the process of unloading ; discharge a cargo. No ship could unload in any bay or estuary which he (the king] had not declared to be a port. Macaulay, Hist. Eng., xviii.

unloader.c: unloader (un-16’dér), m. One who or that which unloads; specifically, a contrivance for unloading, as hay. The Hngineer, UX VIII. 199,

unloadingblock.c: unloading-block (un-l0’ding-blok), n. Insugar- manuf., 2 bench on which the mold containing a sugar-loaf is inverted, and on which the sugar is left standing until removed to the drying-room. In an un- 6627

unloadingmachine.c: unloading-machine (un-lo’ding-ma-shén”), n. apparatus for unloading freight from boats, cars, and wagons. The most usual form is a sort of elevator consisting of a series of cups or buckets carried by anendless band. #. H. Knight. Not located or

unlocated.c: unlocated (un-lo’ka-ted), a. placed; specifically, in the United States, not surveyed and marked off: said of land. See locate, 2. The disposal of the unlocated lands will hereafter be a valuable source of revenue, and an immediate one of credit. A, Hamilton, The Continentalist, No. 6.

unlock.c: unlock (un-lok’), v. t [« ME. unlouken, on- louken (pret. unlek, pp. unloken, unlike), < AS. unlucan, unlock, < un-, back, + lucan, lock: see un-2 and lock1.] 1. To unfasten, as something which has been locked; open, as what has been shut, closed in, or protected by a lock: as, to unlock a door or a chest. I have seen her... unlock her closet. Shak., Macbeth, v. 1. 6. Go in; there are the keys, unlock his fetters; And arm ye nobly both. Fietcher, Double Marriage, ii. 3. 2. To open, in general; lay open. Thou’st unlocked A tongue was vowed to silence. Ford, Lover’s Melancholy, ii. 1. Saturday Morning, as soon as my Senses are unlocked, I get up. Howell, Letters, I, vi. 32. 3+. To spread out. Vnlouke hus legges abroad, other lygge at hus ese, Reste hym, and rose hym and his reg turne, Drynke true and deepe and drawe hym thanne to bedde. Piers Plowman (C), x. 148. 4. To disclose; reveal; make known. That sweven hath Daniel wnloke. Gower, Conf. Amant., Prol.

unlocked.c: unlocked (un-lokt’), a. [< un-1 + locked, pp. of lock1, v.] Not locked.

unlodge.c: unlodge (un-loj’), v. t. [< un-2 + lodge.] To deprive of a lodging; dislodge. Carew.

unlook.c: unlook (un-luk’), v. ¢. [< wn-2 + look.] To recall or retract, as look. [Rare.] He... turned his eyes towards me, then from me, as if he would wnlook his own looks. Richardson, Clarissa Harlowe, V. 215.

unlooked.c: unlooked (un-lukt’), a. Not expected or anticipated: rare except in the phrase unlooked for. By some unlook'd accident cut off! Shak., Rich. ITI., i. 3. 214. Unlooked for, not looked for; not sought or searched for; not expected; not foreseen; not anticipated. An accident unlook’d for put new counsels into thir minds. Milton, Hist. Eng., ii.

unloose.c: unloose (un-lés’), v. [< wn-2 (here intensive) + loose.|] I. trans. 1, To loose; unfasten; untie; undo; unravel. The Gordian knot of it he will unloose. Shak., Hen. V., i, 1. 46. 2. To let go or free from hold or fastening; unbind from bonds, fetters, cords, or the like; set at liberty; release. Where I am robb’d and bound, There must I be unloosed. Shak., Hen. VIIL,, ii. 4. 147. II. intrans. To become unfastened; fall in pieces; lose all connection or union. Without this virtue, the publick union must unloose, the strength decay, and the pleasure grow faint. Jeremy Collier.

unloosen.c: unloosen (un-lé’sn), v. ¢ [< wn-2 (here intensive) + loosen.] To unloose; loosen. V. Knom, Essays, li.

unlord.c: unlord (un-lérd’), v. ¢ [<un-2 + lord.] To deprive of the title, rank, and dignity of a lord; reduce or degrade from a peer to a commoner. [Rare.] The worst and strangest of that Any thing which the people demanded was but the wnlording of Bishops, and expelling them the House. Milton, Hikonoklastes, vi. So, after that, We had to disarchbishop and unlord, And make you simple Cranmer once again. Tennyson, Queen Mary, ii. 2.

unlorded.c: unlorded (un-lér’ded), a. Not raised or preferred to the rank of lord. Milton, Reformation in Eng., i.;

unlordly.c: unlordly (un-lérd’li), a. trary. ([Rare.] The Pastorlike and Apostolik imitation of meek and unlordly Discipline. Milton, Reformation in Eng., ii.

unlosable.c: unlosable (un-16’za-bl), a. Not capable of being lost. Also wnloseable. [Rare.] The Epicureans... ascribe to every particular atom an innate and unloseable mobility. Boyle, Works, I. 445. Not lordly; not arbi- unlustrous

unlost.c: unlost (un-lést’), a. Not lost. [Rare.] A paradise unlost. Young, Night Thoughts, ix. 1071

unlove.c: unlove (un-luy’),v. ¢ [< ME. wnloven; < un-1 (in second quot. wn-2) + lovel.] Not to love; to cease to love. [Rare.] I ne kan nor may For al this world withinne myn herte fynde To unioven you a quarter of a day. Chaucer, Troilus, v. 1698. I had learnt to love Mr. Rochester; I could not unlove him now. Charlotte Bronté, Jane Eyre, xviii.
unlove (un’luv),”. The absence of love; hate. [Rare.] Unlove began its work even in the Apostles’ times. Pusey, Hirenicon, p. 62. Not loved. Chaucer. Lack of love-

unloveliness.c: unloveliness (un-Inv’li-nes), n. lines. (@) Unamiableness; lack of the qualities which attract love. Theold man... followed his suit with all means... that might help to countervail his own unloveliness. Sir P. Sidney, Arcadia, ii. (0) Want of beauty or attractiveness to the eye; plainness of feature or appearance.

unlovely.c: unlovely (un-luv’li), a [< ME. wnlovelich; < un-1 + lovely.) Not lovely. (a) Not amiable; destitute of the qualities which attract love, or possessing qualities that excite dislike; disagreeable. I love thee, all unlovely as thou seem’st And dreaded as thou art! Cowper, Task, iv. 128. (6) Not beautiful or attractive to the eye; displeasing to the sight. Dark house, by which once more I stand Here in the long unlovely street. Tennyson, In Memoriam, vii.

unloving.c: unloving (un-luv’ing),a. Not loving; not fond; unkind. J. Udall, On Ephesians, Prol.

unlovingness.c: unlovingness (un-luv’ing-nes),. The character or state of being unloving. Time and its austere experience of the outer world’s unlovingness have made her thankfully take affection’s clasp. R. Broughton, Joan, II. xi.

unluckful.c: unluckful (un-luk’ful), a. Bringing ill luck; mischievous. O Pallas, ladies of cities, why wettest thou thy delite in three the moste vnluckefull beasts of the worlde, the oulette, the dragon, and the people? Udall, tr. of Apophthegms of Erasmus, p. 375. (Davies.)

unluckily.c: unluckily (un-luk’i-li), adv. In an unlucky or unfortunate manner; unfortunately; unhappily; by ill luck. Was there ever so prosperous an invention thus wnluck- ily perverted and spoiled by a... book-worm, a candlewaster? B. Jonson, Cynthia’s Revels, iii. 2. I was once in a mixt assembly that was full of noise and mirth, when on a sudden an old woman unluckily observed there were thirteen of us in company. Addison, Omens.

unluckiness.c: unluckiness (un-luk’i-nes), ». The character or state of being unlucky, in any sense.

unlucky.c: unlucky (un-luk’i), a. 1. Not lucky or fortunate; not favored by fortune; unsuccessful; subject to frequent misfortune, failure, or mishap; ill-fated; unfortunate; unhappy. In short, they were unlucky to have been bred in an unpolished age, and more unlucky to live to a refined one. Dryden, Def. of Epil. to 2d pt. Cong. Granada. 2. Not resulting in success; resulting in failure, disaster, or misfortune. Unlucky accidents which make such experiments miscarry. Boyle. 3. Accompanied by or bringing misfortune, disappointment, disaster, or the like; ill-omened; inauspicious. A most unlucky hour. Shak., Tit. And., ii. 8, 251. Haunt me not with that unlucky face. Dryden, Aurengzebe, iv. 1. 4. Mischievous; mischievously waggish. [Archaic. ]; Why, cries an unlucky wag, a less bag might have served. Sir R. LD’ Hstrange. There was a lad, th’ unluckiest of his crew, Was still contriving something bad but new. Dr. W. King. unlusti, ». [< MBE. unlust, < AS. unlust, displeasure, dislike (= OHG. unlust, MHG. G. unlust, displeasure, = Icel. vlyst, bad appetite, = Sw. olyst = Dan. ulyst = Goth. wnlustus), < un-, not, + lust, pleasure: see lust!.] Displeasure; dislike. He dooth alle thyng... with ydelnesse and unlust. Chaucer, Parson’s Tale.

unlustrous.c: unlustrous (un-lus’trus), a. Not lustrous; not shining. In an eye Base and unlustrous as the smoky light That’s fed with stinking tallow. Shak., Cymbeline, i. 6, 109. (The above is the reading in some modern editions; the old editions have illustrious.] unlute

unlute.c: unlute (un-lit’), v. t [« wn-2 + lute2.] To separate, as things cemented or luted; take the lute or clay from. Upon the unluting the vessel, it infected the room with a scarce supportable stink. Boyle, Works, I. 483.

unmade.c: unmade (un-mad’), a ([< ME. unmad, *un- maked; < uwn-1 + made.] 1. Deprived of form or qualities.— 2. Not made; not yet formed. Taking the measure of an unmade grave. Shak., R. and J., iii. 3. 70. Used with wp: not made up; not worked into shape; not manufactured: as, wvmade-up materials; an wumade-up dress.

unmagistrate.c: unmagistrate (un-maj‘is-trat), v. t. [« wn-2+ magistrate.| To degrade from or deprive of the office and authority of a magistrate. Milton. [Rare.]

unmaiden.c: unmaiden (un-ma’dn),v.t. [< wn-2 + maiden.) To ravish; deflower. [Rare.] He unmaddened his sister Juno. Urquhart, tr. of Rabelais, iii. 12. (Davies.)

unmaidenly.c: unmaidenly (un-ma‘dn-li), a. Not befitting a maiden. Theiwanton gesticulations of a virgin in a wild assembly of gallants warmed with wine could be no other than riggish and unmaidenly. Bp. Hall, Contemplations, John Baptist Beheaded.

unmailable.c: unmailable (un-ma‘la-bl), a That may not be mailed: applied to matter which, by law, regulation, or treaty stipulation, is excluded from the mails, or which, by reason of illegible, incorrect, or insufficient address, cannot be forwarded to its destination. Glossary of U. S. Postal Terms.

unmaimed.c: unmaimed (un-mamd’), a. Not maimed; not disabled in any limb; complete in all the parts; unmutilated; entire. It is the beet grand duty of an interpreter to give his author entire and wamaimed. Pope, Iliad, Pref.

unmakable.c: unmakable (un-ma’ka-bl), a@. That cannot be made. Unmakable by any but a divine power. N. Grew.

unmake.c: unmake (un-mak’), v. ft. [¢ wn-2 + make.] 1. To destroy the essential form and qualities of; cause to cease to exist; annihilate; uncreate; annul, reverse, or essentially change the nature or office of. God when he makes the prophet, does not unmake the man. Locke. God does not make or unmake things to try experiments. Burnet. Power to make emperors, and to unmake them againe. Jewell, A Replie unto M. Hardinge, p. 418. (Hneye. Dict.) Three observers, separately, on distinct occasions were in some way immediately aware when an electromagnet was secretly ‘‘made’-and “‘unmade.” Proc. Soc. Psych. Research, I, 236. 2. To leave unmade, unformed, uncreated, or unfashioned. [Rare.] May make, unmake, do what she list. Shak., Othello, ii. 3. 352.

unmaking.c: unmaking (un-ma’king), n. The act or process of destroying; destruction; undoing; also, that which unmakes.. A wife may be the making or the unmaking of the best of men. Smiles, Character, p. 326.

unmalleability.c: unmalleability (un-mal’é-a-bil’i-ti), n. The property or state of being caouniieanion

unmalleable.c: unmalleable (un-mal’6-a-bl), a. Not malleable; not capable of being extended by rolling or hammering, as a metal; hence, not capable of being shaped by outside influence; unyielding. “I do believe thee,” said the Sub-Prior; ‘*I do believe that thine {i e., thy mind] i is indeed metal ‘unmalleable by force Scott, Monastery, xxxi,

unman.c: unman (un-man’), v. ¢.; pret. and pp. wumanned, ppr. unmanning. [< un-2 + man.] 1. To deprive of the character or qualities of a human being, as reason, etc. Unman not, therefore, thyself by a bestial transformation. Sir T. Browne, Christ. Mor., iii. 14. 2. To emasculate; deprive of virility.—3. To deprive of the courage and fortitude of a man; break or reduce into irresolution; dishearten; deject; make womanish. Such was his fortitude, that not even the severest trials could unman him. Latimer, Life and Writings, p. xl. Having made up my mind to hope no more, I got rid of a great deal of that terror which unmanned me at first. Poe, Tales, I. 172. 4, To deprive of men: as, to man a ship or town. {The daughter rs of Danaus were] turn’d out to Sea in a Ship unmann'd. Milton, Hist. Eng., i.

unmanacle.c: unmanacle (un-man’a-kl), vt. [< wn-2 + manacle.] To release from or as from manacles; set free. Tennyson, Two Voices. 6628

unmanageable.c: unmanageable (un-man’aj-a-bl), a. Not manageable; not readily submitting to handling or management; not easily restrained, governed, or directed; not controllable. Locke.

unmanageableness.c: unmanageableness (un-man‘aj-a-bl-nes), n. The character or state of being unmanageable.

unmanageably.c: unmanageably (un-man’aj-a-bli), adv. In an unmanageable manner; uncontrollably; so as to be unmanageable. Our eyes are sensitive only to unmanageably short waves. Nature, XLII. 172. Her hair was snow-white and unmanageably coarse. L. Wallace, Ben-Hur, p. 484.

unmanaged.c: unmanaged (un-man’ajd), a. Not controlled; not restrained; specifically, not broken in, as a horse; not trained, in general. Like colts or unmanaged horses. Jer. Taylor, Holy Living. An unguided force, and unmanaged virtue. Felton, Dissertation on Reading the Classicks. unmanhood} (un-man’hud), n. [< ME. weman- home; < un-l + manhood.} An unmanly or cowardly act. To slen himself myghte he nat wynne But bothe doon unmanhode and a synne. Chaucer, Troilus, i. 824.

unmanlike.c: unmanlike (un-man‘lik), a4. Not manlike. (a) Unlike man in form or appearance. (6b) Unbecoming a man as a member of the human race; inhuman; brutal. It is strange to see the unmanlike cruelty of mankind. Sir P. Sidney, Arcadia, i. (c) Unsuitable to a man, as opposed to a woman or child; effeminate; childish. By the greatness of the cry, it was the voice of a man; though it was a very unmanlike voice, so to cry. Sir P. Sidney. This is wnmanlike, to build upon such slight airy conjectures. Jer. Taylor, Works (ed. 1835), II. 392.

unmanliness.c: unmanliness (un-man‘li-nes), n. The character of being unmanly; effeminacy. You and yours make piety a synonym for unmanliness. Kingsley, Yeast, ii.

unmanly.c: unmanly (un-man‘li), a. Not manly. (a) Not having the qualities or attributes of a man, as opposed to a woman or child; not having the strength, vigor, robustness, fortitude, or courage of a man; soft: weak; effeminate; womanish; childish: as, a poor-spirited, wn- manly wretch. (b) Unbecoming in a man; unworthy of man; cowardly: as, unmanly fears. Live, live, my matchless son, Blest in thy father’s blessings; much more blest In thine own vertues; let me dew thy cheeks With my unmanly tears. Beau. and Fl., Laws of Candy, v.

unmanned.c: unmanned (un-mand’), p. a. Not tamed; not yet familiar with man: a term in falconry. No colt is so unbroken, Or hawk yet half so haggard or unmanned! B. Jonson, Sad Shepherd, iii. 2. Come, civil night,... Hood my unmann’d blood, bating in my cheeks, With thy black mantle. Shak., R. and J., iii. 2. 14.

unmannered.c: unmannered (un-man’érd), a Uncivil; rude; mannerless. You have a slanderous... tongue, unmanner’d lord. B. Jonson, Catiline’s Conspiracy, ii. 3.

unmannerliness.c: unmannerliness (un-man’ér-li-nes), ». The state or character of being unmannerly; want of good manners; breach of civility; rudeness of behavior.;

unmannerly.c: unmannerly (un-man’ér-li), a. 1. Not mannerly; wanting in manners; not having good manners; rude in behavior; ill-bred; uncivil. I were unmannerly to take you out And not to kiss you. Shak., Hen. VIII, i. 4. 95. Depart, or I shall be something unmannerly with you. Beau. and Fi., King and No King, iii. 3. 2. Not according to good manners: as, an wn- mannerly jest.=Syn. See list under wneivil. unmannerly+ (un-man’ér-li), adv. With ill manners; uncivilly; rudely. Forgive me If I have used myself unmannerly. Shak., Hen. VILL, iii. 1. 176.

unmantle.c: unmantle (un-man’tl), v. t. [¢ wn-2 + mantle.] To deprive of a mantle; uncover. They unmantled him of a new Plush Cloke. Howell, Letters, I. i. 17.

unmanufactured.c: unmanufactured (un-man-i-fak’tird), a. 1. Not made up; still in its natural state, or only partly prepared for use: thus, fiber is wnmanu- Jactured before it is made into thread; thread is unmanufactured before it is woven into cloth. —2. Not simulated: as, unmanufactured grief. [Colloq.]

unmanured.c: unmanured (un-ma-nird’), a. 1}. Untilled; uncultivated. Spenser. . unmask (un-mask’), v unmateriate Many of our subjects... have caused to be planted large Collonies of ye English nation, in diverse parts of y® world altogether unmanured, and Vvoyd of inhabitants. Bradford, Plymouth Plantation, p. 457. 2. Not manured; not enriched by manure. It is one thing to set forth what ground lieth unmanured, and another thing to correct ill husbandry in that which is manured. Bacon, Advancement of Learning, ii. 117.

unmarked.c: unmarked (un-miirkt’), a. 1. Not marked; haying no mark: as, the wumarked (south-point- ing) pole of a magnet.—2. Unobserved; not regarded; undistinguished; not noted. He mix’d, unmark’d, among the busy throng. Dryden, All for Love, iv.

unmarketable.c: unmarketable (un-mir’ket-a-bl), a. Not fit for the market; not salable; of no merely pecuniary value, That paltry stone brought home to her some thought, true, spiritual, unmarketable. Kingsley, Hypatia, xix.

unmarred.c: unmarred (un-miird’), a [< ME. wnmerred; < un-1 + marred.) Not marred or injured.

unmarriable.c: unmarriable (un-mar’i-a-bl), a. Not marriageable. Milton, Divorce, i. 15. F

unmarriageable.c: unmarriageable (un-mar’aj-a-bl), a. Not fit to be married; too young for marriage.

unmarriageableness.c: unmarriageableness (un-mar’aj-a-bl-nes), n. The state of being unmarriageable.

unmarried.c: unmarried (un-mar’id), a. Not married; single: as, an unmarried woman or man. Commonly the word implies that the person to whom it is applied has never been married; but it may be used of a widow or widower, and possibly. of a divorced person, That die unmarried, ere they can behold Bright Phebus in his strength, Shak., W. T., iv. 4. 123.

unmarry.c: unmarry (un-mar’i), v. t [< un-2 + marry1.] To divorce; dissolve the marriage contract of. [Rare.] Alaw... giving permission to unmarry a wife, and marry a lust. Milton, Divorce.

unmartyr.c: unmartyr (un-mir’tér),v. t [< un-2 + martyr, n.] To degrade from the standing or dignity of a martyr. [Rare.] Scotus... was made a martyr after his death,... but since Baronius has unmartyred him. Fuller, Ch. Hist., II. iv. 36.

unmasculate.c: unmasculate (un-mas’ki-lat), v.t [< un-2 + masculate.| To emasculate. The sins of the south unmasculate northern bodies. Fuller, Holy War (1639), p. 225.

unmasculine.c: unmasculine (un-mas’ki-lin), a. Not masculine or manly. Milton. [< un-2 + mask3.] I, trans. To strip of a mask or of any disguise; lay open what is concealed; bring to light. Iam unmasked, unspirited, undone. . Jonson, Volpone, iii. 6. II, intrans. To put off or lay aside a mask. My husband bids me; now I will unmask. Shak., M. for M., v. 1. 206.

unmasterable.c: unmasterable (un-mas’tér-a-bl), a. [< un-2 + master + -able.] That cannot be mastered or subdued. Sir T. Browne, Vulg. Err., iv. 2. [Rare.]

unmastered.c: unmastered (un-mas’térd), a. 1. Not subdued; not conquered.— 2. Not conquerable. He cannot his unmaster’d grief sustain. Dryden.

unmatchable.c: unmatchable (un-mach’a-bl), a. That cannot be matched; not to be equaled; unparalleled. Most radiant, exquisite, and unmatchable beauty. Shak., T. N., i. 5. 181.

unmatchableness.c: unmatchableness (un-mach’a-bl-nes), n. The character of being unmatchable; matchlessness. The presumption of his wunmatchablenesse. Bp. Hall, Epistles, iv. 2. (Davies.)

unmatched.c: unmatched (un-macht’), a Matchless; haying no match or equal. Beauty! O, it is An unmatch'd blessing or a horrid curse. Ford, Broken Heart, ii. 1.

unmatchedness.c: unmatchedness (un-mach’ed-nes), ». The state of being unmatched; incomparableness. [Rare.] His clear unmatchedness in all manners of learning. Chapman, Tliad, Pref.

unmaterial.c: unmaterial (un-ma-té’ri-al), a. Not material. The unmaterial fruits of shades, » Daniel, Musophilus.

unmaterialized.c: unmaterialized (un-ma-té’ri-al-izd), a. Not in bodily shape; not having become an actual fact: as, his schemes were unmaterialized. Not materi- niieber ere (un-ma-té’ ribat), a. ate i | ol ad unmaze

unmaze.c: unmaze (un-maz’), v.t. [< un-2 + maze.] To relieve from terror or bewilderment. ([Rare.] This poor Arpinate... Unmaz'd us, and took pains for all the town. Stapylton, tr. of Juvenal, viii. 312.

unmeaning.c: unmeaning (un-mé’ning), a 1. Having no meaning or signification: as, meaning words. —2. Not having or not indicating intelligence or sense; mindless; senseless; expressionless. Byron, To Thyrza.

unmeaningly.c: unmeaningly (un-mé’ning-li), adv. In an unmeaning manner; without meaning or sense.

unmeaningness.c: unmeaningness (un-mé/ning-nes), ”. The character of being unmeaning. Miss Burney, Camilla, iii. 1.

unmeant.c: unmeant (un-ment’), a. tended; undesigned. But Rheetus happened on a death unmeant. Dryden, Aneid, x. 561.

unmeasurable.c: unmeasurable (un-mezh’ir-a-bl), a [< ME. unmesurable; < un-l + measurable.] Immeasurable. Glotonye is unmesurable appetit to etc or to drynke. Chaucer, Parson’s Tale. Not meant; not in- Their unmeasurable vanity. B. Jonson, Cynthia's Revels, v. 2.

unmeasurableness.c: unmeasurableness (un-mezh’ar-a-bl-nes), 2. The state of being unmeasurable. [Rare.] Showing the unmeasurableness of his Godhed. Fryth, Bok made by Him (an. 1533). (Zneyc. Dict.)

unmeasurably.c: unmeasurably (un-mezh’ir-a-bli), adv. [< . unmesuradbly; < un-l + measurably.) Immeasurably. The nyght folowynge there rose a wonder grete tempest of excedynge moche wynde, and therewithal it rayned and hauled so vnmesurably that no man myght loke forthe aboue the hatches. Sir R. Guylforde, Pylgrymage, p. 72.

unmeasured.c: unmeasured (un-mezh’ard), a. 1. Not measured; plentiful beyond measure; hence, immense; infinite; boundless. The unmeasured cycles of a limitless future. J. R. Macduff, Memories of Patmos, p. 16. Peopling, they also, the unmeasured solitudes of time. Carlyle. 2. Not subject to or obeying any musical rule of measure, time, or rhythm; irregular; capricious. The unmeasured notes of that strange lyre. Shelley.

unmechanize.c: unmechanize (un-mek’a-niz), v. t. [« wn-2 + mechanize.| To undo or destroy the mechanism of; unmake; destroy; throw out of gear. [Rare.] Embryotic evils that could unmechanize thy frame. Sterne, Tristram Shandy, iii. 167.

unmeddle.c: unmeddle (un-med’1),v.i. [< un-2 + meddle.] To undo or repair the effects of meddling. [Rare.] Lord Granville unmeddles and unmuddles. Higginson, English Statesmen (1875), p. 167.

unmeddling.c: unmeddling (un-med’ling), a. Not meddling; not interfering with the concerns of others; not officious. Chesterfield.

unmeddlingness.c: unmeddlingness (un-med’ling-nes), ». Forbearance of interposition, or of busying one’s self with something. ([Rare.] If then we be but sojourners,... here must be an ... unmeddlingness with these worldly concernment. ip. Hall.

unmedicinable.c: unmedicinable (un-mé-dis’in-a-bl), a. 1. Powerless to cure. Away with his vnmedcinable blame Of worded breath: forbear, friends, let me rest. Chapman, Gentleman Usher, iv. 1. (Davies.) 2. That cannot be cured. But these, much-med’cine-knowing men, physicians, may thd ak Raced enable still. Chapman, Iliad, xvi. 24. (Davies.)

unmeditated.c: unmeditated (un-med’i-ta-ted), a. Not meditated; not prepared by previous thought; unpremeditated. [Rare.] Fit strains pronounced, or sung Unmeditated. Milton, P. L., v. 149. unmeekt paca), a [< ME. unmeke, unmek, unmeoc; < un-l + meek.) 1. Not meek or gentle; fierce; cruel; harsh; severe. An unmeke lord. Chaucer, Boéthius, iv. meter 7. 2. Not kind; disdainful. She to me was nought unmeke. Rom. of the Rose, 1. 590.

unmeet.c: unmeet (un-mét’), a. [< ME. unmet, < AS. un- genet, immoderate, immense, mixed with wn- mete, unmaite, < AS. wume#te (= OHG. unmaze, MHG. unmaze, unmeze, immoderate), < un-, not, + mete, moderate: see meet?.] 1. Not meet or fit; improper; not suitable; unbecoming. ’ 6629 The Ladie, hearkening to his senseful speech, Found nothing that he said unmeet nor geason. Spenser, F. Q., VI. iv. 87. White Angel of the Lord! unmeet That soil accursed for thy pure feet. Whittier, The Peace of Europe. 2t. Unseemly; coarse; rustic. Hir voice ful clere was ful and swete, She was nought rude ne unmete. Rom. of the Rose, 1. 752. 38. Not suited or fitted; not adapted. Ah Maud, you milk-white me you are all unmeet for a wife. Tennyson, Maud.

unmeetly.c: unmeetly (un-mét’li), adv. Not fitly; improperly; unsuitably; unworthily. A faire maiden... upon a mangy jade unmeetly set. Spenser, F. Q., VI. vi. 16.

unmeetness.c: unmeetness (un-mét’nes), m. Unfitness; vi- suitableness; unbecomingness. Vast unmeetness in marriage. Milton, Divorce, i, 13.

unmellowed.c: unmellowed (un-mel’6d), a. Not mellowed; not fully matured; not toned down or softened by ripeness or length of years. His head wnmellow’d, but his j jud dement ripe. Shak., T. G. of V., ii. 4. 70.

unmelodious.c: unmelodious (un-me-16’di-us), a. Not melodious; wanting melody; harsh. The unmelodious noise of the braying mules. Sir T, Herbert.

unmentionable.c: unmentionable (un-men’shon-a-bl), a. Incapable of being mentioned; unworthy of or unfit for being mentioned, named, or noticed. Whenever he did anything which appeared to her to savour of an unmentionable place. W.S. Gilbert, Lost Mr. Blake.

unmentionables.c: unmentionables (un-men’shon-a-blz), n. pl. . Trousers or breeches, as an article of dress not to be mentioned in polite circles; inexpressibles. [Colloq. and humorous.]

unmercenary.c: unmercenary (un-mér’se-na-ri), @ canary; not sordid. A generous and unmercenary principle. Bp, Atterbury, Sermons, I. i.

unmerchantable.c: unmerchantable (un-mér’chan-ta-bl), a. Not merchantable; not of a quality fit for the market; unsalable. R&. Carew. No lot of Meats shall be considered suitable for delivery on contract if twenty (20) per cent, of itis unmerchantable. New York Produce Exchange Report, 1888-9, p. 167. unmercied} (un-mér’sid), a. [< wn-1 + mercy + -ed?.)| Unmerciful; merciless. Drayton, Miseries of Queen Margaret.

unmerciful.c: unmerciful (un-mér’si-fil), a. 1. Not merciful; not influenced by merey; unkind; cruel; inhuman; merciless: of persons or things. God never can hear the prayers of an unmerciful man, Jer. Taylor, Sermons, I. iv. 2. Unconscionable; exorbitant. Unmerciful demands. Pope. Unmerciful Parliament, Same as merciless Parliament (which see, under Parliament).

unmercifully.c: unmercifully (un-mér’si-ful-i), adv. In an unmerciful manner; without mercy or tenderness; cruelly; often, especially in colloquial a extremely; very: as, unmercifully cold weather. Not mer- Full fiercely layde the Amazon about, And dealt her blows unmercifully sore. Spenser, F. Q., V. vii. 31.

unmercifulness.c: unmercifulness (un-mér’si-fil-nes), ». The character of being unmerciful; cruelty; inhumanity.

unmeritable.c: unmeritable (un-mer’i-ta-bl), a merit or desert; worthless. This is a slight wemeritable man, Meet to be sent on errands. ak., J. C., iv. 1.12.

unmerited.c: unmerited (un-mer’i-ted), a. 1. Not merited; not deserved; obtained without service or equivalent: as, unmerited promotion. Milton, P. L., xii. 278.—2. Not deserved because of wrong-doing; cruel; unjust: as, wmerited sufferings or injuries; an unmerited disgrace.

unmeritedness.c: unmeritedness (un-mer’i-ted-nes), n. The character or state of being unmerited. The freeness and unmeritedness of God’s grace. Boyle, Works, I. 278.

unmeriting.c: unmeriting (un-mer’i-ting), a. Not meriting; not meritorious or deserving. A brace of unmeriting, proud, violent, testy magistrates. Shak., Coy., ii. 1. 47.

unmerry.c: unmerry (un-mer’i), @. [< ME. unmerge, un- marie; < un-l + merry.) Not merry; not disposed to mirth. Having no unmiter Ther slepeth ay this god unmerge. Chaucer, House of Fame, 1. 74.

unmeted.c: unmeted (un-mé’ted), a. Not meted or measured. [Rare.] Some little of the anxiety I felt in degree so wameted. Charlotte Bronté, Villette, xxxix. (Davies.)

unmethodized.c: unmethodized (un-meth’od-izd),a. Not methodized or regulated by method, system, or pia not systematized. J. Harington, Oceana. p. 12.

unmevablet.c: unmevablet, a. A Middle English form of wn- movable.

unmew.c: unmew (un-mu’),v.¢. [< wn-2 + mew4t.] To set free as from a mew; emancipate; release. [Rare.] But let a portion of etherial dew Fall on my head, and presently unmew My soul; that I may dare, in wayfaring, To stammer where old Chaucer used to sing. Keats, Endymion, i. unmighty}(un-mi’ti),a. [< ME. unmighty, wn- mighty, unmighty, < AS. unmihtig, unmehtig (= OHG. unmahtig), < wn-, not, + mihtig, mighty.} Powerless; incapable of success. He... is unmighty for his shrewednesse. Chaucer, Troilus, ii. 858. unmild} (un-mild’), a. [< ME. unmilde, < AS. unmilde (= OHG. unmilt), < un-, not, + mild, mild.] Not mild; harsh; severe. Gower, Conf. Amant., i. unmildness} (un-mild’nes), ». Want of mildness; harshness. Milton, Divorce, ii. 7.

unmilitary.c: unmilitary (un-mil’i-ta-ri), a. Not according to military rules or customs; not of a military character.

unminded.c: unminded (un-min’ded), a. Not minded; not heeded; not kept in mind. ([Rare. | A poor, aminded outlaw sneaking home. Shak., 1 Hen. IV., iv. 3. 58. Where was your gratitude, who in your coffers Hoarded the rusty treasure which was due To my unminded father? Beau. and Fi., Laws of Candy, v. 1.

unmindful.c: unmindful (un-mind’fil), a. Not mindful; not heedful; not attentive; regardless; heedless; careless: as, unmindful of laws; unmindful of health or of duty. Unmindful of the crown that virtue gives. Milton, Comus, I. 9. For not unmindful of thee are the Gods;... Even here they seek thee out, in Hela’s realm. M. Arnold, Balder Dead. =Syn. Careless, inattentive (to), heedless, unobservant, negligent, forgetful, unheedful.

unmindfully.c: unmindfully (un-mind’ful-i), adv. In an unmindful manner; carelessly; heedlessly.

unmingle.c: unmingle (un-ming’gl), v. t. To separate, as things mixed. [Rare.] It will wamingle wine from the water, tending and the water descending.

unmingleable.c: unmingleable (un-ming’gl-a-bl), a. not be mingled or mixed. [Rare.] The property of oil being unmingleable with water. Boyle, Works, I. 536.

unmingled.c: unmingled (un-ming’gld), a. Not mingled; not mixed; unmixed; unalloyed; pure: as, to view some event with unmingled dread. Springs on the tops of high hills are... pure andun- mingled. Bacon, Nat. Hist., § 396.

unmiraculous.c: unmiraculous (un-mi-rak’a-lus), @ Not miraculous. Young, Night Thoughts, ix.

unmiraculously.c: unmiraculously (un-mi-rak’i-lus-li), adv. In an unmiraculous manner; without a miracle.

unmiry.c: unmiry (un-mir’i), a. Not miry; not muddy; not foul with dirt. [Rare.] With safe unmiry feet. Gay, Trivia, iii.

unmistakable.c: unmistakable (un-mis-ta’ka-bl), a. That cannot be mistaken or misunderstood; clear; evident. Also unmistakeable. Not the Scripture, but unmistakeable and indefectible oral tradition, was the rule of faith. Tillotson. =Syn. Palpable, manifest, obvious, patent, unequivocal, unambiguous, decided,

unmistakably.c: unmistakably (un-mis-ta’ka-bli), adv. In an unmistakable manner; so as not to be mistaken. Also unmistakeably. She went first to the best adviser, God — Whose finger unmistakably was felt In all this retribution of the past. Browning, Ring and Book, i. 116.

unmiterunmitre.c: unmiter, unmitre (un-mi’tér), v. t To deprive of a miter; degrade or depose from the rank and dignity of a bishop. Milton. [Rare.]} Not metrical; the wine as- Bacon. That can- unmitigable

unmitigable.c: unmitigable (un-mit’i-ga-bl), a. Not capable of being mitigated, softened, or lessened. Her most unmitigable rage. Shak., Tempest, i. 2. 276,

unmitigated.c: unmitigated (un-mit’i-ga-ted), a. Not mitigated; not lessened; not softened or toned down; unassuaged; often, especially in colloquial use, unconscionable: as, an unmitigated scoundrel; an unmitigated lie. ‘ With public accusation, uncovered slander, unmitigated rancour. Shak., Much Ado, iv. 1. 308. The unmitigated blaze of vindicatory law. J. W. Alexander, Discourses, p. 62.

unmitigatedly.c: unmitigatedly (un-mit’i-ga-ted-li), adv. With-out mitigation; in an unmitigated degree; utterly. “Lady Delmar” is neither realistic nor idealistic; it is altogether improbable and unmitigatedly melodramatic. The Academy, April 11, 1891, p. 342.

unmixedly.c: unmixedly (un-mik’sed-li), adv. Entirely; purely; without mixture of other qualities; utterly. [Rare.] That superstition cannot be regarded as unmixedly noxious which compels the hereditary master to kneel before the spiritual tribunal of the hereditary bondman. Macaulay.

unmixedunmixt.c: unmixed, unmixt (un-mikst’), a. Not mixed; not mingled; pure; simple; unadulterated; unmingled; unalloyed. Thy commandment all alone shall live,... Unmiz’d with baser matter. Shak., Hamlet, i. 5. 104. God is an unmixed good. T. Brooks, Works, I. 187.

unmoaned.c: unmoaned (un-m6énd’), a. Not bemoaned or lamented. Our fatherless distress was left unmoan’d. Shak., Rich. III., ii. 2. 64.

unmodernize.c: unmodernize (un-mod’ér-niz), v. ¢ To alter from a modern fashion or style; give an ancient or old-fashioned form or fashion to. Unmodernize a poem rather than give it an antique air. Lamb, Essays.

unmodifiable.c: unmodifiable (un-mod’i-fi-a-bl), a. Not modifiable; not capable of being modified.

unmodifiableness.c: unmodifiableness (un-mod’i-fi-a-bl-nes), ». The state or quality of being unmodifiable. A nature not of brutish unmodifiableness. George Eliot, Daniel Deronda, lviii. (Davies.)

unmodified.c: unmodified (un-mod’i-fid), a. Not modified; not altered in form; not qualified in meaning; not limited or circumscribed. An universal, wunmodijied capacity to which the fanatics pretend. Burke, To Sir H, Langrishe.

unmodish.c: unmodish (un-m6’dish),a@. Not modish; not according to custom or fashion; unfashionable; not stylish.: Your Eloquence would be needless —’tis so unmodish to need Persuasion. Steele, Tender Husband, v. 1. Who there frequents at these unmodish hours, But ancient matrons with their frizzled towers, And gray religious maids? Gay, Eclogues, The Toilette.

unmoistened.c: unmoistened (un-moi’snd), a. Not made moist or humid; not wetted; dry. And mayst thou die with an unmoisten’d eye, And no tear follow thee! Fletcher (and another?), Nice Valour, ii. 1.

unmoldunmould.c: unmold, unmould (un-m6ld’),v.% = [« wn-2 + mold.) To change the’ form of; reduce from any form. Unmoulding reason’s mintage, Charactered in the face. Milton, Comus, 1, 529.

unmolested.c: unmolested (un-mo-les’ted), a. Not molested; not disturbed; free from disturbance. Meanwhile the swains Shall unmolested reap what plenty sows. J. Philips, Cider, ii.

unmomentary.c: unmomentary (un-m6’men-ta-ri), a. At the same time, or without a moment’s intervention. [Rare.] From heav’n to earth He can descend, and bee Aboue and here in space »vnmomentarie. Heywood, Hierarchy of Angels, p. 439.

unmoneyed.c: unmoneyed (un-mun’id), a@ Not having money; not possessed of wealth: as, the wumoneyed classes. Also wnmonied. The unnoneyed wight. Shenstone, The School-mistress.

unmonopolize.c: unmonopolize (un-m6-nop’6-liz), v.¢. To free from monopoly; deprive of the character of a monopoly. Also unmonopolise. [Rare.] The unappropriating and unmonopolizing the rewards of learning and industry from the grease clutch of ignorance and high feeding. Milton, Reformation in Eng.,, ii.

unmonopolizing.c: unmonopolizing (un-m6-nop’6-li-zing), a. Not monopolizing; not including in a monopoly; not obtaining the whole of anything. Also wn- monopolising, [Rare.] 6630 This is an important point, as suggesting the disinterested and unmonopolising side of esthetic pleasure. J. Sully, Encye. Brit., I. 216.

unmoor.c: unmoor (un-mor’), v. [< wn-2 + moor2.| I, trans. 1. Naut., to bring to the state of riding with a single anchor, after having been moored by two or more cables.—2. To loose from anchorage or from moorings, literally or figuratively. Thy skiff unmoor, And waft us from the silent shore. Byron, Giaour. II, intrans. To loose from moorings; weigh anchor. Look, where beneath the castle grey His fleet unmoor from Aros bay! Scott, Lord of the Isles, i. 12.

unmoral.c: unmoral (un-mor’al), a. Not moral; non-moral; not a subject of moral attributes; neither moral nor immoral.

unmorality.c: unmorality (un-m6-ral’i-ti), n. morality; unmoral character. The picture is very highly, a trifle too highly, wrought: but what pathos for those who can see behind it! The need of counsel, the lack of previous education, the absolute unmorality. The Academy, Feb. 8, 1890, p. 94.

unmoralized.c: unmoralized (un-mor’al-izd), a. 1. Untutored by morality; not conformed to good morals. [Rare.] A dissolute and unmoralized temper. Norris. 2. Not subjected to moralizing consideration: as, an unmoralized thought. There are no cabinets of wnmoralised or half-moralised conceptions, serving as illustrations of the evolution hypothesis. New Princeton Rev., I. 180. Also unmoralized.

unmoralizing.c: unmoralizing (un-mor’al-i-zing), a 1. Demoralizing.— 2. Not given to or consisting in moral reflections. He was primarily the artist, impersonal, unmoralizing, an eye and a vocabulary. The Atlantic, LXIV. 701.

unmorrised.c: unmorrised (un-mor’ist), @ [« un-1 + morris + -ed?.] Not dressed as a morris-dancer; not disguised by such a dress. [Rare.] What ails this fellow, Thus to appear before me unmorrised? Fletcher, Women Pleased, iv. 1.

unmortise.c: unmortise (un-mér’tis),v. ¢ [< un-2 + mortise.] To loosen or undo as a mortise; loosen the mortises or joints of. In a dark nook stood an old broken-bottomed cane-couch, without a squab or coverlid, sunk at one corner, and unmortised by the failing of one of its worm-eaten legs. Richardson, Clarissa Harlowe, VI. 304. The wrist is parted from the hand that waved, The feet unmortised from their ankle-bones. Tennyson, Merlin and Vivien.

unmosaic.c: unmosaic (un-m6-za’ik), a. The reverse of Mosaic; contrary to Moses or his law. By this reckoning Moses should be most wn-Mosaic. Milton.

unmothered.c: unmothered (un-muPH’érd), a. 1. Not having another; deprived of mother. [Rare.]—2}. Not having the feelings of a mother. IT e’en quake to proceed. My spirit turned edge. I feare me she’s unmother’d, yet I'll venture. C. Tourneur, Revenger’s Tragedy, ii. 1. unmotherly (un-murH’ér-li), a Not resembling or not befitting a mother. Unmotherly mother and unwomanly Woman, that near turns motherhood to shame, Womanliness to loathing. Browning, Ring and Book, IT. 195. unmould, v.t. See unmold.

unmounted.c: unmounted (un-moun’ted), a. 1. Not mounted; not performing regular duties on horseback: as, unmounted police.—2. Not furnished or set with appropriate or necessary appurtenances: as, an wemounted jewel; not affixed to a mount or backing, as of stiff paper or cardboard, as a drawing or a photograph; not provided with a mat of appropriate size and covered with a protecting glass, as a lantern-slide or transparency.

unmourned.c: unmourned (un-mérnd’), a. Not mourned; not grieved for or lamented. But still he goes wunmourn’d, returns unsought, And oft, when present, absent from my thought. Byron, Corsair, ii, 14. unmovability+ (un-mé-va-bil’i-ti), ». [ME. unmoevablete; as unmovable + -ity.] TImmova- bility. Also wnmoveability.
