unmovable.c: unmovable (un-mé’vya-bl),a. [< ME. wamoeva- ble, wumevable; < un-1 + movable.] Immovable. Also unmoveable. It is clept the dede See, for it rennethe nought, but is evere wrmevable. Mandeville, Travels, p. 100. Absence of unmusically The Duke hath all his goods moveable and wumoueable. Hakluyt’s Voyages, I. 242.

unmovably.c: unmovably (un-mé’va-bli), adv. Immoyably. Also unmoveably. Jer. Taylor, Works (ed. 1835), Pref., I. 16.

unmoved.c: unmoved (un-méyd’), a. 1. Not moved; not transferred from one place to another. Locke. —2. Not changed in purpose or resolution; unshaken; firm. Unméved, unshaken, unseduced. Milton, P. L., i. 554. 8. Not affected; not having the passions or feelings excited; not touched or impressed; not altered by passion or emotion; calm; apathetic: as, an unmoved heart; an unmoved look. Who, moving others, are themselves as stone, Unmoved, cold, and to temptation slow. Shak., Sonnets, xciv. Can you stand unmov’d, When an earthquake of rebellion shakes the city, And the court trembles? Fletcher (and another), False One, v. 4. Who could dwell Unmoved upon the fate of one so young. Southey, The Tale of Paraguay. unmovedly+ (un-m6’ved-li), adv. In an unmoved manner; without being moved. If you entreat, I will unmovedly hear. Beau. and F1., Philaster, i. 2.

unmoving.c: unmoving (un-mé’ving), a. 1. Having no motion. Unmoving heaps of matter. Cheyne, Philos. Principles. Alone, in thy cold skies, Thou keep’st thy old unmoving station yet. Bryant, Hymn to the North Star. 2. Not exciting emotion; having no power to affect the passions; unaffecting; not touching or impressive.

unmowedunmown.c: unmowed, unmown (un-m0od’, un-m6n’), a. Not mowed or cut down. Tennyson, Arabian Nights.

unmuddle.c: unmuddle (un-mud’l), v. [< wn-2 + muddle.] To free from muddle. See the quotation under unmeddle. [Rare.]

unmuffle.c: unmuffle (un-muf’l), v. [« wn-2 + muffle.] I. trans. To take a muffler from, as the face; remove a muffler or wrapping from, as a person. II. intrans. To throw off coverings or concealments. Unmufie, ye faint stars, and thou fair moon, That wont’st to love the traveller’s benison. Milton, Comus, 1. 331.

unmultiply.c: unmultiply (un-mul’ti-pli), v. t [< wn-2 + multiply.) To reverse the process of multiplication in; separate into factors. [Rare.] As two factors multiplied together formed a product, it ought to be possible to unmultiply or split up (as “C. W. M.” expresses it) that product into its factors again. Nature, XX XTX. 413.

unmunitioned.c: unmunitioned (un-mt-nish’ond), a. Unfurnished with munitions of war. Cadiz, I told them, was held poor, unmanned, and wn- munitioned. Peeke, Three to One, 1625 (Eng. Garner, i. 634). (Davies.)

unmurmured.c: unmurmured (un-mér’mérd), a. Not murmured at. [Rare.] If my anger chance let fall a stroke, As we are all subject to impetuous passions, Yet it may pass unmurmur’d, undisputed. Fletcher (and another?), Nice Valour, iy. 1.

unmurmuring.c: unmurmuring (un-mér’mér-ing), a. Not murmuring; not complaining: as, unmurmuring patience. Byron, Bride of Abydos, i. 13.

unmurmuringly.c: unmurmuringly (un-mér’mér-ing-li), adv. In an unmurmuring manner; uncomplainingly.

unmuscled.c: unmuscled (un-mus’ld),a. Having the muscles relaxed; flaccid: as, wnmuseled cheeks. Richardson, Clarissa Harlowe, VI. 362. (Davies.)

unmuscular.c: unmuscular (un-mus’ki-lir), a. Not muscular; physically weak. C. Reade, Cloister and Hearth, lii. (Davies.)

unmusical.c: unmusical (un-mi’zi-kal), a. 1. Not musical; not harmonious or melodious; not pleasing to the ear. Let argument bear no unmusical sound, Nor jars interpose, secret friendship to grieve. B, Jonson, Tavern Academy. Milton could not have intended to close, not only a period, but a paragraph also, with an unmusical verse. Lowell, Among my Books, 2d ser., p. 296. 2. Not skilled in or fond of musie: as, wn- musical people.

unmusicality.c: unmusicality (un-mi-zi-kal’i-ti), n. The quality of being unmusical. The idea of unmusicality is a relative one. Pop. Sci. Mo., XXXVII. 356.

unmusically.c: unmusically (un-mii’zi-kal-i), ady. In an unmusical manner; inharmoniously. [Landor’s] voice was sweet, and he could not speak un- nuusically, though in a rage. Stedman, Vict. Poets, p. 65, 3 unmutable

unmutilated.c: unmutilated (un-mi’ti-la-ted), a Not muti- ie not deprived of a member or part; en- ire.

unmuzzle.c: unmuzzle (un-muz’l), v. t [« wn-2 + muzzle.) To loose from a muzzle; remove a muzzle from; hence, figuratively, to free from restraint. Ay, marry, now unmuzzle your wisdom. hak., As you Like it, i. 2. 74.

unmystery.c: unmystery (un-mis’te-ri), v. t. [< wn-2 + mystery1.| "To divest of mystery; make clear or plain. Fuller, Worthies, Hereford, i. 453. (Davies.) [Rare.]

unnail.c: unnail (un-nal’), v. t [< wn-2 + nail.] To remove or take out the nails from; unfasten or loosen by removing nails. Whiles Joseph of Arimatheea and Nicodemus unnail our Lord. Evelyn, Perfection of Painting.

unnamable.c: unnamable (un-na’ma-bl), a. Incapable of being named; indescribable. Also unnameable. A cloud of unnameadile feeling. Poe, Imp of the Perverse.

unnamed.c: unnamed (un-namd’), a. 1. Not named; not having received a name; hence, not known by name; anonymous. Unnamed accusers in the dark. Byron, Siege of Corinth, iv. 2. Not named; not mentioned. Be glad thou art unnamed. Fletcher (and another), False One, ii. 1.

unnapkined.c: unnapkined (un-nap’kind), a. Having no napkin or handkerchief. [Rare.] No pandar’s wither’d paw, Nor an unnapkin'd lawyer’s greasy fist, Hath once slubber’d thee. Beau. and Fl., Woman-Hater, i. 3.

unnapped.c: unnapped (un-napt’), a. Not having a nap; made without a nap, as cloth; deprived of nap.

unnative.c: unnative (un-na’tiv), a. Not native; foreign; not natural; not naturalized, as a word. Whence... this unnative fear, To generous Britons never known before? Thomson, Britannia.

unnatural.c: unnatural (un-nat’i-ral), a. 1. Not natural; contrary to nature; monstrous; especially, contrary to the natural feelings: as, unnatural offenses. Unnatural deeds Do breed unnatural troubles, Shak., Macbeth, v. 1. 80. It is well known that the mystery which overhangs what is distant, either in space or time, frequently prevents us from censuring as unnatural what we perceive to be impossible. Macaulay, History. 2. Acting without the affections of our common nature; not having the feelings natural to humanity; being without natural instincts: as, an winatural parent. Rome, whose gratitude Tow’rds her deserved children is enroll’d In Jove’s own book, like an unnatural dam, Should now eat up her own. Shak., Cor., iii. 1. 293, 8. Not in conformity to nature; not agreeable to the real character of persons or things; not representing nature; forced; strained; affected; artificial: as, unnatural images or descriptions. All violences and extravagances of a religious fancy are -.. unnatural;. I am not sure that they ever consist with humility. Jer. Taylor, Works, I. 72. He will even speak wellvof the bishop, though I tell him it is unnatural in a beneficed clergyman. George Eliot, Middlemarch, i. 6. =Syn. 1-3. Preternatural, etc. See supernatural.—3, Artificial, etc. See factitious. 5

unnatural (un-na’tur), ». [< wn-l + nature.] The absence of nature or of the order of nature; se contrary of nature; that which is unnatural. So as to be rather unnature, after all, than nature. H. Bushnell. unnature?} (un-na’tir),v.¢. [< un-2 + nature.] To change or take away the nature of; endow with a different nature. Sir P. Sidney, Arcadia, iii.

unnaturalism.c: unnaturalism (un-nat’i-ral-izm), n. The character or state of being unnatural; unnaturalness. [Rare.] The expression of French life will change when French life changes: and French naturalism is better at its worst than French unnaturalism at its best. Harper's Mag., LX XIX. 963.

unnaturality.c: unnaturality (un-nat-i-ral’i-ti), n. The quality or state of being unnatural; unnaturalness; unconformity to nature or to reality. [Rare.] What unkindness and wnnaturalitie may we impute to you. Foxe, Actes and Monuments (ed. 1583), IT. 1086.

unnaturalize.c: unnaturalize (un-nat’i-ral-iz), v.¢ [< wn-2 + naturalize.) Tomake unnatural; divest of natural character. Such usurpations by Rulers are the unnaturalizing of nature, disfranchisements of Freedome. NV. Ward, Simple Cobler, p. 51.

unnaturalized.c: unnaturalized (un-nat’i-ral-izd), a 1. Not naturalized; not made natural; unnatural. Adorned with unnaturalized ornaments. Brathwayt, Natures Embassie, Ded. (Encyc. Dict.) 2. Not invested, as a foreigner, with the rights one privileges of a native subject or citizen; en. 6631

unnaturally.c: unnaturally (un-nat’i-ral-i), adv. In an unnatural manner; in opposition to natural feel- hd and sentiments. Shak., 3 Hen. VI., i. 1.

unnaturalness.c: unnaturalness (un-nat’a-ral-nes), n. The state or character of being unnatural; contrariety to nature.

unnavigability.c: unnavigability (un-nav’i-ga-bil’i-ti), n. The quality or state of being unnavigable. Littell’s Living Age, CLXI. 88.

unnavigable.c: unnavigable (un-nav’i-ga-bl), a. Not navigable; incapable of being navigated; that may not be sailed on. That unnavigable stream. Dryden, tr. of Juvenal, x. 12.

unnavigated.c: unnavigated (un-nav’i-ga-ted), a. Not navigated; not passed over in ships or other vessels; not sailed on or over. Cook, Third Voyage. unnear} (un-nér’), prep. Not near; not close to; at a distance from. Now Cities stand wnneere the Ocean’s brim. Davies, Muse’s Sacrifice, p. 51. (Davies.)

unnecessarily.c: unnecessarily (un-nes’e-sa-ri-li), adv. In an unnecessary manner; without necessity; need- mat superfluously. Shak., Tempest, ii. 1.

unnecessariness.c: unnecessariness (un-nes’e-sa-ri-nes), m. The state of being unnecessary; needlessness. Dr. H. More.

unnecessary.c: unnecessary (un-nes’e-sa-ri), ad. and n. [< ME. wnnecessarie; < un-l + necessary.) I. a. Not necessary; needless; not required by the circumstances of the case; useless: as, wnne- cessary labor or care; unnecessary rigor. Onnecessarie Is him to plaunte yf he be wel yowe. Paliadius, Husbondrie (KE. E. T. 8.), p. 143. II. 2.3; pl. unnecessaries (-riz). That which is unnecessary or dispensable. It contains nothing But rubbish from the other rooms, and unnecessaries. unobtrusive.c: unobtrusive (un-ob-tr6’siv), a. Not obtrusive; not forward; modest; inconspicuous. We possess within our own city an instance of merit, as eminent as it is unobtrusive. E. Everett, Orations and Sreeches, I. 324.

unode.c: unode (i’nod), n. unoiled.c: unoiled (un-oild’), a. Not oiled; free from oil. Unoiled hinges. Young, Love of Fame, vi.

unold.c: unold (un-dld’), v. t. [< un-2 + old.] To make young; rejuvenate. Minde-gladding fruit that can nolde a man. Sylvester, tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Schisme.

unona.c: Unona (i-n0’nii), n. [NL. (Linneus filius, 1781); altered from NL. Anona, the name of a related genus.] A genus of plants, of the order Ano- nace, type of the tribe Unonee. It differs from Asimina, the papaw of the United States, in its commonly moniliform fruit, and from others of its tribe in its corolla with flat open petals, and in having numerous ovules in a single series. The 25 species are natives of tropical Asia, except 4 or 5 which are African. They are trees or shrubby climbers, usually with large flowers solitary in or near the axils, their petals often 2 or 3 inches long, reaching 6 inches in U. longiflora, a shrub of Assam. Their young branches are often silky or velvety, with brown, gray, golden, or reddish hairs, or, in U. Desmos and U. discolor, are covered with white dots or tubercles. Many species yield an aromatic bark and fruit, used as a stimulant and febrifuge. U. discolor, cultivated in India, and native also in China and the Malay archipelago, is a small tree or shrub with polymorphous leaves, odorous yellow flowers with silky petals in several varieties, and purple moniliform fruit with fleshy joints, resembling small grapes; from the unripe fruit the Chinese make a purple dye. U. viridiflora, a gigantic climber of Indian forests, is remarkable for the bright-green color of its large flowers. For the former U. hamata, now Artabotrys odoratissima, see tail-grape; for the former U. (now Cananga) odorata, see Cananga. See also Uvaria and Xylopia, with which the species have been much confused.

unonee.c: Unonee (ii-n0’né-6), v. pl. [NL. (Bentham and Hooker, 1862), < Unona + -ex.] A tribe of polypetalous plants, of the order Anonacee, characterized by flowers with densely crowded stamens and six valvate flattened or connivent petals in two rows, all nearly alike, or the inner smallorabsent. It includes 16 genera, of which Unona is the type; Astmina and Trigyneia are American, the others natives mostly of tropical Asia or Africa. rears (un-op’e-ra-tiv), a. Inopera- lie. unpierced.c: unpierced (un-pérst’), Not pierced; not penetrated. Byron, Mazeppa.

unpillared.c: unpillared (un-pil’ird), a. Deprived of pillars; not having or supported by pillars. Pope, Dunceiad, iii. 107.

unpilled.c: unpilled (un-pild’), a. [< un-1 + pilled, pp. of pill.) Unpillaged. Dr. Dee, Petty Navy Royal (1576). (Davies.)

unpillowed.c: unpillowed (un-pil’6d), a. Having no pillow; having the head not supported. Milton, Comus, |. 353.

unpiloted.c: unpiloted (un-pi’lot-ed), a. Unguided through dangers or difficulties. Charlotte Bronté, Jane Eyre, xxxv.

unpin.c: unpin (un-pin’), v. t.; pret. and pp. yar on ppr. wrypimning. [< ME. unpynnen; < wn-2 pint,} To remove the pin or pins that patent (a) To unbolt. He... gan the stewe dore al soft unpynne. Chaucer, Troilus, iii. 698. (6) To unfasten or unloose by taking out the pins: as, to unpin a ribbon or a gown; hence, to loosen the garments of; undress. Emil. Shall I go fetch your night-gown? Des. No, unpin me here. Shak., Othello, iv. 3. 35. The peremptory Analysis that you will call it, I believe will be so hardy as once more to unpinned your spruce fastidious oratory, to rumple her laces, her frizzles, and her bobbins though she wince, and fling never so Peevishly. Milton, Animadversions.

unpinion.c: unpinion (un-pin’yon), v. ¢ [< wn-2 + pinion1.] To loose from pinions or manacles; free from restraint. Clarke.

unpiteous.c: unpiteous (un-pit’é-us), a. [< ME. wnpitous, unpiteous; < wn-1 + piteous.] 1+. Impious; wicked.— 2. Pitiless; cruel. Myn wunpietous lyf draweth a long unagreeable dwell- ynges in me, Chaucer, Boéthius, i. meter 1.

unpiteously.c: unpiteously (un-pit’é-us-li), adv. [< ME. wn- pitously; < unpiteous + -ly2.] 1+. Impiously; wickedly. Wyclif, Heclus. xlvi. 23.—2. In an unpiteous manner; cruelly. Oxford, in her senility, has proved no Alma Mater in thus so unpiteously cramming her alumni with the shells alone. Sir W. Hamilton,

unpiteousness.c: unpiteousness (un-pit’6-us-nes), ». [< ME. unpitousnesse; < unpiteous + -ness.) 1+. Impiety; wickedness. Wyclif, Lev. xix.7.—2. The character or state of being unpiteous or cruel.

unpitied.c: unpitied (un-pit’id), a 1. Not pitied; not compassionated; not regarded with sympathetic sorrow. Not pinked; not Shak., T. of the §., Go, and weep as I did, And be unpitied. Beau. and Fl., Knight of Burning Pestle, iv. 3 Stumbling across the market to his death Unpitied. Tennyson, Aylmer's Field, cee es —,' unplausive 2+. Unmerciful; pitiless. You shall have your full time of imprisonment and your deliverance with an unpitied whipping. ., M. for M., iv. 2. 13.

unpitiful.c: unpitiful (un-pit’i-fil), a. 1. Having no pity; not merciful. 2. Not exciting pity. Future times, in love, may pity her; Sith graces such unpitiful should Tove, Sir J. Davies, Wit’s Pilgrimage.

unpitifully.c: unpitifully (un-pit’i-ful-i), adv. In an unpitiful manner; unmercifully; without mercy. Beat him She va gas £ hak., M. W. of W., iv. 2. 215.

unpitifulness.c: unpitifulness (un-pit’i-fil-nes), n. The state or character of being unpitiful. Sir P. Sidney, Arcadia, iii. ar ete. See wisinnne, etc. unpity, ». [ME., < went + pity.] Inmpiety. Wychf, Rom. i. 18.

unpitying.c: unpitying (un-pit‘i-ing), a. Having no pity; showing no compassion. Hurrying from his castle, with a cry He raised his hands to the unpitying sky. Longfellow, Torquemada.

unpityingly.c: unpityingly (un-pit’i-ing-li), adv. In an unpitying manner; without compassion.

unplace.c: unplace (unplas’), v. t. [< wn-2 + place.] To displace. The papists do place in pre-eminence over the whole church the pope, thereby unplacing Christ, which i is the Head of the church. J. Bradford, Letters (Parker Soc., 1853), II. 142.

unplaced.c: unplaced (un-plast’), a. 1. Not arranged or distributed in proper places; undetermined in regard to place; confused; jumbled. It is a thousand times more credible that four mutable elements and one immutable fifth essence, duly and eternally placed, need no God, than that an army of infinite small portions, or seeds unplaced, should have produced this order and beauty without a divine marshal. Bacon, Atheism (ed. 1887). 2. Having no place, office, or employment under government. Unplaced, unpension’d. Pope, Imit. of Horace, ii. 1.

unplagued.c: unplagued (un-plagd’), a. Not plagued; not harassed; not tormented; not afflicted. Shak., R. and J., i. 5. 19.

unplaint.c: unplaint (un-plan’), a. [ME. unplain; < un-1 + plain,] Not plain; not simple; not open; insincere. Gower, Conf. Amant., 1. unplained} (un-pland’), a. Not deplored; not bewailed or lamented. To die alone, unpitied, unplained, Spenser, Daphnaida. BIR NS (un-plat’), v. t. [< ME. wnpleiten; < un-? + plait. Cf. unplight?.] 1+. To unfold; explain. Unnete may I unpleyten my sentence with wordes. Chaucer, Boéthius, ii. prose 8. 2. To undo the plaits of; unbraid: as, to wn- plait hair. One day she even went the length of unplaiting with swift warm fingers all the wavy coils of that au ed hair. R. Broughton, Not Wisely but Too Well, xxiii.

unplant.c: unplant (un-plant’), v. t [< un-2 + plant1.] To remove, as that which is planted; uproot; deprive of plants; hence, to depopulate. Being inioyned by our Commission not to unplant nor wrong the Saluages, because the channel was so neere the shore where now is Iames Towne, then a thicke group of trees, wee cut them downe. Capt. John Smith, True Travels, II. 99.

unplanted.c: unplanted (un-plan’ted), a. 1. Not planted; of spontaneous growth. Waller, Battle of the Islands, ii—2. Not cultivated; unimproved. Ireland is a country wholly unplanted. The farms have neither dwelling-houses nor good offices, nor are the lands anywhere provided with fences and communications. Burke, On Popery Laws, iv.

unplastic.c: unplastic (un-plas’tik), a 1. Not plastic; not readily molded. WHncyc. Brit., XIX. 637.—2. Not suitable for plastic representation; unsculptural. Thoroughly unplastic in action and conception. C. C. Perkins, Italian Seulpture, p. 244.

unplausible.c: unplausible (un-pla’zi-bl), a. Not plausible; not having a fair or specious appearance. Such unplausible propositions. Barrow, Sermons, III, xlv.

unplausibly.c: unplausibly (un-pla’zi-bli), adv. In an unplausible manner; not plausibly. Public suspicions Saitene unjustly (but not altogether unplausibly) taxed them with Popish leanings. e Quincey, Secret Societies, I.

unplausive.c: unplausive (un-pla’siv), a. Not approving; not applauding; displeased; disapproving. Tis like he'll question me Why such unplausive eyes are bent on him, Shak., T, and C., iii, 3. 43. unpleadable

unpleadable.c: unpleadable (un-plé’da-bl), a. Unfit to be ae or urged as a plea. South, Sermons, = Vals

unpleaded.c: unpleaded (un-plé’ded), a. 1. Not pleaded; not urged.—2. Undefended by an advocate. Otway.

unpleasable.c: unpleasable (un-plé’za-bl), a. Incapable of being pleased. [Rare.] My unpleasable daughter. Burgoyne, The Heiress, ii. 2.

unpleasant.c: unpleasant (un-plez’ant), a. Not pleasant; not affording pleasure; disagreeable. The unpleasant’st words That ever blotted paper. Shak., M. of V., iii. 2. 254, We have also here and there remarked a little of that unpleasant trick... of telling a story by implication and allusion, Macaulay, Hallam’s Const. Hist. Men of worldly minds, finding the true way of life wn- pleasant to walk in, have attempted to find out other and easier roads. J. H. Newman, Parochial Sermons, i. 99.

unpleasantly.c: unpleasantly (un-plez’ant-li), adv. In an unpleasant manner; in a manner not pleasing; disagreeably.

unpleasantness.c: unpleasantness (un-plez’ant-nes), ». 1. The state or quality of being unpleasant; disagreeableness. Hooker, Eccles. Polity.—2. A slight disagreement or falling out; a petty quarrel; an unimportant misunderstanding. ([Colloq.] wae late unpleasantness, the civil war. [Hunorous, The weather-boarding in many places is riddled with bullets— cards left by passing visitors during the late unpleasantness. The Century, XLI. 326.

unpleasantry.c: unpleasantry (un-plez’an-tri), n. 1. Want of pleasantry; absence or the opposite of cheerfulness, humor, or gaiety; disagreeableness. [Rare.] It would have been well for a man of so many peculiarities as Dr. Gower if this were all the unpleasantry to which he subjected himself. Jon Bee, Essay on Samuel Foote, p. xli. 2. An unpleasant occurrence; especially, a slight quarrel or falling out. [Rare.] Now, on the other hand, the goddess and her establishment of hoaxers, at Eleusis, did a vast ‘‘stroke of business” for more than six centuries, without any unpleasantries occurring. De Quincey, Secret Societies, I. If... there are two such imperious and domineering spirits in a family, unpleasantries of course will arise from their contentions. Thackeray, Newcomes, I. xxxiii. 8. A discomfort. [Rare.] The minor unpleasantries attending a hasty toilet. Chambers's Journal, Oct. 9, 1858, p. 235. (Hneyc. Dict.)

unpleased.c: unpleased (un-plézd’), a. Not pleased; displeased. My unpleased eye. Shak., Rich. IL., iii. 3. 193.

unpleasing.c: unpleasing (un-plé’zing), a. Unpleasant; offensive; disgusting; disagreeable; distasteful. Despiteful tidings! O unpleasing news! Shak., Rich. III., iv. 1. 37. A patch of sand is unpleasing; a desert has all the awe of ocean. Lowell, Among my Books, 1st ser., p. 318.

unpleasingly.c: unpleasingly (un-plé’zing-li), adv. In an unpleasing manner. Bp. Hall, Death of Absalom.

unpleasingness.c: unpleasingness (un-plé’zing-nes), n. The state or character of being unpleasing. Milton, Divoree, ii. 21.

unpleasive.c: unpleasive (un-plé’ziv), a. [< un-1 + *pleaside, < please + -ive.} Not pleasing; unpleasant. Grief is never but an unpleasive passion. Bp. Hall, Remains, p. 108.

unpleasurable.c: unpleasurable (un-plezh’ir-a-bl), a. Not pleasurable; not giving pleasure. Coleridge.

unpleasurably.c: unpleasurably (un-plezh’ir-a-bli), adv. So as not to give pleasure; without pleasure. So, as Lady Jackson rewrites the old story once more, one reads it, if but for its subject, not altogether unprofitably or unpleasurably. The Academy, May, 1890. ben! sou (un-pli’a-bl), a. Not pliable. Hol- Mv and.

unpliably.c: unpliably (un-pli’a-bli), adv. In an unpliable manner; without yielding.

unplucked.c: unplucked (un-plukt’), a. Not plucked; not pulled or torn away. fletcher (and another), Two Noble Kinsmen, v. 1.

unplug.c: unplug (un-plug’), v.t. [< un-2 + plug.] To remove a plug from. See unplugged. First, the resistance is measured in the usual manner with the other end of the cable earthed and with no plug in A, and balance is obtained by unplugging a resistance, R. Elect. Rev. (ing.), XXV. 550.

unplugged.c: unplugged (un-plugd’), a. Having the plug removed; also, not plugged: in electrical testing, said of a resistance when the plug which shortcircuits the coils of wire forming the resistance in the box of resistance-coils is taken out. unplumb! (un-plum’),a. [< wn-1 + plumb?2, a.] Not plumb; not vertical. Clarke. unplumb? (un-plum’), v. t& [< wn-2 + plumb2.] To deprive of lead; remove the lead from. [Rare.] Their turpitude purveys to their malice; and they wn- plumb the dead for bullets to assassinate the living. Burke, To a Noble Lord.

unplumbed.c: unplumbed (un-plumd’), a Not plumbed or measured by a plumb-line; unfathomed. The unplumb’d, salt, estranging sea. M. Arnold, Switzerland, To Marguerite.

unplume.c: unplume (un-plém’), v. t [< wn-2 + plume.] To strip of plumes or feathers; degrade. Glan- ville.

unpoco.c: un poco (6n po’k6). In music, a little; slightly; somewhat: as, wn poco staccato, somewhat staccato; wn poco ritardando, retarding a little.

unpoetical.c: unpoetical (un-pd-et’i-kal), a. 1. Not poetical; not having or possessing poetical character; prosaic. ZT. Warton, Hist. Eng. Poetry, IL. 444. —2. Not proper to or becoming a poet. Bp. Corbet, On the Death of Queen Anne.

unpoetically.c: unpoetically (un-p6-et’i-kal-i), adv. In an unpoetical manner; prosaically.

unpointed.c: unpointed (un-poin’ted), a. 1. Not having a point; not sharp.—2}. Having the points unfastened, as a doublet. His doublet loose and wnpoynted. Guevara, Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 255. 3. Having no point orsting; wanting point or definite aim or purpose. The conclusion... here would have shown dull, flat, and unpointed. B. Jonson, Magnetic Lady, iv. 3. 4, Not having marks by which to distinguish sentences, members, and clauses; unpunctuated: as, wrpointed writing.—5. Not having the vowel points or marks: as, an unpointed manuscript in Hebrew or Arabic. The reader of unpointed Hebrew... supplies for himself the vowels, by means of which alone the consonants can be raised into expressive sound. E. Caird, Philos. of Kant, p. 203.

unpoised.c: unpoised (un-poizd’), a. 1. Not poised; not balanced. The Oft on the brink Ofruin... Totter’d the rash democracy; wnpots’d, And by the rage devour’d. Thomson, Liberty. 2}. Unweighed; unhesitating; regardless of consequences. Seize on revenge, grasp the stern-bended front Of frowning vengeance with wnpaiz’d clutch. Marston, Antonio and Mellida, IL., iii. 1.

unpoison.c: unpoison (un-poi’zn), v. t [< wn-2 + poison.] To remove or expel poison from; free from poison. [Rare.] Such a course could not but in a short time have unpot- soned their perverted minds. South, Sermons, V. i.

unpolicied.c: unpolicied (un-pol’i-sid), a 1. Destitute of civil polity or a regular form of government. Warburton, Divine Legation, i. § 5.—2. Void of policy; impolitic; imprudent; stupid. That I might hear thee call great Cesar ass Unpolicied! Shak., A. and C., v. 2. 311.

unpolish.c: unpolish (un-pol’ish), v. t. [< wn-2 + polish.] 1. Toremove polish or gloss from, as varnished wood or blackened boots. Howell, Letters, I. v. 9.— 2. To deprive of politeness or elegance; render rough or inelegant. unpossibility How anger unpolished the most polite! Richardson, Clarissa Harlowe, V. 286. (Davies.)

unpolished.c: unpolished (un-pol/isht), a. 1. Not polished; not brought to a polish: noting surfaces of marble, wood, metal, etc. Unpolish’d gems no ray on pride bestow. Pope, On his Grotto. 2. Deprived of polish. 3. Not refined in manners; uncivilized; rude; plain. Those first wnpolish’d matrons, big and bold. Dryden, tr. of Juvenal’s Satires, vi. 12,

unpolite.c: unpolite (un-po-lit’), a Not polite; not refined in manners; uncivil; rude; impolite. Tatler, No. 140.

unpolitely.c: unpolitely (un-p6-lit’li), adv. Impolitely. Rather conscious and confused, Arthur asked his pardon if he had stared at him unpolitely. Dickens, Little Dorrit, xxiii.

unpoliteness.c: unpoliteness (un-p-lit’nes), n. 1. Lack of polish; want of refinement; coarseness, as of a style of writing. Sad outcries are made of the unpoliteness of the style. q Blackwall, Sacred Classics Defended, 2. Impoliteness.

unpolled.c: unpolled (un-pdld’), a. 1. Not polled; not registered or counted: as, a large unpolled vote. The opposite party bribed the barmaid at the Town Arms to hocus the brandy and water of fourteen unpolled electors. Dickens. 2+. Unplundered; not stripped. Richer than unpoll’d Arabian wealth and Indian gold. Fanshawe, Poems (1673), p. 314.

unpolluted.c: unpolluted (un-po-li’ted), a. Not polluted; not defiled; not corrupted; pure; unspotted. Her fair and unpolluted flesh. Shak., Hamlet, v. 1. 262.

unpope.c: unpope (un-pop’), v. t [< un-2 + pope.] 1. To divest or deprive of the office, authority, and dignities of pope. [Rare.] So, guilty! So, remains I punish guilt! He is unpoped, and all he did I damn. Browning, Ring and Book, II. 170. 2. To deprive of a pope. [Rare.] Rome will never so far unpope herself as to part with her pretended supremacy. Fuller.

unpopular.c: unpopular (un-pop’i-lir), a. Not popular; not having the public favor: as, an wupopular magistrate; an unpopular law. We never could very clearly understand how it is that egotism, so unpopular in conversation, should be so popular in writing. Macaulay, Moore’s Byron.

unpopularity.c: unpopularity (un-pop-i-lar’i-ti), n. The state of being unpopular. Burke, Speech on Econ, Reform.;

unpopularly.c: unpopularly (un-pop’i-lir-li), adv. popular manner; not popularly. unportable+ (un-por’ta-bl), a. [ME. unportable; < un-1 + portable.] 1. Not portable or capable of being carried. Raleigh.—2. Not bearable, as a trouble; insupportable. Wherfore the seyd William, nother hese frendes... durst not, ne yet ne dar not rydyn ne goo abote swythe occupation as he arn used and disposed, to here [their] grete and unportable drede and vexation. Paston Letters, I. 17.

unportioned.c: unportioned (un-por’shond), a. Not endowed or furnished with a portion or fortune. Has virtue charms? I grant her heavenly fair, But if unportioned, all will interest wed. Young, Night Thoughts, vii.

unportuous.c: unportuous (un-por’ti-us), a. [< wn-l + *por- tuous, < L. portuosus, full of ports, < ports, port: see porti.] Having no ports. [Rare.] An unportuous coast. Burke, A Regicide Peace, iii.

unpositive.c: unpositive (un-poz’i-tiv), a. Not positive; not assertive. A dumb, unpositive life, under the power of the world. H. Bushnell, Sermons for the New Life, xvii.

unpossessed.c: unpossessed (un-po-zest’), a. 1. Not possessed; not owned; not held; not occupied. Such vast room in nature unpossessed By living soul. Milton, P. L., viii. 153. 2. Not in possession: used with of. The mind, unpossessed of virtue. V. Knox, Christian Philosophy, § 23. The head is entirely unpossessed of ciliated lobes. W. B. Carpenter, Micros., p. 453.

unpossessing.c: unpossessing (un-po-zes’ing), a. Having no possessions. Thou unpossessing bastard!

unpossibility.c: unpossibility (un-pos-i-bil’i-ti), n. bility. [Rare.] It would be a matter of utter unpossibility. Poe, King Pest. In an un- Shak., Lear, ii. 1. 69. Impossi- unpossible

Ascham, The Scholemaster, p. 46. For us to levy power... Is all unpossible. Shak., Rich. IIL., ii. 2. 126, A thing unpossible to us This story seems to be. True Tale of Robin Hood (Child’s Ballads, V. 370).

unposted.c: unposted (un-pés’ted), a. 1. Not having a fixed post or situation. There were also some Queen’s officers going out to join their regiments, a few younger men, unposted, who expected to be attached to Queen’s regiments, as their own corps were fighting... against us. W. H. Russell. 2. Not posted or informed. [Colloq.]

unpower.c: unpower (un-pou’ér), 7. Lack of power; weakness. Halliwell. [Obsolete or provincial.]

unpowerful.c: unpowerful (un-pou’ér-fil), a..Not powerful; impotent. Cowley, Davideis, i.

unpracticable.c: unpracticable (un-prak’ ti-ka-bl), a. Not practicable; not feasible; not capable of being performed; impracticable. Barrow, Sermons, Il. xiii.

unpractical.c: unpractical (un-prak’ti-kal), a. Not practical. (a) Inclined to give time and attention to matters of speculation and theory rather than to those of practice, action, or utility; careless about things merely profitable; hence, unfitted to deal with realities. For my own part, I am quite willing to confess that I like him [Spenser] none the worse for being unpractical, and that my reading has convinced me that being too poetical is the rarest fault of poets. unpracticality.c: unpracticality (un-prak-ti-kal/i-ti), n. The character of being unpractical.

unpractically.c: unpractically (un-prak’ti-kal-i), adv.) In an unpractical manner; not practically.

unpracticedness.c: unpracticedness (un-prak’tist-nes), n. [« wn- practised + -ness.| The character or state of being unpractised; want of practice.

unpractisedunpracticed.c: unpractised, unpracticed (un-prak’tist), a. 1. Not having been taught by practice; not skilled; not having experience; raw; unskilful. The French soldiers, which from thee youth have been practised and inured in feats of arms, do not crack or advance themselves to have very often got the upper hand and mastery of your new made and unpractised soldiers. Sir T. More, Utopia (tr. by Robinson), i. 2t. Not known; not familiar through use or association. His tender eye, by too direct a ray Wounded, and flying from unpractised day. Prior. 8. Not practised; not put into operation or use. Waragna ordered all his Galla:.. to leave their horses and charge the enemy en foot. This confident step, unknown and unpractised by Galla before, had the desired effect. Bruce, Source of the Nile, II. 627.

unpraiset.c: unpraiset (un-praz’), v. t [< un-2 + praise.] To deprive of praise; strip of commendation. Young.

unpray.c: unpray (un-pra’), v. t [< wn-2 + pray.] To revoke, recall, or negative by a subsequent prayer having a tendency or effect contrary to that of a former one. [Rare.] The freedom and purity of his obedience. as it were, unpray what he had before pr: ayed. Sir M. Hale, Christ Crucified.

More, Works, p. 894. 2+. Unsolicited; unasked. Thow [Death] lest so fele in sondry wyse Agens hire wil, wnpreyed day and nyghte. Chaucer, Troilus, iv. 513.

unpreaching.c: unpreaching (un-pré’ching), a. Not in the habit of preaching. He is no unpreaching prelate. Latimer, Sermon of the Plough.

unpregnant.c: unpregnant (un-preg’nant), a. 1. Not pregnant; not quickened: with of. Like John-a-dreams, unpregnant of my cause, And can say nothing. hak., Hamlet, ii. 2. 595. 2. Not quick of wit; dull. This deed... makes me unpregnant And dull to all proceedings. Shak., M. for M,, iv. 4. 28.
