unprejudice.c: unprejudice (un-prej’6-dis), n. prejudice. Mr. Carlyle is an author who has now been so long before the world that we may feel towards him something of the unprejudice of posterity. Lowell, Study Windows, p. 121.

unprejudiced.c: unprejudiced (un-prej’6-dist), a. [Early mod. E. also unprejudiad; ¢ un-l + prejudiced.] 1. Not prejudiced; free from undue bias or prepossession; not preoccupied by opinion; impartial: as, an unprejudiced mind. The meaning of them may be so plain that any unprejudiced and reasonable man may certainly understand them. Tillotson. 2. Not warped by or proceeding from prejudice: as, an unprejudiced judgment.— 8. Not hurt; unimpaired; undamaged. A pair of most dissembling hypocrites Is he and this base Earle, on whom I vowel, Leauing King Lewis vnpreiudizd in peace, To spend the whole measure of my kindled rage. Heywood, 2 Edw. IV. (Works, ed. Pearson, 1874, I. 102).

unprejudicedly.c: unprejudicedly (un-prej’é-dist-li), adv. In an unprejudiced manner; impartially. [Rare.] Let us consider this evidence as unprejudicedly and carefully as we can. Amer. Nat., XXIII. 897.

unprejudicedness.c: unprejudicedness (un-prej’é-dist-nes), n. The state of being unprejudiced. Olarke.

unprelated.c: unprelated (un-prel’at), v. t To depose from the dignity of prelate; depose from the episcopate. Bp. Hacket, Abp. Williams, ii. 120. (Davies.)

unprelatical.c: unprelatical (un-pré-lat’i-kal), a. Unlike or unsuitable to a prelate. Clarendon, Civil War, I. 257.

unpremeditable.c: unpremeditable (un-pré-med’‘i-ta-bl), a. [< un-1 + *premeditable, < premeditate) + -able.] 1. Not capable of being premeditated or previously thought of. Imp. Dict.—2. Unforeseen; unlooked for; unexpected. A capful of wind - +. comes against you.. such unpremeditable puffs. Sterne, Sentimental Journey, The Fragment.

unpremeditated.c: unpremeditated (un-pré-med‘i-ta-ted), a. 1. Not previously meditated or thought over. My celestial patroness who deigns Her nightly visitation unimplored, And dictates to me slumbering, or inspires Easy my unpremeditated verse. Milton, P. L., ix. 24. Profuse strains of unpremeditated art. Shelley, The Skylark. 2. Not previously purposed or intended; not done by design: as, an wopremeditated offense. =Syn. 1. Unstudied, impromptu, offhand, spontaneous. See extemporaneous.

unpremeditatedly.c: unpremeditatedly (un-pré-med’i-ta-ted-li), adv. In anunpremeditated manner; without premeditation; undesignedly.

unpremeditatet.c: unpremeditatet (un-pré-med’i-tat), a. Unpremeditated. In sudden and unpremeditate prayer I am not always 1; and, when I am not myself, my prayer is not my prayer. Donne, Sermons, xi.

unpremeditation.c: unpremeditation (un-pré-med-i-ta’shon), ”. Absence of premeditation; undesignedness. The Anecdotes of Sierra seem to us to fail in that larklike unpremeditation which belongs to the lyric. The Atlantic, LXV. 563.

unpreparation.c: unpreparation (un-prep-a-ra’shon), ». The state of being unprepared; want of preparation; unpreparedness. Sir M. Hale, Afflictions.

unprepared.c: unprepared (an-pré-pard’), a. 1. Not prepared. (a) Not fitted or made suitable, fit, or ready for future use: as, unprepared provisions. (b) Not brought into a right, safe, or suitable condition in view of future event, contingency, accident, attack, danger, or the like; not put Freedom from » with =e unpride in order; specifically, not made ready or fit for death or eternity. I would not kill thy unprepared spirit. Shak., Othello, v. 2. 31. (c) Not planned; not worked out in advance; extemporaneous: as, an unprepared speech; unprepared speaking. (d) Not brought into a particular mental state; not trained: as, an unprepared student. 2. In music, specifically of a dissonant tone, not held over from a preceding chord or otherwise prepared; reached by a skip.

unpreparedly.c: unpreparedly (un-pré-par’ed-li), adv. In an unprepared manner or condition; without due preparation.

unpreparedness.c: unpreparedness (un-pré-pir’ed-nes), ». The state of being unprepared, unready, or sks ted; want of preparation.

unprepossessed.c: unprepossessed (un-pré-po-zest’), a. Not prepossessed; not biased by previous opinions; not prejudiced.

unprepossessing.c: unprepossessing (un-pré-po-zes’ing), a. Not prepossessing; not attractive or engaging; unpleasing: as, a person of unprepossessing appearance.

unprescribed.c: unprescribed (un-pré-skribd’), a. Not prescribed; not authoritatively laid down; not appointed: as, unprescribed ceremony. Bp. Hall, Letter from the Tower.

unpresentable.c: unpresentable (un-pré-zen’ta-bl), a. Not presentable; not fit for being presented or introduced to company or society; not in proper trim; unfit to be seen. i Be better eat with one who did not respect the truth or the laws than with a sloven and unpresentable person. O. W. Holmes, Emerson, p. 184.

unpressed.c: unpressed (un-prest’), a. 1. Not pressed. My pillow left wnpress'd. Shak., A. and C., iii. 13. 106. 2. Not enforced. Clarendon, Great Rebellion.

unpresuming.c: unpresuming (un-pre-zu ming), a. Not presuming; modest; humble; unpretentious. Modest, unpresuming men, V. Knox, To a Young Nobleman.

unpresumptuous.c: unpresumptuous (un-pré-zump’ti-us), a. Not presumptuous or arrogant; humble; submissive ; modest. Lift to Heav’n an unpresumptuous eye. Cowper, Task, v. 746.

unpretending.c: unpretending (un-pré-ten’ding), a. Not pretending to or claiming any distinction or superiority; unassuming; modest. To undeceive and vindicate the honest and unpretending part of mankind. Pope.

unpretentious.c: unpretentious (un-pré-ten’shus), a. Not pretentious; making no claim to distinction; modest.

unpretentiousness.c: unpretentiousness (un-pré-ten’shus-nes), 7. The character or state of being unpretentious; unassumingness; modesty. The journal is... none the less pleasant for its simplicity and unpretentiousness. Atheneum, No, 3240, p. 322.

unprettiness.c: unprettiness (un-prit’i-nes), ». The state of being unpretty; want of prettiness. She says it is not pretty in a young lady to sigh; but where is the unprettiness of it? Richardson, Sir Charles Grandison, III. 51.

unpretty.c: unpretty (un-prit’i), a. Not pretty; lacking prettiness, attractiveness, elegance, or charm. His English is blundering but not unpretty. Mme, D’Arblay, Diary, 155. (Davies.)

unprevailing.c: unprevailing (un-pré-va’ling), a. Of no force; unavailing; vain. Throw to earth This unprevailing woe. Shak., Hamlet, i. 2. 107.

unpreventableness.c: unpreventableness (un-pré-ven’ta-bl-nes), ». The character or state of being unpreventable; inevitableness. Mind, No. 35, 1884.

unprevented.c: unprevented (un-pré-ven’ted), a. vented; not hindered.—2+. Not preceded by anything. Grace sc. Comes unprevented, unimplored, unsought. Milton, P. L., iii. 281.

unpriced.c: unpriced (un-prist’), a. 1. Having no price set or indicated. The books offered for sale are unpriced, and customers are invited to make their offers. Athenseum, No. 8177, p. 855. 2. Priceless; above or beyond price. Thine ageless walls are bonded With base, unpriced, J. M. Neale, tr. of Bernard of Cluny.

unpridet.c: unpridet (un-prid’), v. t To strip or divest of pride or self-esteem. Be content to be unprided. Feltham, Resolves, i. 33. 1. Not pre-_ unpriest

unpriest.c: unpriest (un-prést’), v. t [¢ wn-2 + priest.] To deprive of the orders or authority of a priest; unfrock. Leo, bishop of Rome, only wnpriests him. Milton, Judgment of M. Bucer, xxiv.

unpriestly.c: unpriestly (un-prést’li), a. Unsuitable to or unbecoming a priest.

unprince.c: unprince (un-prins’), v. & [< un-2 + prince.] To strip of the character or authority of a prince; deprive of principality or sovereignty. [Rare.] Queen Mary... would not unprince herself to obey his Holiness. Fuller, Worthies, Warwick.

unprincely.c: unprincely (un-prins’li), a. Unbecoming a prince; not resembling a prince. Milton, Ans. to Hikon Basilike, § 9.

unprinciple.c: unprinciple (un-prin’si-pl), v. t. [« wn-2 + principle.| To destroy the moral principles of; corrupt. [Rare.] They have been principled, or rather unprincipled, by such tutors. H. Brooke, Fool of Quality, I. 111.

unprincipled.c: unprincipled (un-prin’si-pld), a [« wn-1 + principled.) 1. Not having settled principles; not grounded in principle. [Rare.] So unprincipled in Virtue’s book. Milton, Comus, 1. 367. 2. Having no sound moral principles; destitute of virtue; not restrained by conscience; profligate; immoral. My poor simple, guileless Baynes was trustee to Mrs. Dr. Firmin before she married that most unprincipled man, Thackeray, Philip, xvi. 8. Not resulting from good principles; iniquitous; wicked. I disclaim all such unprincipled liberties —let me but have truth and the law on my side. Irving, Knickerbocker, p. 388.

unprincipledness.c: unprincipledness (un-prin’si-pld-nes), n. The quality or state of being unprincipled; immorality; wickedness.

unprison.c: unprison (un-priz’n), v. t. [< wn-2 + prison.] To release or deliver from prison; set free. Donne, Letter to the Countess of Huntington. [Rare.]

unprivileged.c: unprivileged (un-priv’i-lejd), a. Not privileged; not enjoying a particular privilege, liberty, or immunity. Where even the children of the peer were unprivileged, no lower class could assert any exclusive claim. EH. A. Freeman, Amer. Lects., p. 307.

unprizable.c: unprizable (un-pri’za-bl), a Incapable of being prized or having its value estimated, as being either below valuation or above or beyond valuation. A baubling vessel was he captain of, For shallow draught and bulk unprizable. Shak., T. N., v. 1. 58. Your ring may be stolen too; so of your brace of unprizable estimations; the one is but frail and the other casual, Shak., Cymbeline, i. 4. 99.

unprized.c: unprized (un-prizd’), a. Not valued, as being either below or beyond valuation. Not all the dukes of waterish Burgundy Can buy this unprized precious maid of me. Shak., Lear, i. 1. 262. But seemingly a thing despised; Even by the sun and air unprized. Wordsworth, Italian Itinerant.

unprobably.c: unprobably (un-prob’a-bli), adv. 1. In a manner not to be approved of; improperly. To diminish by the authority of wise and knowing men, things unjustly aud unprobably crept in. $ Strype, Eccles. Mem. 2. Aye a Imp. Dict.

unproclaimed.c: unproclaimed (un-pr6-klamd’), a. Not proclaimed; not notified by public declaration. Assassin-like, had levied war, War unproclaimed. Milton, P. L., xi. 220.

unproductive.c: unproductive (un-pro-duk’tiv), a. 1. Not productive; barren; more especially, not producing large crops; not making profitable returns for labor: as, unproductive land; in polit. econ., not increasing the quantity or exchangeable value of articles of consumption: as, wepro- ductive labor. This nobleman..., desiring that no part of his property or capital should lie unproductive during his absence, made the best arrangement. Arnot, The Parables of Our Lord, p. 524. I call the man in trade an unproductive laborer who seeks to grow rich suddenly by speculation, instead of by faithful, legitimate business. J. F. Clarke, Self-Culture, xii. 2. Not producing some specified effect or result: with of: as, acts unproductive of good.

unproductiveness.c: unproductiveness (un-pro-duk’tiv-nes), n. The state of being unproductive, as land, stock, capital, labor, ete. 6637

unproductivity.c: unproductivity (un-pro-duk-tiv’i-ti), n. The quality or state of being unproductive; un- ak Nineteenth Century, XXIV.

unprofaned.c: unprofaned (un-pro-fand’), a. Not profaned or desecrated; not polluted or violated. Dry- den, Aineid, xi.

unprofessional.c: unprofessional (un-pr6-fesh’on-al), a. 1. Not pertaining to one’s profession.— 2. Not belonging to a profession: as, an unprofessional man.—8. Not befitting a certain profession or a member of a profession; noting keeping with the rules of a certain profession: as, wnpro- Sessional conduct.

unproficiency.c: unproficiency (un-pro-fish’en-si), m. Want of proficiency. Bp. Hall.

unprofit.c: unprofit (un-prof’it), n. Want of profit; unprofitableness; uselessness.

unprofitable.c: unprofitable (un-prof’i-ta-bl), a. [ME. wnprof- itable; <un-1 + profitable.} 1. Not profitable; bringing no profit; producing no gain, advantage, or improvement; serving no useful or desired end; useless; profitless: as, an wnprofita- ble business; an unprofitable servant. Not with grief, for that is unprofitable. Heb. xiii. 17. Any beast unprofitable for service they kill. Capt. John Smith, True Travels, I. 35. 2+. Unimproved; unlearned. Any uncunnynge and unprofitable man, as men ben wont to fynde comunly amonges the people. Chaucer, Boéthius, i. prose 1. =Syn: Bootless, unremunerative, fruitless, futile.

unprofitableness.c: unprofitableness (un-prof’i-ta-bl-nes), n. The state of producing no profit or good; uselessness; inutility. Addison.

unprofitably.c: unprofitably (un-prof’i-ta-bli), adv. In an unprofitable manner; without profit, gain, benefit, pavantoee, or use; to no good purpose or ef- etc. Our wasted oil unprofitably burns, Like hidden lamps in old sepulchral urns. Cowper, Conversation, 1. 357.

unprofited.c: unprofited (un-prof’i-ted), a. Not having profit or gain; profitless. Shak., T. N., i. 4. 22.

unprofiting.c: unprofiting (un-prof’i-ting), a. Unprofitable. B. Jonson, Epigrams, xe.

unprogressiveness.c: unprogressiveness (un-pro-gres’iv-nes),”. The quality or state of being unprogressive; stag- Not pronation. Pop. Sci. Mo., XX. 772.

unprohibited.c: unprohibited (un-pr6-hib’i-ted), a. Not prohibited; not forbidden; lawful. Milton.

unprojected.c: unprojected (un-pré-jek’ted), a. Not planned; not projected. South.

unprolific.c: unprolific (un-pr6-lif’ik), a. Not prolific; barren; not producing young or fruit; not fertile or fruitful. Sir M. Hale.

unpromise.c: unpromise (un-prom’is), v. t [¢ wn-2 + promise.] Torevoke, retract, or recall, as a promise. Promises are no fetters; with that tongue Thy promise past, unpromise it againe.: Chapman, All Fools, ii. 1.

unpromised.c: unpromised (un-prom’ist), a. Not promised or engaged; uncovenanted. Leave nought unpromise. Spenser, F. Q., V. v. 49,

unpromising.c: unpromising (un-prom’i-sing), a. Not promising; not affording a favorable prospect of success, of excellence, of profit, of interest, etc.; not looking as if likely to turn out well: as, an unpromising youth; an unpromising season. Even the most heavy, lumpish, and unpromising infants appear to be much improved by it. Bp. Berkeley, Farther Thoughts on Tar-water. =Syn. Inauspicious, unpropitious, unfavorable, untoward.

unprompted.c: unprompted (un-promp’ted), a. Not prompted; not dictated; not urged or instigated. My Tongue talks, unprompted by my Heart. Congreve, To Cynthia.

unpronounceable.c: unpronounceable (un-pro-noun’sa-bl), a. 1. Not pronounceable; incapable of being pronounced; difficult to pronounce: as, a harsh, unpronounceable word. But two, a youth and maiden, Were left to brave the storm, With unpronounceable Dutch names, And hearts with true love warm. Halleck, Epistles. 2. Unfit for being pronounced, named, or mentioned; unmentionable as being offensive to chaste ears.

unpronounced.c: unpronounced (un-pro-nounst’), a. Not pronounced; not uttered. Milton, Vacation Exercises, iii. unprovable

unprop.c: unprop (un-prop’), v. ft [< un-2 + prop.] To Bethe a prop or props from; deprive of support.

unproper.c: unproper (un-prop’ér), a. 1. Not proper or confined to one person; not peculiar. There ’s millions now alive That nightly lie in those unproper beds Which they dare swear peculiar. Shak., Othello, iv. 1. 69. 2. Not fit or proper; not suited; improper. Jer. Taylor, Real Presence, x. unproperly+ (un-prop’ér-li), adv. Unfitly; improperly. Vnproperly ascribed to Caucasus. Purchas, Pilgrimage, p. 41. unprophetic, unprophetical (un-pro-fet’ik, -i-kal), a. Not prophetic; not foreseeing or not predicting future events. Wretch... of unprophetic soul.

unpropitiable.c: unpropitiable (un-pr6-pish’i-a-bl), a. cannot be propitiated. A noble race is perishing at the hand of that wnpropiti- able avenger who waits on secular misconduct. The Academy, March 28, 1891, p. 296.

unpropitious.c: unpropitious (un-pré-pish’us), a. Not propitious; not favorable; inauspicious. Now flamed the dog-star’s unpropitious ray, Smote every brain, and wither’d every bay. Pope, Dunciad, iv. 9.

unpropitiously.c: unpropitiously (un-pr6-pish’us-li), adv. In an unpropitious manner; inauspiciously.

unpropitiousness.c: unpropitiousness (un-pro-pish’us-nes), n. The quality or state of being unpropitious; unfavorableness; inauspiciousness.

unproportionable.c: unproportionable (un-pro-por’shon-a-bl), a. Wanting due proportion; disproportionable. Besides, the roofe is not to be thought unproportionable. Purchas, Pilgrimage, p. 39. unproportionableness (un-pr6-por’shon-a-bl- nes),”. The character or state of being unproportionable ; unsuitability. Bp. Gauden, Tears of the Church, p. 586. (Davies.)

unproportionate.c: unproportionate (un-pro-por’shon-at), a. Not proportionate; disproportionate; unfit. Daniel, Civil Wars, vi.

unproportioned.c: unproportioned (un-pro-por’shond), a. proportioned; not suitable. To melt this unproportion’d frame of nature. B. Jonson, Every Man out of his Humour, i. 1.

unproposed.c: unproposed (un-pro-p6zd’), a. Not proposed; not offered for acceptance, adoption, or the like: as, the motion or candidate is as yet wn- proposed. Dryden.

unpropped.c: unpropped (un-propt’), a Not propped; not supported or upheld. Dryden, tr. of Ovid’s Metamorph., viii.

unpropriety.c: unpropriety (un-pro-pri’e-ti), n. Lack of propriety; error; incorrectness; unsuitableness; impropriety. [Rare.] The interest of a respectable Englishman may be said, without any unpropriety, to be identical with that of his wife. Macaulay, Mill on Government.

unproselyte.c: unproselyte (un-pros’é-lit), v. t. [< wn-2 + proselyte.] ‘To prevent being made a proselyte or convert; win back from proselytism. [Rare.] This text... happily unproselyted some inclinable to his opinions. Fuller, Ch. Hist., X. iv. 8. (Davies.)

unprosperous.c: unprosperous (un-pros’pér-us), a. Not prosperous; not attended with success; unfortunate; unsuccessful. A soldier must not think himself unprosperous if hebe not successful as the son of Philip. Jer. Taylor, Holy Living, ii. 6.

unprosperously.c: unprosperously (un-pros’pér-us-li), adv. Unsuccessfully; unfortunately. Careticus, flying, secured himself among the Mountains of Wales, where he died after he had unprosperously reigned three Years. Baker, Chronicles, p. 4.

unprosperousness.c: unprosperousness (un-pros’pér-us-nes), ”. The state of being unprosperous; want of success; failure of the desired result. Hammond, Works, IV. 493.

unprotected.c: unprotected (un-pro-tek’ted), a. Not protected; not defended; not supported. Hooker, Keeles. Polity.

unprotectedness.c: unprotectedness (un-pro-tek’ted-nes), n. The state of being unprotected; defenselessness. The Atlantic, LXIV. 353.

unprotestantize.c: unprotestantize (un-prot’es-tan-tiz), v. t. To cause to change from the Protestant religion to some other; render other than Protestant; divest of Protestant characteristics or features. [Rare.] To Romanize the Church is not to reform it. To unprotestantize is not to reform it. Kingsley, Life (1851), ix.

unprovable.c: unprovable (un-pré’va-bl), a. Not capable of being proved, demonstrated, confirmed, or es- Pope, Odyssey, xxii. That Not unprovable tablished. Also spelled wnproveable. Bp. Hall, Dissuasive from Popery.

unproved.c: unproved (un-prévd’), a. [« ME. *unproved; <un-+ + proved.| 1. Not proved; not known by trial; not tested. A fresh unproved knight. Spenser. 2. Not established as true by argument, demonstration, or evidence. There is much of what should be demonstrated left unproved. Boyle.

unprovedness.c: unprovedness (un-prévd’nes), m. [ME. unprovedness; < unproved + -ness.] Inexperience. Wars of Alexander (HK. EH. T.8.), 1. 1019.

unprovide.c: unprovide (un-pro-vid’), v. ¢. [Cun-2 + provide.] To unfurnish; divest or strip of qualifications; in the following quotation, to divest of resolution. Ill not expostulate with her, lest her body and beauty unprovide my mind again. Shak., Othello, iv. 1. 218.

unprovided.c: unprovided (un-pré-vi'ded), a. 1. Not provided; unfurnished; unsupplied: with with, formerly of: as, unprovided with money. Utterly unprovided of all other natural, moral, or spiritual abilities. Bp. Sprat. I shall make the public a present of these curious pieces at such time as I shall find myself unprovided with other subjects. Addison, Frozen Words. 2. Having made no preparation; not suitably prepared; unprepared. Tears for a stroke unseen afford relief; But, unprovided for a sudden blow, Like Niobe we marble grow. Dryden, Threnodia Augustalis, v. 3t. Unforeseen. Spenser.

unprovidedly.c: unprovidedly (un-pr6-vi’ded-li), adv. In an unprovided manner; without provision; unpreparedly. ; unprovident} (un-prov’i-dent), a. Improvident. Beau. and Fl., Thierry and Theodoret, iv.

unprovoked.c: unprovoked (un-pro-vokt’), a. 1. Not provoked; not incited. When all on the sudden, the Smectymnuans, a strange generation of men, unprovoked, unthought of, cry out of hard measure, and fly in my face, as men wrongfully accused. Bp. Hall, Ans. to Vindication of Smectymnuus. 2. Not proceeding from provocation or just cause: as, an unprovoked attack. A rebellion so destructive and so unprovoked. Dryden.

unprovokedly.c: unprovokedly (un-pro-v0’ked-li), adv. In an unprovoked manner; without provocation. unprudence} (un-pré’dens),. [ME.; < un-1 + prudence.| Want of prudence; imprudence; improvidence. The wvnprudence of foolish [is] erring. a Wyclif, Prov. xiv. 18,

unprudential.c: unprudential (un-pré-den’shal), a. Imprudent. The most unwise and unprudential act. Milton, Rikonoklastes, xxiii.

unpruned.c: unpruned (un-prénd’), a. Not pruned; not lopped or trimmed. Fruit-trees all unpruned. Shak., Rich. II., iii. 4. 45.

unpublic.c: unpublic (un-pub’lik), a. Not public; private; not generally seen or known. [Rare.] Virgins must be retired and unpublic. Jer, Taylor, Holy Living, ii. 3.

unpublished.c: unpublished (un-pub’‘lisht), a. 1. Not made public; secret; private. Unpublish’d virtues. Shak., Lear, iv. 4. 16. 2. Not published; stillin manuscript, as a book. The finest Turner etching is of an aqueduct with stork standing in a mountain stream, not in the published series; and next to it are the unpublished etchings of the Via Mala and Crowhurst. Ruskin, Elements of Drawing, 1872.

unpucker.c: unpucker (un-puk’ér), v. t. [< wn-2 + pucker.] To smooth away the puckers of; relax. Let but Teufelsdréckh open his mouth, Heuschrecke’s also unpuckered itself into a free doorway. Carlyle, Sartor Resartus, i. 3.

unpuff.c: unpuff (un-puf’), v.t [<wn-2 + puff.] To take away the vanity of; humble. We might vnpuf our heart, and bend our knee, T’ appease with sighs God’s wrathfull Maiestie. Sylvester, tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, i. 4.

unpunctual.c: unpunctual (un-pungk’tu-al), a. Not punctual; not exact, especially with reference to time. Pope.

unpunctuality.c: unpunctuality (un-pungk-ti-al’i-ti), n. The state or character of being unpunctual. H. Spencer, Study of Sociol., p. 285.

unpunctually.c: unpunctually (un-pungk’ti-al-i), adv. In an unpunctual manner; not punctually. cable (un-pun‘ish-a-bl), a. Not punishable; not capable or deserving of being 6638 punished: applied to persons or things. ton, Answer to Salmasius, v. 157. Where all offend, the crime’s unpunishable. May, tr. of Lucan, v.

unpunishably.c: unpunishably (un-pun’ish-a-bli), adv. With-out being or becoming liable to punishment. Milton, Answer to Hikon Basilike, § 28.

unpunished.c: unpunished (un-pun’isht), a. Not punished; suffered to pass without punishment or with impunity. Mil- Shall innocence In her be branded, and my guilt escape Unpunish'd? Fletcher (and Massinger?), Lovers’ Progress, v. 1.

unpurely.c: unpurely (un-pir’li), adv. Impurely. Bp. Bale, English Votaries, ii. [Rare.]

unpureness.c: unpureness (un-pur’nes), x. Impurity. J. Udall, On Luke ii. [Rare.]

unpurged.c: unpurged (un-pérjd’), a. Not purged. (a) Unpurified. The rheumy and unpurged air. Shak., J. C., ii. 1. 266. (0) Not cleared from moral defilement or guilt. I feare it would but harme the truth for me to reason in her behalf, so long as I should suffer my honest estimation to lye unpurg’d from these insolent suspicions. Milton, Apology for Smectymnuus.

unpurposed.c: unpurposed (un-pér’post), a. Not intended; not designed. Accidents unpurposed. Shak., A. and C., iv. 14. 84.

unpurse.c: unpurse (un-pérs’), v.t. [< ME. wnpursen; <un-2 + purse.] 1. To take out of a purse; expend. [Rare.] Ever was the gold unpursed. Gower, Conf. Amant., v. 2. Torob of a purse or money. Pollok. [Rare.]

unpurveyed.c: unpurveyed (un-pér-vad’), a. [ME., < wn-1+ purveyed.| Unexpected; unforeseen. Hem that she [Fortune] hath left in dyspeyre, unpurveyed. Chaucer, Boéthius, ii. prose 1.

unqualified.c: unqualified (un-kwol’i-fid), a. 1. Not qualified; not fit; not having the requisite talents, abilities, or accomplishments.: The learned are held unqualified to serve their country as counsellors merely from a defect of opulence. Goldsmith, Vicar, xix. 2. Not qualified legally; not having the legal qualifications; specifically, not having taken the requisite oath or oaths; not having passed the necessary examinations and received a diploma or license: as, an unqualified practitioner of medicine. By the statutes for preserving the game, a penalty is denounced against every unqualified person that kills a hare. Blackstone, Com., I., Int., § ii. In the course of time, through relaxation of bardic discipline, the profession was assumed by unqualified persons, to the great detriment of the regular bards. Encye. Brit., VI. 791. 8. Not modified or restricted by conditions or exceptions; absolute: as, unqualified praise. That women and children taken in war, and such men as have not been slain, naturally fall into unqualified servitude, is manifest. H. Spencer, Prin. of Sociol., § 456.

unqualifiedly.c: unqualifiedly (un-kwol’i-fid-li), adv. In an unqualified manner; without qualification; absolutely. Him of Cyprus, to whom the Syriac versions wnquali- Jjiedly attribute them. Amer. Jour. Philol., VIII. 91.

unqualifiedness.c: unqualifiedness (un-kwol’i-fid-nes), ». The character or state of being unqualified. The advertency and unqualifiedness of copiers. Bibliotheca Biblica, I. 65. (Eneyc. Dict.)

unqualify.c: unqualify (un-kwol’i-fi), v. ¢. [< wn-2 + qualify.] To divest of qualifications; disqualify. [Rare.] Deafness unqualijies me for all company. Swift. unqualitied+ (un-kwol’i-tid), a. Deprived of the usual qualities or faculties. He is unqualitied with very shame. Shak., A: and C., iii, 11. 44.

unquantified.c: unquantified (un-kwon’ti-fid), a. Not quantified. Unquantified proposition. Sce proposition.

unquarrelable.c: unquarrelable (un-kwor’el-a-bl), a. [< wn-1 + quarrel1 + -able.] Incapable of being quarreled with, objected to, or impugned. Such satisfactory and unquarrelable reasons. Sir T. Browne, Vulg. Err., vi. 10.

unqueen.c: unqueen (un-kwén’),v.¢. [< wn-2 + queen.] To divest of the dignity of queen. [Rare.] Although unqueen’d, yet like A queen, and daughter to a king, inter me. Shak., Hen. VIII., iv. 2. 171.

unquenchable.c: unquenchable (un-kwen’cha-bl),a.and. I, a. Not quenchable; incapable of being quenched, extinguished, allayed, or the like: as, wnquench- able fire, thirst, etc. unquit Such an extinction of originality in what would be evolutional closure will always be prevented by the feverish activity of the unquenchable passions of human nature. Maudsley, Body and Will, p. 168 II, ». That which cannot be quenched; figuratively, one whose zeal cannot be quenched. (Colloq.]

unquenchableness.c: unquenchableness (un-kwen’cha-bl-nes), 2. The state of being unquenchable. Hakewill, Apology, iv. 4.

unquenchably.c: unquenchably (un-kwen’cha-bli), adv. In an unquenchable manner}; so as to be unquenchable. That lamp shall burn wnguenchably. Scott, L, of L. M., ii.

unquestionability.c: unquestionability (un-kwes’chon-a-bil‘i-ti),. The character or state of being unquestionable; also, that which cannot be questioned or doubted; a certainty. Our religion is... a great heaven-high Unquestionability. Carlyle, Past and Present, ii. 6.

unquestionable.c: unquestionable (un-kwes’chon-a-bl), a. 1. That cannot be questioned or doubted; indubitable; certain: as, unquestionable evidence or truth; unquestionable courage. King Henry the Seventh being deceased, his only Son Prince Henry... by unquestionable Right succeeded in the Crown, at the Age of eighteen Years. Baker, Chronicles, p. 254. 2. Averse to being questioned; averse to conversation. An unquestionable spirit, which you have not. Shak., As you Like it, iii, 2. 398.

unquestionableness.c: unquestionableness (un-kwes‘chon-a-bl-nes), n. The character or state of being unquestionable; unquestionability.

unquestionably.c: unquestionably (un-kwes’chon-a-bli), adv. Without doubt; indubitably. At fit how [Anacktus] setts on alone toward the Camp; is ment, examin’d, and at last unquestionably known. Milton, Hist. Eng., i.

unquestioned.c: unquestioned (un-kwes’chond), a. 1. Not called in question; not doubted. It is the sober truth of history, unquestioned, because unquestionable. Story, Speech, Salem, Sept. 18, 1828. 2. Not interrogated; having no questions asked; not examined; not examined into. It prefers itself and leaves unquestion’d Matters of needful value. Shak., M. for M., i. 1. 55. 3. Not to be opposed or disputed. Their unquestioned pleasures must be served. B. Jonson.

unquestioningness.c: unquestioningness (un-kwes’chon-ing-nes),. The character of being unquestioning; unquestioning action. [Rare.] The new men... have come to be accepted... with ». cordial unquestioningness. The Century, XX. 3.

unquick.c: unquick (un-kwik’), a. 1. Not quick; slow. Imp. Dict.—2+. Not alive or lively. Daniel, Civil Wars, iii.

unquiescence.c: unquiescence (un-kwi-es’ens), 7. inquietude. unquiet! (un-kwi’et), a. [<wn-l + quiet.] Not quiet; not calm or tranquil; restless; agitated; disturbed; also, causing disturbance. For almost all the world their service bend To Phebus, and in vain my light I lend, Gaz’d on unto my setting from my rise Almost of none but of wnqutet eyes. Beau. and Fil., Majd’s Tragedy, i. A tumbrell or cucking-stool, set up... for the correction of unquiet women. J. Collins, Hist. of Somersetshire (ed. 1791), ITT. 460. unquiet?t (un-kwi’et), v.t [« un-2 + quiet.] To disquiet. Disquiet; Here has fallen a business Between your cousin and Master Manly has Unquieted us all. B. Jonson, Devil is an Ass, iv. 1.

unquiet.c: unquiet (un-kwit’), a. [<¢ ME. unquit; < unit + quit.) 1. Not discharged; not freed from obligation. Gracinus, we must pray you, hold your guards Unquit when morning comes. _ B, Jonson, Sejanus, v. 5. unquit 2. Unpaid. The dai Is past, the dette vn-quit. Holy Rood (E. BE. T. 8.), p. 110.

unquietly.c: unquietly (un-kwi’et-li), adv. In an unquiet manner or state; without rest; in an agitated state; uneasily. One minded like the weather, most unquietly. » MON Shak, Lear, ii, 1. 2

unquietness.c: unquietness (un-kwi’et-nes), ». The state of being unquiet; agitation; excitement; uneasiness; restlessness. Iago. Is my lord angry? Emilia. He went hence but now, And certainly in strange unquietness. ak., Othello, iii. 4. 183.

unquietude.c: unquietude (un-kwi’e-tid), m. Inquietude. A kind of unquietude and discontentment. Str H. Wotton, Education of Children.

unquizzable.c: unquizzable (un-kwiz’a-bl), a. [< wn- + quiz + -able.] Not capable of being quizzed; not open to ridicule. Bach was dressed out in his No. 1 suit, in most exact and unquizzable uniform. Marryat, Frank Mildmay, xv. (Davies.) unraced, a. [ME., < un-1 + raced, pp. of race5.] Unbroken; undestroyed. Tho thinges... ben kept hole and unraced. Chaucer, Boéthius, iv. prose 1.

unracked.c: unracked (un-rakt’), a. Notracked; not having the contents freed from the lees: as, an wn- racked vessel. Bacon, Nat. Hist., § 306.

unraised.c: unraised (un-razd’), a. Not raised. (@) Not elevated. The flat unraised spirits. (6) Not abandoned, as a siege. The siege shulde nat be wnreysed. Berners, tr. of Froissart’s Chron., I. ccexxxviii.

unraked.c: unraked (un-rakt’), a. 1. Not-raked: as, land unraked.—2, Not raked together; not raked up. Where fires thou find’st unraked. Shak., M. W. of W., v. 5. 48. 3+. Not sought or acquired by effort, as by raking. He doubtless will command the People to make good his Promises of Maintenance more honourably unask’d, unrak’d for. Milton, Touching Hirelings.

unransacked.c: unransacked (un-ran’sakt), a. 1. Not ransacked; not searched.—2. Not pillaged. Knolles, Hist. of the Turks.

unraptured.c: unraptured (un-rap’tird), a. Not enraptured, enchanted, charmed, or transported. Man unraptured, uninflamed. Young, Night Thoughts, iv.

unravel.c: unravel (un-rav’el), v.; pret. and pp. unraveled, unravelled, ppr. unraveling, unravelling. [< un-2 + ravel. The prefix is either reversive or intensive, according as ravel is taken to mean ‘tangle’? or ‘untangle.’] I. trans. 1. To disentangle or separate, as threads; especially, to take out the threads of (textile material). See ravel. I have talked with my own heart, And have unravelled my entangled will. Shelley, The Cenci, iii. 1. By means of a prism Sir Isaac Newton unravelled the texture of solar light. Tyndall, Radiation, § 1. 2. To clear from complication or difficulty; unriddle; unfold, These, with fifty other points left unravelled, you may endeavor to solve, if you have time. Sterne, Tristram Shandy, ii. 19. At the first glimpse we see that here there is a mystery to be unravelled. E. A. Freeman, Venice, p. 74. 3+. To separate the connected or united parts of; throw into disorder. Unravelling all the received principles of reason and religion. Tillotson, Sermons, I. i. 4. To unfold or bring to a denouement, as the plot or intrigue of a play. Pope. II. intrans. To be unfolded; be disentangled. Shak., Hen. V., Prol., 1. 9. What webs of wonder shall unravel there! Young, Night Thoughts, vi.

unravelerunraveller.c: unraveler, unraveller (un-rav’el-ér), n. One who or that which unravels. Mythologists are indeed very pretty fellows, and are mighty wnravellers of the fables of the old Ethnicks, discovering all the Old Testament concealed in them. T. Brown, Works, III. 279. (Davies,)

unravelment.c: unravelment (un-rav’el-ment), ». The act or process of unraveling; disentanglement; unfolding. In the course of the unravelment of the conspiracy inst Belle Carlisle we come across many clever touches of character. The Academy, Nov. 15, 1890, p. 447.

unrazored.c: unrazored (un-ra’zord), a. Unshaved. Their wnrazor’d lips. Milton, Comus, 1. 290

unreached.c: unreached (un-récht’), a. Not reached; not attained to. That lofty hill unreached. Dryden. unread}, n. [ME. wnred, unred, < AS. unr&d (= Icel. wrddh = Dan. raad), bad counsel, < un-, not (here ‘bad’), + rd, counsel: see read, n.) Bad advice or counsel. unread? (un-red’), a. [< un-l + read, pp. of readi, v.] 1. Not read; not perused. These books are safer and better to be left publickly unread. Hooker, Eccles. Polity. 2. Untaught; not learned in books. The clown unread, and half-read gentleman. Dryden, Hind and Panther, iii. 408. 6639

unreadable.c: unreadable (un-ré’da-bl), a. Not readable. (a) Incapable of being read or deciphered; illegible: as, unreadable manuscript or writing. (b) Not suitable or fit for reading; not worth reading: as, a dull, unreadable book or poem. Goethe... wasted his time and thwarted his creative energy on the mechanical mock-antique of an unreadable “* Achilleis.” Lowell, Study Windows, p. 217. Books almost unreadable to delicate minds. Littell’s Living Age, CLX1I. 75.

unreadableness.c: unreadableness (un-ré’da-bl-nes), n. The quality or state of being unreadable; illegibility. Athenzum, No. 3300, p. 113.

unreadily.c: unreadily (un-red’i-l), adv. In an unready manner. (a) Unpreparedly. (b) Not promptly; not quickly. (ct) Awkwardly. Men being first inforced to write their acts and monuments in beasts skinnes dried, in barkes of trees, or otherwise perchance as unreadily. Hakluyt’s Voyages, Il. 171.

unreadiness.c: unreadiness (un-red’i-nes), ». The character of being unready, in any sense.

unready.c: unready (un-red’i), a. [< ME. wnredy; < un-1 Min 1. Not ready; not prepared; not ‘ A dismal picture of the general doom; Where souls distracted, when the trumpet blows, And half unready with their bodies come. 2 Dryden, Annus Mirabilis, st. 254. 2. Not prompt; not quick.—3}. Awkward; ungainly. An unready horse, that will neither stop nor turn. Bacon, Youth and Age. 4+. Not dressed; undressed. How now, my lords! what, all wnveady so? Shak., 1 Hen. VI., ii. 1. Enter James, unready, in his night-cap, garterless. Stage Direction in Two Maids of Moreclack. (Nares.) To make unready, to undress or unharness. Come, where have you been, wench? Make me unready. T slept but ill last night. Fletcher, Island Princess, iii. Make unready the horses; thou knowest how. B. Jonson, New Inn, i. 1.
unready (un-red’i), v. t. [< unready, a.] To undress. Hee remained with his daughter, to give his wife time of unreadying herself. (Nares.) Sir P. Sidney, Arcadia, p. 379.

unreal.c: unreal (un-rée’al), a. 1. Notreal; not substantial; having appearance only; illusive; ideal. Hence, horrible shadow! Unreal mockery, hence! Shak., Macbeth, iii. 4. 107. 2. Unpractical; visionary. Those who have most loudly advertised their passion for seclusion and their intimacy with nature, from Pe- triarch down, have been mostly sentimentalists, unreal men. Lowell, Study Windows, p. 205. Fallacy of unreal middle. See fal/acy.—Unreal quantity, an imaginary quantity.

unreality.c: unreality (un-ré-al’i-ti), m. 1. Lack of reality or real existence.—2. That which has no reality or real existence. He (Julius Czesar) was too sincere to stoop to unreality. He held tothe facts of this life and to his own convictions. Froude, Ceesar, p. 549. 38. Unpractical character; visionariness. The unreality of the optimistic religions of the day was what he attacked unceasingly from youth to age, with an energy as honest in its way as Carlyle’s. ‘ The Critic, XIV, 243.

unrealize.c: unrealize (un-ré’al-iz), v. t [< unreal + -ize.] To take away the reality of; make or consider unreal; divest of reality; present or treat in an ideal form. [Rare.] The men, the women,... the lounger, the beggar, the boys, the dogs, are unrealized at once. Emerson, Miscellanies, p. 47.

unreason.c: unreason (un-ré’zn), n. Lack of reason; unreasonableness; irrationality; nonsense; folly; absurdity.—Abbot of unreason. See abbot.

unreasonable.c: unreasonable (un-ré’zn-a-bl), a. 1. Not reasonable or agreeable to reason; irrational. Foritisan wnresonable religion that hath rite nougte of certeyne. Piers Plowman (B), vi. 153. If he [Henry VIII.] seems to act upon pure self-will, he is able to given reason for his acts, and that such a reason as we cannot on mere prejudice determine to be wnreason- able. Stubbs, Medieval and Modern Hist., p. 244. 2. Exceeding the bounds of reason; beyond what is reasonable or moderate; exorbitant; immoderate: as, an unreasonable price. The pretence was infinitely unreasonable, and therefore had the fate of senseless allegations, it disbanded presently. Jer. Taylor, Works (ed. 1835), I. 77. unrecognizably An alarmist by nature, an aristocrat by party, he [Xen- phon] carried to an unreasonable excess his horror of popular turbulence. Macaulay, History. 3t. Not endowed with reason; irrational. The nature of creatures unreasonable. Sir T. Elyot, The Governour, iii. 3. Unreasonable creatures feed their young. Shak., 3 Hen. V1, ii. 2. 26. 4, Not listening to or acting according to reason; not guided by reason; not influenced by reason, I must be most unreasonable to be dissatisfied at any thing that he chooses to put in a book which I never shall read. Trevelyan, in Life of Macaulay, I. 204. 5+. Inconvenient. We departed to our lodging, desiring to know whether our coming the next day might not be uneasy or unreasonable to her. Penn, Travels in Holland, etc. =Syn. Absurd, Silly, Foolish, etc. (see absurd), obstinate, wrongheaded, extravagant, unfair, unjust, extortionate.

unreasonableness.c: unreasonableness (un-ré’zn-a-bl-nes), ». The state or character of being unreasonable, in any sense.

unreasonably.c: unreasonably (un-ré’zn-a-bli), adv. In an unreasonable manner; contrary to reason; foolishly; excessively; immoderately.

unreasoned.c: unreasoned (un-ré’znd), a. Not reasoned or argued; not due to reason or reasoning; not founded on reason; not thought out. Old prejudices and unreasoned habits. Burke, Rev. in France. The unreasoned denial of a fact is quite as illogical as its blind acceptance. Nineteenth Century, XXIV. 586.

unreasoning.c: unreasoning (un-ré’zn-ing), a. Notreasoning; not having reasoning faculties; characterized by want of reason. To these rational considerations there is superadded, in extreme cases, a panic as unreasoning as the previous over-confidence. J.S. Mili.

unreasoningly.c: unreasoningly (un-ré’zn-ing-li), adv. In an unreasoning manner; without reasoning or reflection. WN. A. Rev., CXL. 194.

unreasont.c: unreasont (un-ré’zn),v. t [Cunreason,n.] To prove to be unreasonable; disprove by argument. ([Rare.] To unreason the equity of God’s proceedings. South.

unreavet.c: unreavet (un-rév’), v. t To take to pieces; disentangle; loose, The worke that she all day did make, The same at night she did againe unreave. Spenser, Sonnets, xxiii. unreaved} (un-révd’), a. Not taken or pulled to pieces. Could’st thou think that a cottage not too strongly built, and standing so bleak in the very mouth of the winds, could for any long time hold tight and unreaved? Bp. Hall, Balm of Gilead.

unrebated.c: unrebated (un-ré-ba’ted), a. Same as unbated. A number of fencers tried it, with unrebated swords. Hakewill, Apology.

unrebukable.c: unrebukable (un-ré-bu’ka-bl), a. Not deserving rebuke; not obnoxious to censure. 1 Tim. vi. 14. Also spelled unrebukeable.

unrecallable.c: unrecallable (un-ré-kal’a-bl), a. Not recallable; incapable of being called back, revoked, annulled, or recalled. That which is done is unrecallable. Feltham, Resolves, i. 89. unrecalling} (un-ré-kal’ing), a. Not to be recalled. [Rare.] And ever let his unrecalling crime Have time to wail th’ abusing of his time. Shak., Lucrece, 1. 993.

unreceived.c: unreceived (un-ré-sévd’), a. Not received; not taken; not come into possession; not embraced or adopted. Hooker, Eccles. Polity, v. § 54.

unreckonable.c: unreckonable (un-rek’n-a-bl), a. Not capable of being reckoned or counted; immeasurable; immense. Hawthorne, Seven Gables, ii.

unreckoned.c: unreckoned (un-rek’nd), a. Not reckoned, computed, counted, or summed up. Dryden, Don Sebastian, iii. 1.

unreclaimable.c: unreclaimable (un-ré-kla’ma-bl), a. Irreclaimable. Bp. Hall, Sermons, 2 Pet. i. 10.

unreclaimed.c: unreclaimed (un-ré-klamd’), a. Not reclaimed. (a) Not brought to a domestic state; not tamed. A savageness in unreclaimed blood. Shak., Hamlet, ii. 1. 34. Bullocks unreclaimed to bear the yoke. Dryden, tr. of Ovid’s Metamorph., xiii. (0) Not reformed; not called back from vice to virtue: as, sinner unreclaimed. (c) Not brought into a state of cultivation, as desert or wild land. Not

unrecognizable.c: unrecognizable (un-rek’og-ni-za-bl), a. recognizable; incapable of being recognized; irrecognizable. Coleridge.

unrecognizably.c: unrecognizably (un-rek’og-ni-za-bli), adv. In an unrecognizable manner; without or beyond recognition. Trre- unrecognizably The opening through which we had come had closed unrecognizably behind us. The Atlantic, LX VII. 499.

unrecognized.c: unrecognized (un-rek’og-nizd), a. Not recognized, in any sense. As dear Sam Johnson sits behind the screen,... there is no want of dignity in him, in that homely image of labour ill-rewarded, genius as yet unrecognized, independence sturdy and uncomplaining. Thackeray, On Screens in Dining-Rooms.

unrecommended.c: unrecommended (un-rek-o-men’ded), a. Not recommended; not favorably mentioned. JV. Knox, Essays, No. 113.

unrecompensed.c: unrecompensed (un-rek’om-penst), a. Not recompensed, rewarded, or requited. Heaven will not see so true a love unrecompens’d. Fletcher, Wildgoose Chase, iv. 3.

unreconcilable.c: unreconcilable (un-rek’on-si-la-bl), a. Inrree- oncilable. Bp. Hall, No Peace with Rome.

unreconcilably.c: unreconcilably (un-rek’on-si-la-bli), adv. Irreconcilably. Bp. Hall, Contemplations, ii. 381.

unreconciled.c: unreconciled (un-rek’on-sild), a. Not reconciled. (a) Not made consistent: as, unreconciled statements. (b) Not restored to friendship or favor; still at enmity or opposition: as, a sinner unreconciled to God. (ct) Not atoned for. Any crime Unreconciled as yet to heaven and grace. Shak., Othello, v. 2. 27. (dt) Irreconcilable; implacable. I’m even he that once did owe unreconcil’d hate to you. Beau. and Fl., Woman-Hater, iii. 2. unreconciliable} (un-rek-on-sil’i-a-bl), a. Unreconcilable. Shak., A. and C., v. 1. 47.

unreconstructed.c: unreconstructed (un-ré-kon-struk’ted), a. Not reconstructed; specifically, in U. S. politics, not yet reorganized as a State of the Union: applied to seceded States after the civil war; also, loosely, to citizens of the South not reconciled to the results of that war. On Thursday, Mr. Butler’s Committee on Reconstruction reported in favor of extending for a month the time during which an unreconstructed Southerner may retain his Government employment. The Nation, VIII. 221.

unrecorded.c: unrecorded (un-ré-kér’ded), a. 1. Not recorded; not registered; not made part of any record: as, an unrecorded deed or lease. The unrecorded English words actually in use among the people. Amer, Jour. Philol., X. 290. 2. Not kept in remembrance by writing or by public monuments. Not unrecorded in the rolls of fame. Pope.

unrecounted.c: unrecounted (un-ré-koun’ted),a. Not recounted; not related or recited. Shak., Hen. VIIL., iii. 2. 48.

unrecoverable.c: unrecoverable (un-ré-kuv’ér-a-bl), a 1. Incapable of being recovered, found, restored, or obtained again; not obtainable from debtor; irrecoverable: as, an unrecoverable article of property; an unrecoverable debt. I have a great many debts due to me in America, and I had rather they should remain unrecoverable by any law than submit to the Stamp Act. Franklin, Autobiog., p. 369. 2. Not capable of recovering; incurable; irremediable. ’Tis the dead palsy, that, without almost a miracle, leaves man unrecoverable. Feltham, Resolves, ii. 14. Loss of memory is so commonly associated with unrecoverable cases. Amer. Jour. Psychol., I. 333.

unrecoverably.c: unrecoverably (un-ré-kuv’ér-a-bli), adv. In an unrecoverable manner; irrecoverably; in- eurably. Long sick, and unrecoverably. Bp. Hall, Meditations and Vows, ii.

unrecovered.c: unrecovered (un-ré-kuv’érd), a. 1. Not recovered; not found or restored.— 2+. Irrecoy- erable. Chapman, Iliad, ix. 247. (Davies.)

unrecruitable.c: unrecruitable (un-ré-kr6’ta-bl), a. Not capable of being recruited, in any sense. Milton, On Edueation.

unrecumbent.c: unrecumbent (un-ré-kum’bent), a. Not reclining or reposing. Cowper, Morning Walk. unrecuring} (un-rée-kir’ing), a. Incapable of being cured; incurable. [Rare.] Seeking to hide herself, as doth the deer That hath received some unrecuring wound. Shak., Tit. And., iii. 1, 90.

unredeemed.c: unredeemed (un-ré-démd’), a 1. Not redeemed; not ransomed: as, an unredeemed captive; an wiredeemed sinner. Jer. Taylor, Sermons, III. ii.—2. Not recalled into the treasury or bank by payment of the value in money: as, unredeemed bills, notes, or stock.—8. Not fulfilled, as a promise or pledge. No one takes the trouble to recollect his contrary opinions or his unredeemed pledges. Macaulay, Athenian Orators., 4. Not counterbalanced or alleviated by any countervailing quality; unmitigated. 6640 The unredeemed ugliness... of a slothful people. Carlyle. 5. Not taken out of pledge or pawn. Pawnbrokers lose on an average 10 per cent. on wnre- deemed goods. The Echo, Jan. 14, 1888. (Hneye. Dict.)

unreduct.c: unreduct (un-ré-dukt’), a. Not reduced. Thought unreduct to act Is but an embryon in the truest sense. Middleton, Family of Love, iii. 1.

unreel.c: unreel (un-rél’), v. [< un-2 + reel.] I, trans. To unwind from a reel, as a line or thread. A measured mile course was laid off, unreeling from an anchored stake buoy one mile of fine wire. The Engineer, LX VIII. 413. II, intrans. To become unwound from a reel. The line will unreel faster than it is needed, and get into a snarl. Tribune Book of Sports, p. 163.

unreeve.c: unreeve (un-réy’), v. t.; pret. and pp. unreeved, unrove, ppr. unreeving. [< un-2 + reeve3.] Naut., to withdraw or take out (a rope) from a block, thimble, etc.

unrefined.c: unrefined (un-ré-find’), a 1. Not refined; not purified: as, unrefined sugar.—2. Not refined or polished in manners, taste, or the like. These early and unrefined ages. Burke, Vind. of Nat. Society.

unreformable.c: unreformable (un-ré-fér’ma-bl), a. Not reformable; not capable of being reformed or amended. Hooker, Eccles. Polity, vii. § 24.

unreformation.c: unreformation (un-ref-dr-ma’shon), ». The state of being unreformed; want of reformation. Bp. Hall, Sermons, Hecles. iii. 4. [Rare.]

unreformedness.c: unreformedness (un-ré-f6r’med-nes), n. The quality or state of being unreformed. Contemporary Rev., LIV. 345. ([Rare.]

unseasonableness.c: unseasonableness (un-s6’zn-a-bl-nes), ». The character or state of being unseasonable. Sir M. Hale, Orig. of Mankind.

unseaworthiness.c: unseaworthiness (un-sé’wér’THi-nes), n. The state of being unseaworthy.

unseconded.c: unseconded (un-sek’un-ded), a 1. Not seconded; not supported; not assisted: as, the motion was unseconded; the attempt was unseconded. Shak., 2 Hen. IV., ii. 3.34.—2+. unsectarian.c: unsectarian (un-sek-ta’ri-an), a. Not sectarian; not intended or adapted to promote a sect; not characterized by any of the peculiarities or prejudices of a sect.

unseduced.c: unseduced (un-sé-dist’), a. Not seduced. Shak., Cymbeline, i. 4. 173.

Shak., Hamlet, iii. 2. 29. 8t. Unreasonable. I may not endure that thou dwelle In so unskilful an opynyon That of thy wo is no curation, Chaucer, Troilus, i. 790.

unstarch.c: unstarch (un-stiireh’),v.¢. To take the starch or stiffening from; hence, to free from stiffness, reserve, formality, pride, haughtiness, or the like; relax. One that weighs His breath between his teeth, and dares not smile Beyond a point, for fear t’ unstarch his look. B, Jonson, Cynthia’s Revels, iii. 2.

unstate.c: unstate (un-stat’), v. ¢ 1. To deprive of state or dignity. Shak., Lear, i. 2. 108.—2. To deprive of statehood; cause to cease to be a state. N. Ward, Simple Cobler, p. 23.

unstation.c: unstation (i-ni-ta’shon), n. [< unit + -ation.] 1. Expression in terms of units; measurement in accordance with a system of units.— 2. The operation of adding to the units of a number, written in the Arabic notation, (10—N) times the tens (where N is any number less than 10), (10—N)? times the hundreds, etc., and repeating the process until a digit is obtained. This (diminished by any multiple of N which it exceeds) is the remainder after dividing the original number by N. unite! (i-nit’), v.; pret. and pp. united, ppr. uniting. [< LL. wnitus, pp. of were (> It. unite = Sp. Pg. unit = F. uni), make one or as one, join together, < L. unus, one: see one, a. Cf. one, v., and adunation.] I, trans. 1. To ecom- bine or conjoin so as to form one; make to be one and to be no longer separate; incorporate in one: as, to white two kingdoms or two armies. Unite Your troops of horsemen with his bands of foot. Shak., 1 Hen. VI., iv. 1. 164, As thou hast united our nature to thy eternal being, thou mightest also unite my person to thine by the interior adunations of love, and obedience, and conformity. Jer. Taylor, Works (ed. 1835), I. 37. 2. To connect, conjoin, bring together, or associate by some bond, legal or other; join in interest, affection, fellowship, or the like; ally; link together; associate; conjoin; couple; combine: as, to unite families by marriage; to unite nations by treaty; to white fresh adherents to a cause. Hymen did our hands Unite commutual in most sacred bands. Shak., Hamlet, iii. 2. 170. 8. To make to agree or be uniform; harmonize. The king proposed nothing more than to unite his kingdom in one form of worship. Clarendon, Great Rebellion. 4. To cause to adhere; attach; connect together: as, to white bricks or stones by means of cement. The peritoneum, which is a dry body, may be united with the musculous flesh. Wiseman, Surgery. =Syn. 1. To consolidate, amalgamate, blend, merge. TL. intrans. 1. To become one; become combined or incorporated; be consolidated; coalesce; combine; commingle. Virgin Mother, hail, High in the love of Heaven; yet from my loins Thou shalt proceed, and from thy womb the Son Of God Most High; so God with man unites. Milton, P. L., xii. 382. 2. To join in action; concur; act in concert. If you will now white in your complaints, And force them with a constancy, the cardinal Cannot stand under them. Shak., Hen. VIII, iii. 2. 1. unite! (G@-nit’),a. [< LL. units, pp. of unite, unite: see wnitel,v.] United; joint. Webster. unite! (a-nit’),». [« wnitel, v., with ref. to the union of the kingdoms of England and Scot- must ul- unite land alluded to on the coin in the motto ‘‘Fa- ciam eos in gentes una,” ‘I will make them one nation’ (Ezek. xxxvii. 22).] An English gold coin issued by James I. and current for 20 shillings; a jacobus. A gold coin of the same name and value was issued under Charles I., when it was also called carolus (which see), and under the Common-wealth and Charles II. unite?}, ». An obsolete spelling of wit.

unstatutable.c: unstatutable (un-stat’u-ta-bl), a. statute; not warranted by statute. the Power of the Bishops.

unstatutably.c: unstatutably (un-stat’a-ta-bli), adv. In an unstatutable manner; without warrant of statute. Encyc. Brit., V. 228.

[< ME. wnstedefastnesse; < unsteadfast + -ness.] The state or character of being unsteadfast; inconstancy; fickleness. Bp. Hall, An Humble Remonstrance.

unsteadily.c: unsteadily (un-sted’i-li), adv. In an unsteady manner; without steadiness. 4 Unsteadily they rove, And, never fix’d, are Fugitives in Love. Congreve, tr. of Ovid’s Art of Love.

unsteadiness.c: unsteadiness (un-sted’i-nes), n. The state or character of being unsteady.

unsteady.c: unsteady (un-sted’i), a Not steady. (a) Not firmly established or settled. (6) Not firm; shaking; staggering ; reeling; wavering; trembling; fluctuating: as, an unsteady hand; an unsteady flame. (c) Not constant in mind or purpose; fickle; changeable; unstable; unsettled; wavering: as, an unsteady mind. (d) Not regular, constant, or uniform; varying in force, direction, etc.: as, unsteady winds. (e) Irregular in habits; dissipated.
unsteady (un-sted’i), v.¢ [<wnsteady,a.] To make unsteady; cause to be fluctuating. The Engineer, UXX. 506.

unsteel.c: unsteel (un-stél’), v. ¢ To make unlike steel; disarm; soften. Richardson, Clarissa Harlowe, V. 310. (Davies.) [Rare.]

unstercorated.c: unstercorated (un-stér’k6-ra-ted), a. Not stercorate or manured. Scott, Pirate, iv.

unstick.c: unstick (un-stik’), v. t. To free, as one thing stuck to another; loose. Richardson, Clarissa Harlowe, VII. 380. (Davies.)

unsting.c: unsting (un-sting’), v. t Todisarm ofa sting; deprive of the power of giving acute pain. South. [Rare. }

unstitch.c: unstitch (un-stich’), v. ¢ To undo by picking out stitches; rip.

unstockinged.c: unstockinged (un-stok’ingd), a. Not wearing stockings. Scott, Kenilworth, vii. [Rare.]

unstooping.c: unstooping (un-stdé’ping), a. Not stooping; not bending; not yielding. Onstooping firmness. Shak., Rich. IL, i. 1. 121.

unstringed.c: unstringed (un-stringd’), a. Not stringed: as, an wistringed viol. Shak., Rich. IL., i. 3. 162.

Not having studied; unacquainted; unskilled; unversed. Not so unstudied in the nature of councils as not to know, etc. Bp. Jewell, Life (1685), p. 30. 4. Not devoted to or occupied by study; not passed in study. The defects of their unstudied years. Milton, Tetrachordon.

unstuffed.c: unstuffed (un-stuft’), a. Not stuffed; not crowded. Shak., R. and J., ii. 3. 37.

unstufft.c: unstufft (un-stuf’), v. t. [< ME. unstuffen.] To empty; hence, to depopulate. He seide he wolde not lete the reame be unstuffed of + peple, but thei myght hem well deffende yef eny enmyes entred in to the londe, Merlin (E. E. T. S.), ii. 358.

unsubduable.c: unsubduable (un-sub-dii’a-bl), a. Not capable of being subdued or conquered; unconquerable; invincible. Southey, Kehama, xviii. 5.

unsubdued.c: unsubdued (un-sub-dad’), a. Not subdued; not brought into subjection; not conquered: as, nations or passions unsubdued. Unsubdued pride and enmity against David. J, Edwards, Works, III. 48.

Not having good substance; not strong or stout: as, an unsubstantial building; unsubstantial cloth. —4. Not giving substance or strength; weak; not strengthening or invigorating. Hawthorne, Septimius Felton.

unsuccessfully.c: unsuccessfully (un-suk-ses’ful-i), adv. In an unsuccessful manner; without success; unfortunately. South.

unsuccessfulness.c: unsuccessfulness (un-suk-ses’fil-nes), m. The state of being unsuccessful. Milton, Ans. to Eikon Basilike, § 18.

unsuccessive.c: unsuccessive (un-suk-ses’iv), a. Without sue- cession. While God to his dimsighted, doubtful thought Duration boundless, unsuccessive taught. Bp. Ken, The Monk and the Bird.

unsupportedly.c: unsupportedly (un-su-por’ted-li), adv. In an unsupported manner; without support.

unsuppressed.c: unsuppressed (un-su-prest’), a. Not suppressed; not held or kept under; notsubdued; not quelled; not put down: as, unsuppressed laughter or applause; unsuppressed rebellion.
