unswell.c: unswell (un-swel’), v. 7. [« ME. wnswellen; < un-2 + swell.) To cease from swelling. Ebben gan the welle Of hire teres and the herte wnswelle. Chaucer, Troilus, iv. 1146.

unswept.c: unswept (un-swept’), a. Not swept. (a) Not cleaned by passing or rubbing a brush, broom, or besom over. Shak., M. W. of W., v. 5. 48. (0) Not cleaned up or removed by sweeping, as dust. Shak., Cor., ii. 3. 126. (c) Not moved or passed over with a sweeping motion or action. Foam unswept by wandering gusts. Cowper, Iliad, xi.

unswerving.c: unswerving (un-swér’ving), a. Not deviating from any rule, standard, or course; undeviating; unwavering; firm.

unsworn.c: unsworn (un-sworn’), a. Not sworn. (a) Not bound by an oath; not having taken an oath: as, “an unsworn witness. (b) Not solemnly pronounced or taken. Her solenin oath remained unsworn. Cowper, Odyssey, x.

unsyllabled.c: unsyllabled (un-sil’a-bld), a. Not syllabled; not articulated, uttered, or pronounced; not divided into syllables.

unsymmetrical.c: unsymmetrical (un-si-met’ri-kal), a. Lacking symmetry; asymmetrical: specifically, in botany, said of such flowers as lack numerical symmetry —that is, have the parts in the different cycles of unequalnumber. See symmetrical, 5.

unsymmetrically.c: unsymmetrically (un-si-met’ri-kal-i), adv. In an unsymmetrical manner; without symmetry.

unsymmetry.c: unsymmetry (un-sim’e-tri), m. Want of symmetry; disproportion; asymmetry. Each member of a plant will display... unsymmetry or asymmetry where there is partial or entire departure from a balance of surrounding actions. H. Spencer, Prin. of Biol. (Amer. ed. 1872), § 220. unsympathizability (un-sim”pa-thi-za-bil’i- ti), n. The quality or state of being unsympathizable.

unsympathy.c: unsympathy (un-sim’pa-thi), ». Lack of sympathy. Same as wn- untangle How true the unsympathy as well as the sympathy of nature. Wilberforce, in Life by R. G. Wilberforce, IT. 305. [(Encye. Dict.)

unsystematic.c: unsystematic (un-sis-te-mat’ik), a. Not systematic; not founded upon or in accord with a system; not having a defined system or plan; lacking regular order, distribution, or arrangement. Desultory unsystematic endeavours. Burke, On the Present Discontents (1771). =Syn. See irregular.

unsystematically.c: unsystematically (un-sis-te-mat’i-kal-i), adv. In an unsystematic manner; irregularly. untachet, v. t. [ME., < wn-2 + tache.] To carve. Vntache that curlew. Babees Book (B. B. T.S.), p. 265.

unt.c: unt(ary) + motory.] Having or pertaining to motor influence or effect which is voluntary, or subject to the will: with Remak specifying the somatopleural division of the body, including the muscular system of ordinary language, as distinguished from the splanchnopleural or in- voluntomotory (which see). The volunto-motory, corresponding to the body-wall or somatopleure. Enceyce. Brit., VIII. 167. volunty, ». [< ME. volute, also volente, voul- ente, < OF. volente, volute, F. volonté = Sp. voluntas = It. volunta, will, < L. volunta(t-)s, will, desire: see voluntary.) Will; wish; will and pleasure. or that he ay May not fulfilled his volute. Rom. of the Rose, 1. 5276. For of free choice and hertely volente, She hathe to God avowed chastity. Lydgate, MS. Ashmole 339, f. 15. (Halliweil.) After me made by thy will and wolente To take this woman of the fairy, This here diffame serpent vnto se. Rom. of Partenay (E. E. T. S.), 1. 3473. “Sir,” quod thei,“ yef it be not thus, doth with vs youre volente.” Merlin (E. E. T. 8.), i. 29. And the seid Tuddenham and Heydon wold after theyr volente have it hald yn been of the maner of Hetersete, which sufficient evidences that ye have specifyeth no thyng so. Paston Letters, I. 173. volupere,”. [ME., also volupeer, voluper.] A cap or head-dress worn in the fourteenth century by either sex. The tapes of hir white voluper Were of the same suite of hir color. Chaucer, Miller’s Tale, 1. 55. voluptiet,. See volupty.

untack.c: untack (un-tak’), vt. To separate (that which is tacked); disjoin; loosen; release. Sir, the little ado which me thinks I find in untacking these pleasant Sophismes puts mee into the mood to tell you a tale ere I proceed further. Milton, Reformation in Eng., ii.

untackle.c: untackle (un-tak’1), v. t. [< late ME. untacklen; < un-2 + tackle.| To unhitch; unharness. But vse to untackle them once in a day. Palladius, Husbondrie, p. 62. untainted! (un-tan’ted), a. [< wn-1 + tainted, pp. of taint, v.] 1. Not rendered impure by admixture; not impregnated with foul matter: as, untainted air. Narcissus pining o’er the untainted stream. Keats, To Leigh Hunt. 2. Not sullied; not stained; unblemished. What stronger breastplate than a heart untainted? Shak., 2 Hen. V1., iii. 2. 232. 3. Not rendered unsavory by putrescence: as, untainted meat. untainted?+ (un-tan’ted), a. [< wn-1 + tainted, pp. of taint3, v.] Not attainted; not charged with a crime; not accused. Within these five hours lived Lord Hastings, Untainted, unexamined, free, at liberty. Shak., Rich, IIL, iii. 6. 9.

untaintedly.c: untaintedly (un-tan’ted-li), adv. In an untainted manner; in a manner free from taint, stain, or blemish. South, Sermons, V. i.

untaintedness.c: untaintedness (un-tain’ted-nes), n. The state of being untainted; freedom from taint, stain, or blemish. Bp. Hall, Sermon on 1 Johni. 5.

untaken.c: untaken (un-ta’kn), a. Not taken, in any sense. It cannot stand with the love and wisdom of God to leave such order untaken as is necessary for the due government of his Church. Hooker, Eccles. Polity, iii. 11.

untalented.c: untalented (un-tal’en-ted), a. Not talented; not gifted; not accomplished or clever. This is the sort of stuff you must be satisfied with from a poor untalented girl. Richardson, Sir Charles Grandison, vii. 6. (Davies.)

untalked.c: untalked (un-takt’), a. Not talked or spoken. —Untalked of, not talked or spoken about; not made the subject of talk. Shak., R. and J., iii. 2. 7.

untamable.c: untamable (un-ta’ma-bl), a. Not capable of being tamed, domesticated, subjugated, or subdued; not to be rendered tame, docile, or serviceable to man; incapable of being brought from a wild, savage, barbarous, rude, or violent state: as, an untamable tiger; an untamable savage; untamable passions. Barrow, Sermons, I. iii. Also untameable.

untamableness.c: untamableness (un-ta’ma-bl-nes),. The quality or state of being untamed. Also untame- ableness.

untame.c: untame (un-tam’), a. Not tame; wild. Ida,... nurse of beasts untame. Chapman, Tliad, viii. 41.

untamed.c: untamed (un-tamd’), a. [< ME. untamed, untimid, untamed; as un-1 + tamed.] Not tamed. (a) Not reclaimed from wildness; not domesticated; not made familiar with man: as, an untamed beast. Locke. And her eye has a glance more sternly wild Than even that of a forest child In its fearless and untamed freedom should be. Whittier, Mogg Megone. (b) Not subdued; not brought under control: as, a turbulent, untamed mind. A people very stubborn and untamed. Spenser, State of Ireland.

untamedness.c: untamedness (un-tamd’nes),. The character or state of being untamed. Leighton, Com. on 1 Peter v. (Encyc. Dict.)

untangle.c: untangle (un-tang’gl), v. f. To loose from tangles or intricacy; disentangle; hence, to free from embarrassment, doubt, or uncertainty; resolve; cleanup; explain. Untangle but this cruel chain. Prior, False Friend, iii. untangle If Leonora’s innocent, she may untangle all. Vanbrugh, Love Disarmed.

untappice.c: untappice (un-tap’is), v. [< wn-2 + tappice, tappish.] I, intrans. To come out of concealment. Now I'll untappice. Fletcher and Massinger, A Very Woman, iii. 5. II. trans. To drive out of concealment, as game,

untarnished.c: untarnished (un-tiir’nisht), a. Not soiled; not tarnished; not stained; unblemished: as, untarnished silk; an untarnished reputation.

untasted.c: untasted (un-tas’ted), a. Not tasted; not tried by the taste or tongue; hence, not experienced or enjoyed.

untastet.c: untastet (un-tast’), v. t To take away a taste from; cause to feel disgust or distaste for. Could not by all means might be devis’d Untaste them of this great disgust. Daniel, Civil Wars, viii.

untaught.c: untaught (un-tit’), a. [< ME. untaught, untaught; < un-1 + taught.) Not taught. (@) Not instructed; not educated; unlettered; illiterate. Better unfedde then wn-taughte. Babees Book (E. E. T. §.), p. 348. (6) Unskilled; not having use or practice. Suffolk’s imperial tongue is stern and rough, . untaught to plead for favour. Shak., 2 Hen. VI., iv. 1, 122. (c) Not made the subject of teaching or instruction; not communicated by teaching. With untaught Joy Pharaoh the News does hear, And little thinks their Fate attends on him, and his so near. Cowley, Pindaric Odes, xiv. 12. (d@) Not having learned by experience; ignorant. Insatiate to pursue Vain war with heaven; and, by success untaught, His proud imaginations thus displayed. Milton, P. L., ii. 9. Untaught that soon such anguish must ensue. Wordsworth, Female Vagrant.

untax.c: untax (un-taks’), v. t To remove a tax from. Untaa the clothing of sixty million people. Report of Sec. of Treasury, 1886, I. 1vii.

untaxed.c: untaxed (un-takst’), a. Not taxed. (a) Not charged with or liable to pay taxes. 7. Warton. (b) Not charged with any fault, offense, etc.; not accused. Common speech, which leaves no virtue untawed. Bacon, Learning, i.

unteach.c: unteach (un-téch’),v.t. 1. To cause to forget, disbelieve, or give up what has been taught. If they chanc’t to be taught any thing good, or of their own accord had learn’t it, they might see that presently untaught them by the custome and ill example of their elders. Milton, Apology for Smectymnuus. 2. To make forgotten; make to cease from being acquired by instruction. But we, by art, unteach what nature taught. Dryden, Indian Emperour, i. 1.

unteachable.c: unteachable (un-té’cha-bl), a. Not teachable or docile; indocile. Milton, Tetrachordon.

unteachableness.c: unteachableness (un-té’cha-bl-nes), ». The character or state of being unteachable; absence of docility.

unteam.c: unteam (un-tém’), v. t To unyoke a team from; take a team, as of horses or oxen, from. Justice and authority laid by the rods and axes as soon as the sun unteamed his chariot. Jer. Taylor (ed. 1835), Works, I. 212.

untell.c: untell (un-tel’), v. @ To recall, as what has been told; make as if not told or enumerated. That time could turne up his swift sandy glasse To untell the dayes, and to redeem these hours. Heywood, Woman Killed with Kindness.

untemper.c: untemper (un-tem’pér), v. # To remove the temper from, as metal; hence, to soften; mol- city. I dare not swear thou lovest me; yet my blood begins to flatter me that thou dost, notwithstanding the poor and untempering effect of my visage. Shak., Hen. V., v. 2. 241, The study of sciences does more soften and untemper the courages of men than any way fortified and incite them. Cotton, tr. of Montaigne’s Essays, xix. (Davies.)

untemperate.c: untemperate (un-tem’pér-at), a. Intemperate. Times’ Whistle (EK. E. T. 8.), p. 58. untemperately+ (un-tem’pér-at-li), adv. Intemperately.

untempered.c: untempered (un-tem’pérd), a. Not tempered. (a) Not duly mixed for use: as, untempered lime. So it was not long that this untempered mortar would hold together these buildings. Purchas, Pilgrimage, p. 273. (6) Not brought to the desired state of hardness: as, wn- tempered steel. (c) Not brought to a fit or proper state generally; not regulated, moderated, or controlled; not mollified: as, untempered severity. Johnson, Life of Waller. The untempered spirit of madness. Burke, Appeal from Old to New Whigs. 6650 untempter} (un-temp’tér), ». [ME., < wn-l + tempter.] One who does not tempt. Sothely God is untempter of eyl thingis. Wyclif, Jas. i, 18.

untemptible.c: untemptible (un-tempt’i-bl), a. Not capable of being tempted. Absolute purity is untemptible, as in God. Bushnell, Sermons for New Life, xiv.

untemptibly.c: untemptibly (un-tempt’i-bli), adv. So as not to be tempted. Bushnell.

untenability.c: untenability (un-ten-a-bil’i-ti), ». The quality or state of being untenable; indefensibleness.

untenable.c: untenable (un-ten’a-bl), a 1. Not tenable; that cannot be held in possession: as, an wn- tenable post orfort. Clarendon.—2. That cannot be maintained by argument; not defensible: as, an untenable doctrine. All others give up such false opinions as untenable. Goldsmith, The Bee, No. 1.

untenableness.c: untenableness (un-ten’a-bl-nes),. The character or state of being untenable; untenability.

untenant.c: untenant (un-ten’ant),v.¢. [< wn-2 + tenant1.] To deprive of a tenant or tenants; expel or remove a dweller from; evict; dislodge. He gets possession of their affections, whence all the power of man cannot untenant him. Rev. T. Adams, Works, I. 202. (Davies.)

untenantable.c: untenantable (un-ten’an-ta-bl), a. Not fit to be tenanted or occupied as a dwelling; uninhabitable. Frozen and untenantable regions. Wheweill.

untenanted.c: untenanted (un-ten’an-ted), a. Not occupied by a tenant; not inhabited. Sir W. Temple.

untender.c: untender (un-ten’dér), a. 1. Not tender; not soft.—2. Wanting sensibility or affection. Lear. So young, and so untender? Cor, So young, my lord, and true. Shak.,:King Lear, i. 1. 108.

untendered.c: untendered (un-ten’dérd), a. Not tendered; not offered: as, untendered money or tribute. Shak., Cymbeline, iii. 1. 10.

untent.c: untent (un-tent’), v.¢t. [« wn-2 + tent.] To bring out of tent. [Rare.] Why will be not upon our fair request Untent his person, and share the air with us? Shak., T. and C., ii. 3. 178.

untented.c: untented (un-ten’ted), a 1. Not inclosed in or provided with a tent or tents: as, an wn- tented army.— 2. Having no tents erected upon it: as, an untented field.—3. Not having a medical tent applied; hence, not having the pain lessened. [Rare.] The wntented wounding of a father’s curse Pierce every sense about thee! Shak., Lear, i, 4. 822. Ineautious; careless. Without In an unten-

unterdenlinden.c: Unter den Linden (on'ter den lin'den). [G., ‘ under the lindens.’] A famous street in Berlin which extends from the BrandenburgerThor eastward about three fifths of a mile. On it are the imperial and princely palaces, the university, the academy the statue of Frederick the Great, etc. Width, 160 feet Unterpfalz. See Palatinate. Untersberg (on'ters-berG). A mountain in the Salzburger Alps, situated near the border between Salzburg and Bavaria, 8 miles southwest of Salzburg: celebrated in folk-lore (legends of Charles the Great). Height, 6,480 feet.

unterminated.c: unterminated (un-tér’mi-ni-ted), a. end; having no termination. Any unterminated straight line extending in the same direction as this last one which intersects one of the two former, shall also intersect the other. Nature, XLIII. 554. untetchet,”. [ME.,< wn- + tetche, tache.] An evil habit; a disgraceful act. Seththe forsothe til this time * non wn-tetche he ne wrought, But hath him bore so buxomly ° that ich burn him preyseth. William of Palerne (E. E. T. §.), 1. 509.

untersee.c: Untersee (on'ter-za). [G.,‘ lower lake.’] The name given to the western arm of the Lake of Constance. Length, about 13 miles.

unterseen.c: Unterseen (on'ter-za-en). A village in the canton of Bern, Switzerland, situated between the Lakes of Thun and Brienz, near Interlaken.

unterwalden.c: Unterwalden (on'ter-val-den). [G.,‘ lower forest.’] One of the Forest Cantons of Switzerland, bounded by Lucerne, the Lake of Lucerne, Uri, and Bern. It comprises the two half-cantons Nidwald and Obwald. The surface is mountainous; highest point the Titlis. The chief towns are Stanz and Sarnen; the language is German; the religion Roman Catholic. It has two representatives in the National Council. Unterwalden united with the other Forest Cantons in the leagues of the INh-Hth centuries. It was assigned to the canton of Wald- statten in 1798; the resistance of Nidwald was suppressed by the trench. It became again a canton in 1803, a position secured in 1815 (resistance of Nidwald suppressed by Confederate troops in 1815), and joined the Sonderbund Area, 295 square miles. Population (1888), 27,585. Untrussing of the Humorous Poet, The. See Satiromastix. Unukalhai (tUnuk-al-ha'i). [Ar.runuq-al-haiya, the neck of the serpent.] The third-magnitude star a Serpentis.

untether.c: untether (un-tefH’ér), v. t. [< wn-2 + tether.] To release from a tether; set free, as an animal confined to a certain range by a rope or chain. Atheneum, No. 3277, p. 226. unthank}} (un-thangk’), n. [< ME. unthank, unthonk, unthone, < AS. unthank (= OHG. un- dan, undanch, MHG. G. undank), ingratitude, < un-, not, + thane, thank, gratitude: see wn-l and thank.] 1. No thanks; ingratitude; ill will. Thus shal Ich have unthonke on every syde. Chaucer, Troilus, v. 699. 2. Harm; injury; misfortune. Unthank come on his hand that bound hym so. Chaucer, Reeve’s Tale, 1. 162. unthank?} (un-thangk’), v.# [< wn-2 + thank.] To recant or recall, as one’s thanks; unsay, as what has been said by way of acknowledgment. Duke. We are not pleas’d she should depart. Seb. Then I'll unthank your goodness. Shirley, Love's Cruelty, iii. 3.

unthanked.c: unthanked (un-thangkt’), a. 1. Not thanked; not repaid with acknowledgments.— 2. Not received with thankfulness. [Rare.] Unwelcome freedom, and unthanked reprieve. Dryden, Pal. and Arc., i. 387. unthankest. [ME., also wnthonkes, gen. of wn- thank, used adverbially with the possessive pronouns, ‘not of his, her, their, my, thy, your, our [Te & OS eee f I Ncadfa Ie unthread accord’: see unthank, and ef. thanks.] A form used only in the phrases his, thy, etc., wnthankes, not of his, thy, etc., accord; involuntarily.

unthankful.c: unthankful (un-thangk’ful), a. 1. Not thankful; ungrateful; not making acknowledgments for good received. Luke vi. 35.—2. Not repaid with thanks; unacceptable. One of the most unthankful offices in the world. Goldsmith, The Bee, No. 8 3. Giving no return; unproductive. The husbandman ought not, for one unthankful year, to forsake the plough. B. Jonson, Bartholomew Fair, iii. 1.

unthankfully.c: unthankfully (un-thangk’ful-i), adv. In an unthankful or ungrateful manner; without thanks; ungratefully. Boyle.

unthankfulness.c: unthankfulness (un-thangk’fil-nes), ». Ungratefulness; want of a sense of kindness or benefits; ingratitude. Immoderate favours breed first unthankfulness, and afterward hate. Sir J. Hayward.

unthink.c: unthink (un-thingk’),v.¢. [< wn-2+ think.] To retract in thought; remove from the mind or thought; think differently about. — To unthink your speaking, And to say so no more. Shak., Hen. VIIL, ii. 4. 104, That the same thing is not thought and unthought, resolved and unresolved, a thousand times in a day. J. Howe, Works, I. 71.

unthinkability.c: unthinkability (un-thing-ka-bil‘i-ti), n. [< unthinkable + ~ity (see -bility).] The character of being unthinkable. But genuine determinism occupies a totally different ground; not the impotence but the unthinkability of free-will is what it affirms. W. James, Prin. of Psychol., II. 574.

unthinkable.c: unthinkable (un-thing’ka-bl), a. That cannot be made an object of thought; that cannot be thought; incogitable. What is contradictory is unthinkable. Sir W. Hamilton, Lectures on Metaph. and Logic, ITT. v.

unthinker.c: unthinker (un-thing’keér), n. One who does not think, or who is not given to thinking; a thoughtless person. [Rare.] Thinkers and unthinker by the million are spontaneously at their post, doing what is in them.: Carlyle, French Rey., I. iv. 1. (Davies.)

unthinking.c: unthinking (un-thing’king), a. 1. Not thinking; heedless; without thought or care; thoughtless; inconsiderate: as, «unthinking youth. It is not so easy a thing to be a brave man as the unthinking part of mankind imagine. Steele, Spectator, No. 350. 2. Not indicating thought or reflection; thoughtless. She has such a pretty unthinking Air, while she saunters round a Room, and prattles Sentences. Steele, Tender Husband, i. 1.

unthinkingly.c: unthinkingly (un-thing’king-li), adv. In an unthinking manner; without reflection; thoughtlessly. Pope. t

unthinkingness.c: unthinkingness (un-thing’king-nes), nm. The character of being unthinking or thoughtless. This kind of indifference or unthinkingness. Lord Halifax.

unthorny.c: unthorny (un-thér’ni), a. Not thorny; free from thorns. Sir T. Browne, Vulg. Err., i. 5.

unthought.c: unthought (un-thét’), a. Not thought; not imagined or conceived; not considered: often followed by of, formerly by on. The unthought-on accident is guilty. Shak., W. 'T., iv. 4. 549. This secure chapelry, That had been offered to his doubtful choice By an unthought-of patron. Wordsworth, Excursion, vii. To hold one unthought long, to hold one’s attention so as to keep one from wearying. And I will go to jail-house door, And hold the prisoner unthought Billie Archie (Child’s And ay as he harpit to the king, To had him unthought lang. Glenkindie (Child’s Ballads, IT. 8).

unthoughtfulness.c: unthoughtfulness (un-thét’fil-nes), n. The state or character of being thoughtless; thoughtlessness. A constant equable serenity and unthoughtfulness in outward accidents. Bp. Fell, Hammond, § 2.

unthread.c: unthread (un-thred’), v. t 1. To draw or take out a thread from: as, to unthread a needle.— 2. To relax the ligaments of; loosen. [Rare.] He with his bare wand can unthread thy joints, And crumble all thy sinews. Milton, Comus, 1. 614. 8. To find one’s way through. . They soon unthreaded the labyrinth of rocks. De Quincey, Spanish Nun, § 16, Ballads, VI. 95). ‘sal unthrift

unthrift.c: unthrift (un-thrift’),.anda. [< ME. unthrift; <un-1 + thrift.) I, n. 1. Lack of thrift; thriftlessness; prodigality. For youth set man in alle folye, In unthrift and in ribaudie. Rom. of the Rose, 1. 4926. A hater of folly, idleness, and wnthrift. Harper's Mag., LX XVI. 805. 2}. Folly. He roghte noght what unthrift that he seyde. Chaucer, Troilus, iv. 431. 3. A prodigal; one who wastes his estate by extravagance; one without thrift. Hauing his sonne and here a notable unthrift, & delighting in nothing but in hakes and hounds, and gay apparrell. Puttenham, Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 235. To behold my door Beset with unthrifts, and myself abroad? B. Jonson, Case is Altered, ii. 1. II.+ a. 1. Profuse; prodigal. What man didst thou ever know unthrift that was beloved after his means? Shak., T. of A., iv. 3. 311. 2. Poor; unthrifty. [He] hath much ado (poore penniefather) to keepe his unthrift elbows in reparations. Nashe, Pierce Penilesse, p. 8.

unthriftiheadt.c: unthriftiheadt (un-thrif’ti-hed), n. [< unthrifty + -head.| Unthriftiness. Unquiet Care and fond Unthriftyhead. Spenser, F. Q., IIT. xii. 25.

unthriftily.c: unthriftily (wn-thrif’ti-li), adv. [< ME. unthriftily ; < unthrifty + -ly2.] 1. Poorly. They been clothed so unthriftily. Chaucer, Prol. to Canon’s Yeoman’s Tale, 1. 340. 2. In an unthrifty manner; wastefully; lavishly; prodigally. Why will you part with them [names] here unthriftily? B. Jonson, Epigrams, vii.

unthriftiness.c: unthriftiness (un-thrif’ti-nes), n. The state or character of being unthrifty; prodigality. Staggering, non-proficiency, and unthriftiness of profession is the fruit of self. Rogers, Naaman the Syrian.

unthrifty.c: unthrifty (un-thrif’ti), a. [« ME. unthrifty; < un-1 + thrifty.] 1. Profitless; foolish; wretched. Swich unthrifty wayes newe. Chaucer, Troilus, iv. 1530. 2. Not thrifty; not careful of one’s means; prodigal; profuse; lavish; wasteful. T’ enrich your selues, and your unthrifty Sons To Gentilize with proud possessions. Sylvester, ty. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, i. 3. An unthrifty knave. Shak., M. of V., i. 3. 177. 8. Not thriving; not in good condition; not vigorous in growth. Grains given to a hidebound or unthrifty horse recover him. Mortimer, Husbandry. At the base and in the rear of the row of buildings, the track of many languid years is seen in a border of unthrifty grass. Hawthorne, Scarlet Letter, Int., p. 3. 4. Preventing thrift or thriving; mischievous; wicked. Spenser, F. Q., I. iv. 35. unthrive} (un-thriv’), v. 7. [< ME. unthriven, unthriven, onthryven; < un-2 + thrive.] 1. To fail of success.: For lovers be the folke that ben on lyve, That most disease han and most unthrive, And most endure sorowe, wo, and care. Cuckoo and Nightingale, 1. 142. For upon trust of Calles promise, we may soon onthryve. Paston Letters, Il. 237. 2. To fail to thrive or grow vigorously. Quyk lime, lite of that, lest it wnthryve. Palladius, Husbondrie (E. E. T. §S.), p. 122.

unthrone.c: unthrone (un-thron’), v. 4. To remove from a throne or from supreme authority; dethrone. {The Pope] Thrones and Unthrones Kings. Milton, True Religion, Heresy, Schism.

untidiness.c: untidiness (un-ti’di-nes), n. The character or state of being untidy; lack of neatness; slovenliness. The places the absolute perfection of beauty and untidiness. Edinburgh Rev., CLXVI. 330.

untidy.c: untidy (un-ti’di), a. [< ME. untidy, untidy, un- tydi; <un-1+ tidy1.] 1+. Untimely; unseasonable.—2}. Improper; dishonest.—38. Not tidy; not neat; not orderly or clean. {She shall] haue mo solempne cites and semliche castles Than ge truly han smale tones or] vntydi houses. William of Palerne (E. EB. T. S.), 1. 1455. She omits the sweeping, and her house and furniture become untidy and unattractive. Pop. Sci. Mo., XX XIII. 368.

untie.c: untie (un-ti’),v. [< ME. wnteizen, antigen, < AS. untigan, untigean, untie, < un-, back, + titan, etc., tie: see wn-? and tiel.] IY. trans. 1. To undo, as a knot. Bruted it was amongst the Phrygians, that he which could untie it should be Lord of all Asia. Purchas, Pilgrimage, p. 326. 6651 2. To undo the fastenings, bands, cords, or wrappings of; loosen and remove the things from: as, to untie a bundle; hence, to let or set loose; dissolve the bonds of; liberate. Though you untie the winds, and let them fight Against the churches. Shak., Macbeth, iv. 1. 52. Most haply too, as they untied him, He saw his hat and wig beside him. W. Combe, Three Tours of Dr. Syntax, i. 3. All the evils of an untied tongue we put upon the accounts of drunkenness. Jer. Taylor. 8. To loosen from coils or convolutions. The fury heard, while on Cocytus’ brink Her snakes, untied, sulphureous waters drink. Pope, tr. of Statius’s Thebaid, i. 4. To resolve; unfold; clear. They quicken sloth, perplexities untie. Drayton. II. intrans. To come untied; become loose. Their promises are but fair language,... and disband and untie like the air that beat upon their teeth when they spake the delicious and hopeful words. Jer. Taylor, Works (€d. 1835), I. 887.

untied.c: untied (un-tid’), a. 1. Not tied; free from any fastening or band.— 2}. Figuratively, morally unrestrained; dissolute. There were excesses to many committed in a time so untied as this was. Daniel, Hist. Eng., p. 114. (Davies.)

until.c: until (un-til’), prep. and conj. [Formerly also untill; < ME. until, untill, until, until, ontill; < wn-, as in unto, + till2: see till2 and unto.] I. prep. 1. To; unto: of place. Hire women soon until hire bed hire brought. Chaucer, Troilus, ii. 914. Also zit get he mak tharin Propirtese by preué gyn, That it was like untill a heuyn. Holy Rood (E. E. T. 8.), p. 128. He rousd himselfe full byth, and hastened them untill. Spenser, F. Q., I. xi. 4. 2. To; unto; up to: of time. From where the day out of the sea doth spring, Untill the closure of the Evening. Spenser, F. Q., IIT. iii. 27. II. conj. Up to the time that; till the point or degree that: preceding a clause. Until I know this sure uncertainty, Tl entertain the offer’d fallacy. Shak., C. of E., ii. 2. 187. See ye dinna change your cheer, Until ye see my body bleed. Erlinton (Child’s Ballads, III. 222). ’Tis held a great part of Incivility for Maidens to drink Wine until they are married. Howell, Letters, ii. 54. Until that day comes, I shall never believe this boasted point to be anything more than a conventional fiction. Lamb, Modern Gallantry. We sat and talked until the night, Descending, filled the little room. Longfellow, The Fire of Drift-Wood. The English until with the subjunctive often has a distinctly final sense, and in fact the subjunctive holds its own at that point better than at any other in English. B. L. Gildersleeve, Amer. Jour. Philol., No. 16, p. 422.

untile.c: untile (un-til’), v. t. To take the tiles from; uncover by removing tiles; strip of tiles. Beau. and Fl., Women’s Prize, i. 3.

untillable.c: untillable (un-til’a-bl), a. Incapable of being tilled or cultivated; barren. Cowper, Iliad, i.

untilled.c: untilled (un-tild’), a. [< ME. untiled; < un-1 + tilled.] Not tilled; not cultivated, literally or figuratively. There lines the Sea-Oak in a little shel; There grows vntiil'd the ruddy Cochenel. Sylvester, tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, Eden. His beastly nature, and desert and untilled manners. Jer. Taylor, Holy Dying, ii. 4.

untimbered.c: untimbered (un-tim’bérd), a. 1. Not furnished with timber; not strongly or well timbered. Where ’s then the saucy boat Whose weak untimber'd sides but even now Co-rivall’d greatness? Shak., T. and C., i. 8. 43. 2. Not covered with timber-trees. untime} (un-tim’), ». [ME. untime, untyme, on- tyme; < AS. untima, untime; as un-1 + time.] Unseasonable time. A man shal nat etc in untyme. Chaucer, Parson’s Tale.

untimeliness.c: untimeliness (un-tim‘li-nes),. The character of being untimely; unseasonableness. The untimeliness of temporal death. Jer. Taylor, To Bishop of Rochester.

untimely.c: untimely (un-tim’li), a. [< wn-1 + timely, a.) Not timely. (a) Not done or happening seasonably. Death lies on her like an untimely frost Upon the sweetest flower of all the field. Shak., R. and J., iv. 5. 28. It [Brook Farm] was untimely, and whatever is wn- timely is already doomed to perish. 0. B. Frothingham, Reply, p. 188. (6) Tll-timed; inopportune; unsuitable; unfitting; improper. : unto Some untimely thought did instigate His all-too-timeless speed. | Shak., Lucrece, 1. 43, He kindles anger by untimely jokes. Crabbe, Tales, Works, IV. 8. (c) Happening before the natural time; premature: as, untimely death; untimely fate. The untimely fall of virtuous Lancaster. Shak., Rich. IIl., i. 2. 4.

untimely (un-tim’li), adv. [< ME. untimeliche; < un-l + timely, adv.] In other than the natural time; unseasonably. Can she be dead? Can virtue fall untimely? Fletcher, Humorous Lieutenant, iv. 2. untimeous, untimeously, adv. See untimous, etc.;

untimeously.c: untimeously (un-ti’mus-li), adv. [Also untimeously; < untimous + -ly2.] In an untimous manner; untimely. Scott, Kenilworth, xv.

untimous.c: untimous (un-ti’/mus), a. [Also untimeous; < wn-1 + timous.] Untimely; unseasonable: as, untimous hours. Of untimous persons: He is as welcome as water in a riven ship. He is as welcome as snaw in harvest. Ray, Proverbs (1678), p. 377. His irreverent and untimeous jocularity. Scott, Quentin Durward, I. 304. (The knock] was repeated thrice ere... [he] had presence of mind sufficient to inquire who sought admittance at that untimeous hour. Barham, Ingoldsby Legends, I. 72.

untin.c: untin (un-tin’), v.¢.; pret. and pp. untinned, ppr. untinning. To remove tin from: as, to untin waste tin-plates. The Engineer, LXXI. 42.

untinctured.c: untinctured (un-tingk’tard), a. Not tinctured; not tinged, stained, mixed, or infected; unimbued. Many thousands of armed men, abounding in natural courage, and not absolutely untinctured with military discipline. Macaulay, Nugent’s Hampden.

untinged.c: untinged (un-tinjd’), a. 1. Not tinged; not stained; not discolored: as, water untinged; untinged beams of light.—2. Not infected; unimbued. Swift, To Gay, July 10, 1732.

untirable.c: untirable (un-tir’a-bl), a. Incapable of being tired; unwearied. Shak., T. of A., i. 1. 11.

untired.c: untired (un-tird’), a. Not tired; not exhausted. Shak., Rich. II., iv. 2. 44.

untiring.c: untiring (un-tir’ing), a. Not becoming tired or exhausted; unwearied: as, untiring patience.

untithed.c: untithed (un-tirHd’), a. Not subjected to tithes. R. Pollok.

untitled.c: untitled (un-ti’tld), a. Having no title. (@) Hav-ing no claim or right: as, an untitled tyrant. Shak., Macbeth, iv. 3. 104. False Duessa, now untitled queene. _ Spenser, ¥. Q., V. ix. 42. (0) Having no title of honor or office. The king had already dubbed half London, and Bacon found himself the only untitled person in his mess at Gyray’s Inn. Macaulay, Lord Bacon.

unto.c: unto (un’t6), prep. and conj. [< ME. unto (not found in AS.), < OS. unto, wntuo, unto = OF ries. ont ti, until, = OHG. wnze, wnzi, una, MHG. unze, untie = Goth. unto, up to, until; AS. oth, up to, until, < OS. and, un = OF ries. und, ont = OHG. MHG. wn = Icel. un, unuz, unit = Goth. und, up to, as far as, until; prob. another form of the prep. which appears as the prefix and-, an-2, and with a reversive or negative force as un-2, The same first element appears in until, q.v.] I. prep. To: now somewhat antiquated, but much used in formal or elevated style. Thare men gon un to the See, that schal goon un to Cypre. Mandeville, Travels, p. 125. A semely man to be a kyng, A gracioso face to loke vnto. Political Poems, etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 151. Lawes ought to be fashioned into the manners and conditions of the people to whom they are ment. Spenser, State of Ireland. God made flowers sweet and beautiful, that being seen and smelt unto they might so delight. ‘ Hooker, Eccles. Polity, ii. 5. Come into me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Mat. xi. 28. Tll follow you unto the death. Shak., K. John, i. 1. 154. They also brought a full intelligence in reference unto the particulars they were sent about. NV. Morton, New England’s Memorial, p. 69. Let the North unto the South Speak the word befitting both. Whittier, Texas. To go in unto. See go.—To look unto. See look. II.+ conj. Up to the time or degree that; until; till. Almighty quene, into this yer be gon. Chaucer, Parliament of Fowls, 1. 647. In thys place abide into that ye see Ho bering hym best and ho better haue. Rom. of Partenay (EH. E. T. 8.), 1. 4131. untoiling

untoiling.c: untoiling (un-toi/ling), a. Without toil or labor. Thomson, Castle of Indolence, i. 19.

untold.c: untold (un-told’), a. [< ME. untold; < un-1 + told.] 1. Not told; not related; not revealed. Dryden.— 2. Not numbered; uncounted; that cannot be reckoned: as, money untold. In the number let me pass untold. Shak., Sonnets, exxxvi. Anility and Puerility after all are forces, and might do untold mischief if they were needlessly provoked. J. R. Seeley, Nat. Religion, p. 129. untolerable} (un-tol’e-ra-bl), a. Intolerable. Bp. Jewell, Defence of the Apologie, p. 618.

untomb.c: untomb (un-tém’), v. t. To take from the tomb; disinter. Fuller.

untonality.c: untonality (un-t6-nal’i-ti), n. The state of being without definite tonality. Amer. Jour. Psychol., 1.91. [Rare.]

untonguet.c: untonguet (un-tung’), v. ¢. tongue or of a voice; silence. Such who commend him in making condemn him in keeping such a diary about him in so dangerous days. Especially he ought to untongue it from talking to his prejudice. Fuller, Ch. Hist., XI. ix. 77.

untoninventories.c: Unton Inventories (ed. Nichols), p. 4. 2. A short curtain used upon a bedstead, or in some similar way, either around the frame

untoomlyt.c: untoomlyt (un-tém’li), adv. Hastily. Antenor vntomly turned his way Withoutyn lowtyng or life, legit he noght. Destruction of Troy (E. E. T. §.), 1. 1822.

untooth.c: untooth (un-téth’), v. t To deprive of teeth. Cowper, Odyssey, xviii.

untoothsome.c: untoothsome (un-téth’sum), a. Not toothsome; unpalatable. Shirley, Hyde Park, ii. 4.

untoothsomeness.c: untoothsomeness (un-téth’sum-nes), n. The quality of being untoothsome or unpalatable. Bp. Hall, Contemplations, iii. 287.

untormented.c: untormented (un-tér-men’ted), a. Not tormented; not subjected to torture. Of his wo, as who seyth, untormented. Chaucer, Troilus, i. 1011.

untorn.c: untorn (un-torn’), a. Not torn; not rent or forced asunder. Cowper.

untouchable.c: untouchable (un-tuch’a-bl), a. Not capable of being touched; intangible; unassailable. Untouchable as to prejudice. Feltham, Resolves, ii. 66.

untouched.c: untouched (un-tucht’), a. 1. Not touched, in any physical sense; left intact. Depart untouched. Shak., J. C., iii. 1. 142. The fresh leaves, untouched as yet By summer and its vain regret. William Morris, Earthly Paradise, II. 124. The mineral resources [of Texas] are untouched. Warren, Common School Geography, p. 44. 2. Not mentioned; not treated; not examined. Untouched, or slightly handled, in discourse. Shak., Rich. II1., iii. 7. 19. We are carried forward to explore new regions of our souls as yet untouched and untrodden, H. S. Holland, Logic and Life, p. 50. 8. Not affected mentally; not moved; not excited emotionally. Wholly untouched with his agonies. His heart ’s untouch’d and whole yet. Fletcher, Loyal Subject, v. 1. Time, which matures the intellectual part, Hath tinged my hairs with grey, but left untouched my heart. Southey (Reid’s Brit. Poets, II. 158). I, untouched by one adverse circumstance, Adopted virtue as my rule of life. Browning, Ring and Book, II. 219. untoward! (un-td’iird), a. [< un-1 + toward.] 1. Froward; perverse; refractory; not easily guided or taught. This untoward generation. Acts ii. 40. What means this scorn, thou most untoward knave? Shak., K. John, i. 1. 243. Nay, look, what a rascally untoward thing this poetry is. B. Jonson, Poetaster, i. 1. 2. Inconvenient; troublesome; vexatious; unfortunate; unlucky: as, an untoward event; an untoward vow. An untoward accident drew me into a quarrel. Sheridan, The Rivals, v. 1. =Syn. 1. Wilful, Contrary, etc. (see wayward), intractable. untoward?t, prep. [ME.,< unto + -ward.] To-ward To deprive of a Sir P. Sidney. Whan I am my ladies fro, And thynke untoward hir drawe. Gower, Conf. Amant., iv.

untowardliness.c: untowardliness(un-t0’iird-li-nes),». The character or state of being untowardly.

untowardly.c: untowardly (un-t0’ird-li), a. Awkward; perverse ; froward. Untowardly tricks and vices. Locke, Education.

untowardly (un-t6’iird-li), adv. In an untoward, froward, or perverse manner; perversely. Matters £0 untowardly on our Side in Germany, but the King of Denmark will shortly be in the Field in Person. Howell, Letters, I. iv. 20. 6652

untowardness.c: untowardness (un-t0’iird-nes), n. The state or character of being untoward; awkwardness; frowardness; perverseness. Bp. Wilson. untowent, untown, a. [ME., also untohen, untone, < AS. ungetogen (= MLG. untogen, MHG. ungezogen), uninstructed, untaught, < wn-, not, + token, pp. of tedn, draw, educate, instruct: see wn- and teel, and cf. wanton, earlier wan- town.] Untaught; untrained; rude.

untowered.c: untowered (un-tou’érd), a. Not having towers; not defended by towers. Wordsworth.

untrace.c: untrace (un-tras’), v. t. To loose from the traces or drawing-straps: as, to untrace a horse. And now the fiery horses of the Sun Were from their golden-flaming car untrac’d. Middleton, Father Hubbard’s Tales,

untraceable.c: untraceable (un-tra’sa-bl), Incapable of being traced or followed. South.

untraced.c: untraced (un-trast’), a 1. Not traced; not followed.— 2. Not marked by footsteps. Den- ham, Cooper’s Hill.— 8. Not marked out.

untracked.c: untracked (un-trakt’), a. 1. Not tracked; not marked by footsteps; pathless: as, untracked woods. Sandys, tr. of Ovid’s Metamorph., ii.— 2. Not followed by tracking.

untractable.c: untractable (un-trak’ta-bl), a. ble; intractable. To speak with libertie, and to say you the truth, they say al in this Court that you are a verie good christian, and a verie untractable bishop. Guevara, Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 224. The high-spirited and intractable Agrippina. Gifford, note on Jonson’s Sejanus. There was room among these hitherto intractable irregularities for the additional results of the theory. Whewell. 2+. Difficult; rough. I Toil’d out my uncouth passage, forced to ride The untractable abyss. Milton, P. L., x. 476.

untraded.c: untraded (un-tra’ded), a. 1. Not resorted to or frequented for the sake of trading: as, an untraded place. Hakluyt’s Voyages, iii. 682.— 2. Unpractised; inexperienced. A people not utterly untraded... in his discipline. J, Udall, On Luke i. 3. Unhackneyed; unusual; not used commonly. That I affect the untraded oath. Shak., T, and C., iv. 5. 178.

untrading.c: untrading (un-tra’ding), a. Not engaged in commerce; not accustomed; inexperienced. Untrading and unskilful hands. Locke.

untragic.c: untragic (un-traj’ik), a. Not tragic; hence, comic; ludicrous. Emblems not a few of the tragic and the untragic sort. Carlyle, French Rey., II. vy. 12. (Davies.)

untrained.c: untrained (un-trand’), a. Not trained; not disciplined; uneducated; uninstructed. My wit untrain’d in any kind of art. Shak., 1 Hen. VL, i. 2. 73. I cannot say that Iam utterly wntrain’d in those rules which best Rhetoricians have giv’n. Milton, Apology for Smectymnuus. Not only is the multitude fickle, but the best men, unless urged, tutored, disciplined to their work, give way; untrained nature has no principles. J. H. Newman, Parochial Sermons, i. 286.

untrammeleduntrammelled.c: untrammeled, untrammelled (un-tram’eld), a. Not trammeled, hampered, or impeded.

untrampled.c: untrampled (un-tram’pld), a. Not trampled; not trodupon. Shelley.

untransferable.c: untransferable (un-trins-fér’a-bl), a. Incapable of being transferred or passed from one to another: as, power or right wntransferable. Howell, Pre-eminence of Parliament.

untranslatability.c: untranslatability (un-trans-la-ta-bil’i-ti), n. 1. Not tracta- The quality of being untranslatable. G. P. Marsh, Lects. on Eng. Lang., xxviii.

untranslatable.c: untranslatable (un-trans-la’ta-bl), a. Not capable of being translated; also, not fit to be translated. Gray, To West, April, 1742.

untranslatableness.c: untranslatableness (un-trans-la’ta-bl-nes), n The character of being untranslatable. Cole- ridge.

untranslatably.c: untranslatably (un-trans-la’ta-bli), adv. In an untranslatable manner; so as not to be capable of translation. Atheneum, No. 3238, p. 671.

untransmutable.c: untransmutable (un-trans-mi’ta-bl), a capable of being transmuted. Each character... appears to me in practice pretty durable and untransmutable. Hume.

untransparent.c: untransparent (un-trans-par’ent), a. Not transparent; opaque: literally or figuratively. Boyle, Works, I. 735. In- untrodden

untraveleduntravelled.c: untraveled, untravelled (un-trav’eld),a. 1. Not traveled; not trodden by passengers: as, an untraveled forest. Untravelled parts. Sir T. Browne, Vulg. Err. 2. Not having traveled; not having gained experience by travel; hence, provincial; narrow. An untravelled Englishman. Addison, Spectator, No. 407.

untread.c: untread (un-tred’), v. t To tread back; go back through in the same steps; retrace. Untreading a good part of the aforesaid alley. Sandys, Travailes (1652), p. 131.

untreasure.c: untreasure (un-trezh’ir), v. ¢ 1. To deprive of a treasure. They found the bed untreasured of their mistress. Shak., As you Like it, ii. 2. 7. 2. To bring forth, as treasure; set forth; display. [Rare in both uses. J The quaintness with which he wntreasured... the stores of his memory. Mitford.

untreatable.c: untreatable (un-tré’ta-bl), a. [< ME. untreta- ble; < un-1 + treatable.| 1+. Unmanageable; inexorable; implacable. Thow shalt nat wenen, quod she, that I bere wntretable batable ayenis fortune. Chaucer, Boéthius, ii. prose 8. 2+. Not practicable. Dr. H. More.—8. Incapable of being treated, in any sense.

untrembling.c: untrembling (un-trem’ bling), a. Not trem- pie or shaking; firm; steady. J. Philips, der, i.

untremblingly.c: untremblingly (un-trem’bling-li), adv. In an untrembling manner; firmly.

untrespassing.c: untrespassing (un-tres’pas-ing), a. Not trespassing; not transgressing. Others were sent more cheerefull, free, and still as it were at large, in the midst of an untrespassing honesty. Milton, Apology for Smectymnuus.

untressed.c: untressed (un-trest’),a. [ME.,<wn-1 + tressed, pp. of tress.] With hair unarranged; not done up in tresses, as hair. Hir gilt heres with a golden three Ybounden were, untressed as she lay. Chaucer, Parliament of Fowls, 1. 268.

untried.c: untried (un-trid’), a. 1. Not tried; not attempted. By subtil Stratagems they act their Game, And leave untry’d no Avenue to Fame. Steele, Conscious Lovers, Prol. The generous past, when all was possible, For all was then untried. Lowell, Under the Willows. 2. Not yetfelt or experienced: as, untried sufferings. Remains there yet a plague untried for me? Beau. and Fi., Philaster, iv. 2. 3. Not subjected to trial; not tested or put to the test. By its perfect shape, its vigor, and its natural dexterity in the use of all its untried limbs, the infant was worthy to have been brought forth in Eden. Hawthorne, Scarlet Letter, p. 114. 4+. Unnoticed; unexamined. I slide O’er sixteen years and leave the growth untried. hak., W. T., iv. 1. 6, 5. Not having passed trial; not heard and determined in law: as, the cause remains wn- tried.

untrifling.c: untrifling (un-tri’fling), a. Not trifling; not indulging in levities. Savage.

untrim.c: untrim (un-trim’),v.¢. To deprive of trimming; strip; disorder. By chance or nature’s changing course untrimm’d. k., Sonnets, xviii.

untrimmed.c: untrimmed (un-trimd’), a. 1. Not trimmed; not pruned; not clipped or cut; not put in order: as, an ‘untrimmed wick; untrimmed leaves of a book. So let thy tresses, flaring in the wind, Untrimmed hang about thy bared neck. Tancr. and Gism., O. Pl., ii. 221. 2+. Virgin. The devil tempts thee here, In likeness of a new untrimmed bride. Shak., K. John, iii. 1, 209, 3. Not furnished with trimmings.

untrimmedness.c: untrimmedness (un-trimd’nes), n. of being untrimmed. ([Rare.] It [an old castle] is not particularly “kept up,” but its quiet rustiness and untrimmedness only help it to be familiar. H. James, Jr., Portraits of Places, p. 167.

untristet.c: untristet, a. See intrust. untriumphable+ (un-tri’um-fa-bl), a. Admitting no triumph; not an object of triumph. S. Butler, Hudibras.

untroddenuntrod.c: untrodden, untrod (un-trod’n, un-trod’), a. Not having been trod; not na over; unfrequented. Shak., J. C. vy Wi. Ley (Nares.) The state untrodden What path introd Shall I seek out to scape the flaming rod Of my offended, of my angry God? Quarles, Emblems, iii. 12. The path from me to you that led, Untrodden long, with grass is grown. Lowell, Estrangement.

untroth.c: untroth (un-tréth’),n. [A var. of untruth, as troth is of truth.) 1. Untruth; falsehood. If you find my words to be untroth, Then let me die to recompense the wrong. Greene, Alphonsus, ii. 2. An untruth; a falsehood. There will be a yard of dissimulation at least, city-mea- sure, and cut upon an untroth or two. Fletcher and Rowley, Maid in the Mill, iv. 1.

untroubled.c: untroubled (un-trub’ld), a. 1. Not troubled; not disturbed by care, sorrow, or business; not agitated; unmoved; unruffled; not confused; free from passion: as, an untroubled mind. Quiet, untroubled soul, awake! Shak., Rich. III., v. 3. 149. 2. Not disturbed or raised into waves or ripples: as, an untroubled sea.— 3. Not foul; not turbid: as, an untroubled stream. Bodies clear and untroubled. Bacon.

untroubledness.c: untroubledness (un-trub’ld-nes), ». The state of being untroubled; freedom from trouble; uneoneern. Hammond, Works, IV. 479.

untroublet.c: untroublet (un-trub‘1), v. t. To free from trouble; disabuse. Leighton, Com. on 1 Pet. v.

untrowable.c: untrowable (un-tro’a-bl), a. [ME., < un-1 + trow + -able.] Not to be credited; incredible. Wyclif. untruced} (un-trést’), a. Not interrupted by a truce; truceless. All those four [elements] Maintain a natural opposition And untruec’d war the one against the other. Middleton, No Wit Like a Woman’, iii. 1.

untrue.c: untrue (un-tr6’), a [< ME. untrewe, ontrewe (= MLG. wntriwe = G. untrue = Ieel. utryggr); < un-1 + true.} 1. Not true to the fact; contrary to the fact; false. And he shewed him trewe tidynges and wntrewe, for he made him heleue howe all the countre of Wales wolde gladly haue hym to be their lorde. Berners, tv. of Froissart’s Chron., I. 332. By what construction shall any man make those comparisons true, holding that distinction untrue? Hooker, Bccles. Polity. 2. Not true to one’s duty; not faithful; inconstant; not fulfilling the duties of a husband, wife, vassal, friend, etc.; not to be trusted; false; disloyal. Lete vs take hede to saue the peple and the londe fro these wn-trewe and misbelevynge Sarazins that thus sod- enly be entred vpon vs. Merlin (BE. E. T. §.), ii. 174. For further I could say this man’s untrue. Shak., Lover’s Complaint, 1. 169. 3. Not true to a standard or rule; varying from a correct form, pattern, intonation, alinement, or the like; incorrect. Henry chastised the olde untrewe measure, and made a yere of the length of his owne arme. Fabyan, Chronycle, cexxvi. (Encyc. Dict.) The millboards must be squared truly, or the volume will stand unevenly and the finisher’s design be untrue. W. Mathews, Modern Bookbinding (ed. Grolier Club), p. 35. In the case of crank-pins wearing untrue, there is nothing for it but filing to caliper. The Engineer, LXIX. 159.
untrue (un-tré’), adv. [< ME. untrewe; < untrue, a.) Untruly. Elles he moot telle his tale wntrewe. : Chaucer, Gen. Prol. to C. T., 1. 735.

untrueness.c: untrueness (un-tré’nes), ». [< ME. wntrewe- nesse; < untrue + -ness.] The character of being untrue.

untruism.c: untruism (un-tré’izm), ». [< untrue + -ism.] Something obviously untrue; the opposite of atruism. [A nonce-word.] Platitudes, truisms, and untruism. Trollope, Barchester Towers, vi.

untruly.c: untruly (un-tr6’li), adv. Inan untrue manner; not truly; falsely. Master More untruly reporteth of me in his dialogue. Tyndale, Ans. to Sir T. More, etc. (Parker Soc., 1850), p. 14.

untruss.c: untruss (un-trus’), v.¢. To untie or unfasten; loose from a truss, or as from a truss; let out; specifically, to loose, as to let down the breeches by untying the points by which they were held up; undress. Give me my nightcap, so! Quick, quick, untruss me. Fletcher (and another), Elder Brother, iv, 4. Our Muse is in mind for th’ untrussing a poet. B. Jonson, Poetaster, v. 1. The Clerk of Chatham was untrussing his points preparatory to seeking his truckle-bed. Barham, Ingoldsby Legends, I. 71. 6653

untrussed.c: untrussed (un-trust’), a. Not trussed; not tied up; not bundled up. Fairfax, Godfrey of Bou- logne, xviii. Behold the sacred Pales, where with haire Untrust she sits, in shade of yonder hill. L. Bryskett, Pastorall Aeglogue.

untrusser.c: untrusser (un-trus’ér), ». One who untrusses; hence, one who unmasks and scourges folly; one who prepares others for punishment by untrussing them. Neither shall you at any time, ambitiously affecting the title of the untrussers or whippers of the age, suffer the itch of writing to overrun your performance in libel. B. Jonson, Poetaster, v. 3.

untrusst.c: untrusst (un-trus’), ». Same as untrusser. Thou grand scourge, or second untruss of the time. B. Jonson, Every Man out of his Humour, ii. 1.

untrustful.c: untrustful (un-trust’fal), a. 1. Not trustful or trusting.—2. Not to be trusted; not trustworthy; not trusty. Scott. [Rare.]

untrustiness.c: untrustiness (un-trus’ti-nes), x. The character of being untrusty; unfaithfulness in the discharge of a trust. Sir T. Hayward.

untrustt.c: untrustt (un-trust’), 2. [< ME. untrust, untrist (= Ieel. atraust); < un-) + trust!.] Lack of trust; distrust. Ye have noon other countenance I leave, But speke to us of untrust and reprieve. Chaucer, Merchant’s Tale, 1. 962. untrustt, a. [ME., also untriste (= Icel. wtraustr), faithless: see untrust, n.] Faithless; distrustful. Why hastow made Troylus to me wntriste[var. wntruste]? Chaucer, Troilus, iii. 839.

untrustworthiness.c: untrustworthiness (un-trust’wér’fHi-nes), n. The character of being untrustworthy. Much has been said about untrustworthiness of historical evidence. H. Spencer, Prin. of Sociol., p. 75.

untrustworthy.c: untrustworthy (un-trust’ wer’ Hi), a. Not trustworthy, in any sense: as, an untrustworthy servant; an untrustworthy boat. It wants it [sifting] all the more because it is so closely connected with the early Venetian history, than which no history is more utterly untrustworthy. E. A. Freeman, Venice, p. 228.

untrusty.c: untrusty (un-trus’ti), a. [< ME. untrusty, on- trusty, ontristy; < un-1 + trusty.] Not trusty; not worthy of confidence; unfaithful. Thomas Lodge (Arber’s Eng. Garner, I. 14).

untruth.c: untruth (un-tréth’),». [Also untroth, q. v.; < ME. ontreuthe, untrouthe, untrowthe, < AS. un- trewth, untruth; as wn-l1 + truth.] 1. The character of being untrue; contrariety to truth; want of veracity. He who is perfect and abhors untruth. Sandys. 2. Treachery; want of fidelity; faithlessness; disloyalty. Untruth has made thee subtle in thy trade. Ford, Lover’s Melancholy, iv. 3. 8. A false assertion; a falsehood; a lie. Moreover, they have spoken untruths;... and, to conclude, they are lying knaves. Shak., Much Ado, v. 1. 220.

untruthful.c: untruthful (un-tréth’ful), a. Not truthful; wanting in veracity; contrary to the truth. Clarke.

untruthfully.c: untruthfully (un-tréth’ful-i), adv. In an untruthful manner; falsely; faithlessly.

untruthfulness.c: untruthfulness (un-tréth’ful-nes),. 1. The character or state of being untruthful; falseness; unveracity.—2. Inaccuracy; incorrectness: as, the untruthfulness of a drawing.

untuck.c: untuck (un-tuk’), v. ¢. To unfold or undo; release from being tucked up or fastened. For some, wntuck’d, descended her sheaved hat. Shak., Lover’s Complaint, 1. 31.

untuckered.c: untuckered (un-tuk’érd), a. Wearing no tucker: said of a woman.

untufted.c: untufted (un-tuf’ted), a. Without tufts or projecting bunches, as of scales or hairs: specifically noting certain moths.

untunable.c: untunable (un-ti’na-bl), a. 1. Not capable of being tuned or brought to the proper pitch.— 2. Not harmonious; discordant; not musical. Then in dumb silence will I bury mine [news], For they are harsh, untuneable, and bad. Shak., T. G. of V., iii. 1. 208. Also untuneable.

untunableness.c: untunableness (un-tii’na-bl-nes), ”. The state of being untunable; want of harmony or concord; discord. T. Warton.

untunably.c: untunably (un-ti’na-bli), adv. able manner; discordantly. Plutarch, p. 586.

untune.c: untune (un-tiin’), v.¢t. 1. To put out of tune; make incapable of consonance or harmony. Untune that string. Shak., T. and C., i. 3. 109. In an untun- Holland, tr. of unusefully Naught untunes that Infant's voice; no trace Of fretful temper sullies her pure cheek, ; Wordsworth, Sonnets, iii. 16. 2. To disorder; confuse. Untuned and jarring senses.

untuned.c: untuned (un-tind’), a. al; unharmonious. With boisterous untuned drums. Shak., Rich. II., i. 3. 134,

unturf.c: unturf (un-térf’), v. ¢ To remove turf from; deprive of turf. Nature, XLIII. 80.

unturn.c: unturn (un-térn’), v.¢. To turn in the reverse way, asia a manner to open something. [Rare.] Think you he nought but prison walls did see, Till, so unwilling, thou unturn’dst the key? Keats, The Day Leigh Hunt Left Prison.

unturned.c: unturned (un-térnd’), a. Not turned.—Toleave no stone unturned. See stone.

untutored.c: untutored (un-ti’tord), a. taught; rude; raw. Some untutor’d youth. Shak., Sonnets, exxxviii.

untwine.c: untwine (un-twin’),v. I, trans. 1. To untwist; open or separate after having been twisted; untie; disentangle; hence, figuratively, to explain; solve. This knot might be wntwined with more facilities thus. Holinshed, Sundrie Invasions of Ireland. (Encyc. Dict.) On his sad brow nor mirth nor wine Could e’er one wrinkled knot untwine. Scott, Rokeby, iii. 22. 2. To unwind, as a vine or anything that has been twined around something else: literally or figuratively. It requires a long and powerful countersympathy in a nation to untwine the ties of custom which bind a people to the established and the old. Sir W. Hamilton. II. intrans. To become untwined. His silken braids wntwine, and slip their knots. Milton, Divorce, i. 6.

untwist.c: untwist (un-twist’),v. I. trans. 1. To separate and open, as threads twisted; turn back from being twisted. Swift.—2. Figuratively, to disentangle; solve: as, to wntwista riddle. Fletcher, A Woman Pleased, v. 1. II. intrans. To become separate and loose or straight from having been twisted.

untwist (un-twist’),n. [< wntwist, v.] A twist in the opposite direction. Each coil of the cable in the tank as it comes out receives a twist in the opposite direction, or untwist. Elect. Rev. (Eng.), XXIV. 467.

unum.c: Unum (one), Verum (true), Bonum (good); or five, Ens being omitted. ()) That which is altogether beyond the bounds of human cognition and thought. Compare I., 3.—38. In math., a transcendental expression or function.

ununderstandable.c: ununderstandable (un-un-dér-stan’da-bl), a. Not to be understood; incomprehensible. Pi- lazzi Smyth. ([Rare.]}

ununderstood.c: ununderstood (un-un-dér-stid’), a. Not understood; not comprehended. fuller, Ch. Hist., IX. 1.50. [Rare.]

unungun.c: Unungun (u-nung'un), or Aleut. [‘People.’] A division of the Eskimauan stock of North American Indians, inhabiting the Aleutian Archipelago. Number (1894), about 2,200. See Eskimauan.

ununiform.c: ununiform (un-i’ni-f6rm), a. wanting uniformity. [Rare.] An ununiform piety. Decay of Christian Piety.

ununiformness.c: ununiformness (un-i’ni-férm-nes), ». The character or state of being ununiform; want of uniformity. [Rare.] A variety of parts, or an ununiformness, Clarke, Answer to Sixth Letter.

unurged.c: unurged (un-érjd’), a. Noturged; not pressed with solicitation; unsolicited; voluntary; of one’s own accord. Shak., K. Jobn, v. 2. 10.

unusage.c: unusage (un-ii’zaj), n. [< wn-l + usage.) 1. Unusualness; infrequency. Defawte of unusage and entrecomunynge of marchaun- dise. Chaucer, Boéthius, ii. prose 7. 2. Want of use. Halliwell.

unused.c: unused (un-izd’), a. 1. Not put to use; not employed; not applied; disused. Shak., Sonnets, iv.— 2. That has never been used.—8. Not accustomed; not habituated: as, hands unused to labor; hearts unused to deceit. Unused to the melting mood. Shak., Othello, v. 2. 349. Her gaoler’s torches fill with light The dreary place, blinding her unused eyes. William Morris, Earthly Paradise, I. 263. 4. Unusual; unwonted. Bitter pain his vexed heart wrought for him, And filled with unused tears his hard wise eyes. William Morris, Earthly Paradise, III. 145.

unusedness.c: unusedness (un-i’zed-nes), n. Unwontedness; unusualness. Sir P. Sidney, Arcadia, vii. [Rare.]

unuseful.c: unuseful (un-is’ful), a. Useless; serving no purpose. Jer. Taylor, Works (ed. 1835), IT. 292. Those hands that gave the casket may the palsy For ever make unuseful, even to feed thee! Fletcher, Wife for a Month, i. 2.

unusefully.c: unusefully (un-is’fil-i), adv. Ina useless manner. Jer. Taylor, Works (ed. 1835), I. 236. Shak., Lear, iv. 7. 16. Not tuned; unmusi- Uninstructed; un- Not uniform; unusefulness

unusefulness.c: unusefulness (un-is’ful-nes),, The character of being unuseful. WN. A. Rev., CXLII. 304.

unusual.c: unusual (un-t’zhé-al), a. Not usual; not frequent; not common; rare; strange: as, an wn- usual season; a person of unusual erudition. Some comet or unusual prodigy. Shak., T. of the §., iii. 2. 98. The territory to whose free population Roman citizenship was now extended was of very unusual size according to the measure of ancient cities. E. A. Freeman, Amer. Lects., p. 317. =Syn. Uncommon, unwonted, singular, remarkable, odd.

unusuality.c: unusuality (un-a-zh6-al’i-ti), n. [< unusual + -ity.] The state or character of being unusual; unwontedness; rarity. It is to be said of Sallust, far more plausibly than of Carlyle, that his obscurity, his unusuality of expression, and his Laconism... bore the impress of his genius, and were but a portion of his unaffected thought. E, A, Poe, Marginalia, lvi.

unusually.c: unusually (un-ii’zhé-al-i), adv. In an unusual manner; not commonly; not frequently; rarely; unwontedly. Paley.

unusualness.c: unusualness (un-i’zhé-al-nes),. The state of being unusual; uncommonness; infrequency; rareness of occurrence; rarity.

unutterability.c: unutterability (un-ut’ér-a-bil’i-ti), n. 1. The character of being unutterable; unspeakableness.—2. Pl. unutterabilities (-tiz). That which cannot be uttered or spoken. They come with hot unutterabilities in their heart. Carlyle, French Reyv., II. i. 3.

unutterable.c: unutterable (un-ut’ér-a-bl), a. Incapable of being uttered or expressed; ineffable; inexpressible; unspeakable: as, wnutterable anguish; wnutterable joy. He is, sir, The most unutterable coward that e’er nature Bless’d with hard shoulders. Beau, and Fl., Thierry and Theodoret, ii. 4. He with sighs unutterable by any words, much less by a stinted Liturgie, dwelling in us makes intercession for us. Milton, Fikonoklastes, xvi.

unutterably.c: unutterably (un-ut’ér-a-bli), adv. In an un- - utterable manner; unspeakably; beyond expression. There would have been something sad, unutterably sad, in all this. Hawthorne, Scarlet Letter, p. 43.

unvaccinated.c: unvaccinated (un-vak’si-na-ted), a. Not vae- crinated; specifically, having never been successfully vaccinated.

unvaluable.c: unvaluable (un-val’i-a-bl), a. 1. Being above price; invaluable; priceless. I cannot cry his caract up enough; He is unvaluable. B. Jonson, Magnetick Lady, i. 1. 2. Valueless; worthless. If nature... deny health, how unvaluable are their riches! Rev. T. Adams, Works, I. 424.

unvalued.c: unvalued (un-val’ad), a. 1. Not valued; not prized; neglected. Shak., Hamlet, i. 3. 19.— 2+. Inestimable; not to be valued. Each heart Hath, from the leaves of thy wnvalued book, Those Delphick lines with deep impression took. Milton, Epitaph on Shakspere. Art or nature never yet could set A valued price to her wnvalued worth. Middleton, Family of Love, i. 2. 3. Not estimated; not having the value set; not appraised: as, an estate wavalued.

unvanquishable.c: unvanquishable (un-vang’kwish-a-bl), a. Incapable of being conquered. J. Udall, On John Xvii.

unvanquished.c: unvanquished (un-vang’kwisht), a. Not conquered; not overcome. Shak., 1 Hen. VI, v. 4. 141.

unvaried.c: unvaried (un-va’rid), a. Not varied; not altered; not diversified; unchanged. The same unvary’d chimes. Pope, Essay on Criticism, ii. 348. So far as its [Salem’s] physical aspect is concerned, with its flat wnvaried surface, covered chiefly with wooden houses. Hawthorne, Scarlet Letter, p. 231.

unvariegated.c: unvariegated (un-va’ri-e-ga-ted), a. Not variegated; not diversified; not marked with different colors. Edinburgh Rev.

unvarnished.c: unvarnished (un-vir’nisht), a. 1. Not overlaid with varnish.—2, Not artfully embellished; plain. A round unvarnish'd tale. Shak., Othello, i. 3. 90.

unvarying.c: unvarying (un-va’ri-ing), a. Not altering; not liable to change; uniform; unchanging. Locke.

unvaryingly.c: unvaryingly (un-va’ri-ing-li), adv. In an unvarying manner; uniformly. George Eliot, Silas Marner, xvii. Not variable; 6654

unvassal.c: unvassal (un-vas’al), v. t. [« un-2 + vassal.] To cause to be no longer a vassal; release from vassalage. ([Rare.]

unveil.c: unveil (un-val’), v. [Early mod. E. unvail; ¢ un-2 + veil.] I. trans. To remove a veil from; uncover; disclose to view; reveal: as, to unveil statue. Shak., T. and C., iii. 3. 200. II. intrans. To become unveiled; be disclosed to view; remove a veil; reveal one’s self. Unveil, O Lord, and on us shine In glory and in grace. J. H. Newman, The Two Worlds. Non-vaseular; Also unvail.

unveiledly.c: unveiledly (un-va’led-li), adv. Plainly; without disguise. Boyle, Works, IV. 18. [Rare.]

unveiler.c: unveiler (un-va’lér), ». One who unveils; ee one who expounds. Boyle, Works,

unvenerable.c: unvenerable (un-ven’e-ra-bl), a. Not venerable; not worthy of veneration; contemptible. Shak., W. 'T., ii. 3. 77.

unvenomed.c: unvenomed (un-ven’umd), @. Having no venom; not poisonous: as, a toad unvenomed. Bp. Hall, Satires, Postscript.

unvenomous.c: unvenomous (un-ven’um-us), a. Same as wn- venomed. Bp. Gauden, Tears of the Church, p. 297. (Davies.)

unvented.c: unvented (un-ven’ted), a. Not vented; not uttered; not opened for utterance or emission. Fletcher, Mad Lover, ii. [Rare.]

unveracious.c: unveracious (un-vé-ra’shus), a. Not veracious; not having a strict regard for truth; untruthful; dishonest; false.

unveracity.c: unveracity (un-vé-ras‘i-ti), n. rarity; untruth; falsehood. A certain very considerable finite quantity of Unveracity and Phantasm. Carlyle.

unverdant.c: unverdant (un-vér’dant), a. Not verdant; not green; having no verdure. Congreve, tr. of Ovid’s Art of Love, iii. unveritable} (un-ver’i-ta-bl), a. Not veritable; not true. Puttenham, Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 21.

unversed.c: unversed (un-vérst’), a. 1. Not skilled; not versed; unacquainted. A mind in all heart-mysteries unversed. Wordsworth, Excursion, vi. 2. Not put in verse: as, thoughts wnversed.

unvexed.c: unvexed (un-vekst’), a. Not vexed; not troubled; not disturbed; not agitated or disquieted. Donne, Anatomy of the World,i. Also invest. In the noon now woodland creatures all Were resting neath the shadow of the trees, Patient, unvexed by any memories. William Morris, Earthly Paradise, II. 174.

unvicar.c: unvicar (un-vik’ir), v. ¢ To deprive of the office or position of vicar. IfI had your authority, I would be so bold to unvicar im. Strype, Cranmer, II. vii. (Davies.)

unviolable.c: unviolable (un-vi’6-la-bl), a. Not to be violated or broken. Shak., Rich. IIL, ii. 1. 27. [Rare.]

unviolated.c: unviolated (un-vi’6-la-ted), a. 1. Not violated; not injured. Th’ unviolated honour of your wife. Shak., C. of E., iii. 1. 88. 2. Not broken; not transgressed: as, an wvio- lated vow. Milton, S.A., 1. 1144.

unvirtue.c: unvirtue (un-vér’ti), n. Absence of virtue; vice. [Rare.] They think their children never do unvirtuous things; and yet they reek with unvirtue. H. W. Beecher, Christian Union, March 3, 1887.

unvirtuous.c: unvirtuous (un-vér’ti-us), a. Not virtuous; Serpe of virtue. Shak., M. W. of W., iv. 2.

unvisible.c: unvisible (un-viz’i-bl), a. Invisible. Chaucer. unvisibly+ (un-viz’i-bli), adv. Invisibly. Bp. Gardiner.

unvital.c: unvital (un-vi’tal), a. Not vital; not essential to life; hence, fatal. [Rare.] Lavoisier showed that the atmospheric air consists of pure or vital, and of an wnvital air, which he thence called azote. Whewell,

unvitiated.c: unvitiated (un-vish’i-a-ted), a. Not vitiated; not corrupted; pure. B. Jonson, Magnetick Lady, iv. 3.

unvizard.c: unvizard (un-viz’iird), v.t [< un-2 + vizard.] To divest of a vizard or mask; unmask. O what a death it is to the Prelates to be thus un-vis- added, thus uncas’d. Milton, On Def. of Humb. Remonst. Not ven- Want of ye- In an un- ? a ott unwares

unvoiced.c: unvoiced (un-voist’), a. 1. Not spoken; unuttered; not articulated or pronounced. EHmer- son.—2. In phonetics, not uttered with voice as distinct from breath; unintonated; surd.

unvoidable.c: unvoidable (un-voi’da-bl), a. Incapable of being made void; irreversible. He will from on high pronounce that unvoidable sentence. Bailey, tr. of Colloquies of Erasmus, p. 178. (Davies.) unvoluntary} (un-vol’un-ta-ri), a. Involuntary. Fuller.

unvoluptuous.c: unvoluptuous (un-vo-lup’ti-us), a. Free from voluptuousness; not sensuous. George Eliot, Middlemarch, xxiii.

unvote.c: unvote (un-vot’), v. ¢ undo by vote. This was so sacred a rule that many of those who voted with the court the day before, expressed their indignation against it, as subverting the very constitution of parliament, if things might be thus voted and unvoted again from day today. Bp. Burnet, Hist. Own Times, an, 1711.

unvowed.c: unvowed (un-voud’), a. Not vowed; not consecrated by solemn promise.. If vnuowed to another Order,... he vows in this order. Sandys, Travailes, p. 229. (Davies.)

unvoyageable.c: unvoyageable (un-voi’aj-a-bl), a. 1. Incapable of being navigated; innavigable. De Quin- cey.—2. Not to be crossed or passed over; impassable. This unvoyageable gulf obscure. Milton, P. L., x. 366. Not vulgar or com- To retract, annul, or

unvulgar.c: unvulgar (un-vul’ gir), a. mon. Heat my brain With Delphic fire, That I may sing my thoughtkin some unvulgar strain. B. Jonson, Underwoods, xliv.

unvulgarize.c: unvulgarize (un-vul’gir-iz), v. t. To divest of vulgarity; make not vulgar or common. Lamb.

unwaited.c: unwaited (un-wa’ted), a. Not attended: with on. To wander up and down unwaited on. Fletcher, Mad Lover, ii.

unwakeful.c: unwakeful (un-wak’fil), a. Sleeping easily and soundly; characterized by sound sleep.

unwakefulness.c: unwakefulness (un-wak’fil-nes), n. The quality or state of being unwakeful; sound sleep.

unwakened.c: unwakened (un-wa’knd), a. Not wakened; not roused from sleep or as from sleep. Milton, P. L., v. 9. “eS (un-wol’et), v. t. To take from a wal- et. The lacquey laughed, unsheathed his calabash, and un- walleted his cheese. Jarvis, tr. of Don Quixote, II. iv.14. (Davies.)

unwandering.c: unwandering (un-won’dér-ing), a. Not wandering; not moving or going from place to place. Cowper, Iliad, xiii. “

unwapperedt.c: unwapperedt (un-wop’érd), a. Not caused or not having reason to tremble; not made tremu- _ lous; unpalsied; hence, fearless and strong through innocence. We come towards the gods, Young and unwapper'd, not halting under crimes Many and stale. Fletcher (and another), Two Noble Kinsmen, v. 4.

unwarded.c: unwarded (un-war’ded), a. Unwatched; unguarded. J. Brende, tr. of Quintus Curtius, fol. 81.

unwarely.c: unwarely (un-war’li), adv. [< unwarely, unwar- ly, unwarliche, < AS. unwerlice, unexpectedly, under, unexpected: see unware, a.) Unawares; unforeseen; unexpectedly. Elde is comen unwary upon me. Chaucer, Boéthius, i. meter 1.

unwareness.c: unwareness (un-wir’nes), m. [< unware + -ness.| The condition of being unexpected. Hakluyt’s Voyages, I. 201.

unwarest.c: unwarest (un-warz’), adv. [< ME. *unwares, <¢ AS. unwares, < under, unexpected: see wn. ware.) Unawares; by surprise. A great sort of Turks entred into the bulwarke of Spaine,... and drove our men out, I can not tell how, unwares or otherwise. Hakluyt's Voyages, I. 84. ” unwarily

unwaret.c: unwaret (un-war’),a. [< ME. wawar, onward, <¢ AS. wwwer, unheeding, unheeded, unexpected, <un-, not, + wer, heedful: see wn-1 and ware.] Unexpected; unforeseen. Upon thy glade day have in thy mynde The unwar wo or harm that comte bihynde. Chaucer, Man of Law’s Tale, 1. 329.

unwaret (un-wir’), adv. [ME. uwnwar; prop. predicate use of unware, a.] Unawares; unexpectedly. On thee, Fortune, I pleyne, That unwar wrapped hast me in thy cheyne. Chaucer, Franklin’s Tale, 1. 628. He put vp his goode swerde for route leste he slough eny man vn-war. Merlin (E. EB. T.8.), iii. 498.

unwarily.c: unwarily (un-wa’ri-li), adv. In an unwary manner; without vigilance and caution; heedlessly; unexpectedly. Shak., K. John, v. 7. 63.

unwariness.c: unwariness (un-wa’ri-nes), n. The character of being unwary; wanton caution; carelessness; heedlessness; recklessness.

unwarlike.c: unwarlike (un-war’lik), a. Not warlike; not fit for war; not used to war; not military. The unwarlike disposition of Ethelwolf gave encouragement, no doubt, and easier entrance to the Danes. Milton, Hist. Eng., v.

unwarm.c: unwarm (un-warm’), v. i. [< wn-2 + warm.] To lose warmth; become cold. [Rare.] With horrid chill each little heart wnwarms., Hood.

unwarned.c: unwarned (un-wirnd’), a. Not warned; not cautioned; not previously admonished of danger. Locke.

unwarnedly.c: unwarnedly (un-war’ned-li), adv. Without warning or notice. [Rare.] They be suddenly and unwarnedly brought forth. Bp. Bale, Select Works, p. 88.

unwarp.c: unwarp (un-wiarp’), v. t [< un-2.+ warp.] To reduce from the state of being warped. Lvelyn.

unwarped.c: unwarped (un-warpt’), a. Not warped; not biased; impartial; unbiased. Thomson, Spring.

unwarrantability.c: unwarrantability (un-wor’an-ta-bil’i-ti), 7. The character of being unwarrantable; unwarrantableness.

unwarrantableness.c: unwarrantableness (un-wor’an-ta-bl-nes), n. The character or state of being unwarrantable. Bp. Hall, Ans. to Vind. of Smectymnuus, § 3.

unwarrantably.c: unwarrantably (un-wor’an-ta-bli), adv. Inan unwarrantable manner; in a manner that cannot be justified. Bp. Hall.

Not guaranteed; not assured or certain. Upon hope of an unwarranted conquest. Bacon. 8. Not guaranteed to be good, sound, or of a certain quality: as, an unwarranted horse.

unwary.c: unwary (un-wa’ri), a. [<un-l+wary. Cf. unware, the earlierform.] 1. Not wary; not vigilant against danger; not cautious; unguarded; precipitate; heedless; careless. Milton, P. upanishad.c: upanishad (6-pan’i-shad), ». [Skt.] In Sanskrit lit., name given to a series of treatises of theosophie and philosophic contents. They are of different dates. They exhibit the earliest attempts of the Hindu mind to penetrate into the mysteries of creation and existence. An upanishad is a passage of more philosophic or theosophic character, an excursus into a higher and freer region of thought, away from the details of the ceremonial and their exposition. Whitney, Amer. Jour. Philol., VII. 1.

upanishads.c: Upanishads (o-pa-ni-shadz'). [Skt., from up unto, ni, down, and -f sad, to sit; and so, literally, ‘a sitting down by,’ ‘setting oneself at the feet of another,’ ‘confidential communication,’ ‘ esoteric doctrine.’] With the Aranyakas the oldest speculative treatises of the Hindus: they lie at the root of the philosophical side of Hinduism Not only are they viewed as shruti, or revelation, equally with the Mantras and Brahmanas, but they are practically the only Veda of all educated Hindus at the present day. Properly each Brahman a had its Aranyakas or ‘forest treatises,’ intended for the Vanaprasthas or ‘dwellers in the forest (that is, Brahmans who, having passed the two earlier stages of the brahmachari, or student, and the grihastha, or householder, retire into the forest to devote themselves to self-mortification and religious meditation); but the mystical doctrines of the latter were so mingled with extraneous matter that the chapters called Upanishads appear to have been added to investigate more exclusively and definitely such problems as the origin of the universe, the nature of deity, the nature of the soul, and the connection of spirit and matter. Some of the most important are the Aitareya Upanishad and the Kaushitakibralimana Upanishad of the Rigveda- the Taittiriya belonging to the Taittiriyasanhita of the Yaiur- veda; the Brihadaranyaka attached totheShatapathabrah- mana of the Vajasaneyisanhita of that Veda, and the Islia or Ishavasya, forming the 40th chapter of the latter Sanhita ; the Chhandogya and Kena belonging to the Sama- veda; and the Prashna, Mundaka, Mandukya, and Katha belonging to the Atharvaveda. Following the stratifica- 1021 tory principle, in general the only guide in determining the age of Sanskrit works, the ancient Upanishads — that is, those which occupy a place in the Sanhitas, Brahmanas, and Aranyakas — are believed to be older than 600 B. c. or anterior to Buddhism, though the germs of the doctrines contained in them are to be found in some of the latest hymns. The others range through a long period, and are very numerous. The ancient Vedic literature first became known outside of India through these Upanishads. They were translated from Sanskrit into Persian by or for Dara Shukoh, the eldest son of the Mogul emperor Shah Jehan who held the liberal religious views of Akbar. He had heard of the Upanishads in Kashmir in 1640, invited several pandits to Delhi to assist in their translation, and finished the work m 1657. Translated into Persian, then the most widely read language of the East, they became generally accessible. In 1775 a manuscript of this Persian transla- sent by the French resident at the court of Shuja ud Daula to Anquetil Duperron, the discoverer of the Avesta; and later another manuscript. Anquetil Duperron collated the two, and translated the work into French m j Batin, publishing the latter version in 1801 and 180- under the title of Oupnekhat, a corruption of Upanishad. This Latin translation was studied by Schopen¬ hater Twelve of them are translated by Max Muller, with introductions and notes, in the “ Sacred Books of the East ” I. and XV.

upas.c: upas (u’pas),. [= F. upas, < Malay (Java) upas, poison; in the Celebes and Philippine Islands po or hip.]|| 1. The poisonous sap of different trees of the Malayan and Philippine Islands, more or less used for arrow-poison. The upas-antiar is yielded by the antiar or upas-tree. (See def. 2andantiar.) The upas tieuté, or upas raja, is from the cietat or tjettek, Strychnos Tieuté, one of the strychnine- rees. 2. The tree Antiaris toxicaria, one of the largest Javanese trees, having a cylindrical stem 60 or 70 feet high below the branches. Upon incision a poisonous milky juice flows from the trunk, concreting into a gum, which is mixed with the seed of Capsicum Jrutescens and various aromatic substances to form one cS kind of arrow-poison. The action of the poison is first purgative and emetic, then narcotic, destroying life by tetanic convulsions. Fable invests this tree with a deadly influence upon whatever comes under its branches. It is true that when the tree is felled or the bark extensively wounded it exhales an effluvium producing cutaneous eruptions; otherwise the upas may be approached and ascended like other trees. See Anttaris and sack-tree. upas Fierce in dread silence, on the blasted heath, Fell was sits, the hydra-tree of death. Erasmus Darwin. 3. Figuratively, something baneful or pernicious from a moral point of view: as, the upas of drunkenness.;

upbear.c: upbear (up-bar’), v. t. 1. To bear, carry, or raise aloft; lift; elevate; sustain aloft. One short sigh of human breath, upborne Ev’n to the seat of God. Milton, P. L., xi. 147. Swift as on wings of winds wpborn they fly. ; Pope, Odyssey, viii. 127. 2. To support; sustain. His resolve Upbore him, and firm faith. Tennyson, Enoch Arden. Language... upborne by... thought. Lowell, Among my Books, 2d ser., p. 325. 3+. To hold up; commend. Ne him for his desire no shame, Al were it wist, but in pris and unborn Of alle lovers, wel more than before. Chaucer, Troilus, i. 375.

upbind.c: upbind (up-bind’), v. t To bind up. Thy injur’d robes upbind! Collins, Ode to Peace, st. 3.
